**66,2,6** and thinking it out by himself he fashioned words of this kind, finding them not from the divine Scripture and the voice of the Holy Spirit but from the reasonings of wretched human nature,

**66,2,7** saying: For what reason are the things within the whole bounded vessel of creation unequal—black and white, red and green, moist and dry, sky and earth, night and daylight, soul and body, good and bad, just and unjust—except that all these certainly consist of two things?

**66,2,8** And the devil, campaigning still further against human nature, bred in his mind the dreadful notion, so that he should imagine what is not and fail to recognise what is, in order to set up a kind of war in the minds of the deceived, those who think that there is something besides him who is, and that, so to speak, all things are worked from two roots or two principles—which is the most impious and wicked thing of all.

**66,2,9a** But about this I shall speak again.

**66,2,9b** For blinded in his mind in these matters, the aforesaid Scythianus took his pretexts from Pythagoras and thought in this way, and fashioned for himself four books, giving one the name of Mysteries, the second of Chapters, the third gospel, the fourth of Treasures;

**66,2,10a** in them he yoked together the equally matched and equally balanced figures of two principles in each subject, so the poor man supposed, and so on this point he fancied, as though he had found something great for life.

**66,2,10b** And in reality he found a great evil for life, against himself and those led astray by him.

**66,3,1** Since the man was in this state, and had heard the way in which the prophets and the Law prophesied about the constitution of the world and about the one sole Ruler, the ever-existing Father who never ceases to be, and about his Son and the Holy Spirit,

**66,3,2** he wished—carried along by a certain excessive self-indulgence, scoffing in his untaught mind, and driven by heavy wantonness within himself—to make the journey to Jerusalem about the times of the apostles,

**66,3,3** supposedly to hold discussion there with those who proclaimed the teaching on the monarchy and on the creatures of God.

**66,3,4** The poor man went up and began to dispute with the presbyters there, who lived according to the legislation of God given to Moses and the prophetic teaching of each prophet:

**66,3,5** How do you say that there is one God who made night as well as day, flesh as well as soul, dry as well as wet, heaven as well as earth, darkness as well as light?

**66,3,6a** They showed him clearly—for the truth is not hidden—but the contradicter was not ashamed.

**66,3,6b** Unable to accomplish anything, he nevertheless carried on in the shamelessness of his perversity.

**66,3,7** When he could achieve nothing, but rather came off the worse, he attempted, by means of the magic books he had (for he was also a sorcerer, from the wisdom of the Indians and Egyptians and of heathen myths, having trafficked in the dreadful and destructive arts of sorcery),

**66,3,8** some apparition, going up on a roof to attempt it; yet, achieving nothing, he fell from the roof and came to the end of his life.

**66,3,9** He had spent a good many years there.

**66,3,10** He had only one disciple with him, the aforesaid Terebinthus, to whom he also entrusted his property, as to one most trustworthy and serving him with goodwill; when Scythianus died, Terebinthus buried him most affectionately, and after the burial resolved not to go back to the woman, who had been joined to Scythianus from harlotry, or rather from captivity, but ran away, taking everything he had, gold and silver and the rest,

**66,3,11** to the country of the Persians, and changed his name so as not to be detected, taking for himself, instead of Terebinthus, as I have explained above, the name of Buddas.

**66,3,12a** This man in turn received an evil succession of inheritance, the four books of Scythianus and the practices of magic and trickery.

**66,3,12b** For he too had been most carefully educated in letters.

**66,3,13** When he too was holding discussions in the country of the Persians, having lodged with a certain old widow, and had disputed about the two principles with the temple-wardens of Mithras and priests of the idol, with a certain prophet Parcus and with Labdacus, and was unable even to argue against the presidents of the idolatry, but stood refuted by them and came away in disgrace,

**66,3,14** then, conceiving the same plan as the aforesaid Scythianus, he went up to the upper room, attempting supposedly to work some magic so that no one would contradict him; he was hurled down by an angel, fell, and thus died through the divining operation he had wished to undertake.

**66,3,15** The old woman laid out his body and came into possession of his money; and having no child, nor any relation, she remained so for a long time.

**66,3,16a** Later she bought Cubricus, also called Mani, and took him into her service.

**66,3,16b** And when she died she left him the effects of the evil inheritance, like venom left behind by an asp, to bring corruption and destruction on many.

**66,4,1a** So once more Cubricus, who called himself Mani, lived among them and held discussions among them.

**66,4,1b** And since no one was persuaded by him, but all who heard the teaching of Manichaeus were indignant and repelled by its novelty, its dreadful myth-making and its empty deceit,

**66,4,2** he, seeing the tokens of his evil-scheming words overturned, and befuddled in mind, devised for himself some pretext by which he might establish this fabricated sensationalism of his own.

**66,4,3** And when a report spread that the son of the king of the Persians had fallen into some illness and was lying in the royal city of Persia—for Mani was not living there, but somewhere else, far from the king’s city—blinded by his own wickedness,

**66,4,4a** and supposing that from the books he had found belonging to his master Terebinthus, also called Buddas, the successor of Scythianus, he could perhaps work some cures on the king’s son, he set out from his own place and hurried there, and boldly made his claims known, promising to help.

**66,4,4b** But the fantasy of his hope did not prosper for the sorcerer.

**66,4,5a** For he fell short of his expectation, having applied certain kinds of drugs to the king’s sick boy.

**66,4,5b** In the end, at any rate, the youth died in his hands, so that all his promises, empty and joined with falsehood, might be exposed.

**66,4,6** When this turned out so, he was thrown into prison by royal command.

**66,4,7a** For the kings of the Persians do not inflict punishments at once on those who commit offences that bear the graver charges, but devise some more elaborate sentence of death, with tortures, by which to dispose of those under threat.

**66,4,7b** So much for this.

**66,5,1** Mani, also called Cubricus, remained in confinement, and was visited by his own disciples.

**66,5,2** For the charlatan had already gathered for himself an army, so to speak, whom he called disciples, about twenty-two in number already.

**66,5,3** Choosing three of them, one called Thomas, and Hermeias and Addas, he formed a plan, having heard about the sacred books in Judaea and in the whole world—I mean the Christian books, of the Law and the Prophets, of the gospels and the Apostles.

**66,5,4** So he gave gold to the aforesaid and sent them to the regions of Jerusalem.

**66,5,5** This he did before he was shut up in prison, when, holding discussions with many, he was unable to establish his own doctrine.

**66,5,6** Since he had heard about Christ’s name and his servants—the Christians, I mean—he had resolved to deceive those who had gone astray by means of the name of Christ’s cause.

**66,5,7a** They went off and bought them, for they did not delay.

**66,5,7b** Hurrying back, since they no longer found him in the free air but in prison, they went in there too and showed him the books.

**66,5,8a** He took them, searched them through and tampered with them, weaving his own lie into the truth at any point where he came upon a figure of speech or a term able to produce a likeness of his own way of thinking.

**66,5,8b** And from then on he strengthened the fabrication of his own fodder.

**66,5,9** But meanwhile, having earnestly entreated the keeper of the prison, he gave him much silver, and got away as a fugitive, leaving the country of the Persians, and made for the Roman realm.

**66,5,10** Being by now midway between Mesopotamia and Persia, and still in the desert regions, he heard about a great man distinguished in the highest piety, Marcellus by name, who lived in Kaschar, a city of Mesopotamia, a man Christian in every respect and most admirable in works of righteousness, providing for widows and the poor, and for orphans and the needy [...]; he planned to entangle the man,

**66,5,11** so that, having brought him under his hand, he might through him gain mastery not only over Mesopotamia but also over the whole region towards Syria and the Roman realm.

**66,5,12a** He wrote him a letter through Turbo, one of his disciples, from the bank of the river Stranga, from a fort called Arabion; and the letter contained the following.

**66,5,12b** Take it, I pray you, and read the device of the deceiver’s depravity.

**66,6,1** “Manichaeus, an apostle of Jesus Christ, together with all the holy ones and virgins who are with me, to Marcellus, beloved child: grace, mercy and peace from God the Father and from our Lord Jesus Christ; and the right hand of light will preserve you from this present evil age, from its mishaps, and from the snares of the wicked one, amen.

**66,6,2** On perceiving your love, which is very great, I rejoiced greatly, but I was grieved that your faith is not in accordance with right reason.

**66,6,3** Therefore, having been sent to set the human race right, and sparing those who have surrendered themselves to deceit and error, I judged it needful to send you this letter:

**66,6,4** in the first place for your own soul’s salvation, and next for that of those who happen to be with you as well, so that you may not hold an undiscerning judgement, as the guides of the simpler sort teach, who say that good and evil come from the same source and introduce one principle,

**66,6,5** not distinguishing nor dividing darkness from light, and the good from the evil and bad, and the outer man from the inner, as we said before, but never cease mixing and mingling the one with the other.

**66,6,6a** But you, my child, do not, like most men, unite both without reason and simply, as chance may have it, nor ascribe them to the God of goodness.

**66,6,6b** For they refer the beginning and the end and the father of these evils to God, “whose end is near to a curse.”

**66,6,7** For they do not even give credence to the words spoken in the gospels by our Saviour and Lord Jesus Christ himself, that “a good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor indeed can a bad tree bear good fruit.”

**66,6,8** And I am filled with amazement at how they dare to call God the maker and creator of Satan and his evil deeds.

**66,6,9** And would that their futile labour had gone only so far, and that they did not say that Christ, the Only-begotten who came down from the bosom of the Father, is the son of one Mary, a woman, begotten of blood and flesh and the other foulness of women!

**66,6,10** And so as not to tax your forbearance by writing much in this letter at great length, lacking as I do natural eloquence, I shall be content with this.

**66,6,11a** But you will learn the whole when I am present with you, if indeed you still have a care for your own salvation.

**66,6,11b** For I do not throw a noose over anyone, as the more foolish of the many do.

**66,6,11c** Consider what I say, most honoured child.”

**66,7,1a** On reading this letter the most estimable Marcellus, a most God-fearing and distinguished man, wondered and was astounded.

**66,7,1b** For it happened that Archelaus, the bishop of the city, was at home with him on that day, on which the servant of God took the letter of Manichaeus into his hands.

**66,7,2** Archelaus, learning the reason and reading the letter, ground his teeth, roaring like a lion, and taking up zeal for God he was eager rather to set out to him and to lay hands on such a man, as an intruder from the barbarians, the land from which he had set out, risen up for the destruction of the sons of men.

**66,7,3a** But the sensible Marcellus calmed the bishop by entreaty, and urged Turbo to complete the journey to Mani at the fort of Arabion, where he was waiting for Turbo.

**66,7,3b** This stronghold lies between the Persians and Mesopotamia.

**66,7,4** But he declined to go to Manichaeus, and Marcellus, without forcing Turbo, sends one of his own couriers, having written him a letter of this kind.

**66,7,5a** (Letter of Marcellus to Manichaeus.)

**66,7,5b** “Marcellus, a man of note, to Manichaeus, who is made known through his letter, greeting.

**66,7,5c** I received the letter written by you, and I welcomed Turbo in accordance with my own kindliness, but I have in no way understood the meaning of the letter, unless you come and explain each point to us in plain speech, as you promised in your letter.

**66,7,5d** Farewell.”

**66,8,1** When Mani learned this, he considered that it was not good that Turbo’s stay had become a detention; and though he often deceived even himself, reckoning things otherwise than they were, to reassure his own mind, nevertheless, seizing the pretext afforded by the letter, he came at a run to Marcellus.

**66,8,2** But Bishop Archelaus, who had in himself, along with his words, zeal for the faith as well, deliberated whether it was possible straightaway to hunt the man down like a leopard or a wolf or some other wild beast and hand him over to death, so that the flocks might not be harmed, as he perceived the entry of such a beast on the attack.

**66,8,3** But Marcellus rather begged, with long-suffering, that the bishop should hold the discussion with him forbearingly.

**66,8,4** The bishop had already learned the whole subject of Mani’s opinion; for Turbo had related to them, to him and to Marcellus, the whole empty babble of the heresy:

**66,8,5a** how Mani introduces two principles without beginning, always existing and never ceasing to be, opposed to each other, and gives the one the name of light and good, and the other of darkness and evil, so that they are God and devil.

**66,8,5b** At times, too, he calls the pair of them gods, a good god and a wicked god.

**66,8,6a** And he says that all things are from the two principles and are constituted of them.

**66,8,6b** And that the one principle makes all good things, and the other likewise the bad.

**66,8,6c** And that the substances of these two principles are present in the world, and that the body was made by the one principle, and the soul is the other’s,

**66,8,7** and it is this that is the soul in men and in every living creature, bird, reptile and beast; and not only so, but he says that in plants too the sap of life is a movement of soul, which he says is present in men as well.

**66,9,1** Among the other things he asserts in his myth-making and teaching, he says that one who eats flesh eats a soul, and that such a one is liable to become something of the same kind himself:

**66,9,2a** if he ate a pig, he becomes a pig in turn, or a bull, or a bird, or one of the creatures that are eaten.

**66,9,2b** That is why these people do not partake of anything that has a soul.

**66,9,2c** And if, he says, someone plants a fig tree, or an olive, or a vine, or a sycamore, or a persea, he himself, when he dies, has his soul bound in turn among the boughs of the trees that he planted, and it cannot pass beyond them.

**66,9,3** And if, he says, someone marries a wife, after his departure from here he is embodied anew in turn and becomes a woman, so that he himself may be married.

**66,9,4** And if, he says, someone has murdered a man, after his release from the body his soul is turned again into the body of a leper, or into a mouse, or into a snake, or will be something of that kind again, like those whom he murdered.

**66,9,5** He said again that the Wisdom from above, of the good God,

**66,9,6** taking counsel for the soul that had been poured out in all things (for he says, he and the Manichaeans who derive from him, that the soul is a portion of God, and that, torn away from him, it was cast down into bodies in captivity to the rulers of the opposing principle and root)—in this way, he says, because it is food for the men who seized it and supplies them with strength, and they have divided it up among bodies,

**66,9,7** for this reason, he says, the aforesaid Wisdom set these luminaries in heaven, sun and moon and stars, having made this device through the twelve elements of which the Greeks speak.

**66,9,8a** And he insists that these elements draw up the souls, which are luminous, of the men and the other living creatures that die.

**66,9,8b** And that they are carried to the boat.

**66,9,8c** For he means sun and moon to be ships; and the small ship is loaded for up to fifteen days, according to the filling of the moon, and so crosses over and from the fifteenth day unloads them into the great ship, that is, the sun.

**66,9,9** And the sun, the great ship, ferries them across to the aeon of life and the land of the blessed.

**66,9,10a** And so he says that the souls ferried over through the sun and moon—those of the people who are in the knowledge of this vulgar babble of theirs—having been purified, are deemed worthy of the ferrying, this mythology of his.

**66,9,10b** And again, that a soul is no longer saved unless it partakes of this same knowledge.

**66,9,10c** And great indeed is the tragic drama of this fiction.

**66,9,10d** Matters stood so, and Archelaus had grasped the question for the confrontation, being most ready because of the man’s manifold knowledge of God, and because, through what Turbo had told him beforehand, he had learned exactly everything about the man’s sorcery; and look, Mani arrived, with the men he had with him.

**66,9,10e** Straightaway, then, and at once they proceed to a public debate, in Kaschar itself, having first chosen together judges for their confrontation over the question, one Marsipus by name, and Claudius and Aegialeus and Cleobulus: the first a philosopher of the outside learning, the next a physician-sophist, the next a grammarian by nature, and the other a sophist.

**66,9,10f** And many words were spoken on both sides, Mani putting forward the matters of his mythical teaching and Archelaus, like a hoplite winning the prize of valour, demolishing by his own strength the darts of the opposing side; Mani in the end came off the worse, and the judges adjudged the prize to the truth—which was no wonder, since the truth is self-established and cannot be demolished, even if lawlessness, carried along by shamelessness, should resist the bond of the truth, since falsehood has neither subsistence nor foundation, like the shadow of darkness, and like the slipperiness of the serpent’s progress and its want of support from its lack of feet.

**66,11,1a** From there Mani ran away, when the crowds wanted to stone him, had not Marcellus come forward into the midst and shamed the crowds by his venerable presence; otherwise the wretch would long ago have been dead, remaining a corpse.

**66,11,1b** Withdrawing, he came to a village of Kalchara called Diodoris,

**66,11,2a** in which at that time one Trypho, a most reasonable man, happened to be presbyter of the people there.

**66,11,2b** Coming to him, Mani again stirred up trouble with his boasting, finding the man good in other respects and admirable in piety, but poor in speech.

**66,11,3a** But even so he was not able, as he had supposed, to mock the servant of Christ.

**66,11,3b** For God always makes ready the gifts from the Holy Spirit for those who hope in him, and supplies them, as he also promised, being free from falsehood, “Do not be anxious what you will say.

**66,11,3c** For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of my Father who speaks in you.”

**66,11,4** Then, when he wished to debate again with Trypho the presbyter, and Trypho had opposed him on many points and had written to Archelaus on this matter,

**66,11,5a** “A certain man has come here, just like a savage wolf, and is attempting to destroy the sheepfold.

**66,11,5b** But I beg you, send me word what I should do about him, or with what words I should answer their false teaching.

**66,11,5c** And if you yourself think fit to come, you would free the fold of Christ and his flocks from care.”

**66,11,5d** He sent him two arguments to hold ready against Mani, and let him know that he should await his arrival.

**66,11,6** Mani came forward very early in the middle of the village, calling him to make a beginning and challenging Trypho to come to a debate.

**66,11,7** And when Trypho appeared and answered him point by point on what he asked, according to the understanding given him by God, and had quietly, after a fashion, confounded the deceiver on the matter about which he was himself in doubt, Archelaus came on the scene like a strong householder caring for his own, and advancing boldly he rebuked the one who was trying to plunder.

**66,11,8** The moment Mani caught sight of Archelaus, he said in a wheedling tone, by way of pretence, “Let me debate with Trypho; for your dignity is beyond me, because you are the bishop.”

**66,11,9a** But Archelaus, after refutations of his argument, showed him to be a greater hypocrite and silenced him.

**66,11,9b** And having furnished the solutions to the arguments put forward by him, he put him to shame once more, so that he could no longer open his mouth.

**66,11,9c** The people, seized with zeal once again, tried to lay hands on the wretch.

**66,11,9d** But he escaped the crowds and arrived again at the aforesaid fort of Arabion.

**66,12,1** From there the king of the Persians, learning of Mani’s place of refuge, sent and seized him in the aforesaid fort, dragged him off ignominiously to Persia, and ordered his skin to be flayed off with a reed, and so paid him his punishment.

**66,12,2a** And so, flayed with a reed, his skin stuffed with chaff they still keep to this day in Persia; and thus he ended his life.

**66,12,2b** That is why the Manichaeans themselves make their beds on reeds.

**66,12,3** When he had died in this way and left behind his disciples whom we have mentioned, Addas and Thomas and Hermeias—before he received his penalty in the manner described, they had been sent out by him: Hermeias to Egypt, whom many met.

**66,12,4** For the heresy is not an old one, and those who had met the aforesaid Hermeias, who was a disciple of Mani, related to us what concerned him.

**66,12,5** Addas went to the upper regions, and Thomas to Judaea; and through them the doctrine has been strengthened up to the present.

**66,12,6a** Mani used to say that he himself was the Paraclete Spirit; and sometimes he calls himself an apostle of Christ, sometimes the Paraclete Spirit.

**66,12,6b** And great is the heterodox inconsistency of his blindness.

**66,13,1** From here on, then, beloved, we have need to speak to the heresy and to its futile thinking.

**66,13,2** For all that went before I have set out by way of history; and this is where the most pernicious Mani begins to teach and write and speak, in his discourse on the faith.

**66,13,3** For he published various books, one of them composed in alphabetic sections, equal in number to the twenty-two letters of the alphabet of the Syrians;

**66,13,4** for most of the Persians, besides the Persian letters, also use the Syrian script, just as among us many nations use the Greek, although almost every nation has letters of its own.

**66,13,5a** Others, supposedly, pride themselves on the most profound dialect of the Syrians, the dialect of Palmyra, both the dialect itself and its letters.

**66,13,5b** These letters are twenty-two; for this reason the same book too is divided into twenty-two sections of discourse.

**66,13,6a** To this one he gives the name Mysteries of Manichaeus, and to another, Treasure.

**66,13,6b** And having cobbled together other books too, he puts on airs: the so-called Little Treasure, and another on astrology.

**66,13,7a** For they are not wanting in such curious arts; rather, astronomy lies ready to hand for them as a boast, together with phylacteries—amulets, I mean—and some other spells and tricks.

**66,13,7b** The same Mani, then, begins in his book by saying:

**66,14,1** “God and matter existed, light and darkness, good and evil, in all respects utterly contrary, so that neither has anything at all in common with the other.”

**66,14,2a** And this is the preface of the charlatan.

**66,14,2b** From here he begins his evil contrivance.

**66,14,2c** The book is a long one, containing worthless things of this sort, whose awkwardness and the contradictoriness of whose words must still be grasped from the very beginning of its design.

**66,14,3a** For even if the rest of the drivel and the mythical subject-matter is long, all his wickedness will be displayed from the introduction.

**66,14,3b** For his ‘God and matter existed’ sets forth something in no way short of the futile supposition of the Greeks.

**66,14,4a** But this empty notion of his calumny is easily caught, simple and easily overthrown.

**66,14,4b** For that two things should together be contemporaneous and everlasting is impossible, on sound reasoning and sensible understanding, in the judgement of one who knows how to judge soundly.

**66,14,4c** And this will be recognisable to everyone who possesses understanding.

**66,14,5a** For if the two are contemporaneous, they do not differ even in name.

**66,14,5b** For everything contemporaneous is also co-eternal, and what is co-eternal is also ever-existing, and this is God, above all when it has received its beginning from no cause.

**66,14,5c** For nothing is everlasting except God alone.

**66,14,6a** For you have set out these principles under different names, O barbarian in mind and enemy of human nature.

**66,14,6b** The one you set out as light, the other as darkness; again, one as good and the second as evil.

**66,14,6c** And you say that these are in all respects utterly contrary, so that neither has anything at all in common with the other.

**66,14,6d** So you separate them from each other; for clearly they are contrary, as you said.

**66,14,7** But if they are by nature together, they will be found friendly and harmonious and together with one another, living together and sharing with each other, and not separated from each other at all, because of an excess of friendship.

**66,14,8a** But if they are apart from each other, each of them is certainly bounded.

**66,14,8b** And everything bounded is not perfect.

**66,14,8c** For it is delimited by being bounded.

**66,14,9** Besides, a boundary will be sought to mark off the two, lest, touching each other at their extremities, both should join their own selves to each other through their extremities, and the one should share with the other and abolish the boundary of their opposition; and if you grant something that separates them, between the two,

**66,14,10** the separating thing will no longer be like them, nor yet will it be other than both.

**66,14,11** For if on one side the separating thing is assimilated to one of the two everlasting things mentioned before, the separating thing would no longer be foreign to the one it is assimilated to, but joined to the one it is assimilated to, and through the part made equal there will be a junction, and there will no longer be a boundary set in the separation of the two natures from each other.

**66,14,12a** But if it is neither like the two nor partaking in part of either, then the everlasting and ever-existing things are no longer two, but now three; and there are no longer two principles, and two first things opposed to each other, but a third, other thing, opposed to both and unlike both, separating between the two and having nothing in common with either, because it is alien and takes the likeness of neither.

**66,14,12b** And so these will now be no longer two, but three.

**66,14,13a** Besides, another will be sought, the one who mediated and inserted this boundary, a fourth.

**66,14,13b** For the two could not have set up the boundary, or the wall, unless there were another, the setter of the boundary, who inserted the separating thing between the two, and one, moreover, learned in knowledge, sensible in manner, reasonable and of higher repute, so as to be able to persuade both to an agreement of peace.

**66,14,14a** There will, then, be one who sets the boundary, and one thing that separates, and two things bounded, and no longer only two principles, but both three and four.

**66,14,14b** And in this way one may turn one’s mind to many principles, and leave aside what is and imagine what is not.

**66,15,1a** Now while the wretch seeks, supposedly, not to mingle evil with God—and indeed it is absurd to attach it to God.

**66,15,1b** For it is acknowledged in the stamp of the church’s teaching that the divine is entirely foreign to evil and unmixed with it.

**66,15,2a** For God made nothing evil, but all things very good, being good by nature, incomprehensible in essence, containing all things, but himself contained by nothing.

**66,15,2b** Evil, then, neither always existed nor came into being from God.

**66,15,3** Since, then, evil neither exists nor always exists, nor came into being from God, it remains to inquire in what way that which does not always exist, but has had a beginning of being, and ceases and perishes and does not remain to the end—from where it had its beginning.

**66,15,4** And when we inquire into this, we must first consider what kind of thing evil is and in what evil arises, and whether it is something circumscribed, or a body, so to speak, or has subsistence, or can even possess a root.

**66,15,5** And when we examine these questions among ourselves, evil will be found to be without subsistence and to have no root, but to extend only as far as deeds, as the outcome of the practical activity of men.

**66,15,6a** For evil exists in our doing it, and in our not doing it, it does not exist, while our understanding discovers what it is: to do wickedly, which does not please God, and which can neither contradict God nor fight against the divine.

**66,15,6b** For whatever can be cut off and destroyed by men is all the more unable to hold out against God.

**66,16,1** At the same time we must also think thus about the devil: that he was not created evil by nature from the creation, but later devised for himself the doing of evil; it was not unknown what he would become, but he was created well together with all, most usefully, because of the abundance of righteousness,

**66,16,2** since God, through the abundance of his goodness, willed all beings and all things to exist and set his good things before all, and by the grant of free will allowed all to use their own will, each for whatever undertaking he might wish, so that he himself might be blameless of evil things, and there might be a distinction of those who advance in virtue and in turn carry off the prizes of his love for mankind and his goodness.

**66,16,3** But this maniacal Mani, wishing to remove God from evil, has rather set up evil against him on equal terms.

**66,16,4** At the same time he is not ashamed to vilify the whole creation; trading on the faults that arise among us as pretexts, and weaving the equally balanced pairs into the whole work of creation, he has rather turned out to be the advocate and protector of the very evil he professes to renounce, and instead of hatred towards it he embraces a kind of friendship and fellowship with it, since he gives it substance and proclaims it everlasting, ever existing with God and never ceasing to be.

**66,16,5** And while he calls it by certain names, he will be detected through all his arguments as having fallen from the truth, since the whole creation was well created by God, as the very testimonies he himself adduces show.

**66,17,1a** And first, that he has called it matter, and according to the same thought reckons it to be corruption.

**66,17,1b** And first, if it is corruption, it would then be the corruption of something.

**66,17,1c** And if it is a corruption of other things, while itself is permanent, then long ago it would have corrupted the things that are, and it alone would have subsisted through so long a time, exercising the activity of its own power and not being cut off;

**66,17,2** but if it is the corruption of itself, corrupting, subduing, consuming and destroying, it is being destroyed and will not stand, being something that consumes and corrupts itself.

**66,17,3a** How, then, has it stood for so long a time, existing, according to the charlatan’s account?

**66,17,3b** At the same time it will have no fellowship at all with life, nor will it be found together with life or with goodness.

**66,17,4** But since in each of the creatures he vilifies there is goodness as well, his argument about evil has collapsed on every side, because the one of the things he speaks of shares with the other—as one may say of snakes and the other venomous reptiles.

**66,17,5** For in all the things that have been fashioned for usefulness, but are vilified by him by their very name, the opposite of evil is also found—as one may say of the snake and the rest.

**66,17,6a** For in the very creatures he vilifies, from which comes venom for death, there is also an antidote, serving as a remedy against death and harm.

**66,17,6b** And day is for men’s work, as also for being given light and seeing; but night too, which he vilifies by name, is found to be a rest given to men by God.

**66,17,7** And so each thing is found to be good in itself, and unable to take its name from the sins among us, or to receive on equal terms a name shared with evil.

**66,18,1** For everything is good and pleasing, and nothing is to be rejected, since, as it says, “lo, all things are exceedingly good”; and evil has no root anywhere.

**66,18,2** For this reason God too, when in his goodness he created the whole world from the beginning, added ‘good’ to each of the created things, saying, “And God saw that it was good”, so that he might bear witness to the good and do away with the cunning of those who plot against human nature, who by wicked myths have contrived to blot out the truth from among men.

**66,18,3a** For on the first day he made the heaven and the earth, and the light, and what is on the earth.

**66,18,3b** “And he saw, and lo, it was good,” the Scripture declares.

**66,18,4a** Did he not know, then, that he was about to make something good, seeing that after it came to be he says, “Behold, it is good”?

**66,18,4b** And so in order over the waters, over the sea, over the growing plants, over the trees, over the lights in heaven, over the cattle, over the birds and the creeping things and the fishes.

**66,18,5** For over each one he would say, “And God saw, and lo, it was good,” not as one who was ignorant beforehand, nor as one who had come to know that it was good through experience after it had come to be; but from the fact that all things are good he foretold that evil exists nowhere, because of the opinion of the evil-minded;

**66,18,6** and since all things are good and are attested as good, he spoke the word ‘good’ in accordance with the truest testimony to the good — this being, for every good thing, a removal of all evil — so that, from the whole being good, the account of evil devised by men might be done away with, so that he might utterly remove the whole mischievous supposition of those who bring in that teaching.

**66,18,7** Then, coming to man, he did not say that he was good — not that man is evil, the most excellent of all the things created on the earth, created by God with unspeakable wisdom for ruling, to whom God was about to hand over the lordship of all the things created by him, as he says,

**66,18,8** “Let us make man after our image and after likeness, and let them rule over the fishes of the sea, and the birds of the heaven, and the creeping creatures of the earth, and cattle, and wild beasts, and all things that are on the earth”.

**66,18,9** But since he was created after the image of God, the divine writing was content with so great a dignity, and had no need of any further addition.

**66,18,10** For if he possessed the image of goodness itself — I mean of the Lord God, the good maker of all creation, from whom is every fountain of goodness, from whom the good is present in all things — how did he still need to hear a testimony that “behold, it is good”, when he possessed the image of the good itself?

**66,18,11** Afterwards, at the end of the whole, after making all the creation, the divine word set its seal upon all things and set forth the same testimony, saying,

**66,18,12a** “And God saw all things that he had made, and behold, they were very good,” speaking with the addition of “very”.

**66,18,12b** Now this happened to be the sixth day, and the seventh was a day of rest, so that, the root of the doctrine of evil having been taken away, no one might any longer find a pretext to dare this — to think of evil as everlasting.

**66,18,13a** For the very account concerning it has been done away with.

**66,18,13b** For evil existed nowhere, since all things were exceedingly good, having come into being from a good God and been attested by him.

**66,19,1a** Now the name ‘matter’ is twofold.

**66,19,1b** For in one sense, as I have said, according to the mind of the wretch, it is the name of an activity and of a consuming corruption.

**66,19,1c** But we are accustomed to call ‘matter’ the material for the fashioning of each thing among those who practise the crafts, so that one says ‘matter of timber’, ‘matter of the potter’s work’, ‘matter of gold’, ‘matter of silver’.

**66,19,1d** And there is also spoken of in bodies a certain matter of working, that which gathers from the injury caused by sores.

**66,19,1e** Let him speak, then, this soothsayer who has lately arrived and who professes to announce the things before the ages.

**66,19,2** For this man dared even to call himself the Paraclete Spirit; and at other times he styles himself, as I have said, an apostle of Jesus Christ, though he never put on the form of a dove, nor is he the Paraclete Spirit sent from heaven to the apostles as power for a garment of incorruption,

**66,19,3a** which the Only-begotten promised to send, appointing it not for many days after those, but for immediately upon his going up, as he said, “If I go away, he will come”.

**66,19,3b** And at once, in the upper room, they were filled with the Holy Spirit, when they had returned from the Mount of Olives,

**66,19,4** as it is written, “And there appeared to them tongues of fire, parting asunder, and the house was filled as if by a forceful breath, and the Spirit sat upon each one of them, and they spoke in tongues the wonderful works of God, and each one heard in his own tongue.”

**66,19,5** And they were from every race of those under heaven, and each was comforted through the Spirit — the apostles through the gift, and all the nations through the sounding of the wonderful teaching of God.

**66,19,6** For if this charlatan — this man truly mad, who lives up to his own name — were the Paraclete Spirit which the Lord promised to the disciples, then the apostles passed away deprived of the promise, though they had heard from the Lord who cannot lie, “You will receive the Holy Spirit’s gift not many days from now”.

**66,19,7a** And the deceiver will be found to be lying against Christ, as though he had not fulfilled the things he had said.

**66,19,7b** For the generation of the apostles passed away — I mean from Peter to Paul and to John, who also lingered long in the world, until the times of Trajan.

**66,19,7c** And James passed away, who was the first to be bishop in Jerusalem, who was called the brother of the Lord, but was a son of Joseph, born of his own wife together with his other brothers;

**66,19,8a** the Lord Jesus Christ, born according to the flesh of Mary the ever-virgin, lived among them and so came to be called their brother, in the rank of brothers; and all the saints who shared his throne passed away.

**66,19,8b** And with them Symeon, the son of his father’s brother, the son of Clopas, the brother of Joseph.

**66,19,9a** Their times I have set down below in order and in sequence from James the bishop — the bishops in succession in Jerusalem, and those under each emperor — down to the time, already indicated, of Aurelian and Probus, in which this Mani became known, a certain man, a Persian, who brought forth into the world this outlandish teaching.

**66,19,9b** And it is as follows.

**66,20,1a** 1. James, who was struck with a club in Jerusalem and suffered martyrdom, until Nero.

**66,20,1b** 2. Symeon was crucified under Trajan.

**66,20,1c** 3. Judas.

**66,20,1d** 4. Zacharias.

**66,20,1e** 5. Tobias.

**66,20,1f** 6. Benjamin.

**66,20,1g** 7. John, until the nineteenth year of Trajan.

**66,20,1h** 8. Matthias.

**66,20,1i** 9. Philip.

**66,20,1j** 10. Seneca.

**66,20,1k** 11. Justus, until Hadrian.

**66,20,1l** 12. Levi.

**66,20,1m** 13. Vaphris.

**66,20,1n** 14. Josis.

**66,20,1o** 15. Judas, until the eleventh year of Antonius.

**66,20,1p** These, then, were bishops of Jerusalem from the circumcision.

**66,20,1q** And these were from the gentiles: 16. Mark.

**66,20,1r** 17. Cassian.

**66,20,1s** 18. Publius.

**66,20,1t** 19. Maximus.

**66,20,1u** 20. Julian.

**66,20,1v** These all until the tenth year of Antoninus Pius.

**66,20,1w** 21. Gaianus.

**66,20,1x** 22. Symmachus.

**66,20,1y** 23. Gaius, until the days of Verus, his eighth year.

**66,20,1z** 24. Julian.

**66,20,1aa** 25. Capito.

**66,20,1ab** 26. Maximus, until the sixteenth year of Verus.

**66,20,1ac** 27. Antoninus.

**66,20,1ad** 28. Valens.

**66,20,1ae** 29. Dolichianus, until Commodus.

**66,20,1af** 30. Narcissus.

**66,20,1ag** 31. Dius, until Severus.

**66,20,1ah** 32. Germanio.

**66,20,1ai** 33. Gordius, until Antoninus.

**66,20,1aj** 34. Narcissus, the same, until Alexander the son of Mamaea — not the Macedonian, but another.

**66,20,1ak** 35. Alexander, until the same Alexander.

**66,20,1al** 36. Mazabanes, until Gallus and Volusian.

**66,20,1am** 37. Hymenaeus, until Aurelian.

**66,20,3a** In all, from the ascension of Christ to Mani and the emperors Aurelian and Probus, 276 years according to some chronographers, but according to others 246.

**66,20,3b** And from then until now, other bishops: Bazas, Hermon, Macarius, Maximus, Cyril, Herennius, another Cyril, and Hilarion, who now holds the church, and who has also been accused of communion with the Arians.

**66,20,4a** And the emperors in order, whose times are also attached: the remainder of Aurelian’s reign, one year; Tacitus, six months; Carus and Carinus and Numerian, two months.

**66,20,4b** Diocletian, twenty years.

**66,20,4c** Maximianus, Licinius, Constantine, Constantius, Julian, Jovian, Valentinian, Valens and Gratian.

**66,20,5** So that from the aforesaid Mani until the present — that is, the thirteenth year of Valens, the ninth year of Gratian, the first year of the younger Valentinian, and the hundred and seventh year of Diocletian —

**66,20,6** so that in the fourth year of Aurelian, and in the times of Hymenaeus bishop of Jerusalem, the error and illusion of the working of the devil who dwells in the world should be sent forth upon the world as a visitation, and by its deceit should draw away from the truth those who were persuaded by him.

**66,21,1** His trickery, then, has been exposed on every side, so that the mind of the intelligent, once it knows all things precisely, will condemn his counterfeit invention;

**66,21,2** and all the rest of what pass for his clever arguments are full of nonsense, crooked and unstable, and are laughed at by all intelligent people; to take these apart word by word and to write the answers to them all would swell the refutation in this treatise against him to a great bulk.

**66,21,3** Rebuttals refuting him have already been composed, admirably, by great men: by Bishop Archelaus, as was said earlier; by Origen, as I have heard; by Eusebius of Caesarea and by Eusebius of Emesa; by Serapion of Thmuis; by Athanasius of Alexandria; by George of Laodicea; by Apollinarius of Laodicea; by Titus; and by many of those who have spoken against him.

**66,21,4** But it will do no harm, out of our own poverty too, to say a few things to the shame of the pitiable man, for the overthrow of his mind, which has gone astray in every way, as we have also said already.

**66,21,5** I would have wished to make my refutation of him without harsh words, and I could have done it with forbearance, were it not that he is not ashamed to blaspheme the Master of all with an unbridled tongue, denying outright the very Maker, who fashioned this whole vault of heaven and earth and of all things in them, and all things in the world, and imagining some other god who does not exist, while forsaking the one who does.

**66,21,6** For he has fallen from the truth, and what the ridiculous proverb tells has befallen him: like the raven which, having food about its mouth and seeing the shadow of the food in the water, wished to get the other food, and lost what it had and did not gain what was not there.

**66,21,7a** And who will bear with the blasphemer?

**66,21,7b** For if we have fathers according to the flesh, and cannot bear to hear them reproached by anyone, how much more, if we should hear the Lord God of all being blasphemed by that most grievous Mani?

**66,21,8** So when, in the mercy of God, rains are sent according to his goodness, he in his blasphemy is not ashamed to say that the rains are not from God, but from an outflow of the archons.

**66,22,1** And as for telling the rest, who would not burst out laughing, so that the pieces of Philistion may well be more worth having than this man’s mime-talk?

**66,22,2** For in his myth-making he teaches that an Omophorus carries the whole earth, and that every thirty years, he says, when one shoulder grows weary, he shifts it to the other shoulder, and that this is how earthquakes come about.

**66,22,3** Yet were this the case, the matter would be according to nature, and no longer divinely sent.

**66,22,4a** But the words of the Saviour refute the sorcerer, for he said, “Be good, as your heavenly Father, for he makes his sun rise on the just and the unjust, and sends his rain on the wicked and the good”.

**66,22,4b** And the saying, “There shall be earthquakes in various places, and famines and plagues”.

**66,22,5a** And if earthquakes came about by nature, or according to a regular course — well, often when earthquakes occur in a region, it has even happened that the earth was shaken many times each night for a whole year.

**66,22,5b** Was it, then, because the Omophorus’ shoulders had been wounded that he was carried along, unable to bear the toil, and made the shaking continuous?

**66,22,6a** And who will bear with such foolish talk?

**66,22,6b** And what other plausible tale did he not dare to tell?

**66,22,6c** For this man asserts — so he says — that the souls which have come to the knowledge of his error are received up into the moon, the soul being of a luminous substance.

**66,22,7** For this reason, he says, the moon waxes and wanes, being filled from the souls that die in the knowledge of this unbelief.

**66,22,8** Then, he says, they are unloaded from the moon — the smaller vessel, he says — and are taken over into the sun and deposited in the aeon of the blessed, he says.

**66,22,9** But wickedness, being always blind, does not know its own shame, as it is refuted by its own words, being unable to bring its lies to completion.

**66,23,1** For first, a single man was formed, Adam, from whom sons and daughters were born; and at the beginning of the making of the world, about the hundredth year of Adam, more or less, Abel is killed, being some thirty years old, more or less.

**66,23,2** After this first man to be killed, Adam the first-formed dies on the earth after 930 years, the sun and the moon and the stars having been fixed and created in heaven from the fourth day.

**66,23,3a** What then shall we say, you there?

**66,23,3b** Shall we acknowledge the refutation of your folly?

**66,23,3c** For how could nine hundred and thirty years have passed without the moon waning and waxing?

**66,23,4a** With what souls of the dead, then, was the moon being filled and made full?

**66,23,4b** Tell me.

**66,23,4c** But the Manichaean did not know that there are intelligent people, who are persuaded not by false words but by the truest proofs.

**66,23,5a** Then let us grant that it is so — which it is not, God forbid — and that the moon is loaded and filled from the souls of the Manichaeans.

**66,23,5b** How will such a hypothesis still hold together?

**66,23,6** For if no Manichaean died after the fifteenth day of the moon, but a fixed term were appointed for the Manichaeans to die up to the fifteenth of the moon, and after the fifteenth no longer to die until the moon’s cargo was unloaded, so that it might begin to load again from the new moon, then the lie of these people might have been plausible; but as it is, it is implausible.

**66,23,7a** For they die every day, and the elements appointed by God know their own course.

**66,23,7b** And again, the cargo of souls supposed to be in the moon will not stand.

**66,24,1** And again some of them hold that, by a contrivance of cunning, he says, the mother of all things permitted a power of her own to descend from heaven in order to rob the archons and to strip from them the power which they had taken from above.

**66,24,2a** For he means to say that the principalities and authorities, having waged war against the living God, snatched from him a great and incomprehensible power, which he also names soul.

**66,24,2b** And oh, the great absurdity of this!

**66,24,3a** For everyone who is robbed and overpowered has been brought low.

**66,24,3b** If, then, the principalities overpowered the good God and tore a power away from him out of his panoply, they will be stronger than he.

**66,24,4** And he, having given way to them at first, cannot afterwards take back from them the power snatched from him — or rather, the panoply — he who from the beginning was unable to hold out against his enemies.

**66,24,5** And besides, even if at some time he should again come to victory and, prevailing over those of the opposite side, take back the power snatched from him, since the root and beginningless beginning of evil still remains and cannot be wholly done away with, it will prevail once more, enlisting greater power for itself, and, growing strong through some domination, would again take away from the good God the power that had been recovered by him;

**66,24,6** and evil will for ever stand against him and never be brought to an end, perpetually snatching and being snatched.

**66,24,7** But if those who are damaged in their wits and deceived in every way should say that, when in due time the good God sets free the panoply of the part snatched from him, he will then destroy and exterminate the principalities and the authorities of the opposing power — if this is indeed to come about, and if the good God will utterly destroy and exterminate them, then the charlatan’s doctrine has collapsed, which says that the good one is not just, nor passes sentence on the sinner in judgment, neither handing anyone over to torments nor killing.

**66,24,8** For if he attempts at all to destroy and exterminate the devil — or rather the opposing activity — then either, according to Mani, he will no longer be good, as his doctrine holds, or, while still being good, he destroys the evil; and then this one will be the Lord who made the heaven and the earth, as he is in truth, who renders to each according to his works, who from surpassing goodness grants the good to the good man who has laboured in goodness, and assigns what is just to him who has done evil deeds.

**66,24,9** And his doctrine has been refuted on every side, as it secretly corrupts the hearts of men toward what is contrary.

**66,25,1** I shall fittingly set out below, word for word and in order, his way of thinking, from what Archelaus composed against him in his disputation against him, as Turbo himself, one of his disciples, of whom I made mention above, revealed it.

**66,25,2a** So when Archelaus the bishop and Marcellus and those with them questioned Turbo about the teaching of Mani, Turbo answered, saying what I have quoted from the book.

**66,25,2b** And it is as follows.

**66,25,3a** (The beginning of the godless doctrines of Mani.)

**66,25,3b** If you wish to learn the faith of Mani from me, hear it briefly.

**66,25,3c** He worships two gods, unbegotten, self-generated, eternal, the one opposed to the other.

**66,25,3d** And he presents one as good and the other as wicked, naming the one light and the other darkness.

**66,25,3e** And he says that the soul in men is part of the light, and that the body and the handiwork of matter are part of the darkness.

**66,25,4a** And he says that a mixture or blending of these came about in this way, likening the two to this example: like two kings fighting against each other, who were enemies from the beginning, each holding his own possessions in his own region.

**66,25,4b** And in a hostile encounter the darkness came out from its own borders and fought against the light.

**66,25,5a** And when the good Father knew that the darkness had come into his land, he put forth from himself a power called the Mother of Life, and she put forth the First Man — the five elements.

**66,25,5b** And they are wind, light, water, fire and matter.

**66,25,6a** And having put these on, as equipment for war, he went down below and made war on the darkness.

**66,25,6b** But the archons of the darkness, fighting back against him, ate of his panoply, which is the soul.

**66,25,7a** Then the First Man was terribly afflicted down there by the darkness.

**66,25,7b** And had the Father not heard him when he prayed, and sent another power put forth by him, called the Living Spirit, and had it not come down and given him its right hand and brought him up out of the darkness, the First Man would long ago have been held fast and in peril.

**66,25,8a** From that time, then, he left the soul below.

**66,25,8b** And for this reason, when Manichaeans meet one another, they give one another their right hands for a sign, as men saved from darkness.

**66,25,8c** For he declares that every sect is in the darkness.

**66,25,8d** Then the Living Spirit created the world; and, itself bearing three other powers, it came down and brought up the archons, and made them fast in the firmament, which is the sphere, their body.

**66,26,1a** Then again the Living Spirit created the lights, which are remnants of the soul, and in this way made the firmament revolve.

**66,26,1b** And again it created the earth in eight forms.

**66,26,1c** And the Omophorus carries it from below, and when he grows weary of carrying, he trembles and becomes the cause of an earthquake outside the appointed time.

**66,26,2a** For this reason the good Father dispatched his Son out of the bosom into the heart of the earth and into its lowest parts, so that he might give him a fitting desire.

**66,26,2b** And whenever an earthquake occurs, either he is trembling from weariness, or he is shifting it over to the other shoulder.

**66,26,3** Then, too, matter created the plants of itself; and when they were being plundered by certain archons, it summoned all the foremost of the archons, and took one power from each of them, and fashioned man after the pattern of that First Man, and fastened the soul within him.

**66,26,4a** This is the account of the blending; and when the living Father saw the soul afflicted in the body, being compassionate and merciful, he sent his beloved Son for the salvation of the soul.

**66,26,4b** For it was on this account, and on that of the Omophorus, that he sent him.

**66,26,4c** And the Son came and changed himself into human form, and was seen by men as a man, not being a man, and people assumed that he had been born.

**66,26,6a** Having come, then, he carries out the work of making for the salvation of souls, and constructed a machine with twelve buckets, which, turned by the sphere, draws up the souls of the dying.

**66,26,6b** And the great light takes these with its rays, purifies them and passes them on to the moon, and in this way the disc of the moon, as it is called among us, is filled.

**66,26,6c** For he says that the two lights are ships, or ferry-boats.

**66,26,7a** Then, when the moon has been loaded, it ferries them across to the east, and so it wanes, being lightened of its cargo, and in this way it fills the ferry-boat.

**66,26,7b** And again it unloads, as the souls are drawn up by the buckets, until he saves his own portion of the soul.

**66,26,7c** For he says that every soul and every moving living creature partakes of the substance of the good Father.

**66,26,8a** So when the moon passes on its cargo of souls to the Father’s aeons, they remain in the Column of Glory, which bears the name of the perfect air.

**66,26,8b** And this air is a column of light, because it is full of the souls that are being purified.

**66,26,8c** This is the cause through which souls are saved.

**66,27,1** And the cause of men’s dying, again, is this: a certain virgin, beautiful, adorned and very alluring, tries to plunder the archons in the firmament, who were brought up by the Living Spirit and crucified, appearing to the males as a shapely female, and to the females as a handsome and desirable youth.

**66,27,2** And the archons, whenever they see her adorned, are goaded to frenzy by the love-charm, and, being unable to catch her, burn terribly with amorous longing, their minds carried away.

**66,27,3a** So when, as they run, the virgin vanishes, then the great archon puts forth the clouds from himself, so as to darken the world in his anger.

**66,27,3b** And so, if he is sorely distressed, he is worn out like a man who sweats.

**66,27,3c** And his sweat is the rain.

**66,27,4a** Likewise the archon of the harvest too, if he is plundered by the virgin, pours out pestilence over the whole earth, so as to put men to death.

**66,27,4b** For this body is called a world, in relation to the great world.

**66,27,4c** And all men have roots below, bound to those above.

**66,27,4d** So whenever he is plundered by the virgin, he then begins to cut the roots of men.

**66,27,5a** And when their roots are cut, then pestilence begins to arise, and so they die.

**66,27,5b** And if in his toil he shakes the upper parts of the root, an earthquake comes about and follows, as the Omophorus is moved along with it.

**66,27,5c** This is the cause of death.

**66,28,1a** And I will tell you this too, how the soul is poured over into five bodies.

**66,28,1b** First a little of it is purified; then it is poured over into the body of a dog, or of a camel, or of another animal.

**66,28,1c** And if it is a soul that has committed murder, it is transferred into the bodies of lepers; and if it is found to have reaped, into those who stammer.

**66,28,1d** And these are the names of the soul: mind, thought, understanding, reflection, reasoning.

**66,28,2a** And the reapers, all who reap, resemble the archons who have been in the darkness from the beginning, when they ate of the panoply of the First Man.

**66,28,2b** Therefore they must be poured over into grass, or into beans, or into barley, or into ears of grain, or into vegetables, so that they may be reaped and cut.

**66,28,3a** And again, if anyone eats bread, he too must become bread and be eaten.

**66,28,3b** If anyone kills a little bird, he will be a little bird; if anyone kills a mouse, he too will be a mouse.

**66,28,4** Again, if anyone is rich in this world, when he goes out of his tabernacle he must be poured over into the body of a poor man, so that he goes about begging, and after this departs into everlasting punishment.

**66,28,5a** And since this body belongs to the archons and to matter, he who plants a persea tree has to go through many bodies until that persea tree is brought down.

**66,28,5b** And if anyone builds himself a house, he will be torn apart into all the bodies.

**66,28,5c** If anyone bathes, he fixes his own soul fast in the water.

**66,28,6a** And if anyone does not give pious offerings to his elect, he will be punished through the generations, and is re-embodied in catechumens’ bodies, until he has given pious offerings in abundance.

**66,28,6b** And for this reason they bring to the elect whatever is finest among foods.

**66,28,7a** And whenever they are going to eat bread, they first pray, addressing the bread in this way: “It was not I who reaped you, nor I who ground you, nor did I press you or throw you into an oven; another did all this and carried you to me; I ate without blame.”

**66,28,7b** And when he has said these words to himself, he tells the catechumen, “I prayed on your behalf,” and so the man goes away.

**66,28,8a** For, as I told you a little while ago, if anyone reaps, he will be reaped; so too, if he puts grain into a mill, he too will be put in; or having kneaded, he will himself be kneaded; or having baked bread, he will be baked.

**66,28,8b** That is why doing work is forbidden to them.

**66,28,9a** And again, there are certain other worlds, for the lights when they set from this world, out of which they rise.

**66,28,9b** And if anyone walks on the ground, he harms the earth; and he who moves his hand harms the air, since the air is the soul of men and of animals and of birds and of fishes and of creeping things.

**66,28,9c** And if anyone is in the world — I have told you that this body is not God’s, but is of matter, and is darkness, and must itself be darkened.

**66,29,1a** And concerning paradise: it is not called a world.

**66,29,1b** And the plants in it are lust and other deceits, which corrupt the reasonings of those men.

**66,29,1c** But the plant in paradise by which they recognise the good—that is Jesus, the knowledge of him which is in the world.

**66,29,1d** And he who receives it distinguishes the good and the evil.

**66,29,2a** The world, however, is not God’s either, but was moulded out of a portion of matter, and that is why everything perishes.

**66,29,2b** And what the archons plundered from the First Man is what fills the moon, what is purified daily from the world;

**66,29,3a** and if the soul goes out without having known the truth, it is handed over to the demons, so that they may subdue it in the gehennas of fire, and after the chastisement it is poured over into bodies, so that it may be subdued.

**66,29,3b** And so it is cast into the great fire until the consummation.

**66,30,1a** And concerning the prophets among us he speaks thus: that they are a spirit of ungodliness, or of the lawlessness of the darkness which came up from the beginning.

**66,30,1b** And for this reason, having been led astray, they did not speak.

**66,30,1c** For the archon blinded their mind.

**66,30,2** And if anyone follows their words, he dies for ever, bound into the Clod, because he did not learn the knowledge of the Paraclete.

**66,30,3a** And he gave a command to his elect alone, who are not more than seven in number: “When you stop eating, pray, and put on your head oil exorcised with many names, for the strengthening of this faith.”

**66,30,3b** But the names were not disclosed to me.

**66,30,3c** For only the seven use them.

**66,30,4a** And again, the name that is precious and great among us, Sabaoth, he says is itself the nature of man and the father of lust.

**66,30,4b** And for this reason the simple-minded worship lust, regarding it as a god.

**66,30,5a** And concerning Adam, how he was created, he speaks thus: that the one who spoke the words, “Come, and let us make man after our image and after likeness,” or after the form which we saw, is an archon, who said to the other archons, “Come, give me of the light which we took, and let us make man after the form of us archons, after the one which we saw, which is the First Man.”

**66,30,5b** And so he created man.

**66,30,6a** And they created Eve likewise, giving her of their lust, so as to deceive Adam.

**66,30,6b** And through these the forming of the world came about, from the archon’s handiwork.

**66,31,1** And he says that God has no part with the world itself, nor rejoices over it, because he was plundered by the archons from the beginning and affliction came upon him; for this reason he sends and plunders his soul from them daily through these lights, sun and moon, by means of which the entire world and the whole of creation is snatched away.

**66,31,2** And he says that the one who spoke with Moses and the Jews and the priests is the archon of the darkness; so that the Christians, the Jews and the pagans are one and the same thing, as they worship the same god.

**66,31,3a** For he deceives them in his lusts, not being a god of truth.

**66,31,3b** For this reason, then, all who hope in that god, the one who talked with Moses and with the prophets, are destined to be bound with him, because they did not hope in the God of truth.

**66,31,3c** For that one spoke with them according to their lusts.

**66,31,4** And after all this, at the end, he says, as he himself wrote, that when the Elder displays his image, then the Omophorus lets the earth go, and so the great fire is released and consumes the whole world.

**66,31,5a** Then again he releases the Clod together with the new aeon, in order that every soul of the sinners may be bound for ever.

**66,31,5b** And these things will happen when the Statue comes.

**66,31,6** And the emanations, all of them — Jesus, the one in the small ship, and the Mother of Life, and the twelve helmsmen, and the Virgin of Light, and the third Elder, who is in the great ship, and the Living Spirit, and the wall of the great fire, and the wall of the wind and of the air and of the water and of the inner living fire — dwell by the lesser light, until the fire consumes the whole world in however many years, the number of which I have not learned.

**66,31,7** And thereafter the two natures will be restored, and the archons will inhabit their own lower regions, and the Father the higher, having recovered what belongs to him.

**66,31,8a** And he handed down all this teaching to his three disciples, bidding each to journey to a region.

**66,31,8b** And Addas received the regions of the east, and Thomas has been allotted the land of the Syrians, and another, Hermeias, made the journey to Egypt.

**66,31,8c** And to this day they spend their time there, wishing to establish the system of the doctrine.

**66,32,1a** These are the things I have quoted from the aforesaid book of Archelaus.

**66,32,1b** And so his school of a tare-like sowing was established in the world, he having vomited forth the tares of his teaching.

**66,32,2a** And how much one might bring forward against such great slander from this mime-talker, as would surely be plain to everyone.

**66,32,2b** And even if his statements are not scraped down one by one for their overthrow, they will suffice for his shame merely through its being known that these things pass current among them, though they are incoherent and have no force.

**66,32,3a** For he undoes his first statements by his second, and his second utter things different from his first.

**66,32,3b** For at one time he would have the world come into being from God, at another from the archons, and God have no responsibility toward the world, but the world be perishing; at one time he says that the firmament is the skins of the archons, at another that they are crucified above in the vault, and run about and gather clouds and rage and are driven to frenzy at the sight of the virgin and at the beauty of the youth.

**66,33,1a** Oh, what great shame!

**66,33,1b** For what is more wretched, more distasteful and more shameful than this — that the Spirit of truth should shape itself as a female, and at another time be seen by the archons in male form?

**66,33,1c** For it is a shameful outrage for a man to be made womanish and to exist in the form of a female; and again it is most shameful for women to play the man and to bear the guise of a man.

**66,33,2a** And how will a spirit that is of virtue, and divine, not rather be found to be insulted by this fabricator Mani?

**66,33,2b** And how are those who have been flayed driven to frenzy?

**66,33,2c** Tell me, you there.

**66,33,2d** And how were they flayed after being crucified?

**66,33,2e** And if they have been crucified, how do they run after the power that vanishes?

**66,33,3a** And who will bear with the blasphemer, who lays it down that we are nourished from the sweat of archons, and that the rain is sent down to us from a shameful excretion?

**66,33,3b** And from where does he himself drink his drink, drawing it from the rains, together with his own disciples?

**66,33,3c** And how would he not be ridiculous, overcome by the need of bodily things, drinking sweat?

**66,33,4** For indeed sin is of different kinds, and the punishment will not be as great for one who sins involuntarily as for one who commits the sin with a willing mind.

**66,33,5** For other men — even if it were so, which God forbid (for the mad deceiver is imagining it) — not knowing that it is sweat and shameful excretions that they draw and drink, are more deserving of pardon and of mercy than he who, pricked in his conscience to no purpose, because of the defeat of his weakness makes use of these drinks of his and of the other uses that come from the flesh.

**66,34,1a** And there are many things in which this man, with a mouth of false speaking, has deceived those who were persuaded by him.

**66,34,1b** For what is there in him that is not ridiculous?

**66,34,2** His holding that the seeds of herbs and of crops and of pulses are souls — so that we shall even attempt to say something ridiculous, following his own myth-making, for his refutation: that if the grains of lentil and bean and chickpea and the rest are souls, and the bull’s soul too is the same, then by their own reasoning those who eat meat are more praiseworthy than those who practise the disciplined ways of life.

**66,34,3** For according to his rhapsodic invention he is afraid that,

**66,34,4a** if he partakes of things with souls — animals and the rest — he himself may become like them.

**66,34,4b** Rather the contrary.

**66,34,4c** For if fifty men, or even a hundred, come together, they will all be fed from one bull — to speak according to his vain false charge.

**66,34,4d** Nevertheless, for his refutation it must be said that the fifty, or the hundred, are answerable for a single soul, whereas he who eats the grains of the seeds will rather, in a single gulp of his partaking, be the cause of thirty and forty souls.

**66,34,4e** And all his ideas are vain and laughable.

**66,35,1** For to everyone who has understanding in the Lord the proofs of the truth are surely plain from the true teaching itself; for indeed nothing is truer than the Saviour for the revelation of the life of men.

**66,35,2** For this barbarian, the Persian who has come among us, a slave in his mind — for it would be no reproach that he was a slave in body — he says, then, that all souls are equal, and that one and the same soul is found in all: in men and cattle and wild beasts and birds and creeping things, and in creatures of the air and of the sea, in wild creatures, and in the seeds of crops, in trees and in all other visible things.

**66,35,3a** And this is not how our Lord showed it.

**66,35,3b** Or else, when he came to save mankind, he would also have been seeing to the healing and treatment of the cattle, and bringing about the raising of fallen animals.

**66,35,4** But he does not relate it so, nor teach it so — God forbid; rather, he knows how to save the souls of men, which he summed up comprehensively in the riddle when he said, “I came only for the sheep that was lost,” meaning the whole of human nature.

**66,35,5a** And what does it say?

**66,35,5b** “He healed all whom they brought to him, the moonstruck and those held by various diseases”.

**66,35,5c** They brought to him the blind, the deaf, the crippled, the paralysed, the maimed, and he extended his kindness and healing over all; but nowhere is it written that they brought animals to him.

**66,35,6** Then again, coming into the region of the Gergesenes, as Mark says, or within the borders of the Gergesenes, according to Luke, or of the Gadarenes, according to Matthew, or of the Gergesenes, as certain copies read — for the place lay between the three allotments —

**66,35,7a** “And lo, two men possessed by demons, very savage, coming out of the tombs, and they shouted, saying, ‘Ah, what have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God, that you have come before the time to torment us?

**66,35,7b** We know who you are, the Holy One of God.’

**66,35,7c** And there was a herd of swine feeding there, and the demons besought him, saying, ‘If you drive us out of the men, dispatch us into the swine.’

**66,35,7d** And they rushed headlong into the sea and were lost in the waters.

**66,35,7e** And those who fed them fled and reported it in the city.”

**66,35,8** And in Matthew two demoniacs are spoken of, but he mentions swine simply, and does not make known the number.

**66,35,9a** But Mark also related the exact number of the swine, saying, “And he came into the region of the Gergesenes, and there met him a demoniac, who was bound with iron chains and tore the bonds apart, and lived among the tombs, and cried out, ‘Ah, what have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God?

**66,35,9b** You have come before the time to torment us.’

**66,35,9c** And Jesus asked him, ‘What is your name?’

**66,35,9d** And he said, ‘Legion’, because many demons had entered into him.

**66,35,9e** And they besought him that they might not be sent out of the country, but might enter into the swine; for there was a herd of swine feeding there; and he permitted them to enter into the swine.

**66,35,9f** And the herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea — they numbered some two thousand — and drowned in the sea.

**66,35,9g** And those who tended them ran away, and brought word of it in the city.”

**66,35,10a** Did God the Word, then, who became man for our sake, ask out of ignorance, and did he not know the name of the demon before he asked?

**66,35,10b** No; but the Godhead is accustomed to make the grounds of each matter plain out of the mouth of those who are questioned.

**66,35,11a** So here too, to show the terror and the multitude of the demons, he puts the question, so that the wonderful work may be shown out of that man’s mouth.

**66,35,11b** “And the demons besought him, saying, ‘Do not send us into the abyss, but permit us to enter into the swine.’

**66,35,11c** And he permitted them.

**66,35,11d** And the demons went out into the swine.

**66,35,11e** And the herd of swine rushed down the steep bank into the sea, and they perished in the waters.”

**66,36,1a** Oh, the great love of God for mankind!

**66,36,1b** How he refutes the lie, and shows the truth to his servants through deeds and through words and through all his care!

**66,36,1c** For he showed by deed that the soul is not the same in men and in cattle and in animals.

**66,36,2a** For if the soul were the same, for what reason, wishing to cleanse one man, or to save one soul — that of the demoniac — did he not spare to destroy two thousand souls together, if it was the same?

**66,36,2b** How does he cleanse the one man, or the one soul, yet permit the demons to enter into the other bodies — or rather, souls?

**66,36,3a** Are not the works of the light plain?

**66,36,3b** Are not these words wrought in light?

**66,36,3c** Is not the face of the truth bright?

**66,36,3d** Are not all things smooth to those who understand, and straight to those who find knowledge?

**66,36,3e** Who, having heard these things and compared them, does not convict Mani of stitching together what he ought not, so as to twist the minds of men away from what is?

**66,36,4** But again the wretches — for I have also heard someone arguing thus: when he heard this treatment of the matter from us, the brutish man turned about and thought that perhaps he could prevail against the truth of God, and, putting forward to himself words full of mockery, he thought to work against the truth with falsehood, and says, “But dying was a benefit to the swine; for their souls were released from their bodies and saved.”

**66,37,1** And great is the folly of those who do not see and are blind in mind, and who do not even take in with the sense of hearing the things they themselves say.

**66,37,2a** For if he at all considers the release of souls from the body to be salvation, the Saviour ought rather to have dispatched the demon-possessed man, so that his soul might be saved by being released from a man’s body.

**66,37,2b** So then he had a greater love for the souls that were in the swine than for the soul of the man.

**66,37,3** For for what reason did he not permit the man too to be thrown into the sea with the swine and die, so as to cleanse and save all the souls, both the man’s and the swine’s?

**66,37,4a** But we have not seen it so; rather, he summons Lazarus, four days dead, out of the tomb and raises him, and returns him to the world, not procuring evil for him, nor doing him any foolish thing.

**66,37,4b** “For he loved Lazarus,” says the Scripture.

**66,37,5a** Him whom he loved, then — how did he make him return into the flesh, if the flesh is evil?

**66,37,5b** And how did he not rather leave alone the man who had once died and been saved from the body?

**66,37,6a** And let no one think that Lazarus died again at once.

**66,37,6b** For the holy gospel shows clearly that Jesus was at table and Lazarus was at table with him; and in traditions too we have found that Lazarus was thirty years old at the time when he was raised.

**66,37,7a** And after he raised him he lived another thirty years, and so departed to the Lord, and, having fallen asleep, he was spoken of by a reverent name, as all are until the hour of the resurrection, when the Only-begotten, as he promised, is to restore its body to the soul and its soul to the body, and to give to each according to what he has done, whether good or bad.

**66,37,7b** For had there been no rising of bodies, where would the gnashing of teeth come from?

**66,37,7c** But let not some again speak the words of derangement, saying that teeth were made for us for chewing.
