**66,69,10** For since the love of money, the god of this age, blinded them, the illumination of the gospel did not dawn in their hearts, because they had been blinded by the love of money.

**66,69,11a** For it was this that blinded Judas too, this that killed Ananias and those with him, this that has destroyed many.

**66,69,11b** This is the god of this age: men chose it as their god, laid hold of the honour paid to it, and held the Lord in contempt, as he says, “He will cling to the one and scorn the other; you cannot serve God and mammon.”

**66,69,12a** And do you see the matter interpreted expressly and plainly?

**66,69,12b** For there exists no other god — neither in heaven, nor on the earth, nor in any region — but one Father, of whom all things are, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, by whom all things are, and one Holy Spirit, in whom all things are: the Trinity, which always is, one Godhead, never taking on any addition and never admitting any subtraction.

**66,70,1** But let us go on again to other matters and tear apart the nets of this wild beast, this enemy and avenger, beloved, bringing the strange things he says to the declaration of the truth, for those who wish to learn the things of the truth and to turn their mind away from the evil teaching of every heresy.

**66,70,2** For again he lays hold of the Law and the Prophets, hostile as he is to the truth and to the Holy Spirit, who spoke in the Law and in the Prophets; and, giving his tongue free rein by nature, as he always does, he speaks against God, the maker of all things, who spoke too in the Law and in the Prophets, “who is Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named.”

**66,70,3a** And he says, “From him comes desire, and from him murders, and all the rest.”

**66,70,3b** For he commanded them to snatch away the Egyptians’ garments, and to bring sacrifices to him, and all else that the Law provides; and that the murderer be put to death, so that one is no longer content with the first murder but commits a second as well, he forsooth avenging the first murder; and that he puts desires into the minds of men, speaking of women and of other matters.

**66,70,3c** But sparingly, he says, he prophesied a few things about Christ, so that through the few, by persuasive talk, he might win belief.

**66,70,4a** These were the words of the reckless Mani, which he utters with unbridled tongue against his own Master.

**66,70,4b** But anyone who considers it would see nothing else appearing in this but the doings of a delirious man.

**66,70,4c** For as one who has a delirium arms himself with a sword against himself, and in his seizure, cutting his own flesh, thinks he is warding off enemies, and does not know it, so this man too arms himself against himself, not understanding the texts that he drags in against himself.

**66,70,5a** For if desire is from him, and he works desires, how is it that he who puts desire in writes again and again against desire?

**66,70,5b** He who says, “You shall not desire what is your neighbour’s — not his ox, not his beast of burden, not his slave-girl, not his field, not his wife, not anything that belongs to your neighbour” — if he does away with desire, he is not himself the supplier of desire.

**66,71,1a** How then, he says, did he command them to despoil the Egyptians when they were going out of the land of Egypt?

**66,71,1b** Yes; for he is a righteous judge, as I have said many times already on this point.

**66,71,2a** And to make plain that it is not he who has need of sacrifices, he declares in the prophet, “Did you bring sacrifices to me, house of Israel, for forty years?

**66,71,2b** says the Lord.”

**66,71,3a** To whom, then, were the offerings brought?

**66,71,3b** To him, according to the intention of those who offered them; but he himself did not command them because he had need of them, but in order to accustom them, away from polytheism, to acknowledge one God.

**66,71,3c** For since he saw sacrifices being performed for the gods of the Egyptians — so that they might not, their thoughts turned aside through polytheism, forsake the one and only God.

**66,71,4a** But when over a long time he had drawn their mind together away from polytheism, having weaned them from such a practice, he begins to cut away what he did not want, and he said, “To what purpose do you bring me frankincense from Sheba, and cinnamon from a land far off?

**66,71,4b** Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?

**66,71,4c** For I did not require these things from your hands, but that you practise righteousness and truth towards your neighbour, each towards his brother.”

**66,71,5a** And you see that as time goes on the substance of the power of divine things is revealed, as he himself again says to Samuel, “Anoint Saul as king.”

**66,71,5b** But later he rebukes them, saying, “You anointed a king and rulers not through me, and I did not command you.”

**66,71,6a** But since their minds sought this, God, consoling Samuel the prophet, said, “It is not you they have rejected, but me, says the Lord.

**66,71,6b** Nevertheless, anoint Saul the son of Kish for them.”

**66,71,6c** The divine deals with them as with little children, so as to bear with the weakness of those who are weak and to coax the infant away from its own frailty.

**66,71,7a** Then he speaks the most perfect word: “The sacrifice for God is a crushed spirit; a heart crushed and humbled God will not set at nought.”

**66,71,7b** And, “Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise,” and whatever else there is to say on this.

**66,72,1a** Then the same Mani says: he wanted to set forth an account concerning Christ.

**66,72,1b** For he who spoke in the law is truly great, he who set it forth, knowing also about the things to come.

**66,72,2** For if he knows the things to come, he is not without a share of foreknowledge, but is God, since he knows the things to come; and he wrote them down so that they might come to pass.

**66,72,3a** But if they were contrary to him, he would have written about them, but he would have undone them, so that we might not be persuaded by them.

**66,72,3b** But since he establishes that the things to come are to be fulfilled in Christ, it is then the same Spirit that spoke in the law and in the prophets and in the gospel.

**66,72,3c** For the harmony is one, as he says through Moses, “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers.”

**66,72,4a** And again the Lord says, “Moses wrote about me.”

**66,72,4b** And Moses says, “Every soul that will not hear that prophet shall be utterly destroyed.”

**66,72,4c** And again the Lord: “If you do not believe the writings of Moses, how will you hear my words?”

**66,72,4d** And on every side the truth is seen to be something full of light and without a wrinkle.

**66,73,1** Again, he defines the covenant of the law as a covenant of death, because the apostle said, “But if the covenant of death, engraved in letters on stones,

**66,73,2** came in glory,” and the divine scripture said not only this, but also that “the law is not laid down for the righteous man, but for parricides and matricides and perjurers, and whatever else is opposed to sound teaching.”

**66,73,3a** Since, then, the law is not laid down for the righteous man, is the righteous man therefore lawless?

**66,73,3b** By no means.

**66,73,3c** But since the righteous man has gone ahead and accomplished the things of the law, there is no law against the righteous man who has done the law.

**66,73,3d** But it is laid down against those who have acted lawlessly, judging those who have transgressed.

**66,73,4a** So it is, then, with the covenant.

**66,73,4b** For it said that the murderer should be put to death, the adulterer killed, and the transgressor stoned.

**66,73,4c** And it came in glory; for its glory was great.

**66,73,4d** For it held the opinion of mankind in check, away from wronging one another, being shown forth in the light of a pillar of fire, in fearful trumpets sounding loudly, and in the tent of witness, and coming at that time in great glory.

**66,73,5a** For the covenant of death had to go first, so that, having first died to sin, we might live to righteousness, as Christ bore our weaknesses and took up our diseases, having borne all things up on the cross in his body, so that first the things of death and then that of life might be fulfilled in him for our sake.

**66,73,5b** And for this reason he first dies, in order to establish the covenant of death.

**66,73,6a** Then he has been raised from the dead, so that it might be “from glory to glory, as from the Lord, the Spirit”.

**66,73,6b** For on the cross he triumphed over principalities and powers; in his death he condemned sin; in being buried he buried lawlessness; in tasting death he broke off the sting of death; in going down into Hades he despoiled Hades, set free with valour those who were bound in fetters, and took the trophy of the cross over the devil.

**66,73,7a** And see how this glory reaches from Moses to the Lord.

**66,73,7b** How much more, then, will the covenant of life be in glory, when the stone was rolled away, the rocks were split, the tombs were opened, angels flashed like lightning, women brought the good news, peace was given, the Spirit was given by him to the apostles, the kingdom of heaven was proclaimed, and the gospel enlightened the world?

**66,73,8a** “He who came down is himself also he who went up above all the heavens and who is seated at the Father’s right hand”: the covenant was not death-dealing, but the covenant was against death.

**66,73,8b** And that of death was in glory, so that the surpassing glory might come about against death.

**66,74,1a** Then again the same Mani says: an old and a new covenant cannot belong to one teacher.

**66,74,1b** For the one grows old day after day, while the other is made new day by day; for all that is growing old and ageing comes near to vanishing; but that one belongs to another god and another teacher, and this one to a different god and a different teacher.

**66,74,2a** Now if he could show two old covenants, what he says might have been plausible coming from him, on the ground that there were two who made covenants at that time.

**66,74,2b** Likewise, if he could show two new covenants, one might have taken into one’s mind what was said before.

**66,74,3** But if the old belongs to one and the new to the other, and the new covenant is the good God’s and the old the wicked one’s, then, had the good God not seen the wicked one making a covenant, he would not have known that a covenant ought to be made; and he will rather be one who takes the occasion of his teaching from him, and is inexperienced in affairs.

**66,74,4** For without having seen, he would not have imitated; and the old covenant ought rather to have been the good one’s, so that the wicked one at least might be called the imitator, rather than he who is the true God.

**66,74,5a** For the Lord says in the gospel, “Whatever the Son sees the Father doing, so he himself also does likewise.”

**66,74,5b** And so as not to yield to the one counselling him, so that the devil might not boast and say that the Saviour had done something on his counsel — as he says to him, “Command that the stones become loaves.”

**66,74,5c** But he does not put up with it, so that he might not be supposed to have learned, taking counsel from the devil.

**66,74,6a** And do you see that he says the two covenants belong to one God?

**66,74,6b** For the apostle says, “The first covenant was given from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery.

**66,74,6c** For Mount Sinai is in Arabia.”

**66,74,6d** For though there are two wives, yet the husband is one; so too, though there are two covenants, yet God is one, he who made the two.

**66,74,7a** And for this reason he has not called two of them new, nor two old, but one old and one new.

**66,74,7b** And he says, “A covenant is valid in the case of the dead; therefore not even the first was made without blood.

**66,74,7c** For Moses took the blood of the goats and sprinkled both the book itself and the people.

**66,74,8a** For this reason the second covenant also was given upon the death of the Saviour”; since above all the two agree with one another, the one saying, “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes for whom it is laid up,” and the second, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them.”

**66,74,8b** And there is much to be said about this, but for the sake of brevity I shall pass it over.

**66,75,1** Again, he likens the law and the prophets to trees that are withered and grown old, supposedly on the strength of the saying in which he said, “The law and the prophets until John.”

**66,75,2a** And nothing is more foolish than this.

**66,75,2b** For to whom is it not clear that, once what the prophets proclaimed had been fulfilled, the prophets were brought to their completion?

**66,75,2c** For if prophets were still coming, proclaiming Christ as coming from Mary, Christ had not yet come among us.

**66,75,3** For this matter is like something of the following kind: as a king who is about to travel to a country sends ahead of him horsemen to make ready beforehand and heralds to announce him in advance, and the nearer the king’s arrival draws, the more numerous are the heralds of his arrival, going on ahead and announcing in the cities the news of his arrival.

**66,75,4a** But once the king has come into the city, what further need is there of heralds?

**66,75,4b** What further need of horsemen, or of the others who announce the king’s arrival in advance, when the king himself is within?

**66,75,5a** So too the law and the prophets: until John.

**66,75,5b** But once John had lifted up his voice in proclamation in the wilderness and had shown that “this is the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,” there is no longer need of prophets, that they should come and proclaim to us the coming of Christ from a virgin.

**66,75,5c** But there is need of those who announced his coming in advance, for the confirmation of his coming, that it had been announced beforehand.

**66,75,6** For just as, if someone has a tutor — as the apostle too says, “The law has become our tutor until the coming of the Lord” — and he has come of age and has reached the teacher, he certainly does not cast off the tutor as an enemy; in the same way we too were guided in the law and in the prophets until the coming of the teacher.

**66,75,7** But having found the teacher we do not dishonour the tutor; rather, we even confess our gratitude to him, because, having guided our infancy, he sent us on to the more perfect lessons.

**66,75,8** Or, just as, when someone about to sail on the sea has the large ship, but goes out over the swell along the seashore in a small boat, and the boat carries the man across to the large ship, the man certainly does not send the boat to the bottom because he has found the large ship, but, while being grateful to the boat, he takes hold of the greater vessel of his safety;

**66,75,9** or, to put it another way, as when someone is cast out by the mother who bore him, but is taken up by some chance person and brought up over time, and later, when he has grown to manhood, recognises his own natural father, and such a person has understanding — surely, because he has recognised his own father and is taking possession of his own inheritance, he does not on that account dishonour the one who brought him up; would he not much rather be grateful to his foster-father, for not allowing him to be handed over to death? —

**66,75,10** so too we are grateful to God who gave the law and the prophets, and we are grateful to him for counting us worthy of the new covenant of his Son.

**66,76,1a** And the same Mani says that we are shapes of the rulers, brought into being by the rulers, and thrown down to them as food to be devoured.

**66,76,1b** But there is great ignorance in words of this kind.

**66,76,2** For we do not see things turning out that way.

**66,76,3a** For every creature whatever on the earth, even if it is one of the baser and fiercer beasts, does not attack its own form, but others; for example, lions do not eat lions, because of their own likeness and their sameness of kind; but when a great famine presses upon the beasts in the mountains, and for a long time they find nothing, whether because of snow or through some other want, the lions keep to their dens and holes, living together with their cubs and together with the lionesses.

**66,76,3b** And beast does not attack beast, nor wolf wolf,

**66,76,4** unless perhaps the animal falls into madness and, being rabid, does not know what it is doing.

**66,76,5a** If, then, a wolf does not devour a wolf because their form is of one kind, how are the rulers able to devour us, if we share the same form as they, and why do they not rather cherish us, so as to be seen preserving their own forms?

**66,76,5b** And on every side the charlatan’s words are refuted.

**66,77,1a** Then again he seizes upon the gospel, saying that not all can receive his teaching, but only those to whom it has been given.

**66,77,1b** But the Saviour’s word here was not about teaching, but about eunuchs.

**66,77,2a** But if the Saviour’s “not all can receive” here is fulfilled concerning his teaching, then, if they do not receive it, they do not receive it by their own choice.

**66,77,2b** These, then, will be called praiseworthy or blameworthy on the ground of free will, and the receiving will no longer be by nature; since otherwise, what good would he do by proclaiming his teaching?

**66,77,3** But his argument has fallen to the ground on every side; for the Saviour did not declare the saying to be about teaching, but spoke it on account of the making of eunuchs; and even if he were to call it teaching, Mani’s argument will no longer stand.

**66,77,4a** And the same Mani says: I knew those who are ours.

**66,77,4b** “For indeed the sheep that are mine know me, and I know the sheep that are mine.”

**66,77,4c** But he lies in everything.

**66,77,4d** For, wishing by flattery to snatch souls from among those who were then present at the debate, he spoke this word, sowing a bait beneath, so to speak, so that through the flattery they might be minded to attach themselves to him;

**66,77,5** so that, when they had attached themselves, he might begin to boast and to say that he knew them before they made their way to him.

**66,77,6** And it has turned out for him like the myth of the Greeks about Apollo the soothsayer,

**66,77,7a** who prophesied for others but could not prophesy for himself, and failed of his oracle when he loved Daphne and failed to win her because of her chastity; so too this Mani claimed by divination to know his own, but in reality he had come on account of Marcellus, to bring him under his hand.

**66,77,7b** But his oracle fell through.

**66,77,7c** For neither was Marcellus persuaded by him, nor anyone else of the people of that time on that occasion.

**66,78,1a** Then he said that in the years of old no one was saved, but from Tiberius Caesar’s fifteenth year down to his own times.

**66,78,1b** Now Probus was the emperor at that time, and Aurelian before him, when this Mani was abroad among men.

**66,78,2a** And in this again he is refuted on every side, since the gospel and the apostolic sayings speak of those who had already been saved before.

**66,78,2b** Likewise the Lord says, “From this generation shall be required all the blood of a righteous man poured out upon the earth, from the blood of Abel the righteous to the blood of Zacharias, poured out between the sanctuary and the altar.”

**66,78,2c** How, then, was Abel righteous, how Zacharias, unless salvation already existed, and unless he had already saved through the law and the prophets?

**66,78,2d** He says, “Death reigned from Adam until Moses,” so that you may know that in Moses death was cut short, though not wholly abolished.

**66,78,4a** For it was awaiting Jesus, the perfecter of all things, so that, when he should give himself up for mankind — the immortal dying, the one who cannot be held becoming one who is held, the Life enduring suffering in the flesh — he might also break, through death, him who has the power of death, the sting of sin, and death itself; when at last the saying was fulfilled, “O death, where is your sting?

**66,78,4b** O Hades, where is your victory?”

**66,78,5a** For there, in Moses, death was checked and overturned, having reigned until Moses.

**66,78,5b** And at first there were righteous men, those such as Abel and Enoch, “who was translated so that he should not see death, and he was not found.”

**66,78,6a** But there was not yet the written law, but the law according to nature, from the mind and from tradition, by succession from fathers to their sons.

**66,78,6b** But when the law was set forth in clear light, it became, so to speak, a sword cleaving asunder the power of sin; and when the Saviour came, the sting of death was crushed.

**66,78,6c** And again, death will then be swallowed up in victory.

**66,78,7a** And see how God was saving by many ways.

**66,78,7b** But the perfection of salvation has come about in Christ Jesus our Lord, and will come about, as the gospel too declares, “From his fullness we have all received.”

**66,78,7c** And what, it says, is the fullness?

**66,78,8a** “But the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus.”

**66,78,8b** There it was given; here it came about.

**66,78,8c** If the law, the grace and the truth are from the fullness of Jesus, then the old and the new covenant are in the law and in grace and truth.

**66,79,1** Again, the same Mani makes use of another text, declaring that “Christ redeemed us out of the law’s curse, becoming a curse on our behalf.”

**66,79,2a** Let him tell us, then, with what pieces of silver the purchase was made, and what the price was that was paid so that he might buy us.

**66,79,2b** For he did not say “which he bought,” but “redeemed”.

**66,79,2c** But he knows of the purchase, yet is ignorant of the price; but the truth confesses both.

**66,79,3a** For he redeemed us, and truly bought us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us.

**66,79,3b** And how he bought us the teacher of the church at once adds, declaring, “You were bought with a price, with the precious blood of a lamb without blemish and without spot, Christ.”

**66,79,3c** If, then, it was with the blood that you were bought, you do not belong among those who have been bought, Mani, since you deny the blood.

**66,79,4a** And from whom did he buy us?

**66,79,4b** Speak.

**66,79,4c** Did he purchase us when we belonged to another?

**66,79,4d** Was our former master, then, in want, and, needing the price of us, did he take it and sell us to Christ?

**66,79,4e** And if we were sold to Christ, we no longer belong to the former one.

**66,79,5a** If, then, the former one no longer possesses us, he has come to be outside his own estate, and he has no authority in his own places.

**66,79,5b** How, then, is he at work in the sons of disobedience, as it is written?

**66,79,6** But the man who is mad in every respect understands neither how he bought, nor how we were bought, nor how he became a curse for us — he who has opened his mouth and is unable to speak with confidence about what he says.

**66,79,7a** For see, we behold them, in the regeneration at his coming, saying and crying aloud, “We ate in your name, and in your name we cast out demons.”

**66,79,7b** And he will say to them, “Depart from me, you accursed; I never knew you.”

**66,79,8a** How, then, do they confess him, and he curses them?

**66,79,8b** And what was the curse of the law?

**66,79,8c** Why, the law’s curse was a cross, because of sins.

**66,79,8d** For if anyone was caught in a transgression, the law said, “And if you hang him upon a tree, the sun shall by no means go down on him, on his dead body; but you shall take him down without fail and bury him without fail before sunset, for cursed is everyone who hangs upon the tree.”

**66,79,9** Since, then, the curse had been appointed on account of crucifixion, and he himself came and bore our sins up on the tree, having given himself for us, his blood bought us and his body undid our curses — that is, he undid our sins through the repentance of the cross and through his coming.

**66,79,10** So neither is the law a curse — by no means — nor did the gospel take on the curse, nor the Lord; but through the occasion of his death the death that stood against sin has been undone.

**66,80,1a** Then he says that the law was a ministry of death.

**66,80,1b** We have already said much about this, that it was not itself a minister of death.

**66,80,2a** For it did not tell anyone to kill, but gave command, saying, “You shall not kill.”

**66,80,2b** But since it put the murderer to death — so that through the one man who was put to death the practice of murder might be done away, and many, made afraid on account of one, might restrain their wrongdoing so as to kill no longer — the ministry was of death, not in order to minister death, but in order to bring death upon the murderer, so that many might no longer become murderers.

**66,80,3** But when the Saviour came, since the tutor had by then brought them to sobriety for the greater part of the time, he showed the more perfect lessons in harmony with the law — with “You shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness” —

**66,80,4a** and said, “To him who strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also,” so that the ministry might be one of life, murder being done away altogether.

**66,80,4b** For he who is struck on the cheek does not produce a provocation to murder, but loosens the murderer’s hand, soothing with his humility the malice that is in him.

**66,80,4c** And thus the old and the new covenant agree in all things.

**66,81,1** Then again he lays hold of something, in order to bring in by stealth a scheme of two persons for the establishment of the dyad that he speaks of, and of the two natures, and of the principles without beginning and the roots of which we have already spoken before; wishing to say similar things for the division of realities, and daring to divide in this way,

**66,81,2** he is not ashamed to say that the old covenant said, “Mine is the gold and mine is the silver,” while the new covenant says, “Blessed are those poor in spirit, because the kingdom of heaven belongs to them.”

**66,81,3a** Yet he is unaware that the old covenant in its turn also says, “Rich and poor met one another, but the Lord made them both.”

**66,81,3b** And the new covenant agrees in the same thing, blessing the poor who are poor in fact, and at another time the poor in spirit, so that both may hold good; so that Peter and those with him might also show, in their boasting, the true poverty: “Silver and gold I have none, but what I have, this I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ, stand up and walk about.”

**66,81,4** So that he might indicate that the blessing of the poor in fact is not set against the blessing pronounced on those poor in spirit, who possess something with righteousness, but are poor in being humble-minded; of whom he said, “I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink,” and what follows.

**66,81,5a** Then he explains, saying that these did so from what belonged to them.

**66,81,5b** And do you observe one and the same Spirit in the old covenant, pointing to the poor man and the rich, and likewise in the new covenant?

**66,81,5c** In the same way the Saviour too praises both.

**66,81,6** For as he watched the treasury he saw those who were casting gifts into the Corban, and he did not forbid the gifts of the rich, but he also praised the widow who had cast in the two mites, because of the poverty mentioned before, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “Rich and poor met one another, but the Lord made them both.”

**66,81,7a** And that these things are so, and that the Spirit of the old and of the new covenant is the same, see the apostle speaking about the ancient prophets: “Time will be lacking to me if I tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David and the rest of the prophets, who went about in sheepskins, in goatskins, maltreated, in straits, oppressed — men of whom the world was not worthy.”

**66,81,7b** For we have found Isaiah too clothed in sackcloth, and Elijah likewise.

**66,81,7c** And do you see how, in both the old and the new covenant, the poor are blessed for their piety, and the rich are blessed for their righteousness?

**66,82,1a** Then again the same Mani says: the old covenant, he says, commands keeping the sabbath, and if anyone did not keep the sabbath, he was stoned with stones, just as a man who gathered a load of sticks was handed over.

**66,82,1b** But the new covenant — meaning the Lord in the gospel — said, “I am working, and my Father is working,” and on the sabbath the disciples were plucking ears of grain, and on the sabbath he healed.

**66,82,1c** And not only this, but he also said, “Take up your bed and go to your house.”

**66,82,2a** Oh, the great ignorance!

**66,82,2b** For nothing is worse than inexperience.

**66,82,2c** For ignorance has blinded many.

**66,82,2d** For when has the sabbath not been set aside for a good reason?

**66,82,2e** And at what time was every single day — not the sabbath alone — not bound fast against wickedness?

**66,82,3** For Joshua the son of Nun, the successor of Moses, who is numbered among the prophets, the one chosen by God, who by prayer held back the sun and the moon, as he said, “Let the sun stand against Gibeon, and the moon against the ravine of Aijalon,” is at once found setting aside the sabbath for a good work.

**66,82,4a** For Joshua goes round the walls of Jericho for seven days; for it was not lawful to walk on the sabbaths beyond the measure of the six stades laid down.

**66,82,4b** And the circuit of Jericho happens to be more than twenty stades.

**66,82,4c** And since they went round for seven days, the sabbath certainly fell on one of the days.

**66,82,5a** And this was a command of God, so that he might show his will in the working of wonders.

**66,82,5b** For there were no engines and no contrivances, no rams, no siege towers; but by the sound of a horn trumpet alone and the prayer of a righteous man the walls of the enemy leaned over and fell down.

**66,82,6** For they had to be punished, since the sins of the Amorites had been filled up.

**66,83,1a** For the law was a judge against injustice, and rendered to each according to his own works.

**66,83,1b** And since the Amorites were in sins, having fallen into transgression and having denied the oath which they had sworn, as I have already said somewhere else — but it will do no harm to set out the same things here too.

**66,83,2a** For these are the ready weapons of Mani’s cleverness: that the God of the law is a fine one, who despoiled the Egyptians, drove out the Amorites and Girgashites and the rest of the nations, and handed their land over to the sons of Israel.

**66,83,2b** How did he who says, “You shall not covet,” give them what belonged to others?

**66,83,3** And the ignorant man does not know that they took back their own land, which had been plundered from them, and that what had passed between them was avenged according to the terms of truth and the oath.

**66,83,4** For when Noah had been saved from the flood, together with his wife and his three sons and three daughters-in-law, he alone, dividing the whole world among his three sons, Shem and Ham and Japheth, made the division by casting the lots at Rhinocorura, as the sequence of events also has it; and there is nothing empty-sounding or falsified in this.

**66,83,5a** For Rhinocorura is rendered Neel.

**66,83,5b** And so in fact the natives call it, and from the Hebrew it is rendered “lots”, since it was there that Noah threw the lots for his three sons;

**66,83,6** and the lot fell from Rhinocorura to Gades, comprising Egypt and Mareiandine and Ammon, Libya and Marmaris, Pentapolis, Macate, Macrone and Leptis Magna, Syrtis, Mauretania, as far as the so-called Pillars of Heracles and inner Gades.

**66,83,7a** These are the parts towards the south.

**66,83,7b** And from Rhinocorura the parts towards the east: Idumaea and Midianitis, Alabastritis and Homeritis and Axomitis, and Bugea, and Liban, as far as the country of the Bactrians.

**66,83,8a** And the same lot marks the boundary between it and Shem towards the east.

**66,83,8b** To Shem the lot fell in breadth: Palestine and Phoenicia and Coele, Commagene, Cilicia, Cappadocia, Galatia, Paphlagonia, Thrace, Europa, Rhodope, Lazia, Iberia, Caspia, Cardyaea, as far as Media towards the north.

**66,83,9a** From there this lot marks the boundary of Japheth towards the north.

**66,83,9b** And towards the west, from Europa as far as Spain and Britain, and from there the nations lying alongside: the Eetes and Daunians, Iapygians, Calabrians, Latins, Opici, Magardes, as far as the holding of Spain, and of Gaul, and the upper country of the Scots and the Franks.

**66,84,1** When, then, the lots had been divided in this way, Noah called together his three sons and bound them by an oath that none should set foot on his brother’s lot and take advantage of his brother.

**66,84,2** But Canaan, the son of Ham, being covetous, invaded the land of the Palestinians and seized it, and the land was called Canaan, because he settled in it, having left his own lot because it seemed to be scorching.

**66,84,3** And settling in the land of Shem, which is now called Judaea, he begot these sons: the Amorite and Girgashite and Perizzite and Jebusite and Hivite and Arkite and Hittite and Sinite and Zemarite and Sidonian and Philistine.

**66,84,4a** For this reason the Lord too speaks in the law, showing that their sins were being filled up in the matter of the oath, as he says, “The sins of the Amorites are not yet filled up.”

**66,84,4b** For this reason they stayed at the mountain, passing the time in the wilderness, until those others should make themselves self-condemned and come out to war against the sons of Shem, who had been wronged.

**66,84,5** For Shem begets Arphaxad, Arphaxad Cainan, Cainan Shelah, Shelah Eber, Eber Peleg, Peleg Reu, Reu Serug, Serug Nahor, Nahor Terah, Terah Abraham, Abraham Isaac, Isaac Jacob, Jacob Judah, Judah Perez, Perez Hezron, Hezron Ram, Ram Amminadab, Amminadab Nahshon.

**66,84,6a** In the times of Nahshon, the tribal chief of Judah, and in the days of Joshua the son of Nun, Shem’s sons received their own land, with no injustice in the matter, but righteous judgement.

**66,84,6b** So the walls of Jericho fell of their own accord; for righteousness avenges injustice.

**66,84,7** For seven days they went round the walls, and the sabbath was set aside, so that righteousness might be fulfilled.

**66,85,1** And not only this, but the lampstand of the sanctuary in the tent of witness had seven lamps, and every day the seven lamps were lit alike, and not one of them was idle on any single day at all, but every day the light was the same.

**66,85,2a** For the sabbath was not made for shutting out, but for good work.

**66,85,2b** And while no one at all in the twelve tribes was working, the altar alone did not rest from work, even as the Lord tells us in the gospel, “Your priests in the temple profane the sabbath, and they are without blame.”

**66,85,3a** And “profane the sabbath” means that they set it aside.

**66,85,3b** And how do they set it aside, except by bringing sacrifice to God, that the altar may not stand idle?

**66,85,4** And not only this, but the sun too rises and sets, and the moon waxes and wanes, and winds blow, and fruits sprout, and mothers give birth, and all things happen on the sabbath.

**66,85,5a** For this reason the Lord too, when he came, did not do carpentry on the sabbath, did not work bronze, nor anything else, but, being God, he did the work of God.

**66,85,5b** And he says, “Take up your bed and walk,” so that the work that had been done might be made manifest by the man carrying it, so that all might recognise him who came from heaven to help the sons of men.

**66,85,5c** For indeed he came in reality to set aside the sabbath; but he could not have set it aside if it had been foreign to him.

**66,85,6** For no one undoes another’s work, unless such a person turns contractor for other men’s affairs and meddler in other men’s business, buying himself lawsuits.

**66,85,7** But since the sabbath is his own, for this reason he says that the Son of Man is master of the sabbath also.

**66,85,8a** And he says, “It is not for the sake of the sabbath that man came into being, but the sabbath for the sake of man.”

**66,85,8b** If, then, God made the sabbath for man, he also honoured man above the sabbath, so that man might know rest and the respite of what is to come; for these are copies of the heavenly things.

**66,85,9a** For here it is in part, but those things are the whole perfection.

**66,85,9b** The sabbath in the law, then, was until his coming; and he set that sabbath aside and gave us the great sabbath, which is the Lord himself, our rest and our sabbath-keeping.

**66,85,10a** So no one will separate the old covenant from the new, nor the new from the old; for the harmony is one and the same.

**66,85,10b** But if the unlearned and inexperienced man sees two buckets drawing from one spring, and supposes that because the buckets differ the waters too are different, and then hears the truth from those of understanding — “Taste from the two buckets, and see that the buckets are two, but the spring is one.”

**66,85,11a** So it is: one Lord, one God, one Spirit that has spoken in the law and in the prophets and in the gospel.

**66,85,11b** For this reason there are not two old covenants, nor two new covenants, since those who made the covenants are not two; but there is one who makes the old grow old and renews the new, not abolishing the old to its destruction, but bringing the old to rest, and adding to the second an inheritance of abundance.

**66,86,1a** Again, the same Mani brings in another text, saying: I know of a spirit saved without a body.

**66,86,1b** For this, he says, is what the apostle teaches, saying, “It is heard on all sides that there is fornication among you, and fornication of a sort found not even among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife.

**66,86,1c** And you are puffed up, and did not rather mourn, so that he who has done this deed might be removed from among you.

**66,86,1d** For my part, though away in body yet present in spirit, I have already given judgement on the one who has wrought this deed — when you are gathered together, and the Lord, with my spirit — that such a one be handed over to Satan for the flesh’s destruction, so that the spirit may find salvation in the day of the Lord.”

**66,86,2a** But destruction, in the case of flesh, is complete annihilation.

**66,86,2b** How, then, if the flesh is annihilated in the devil’s hand and the spirit is saved, is there still to be a resurrection of bodies or of flesh?

**66,86,3** And the man who is inexperienced in everything is unaware that the flesh’s works are fornication, adultery, licentiousness and the like; and it is not the flesh itself that he speaks of, but its works:

**66,86,4** when one commits fornication, it is the flesh that is at work; but if one acquires continence, the flesh is no longer flesh, but the flesh has been changed into spirit, as the apostle too says, “He who from the beginning yoked the two together said, ‘On this account a man will forsake his father and his mother and will cleave to his wife, and the two will become a single flesh’; as he who cleaves to a harlot is one body, so he who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit.”

**66,86,5a** So then he who commits fornication has become flesh; not only the flesh itself, but everything, the soul too and the rest, becomes flesh.

**66,86,5b** For by cleaving to the harlot he became flesh, and being carnal he is called wholly flesh.

**66,86,5c** But he who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit — which is to say, body and soul and everything else there is in the man are one spirit in the Lord.

**66,86,6a** And laying down the law about this the same apostle says, “God has set all the members in the body, each one as he willed.”

**66,86,6b** And see how he confesses God as the maker of the body and the one who set the members that are in us, and set them as he willed, by his own wisdom and goodness.

**66,86,7** Then again, in place of the example of our own body, he gives that of Christ: “As we too are Christ’s body, and members from a member, and God’s church, which is Christ’s body.”

**66,86,8** If, then, the church, God’s body, being joined fast to the Spirit, which is to say to the Lord, is one spirit, then whoever sins and departs from it has fallen from the Spirit and become wholly flesh, in soul and body and whatever else is in him.

**66,86,9a** Otherwise how could part be handed over to Satan, and part not be handed over?

**66,86,9b** For he did not say that the flesh was to be handed over to Satan, but to hand over such a one.

**66,86,10a** And he who says “such a one” has handed over the entire man, with the soul and the whole of the man.

**66,86,10b** And if he has handed over the whole, he has declared the whole to be flesh; but he indicated that the spirit is to be saved for the Lord’s day: so that the church should not fall under blame for the fault of the man who had fallen, and the whole church be defiled by the transgression of one, he says, “Hand over the man who has fallen, so that the spirit” — meaning the whole church — “may find salvation.”

**66,87,1a** But, he says, it is written, “Flesh and blood will not inherit God’s kingdom”; and he thinks that in this he is saying something.

**66,87,1b** And in truth fornication is unable to inherit the kingdom of the heavens; neither is adultery, nor licentiousness, nor idolatry — that is, flesh and blood.

**66,87,3a** But if you suppose this about flesh and blood, that it is the flesh itself, how is the saying still fulfilled, “And as many as received him, he gave them authority to become children of God, who were born not of bloods, nor of the flesh, but of God”?

**66,87,3b** Who has come to birth in the world apart from flesh?

**66,87,3c** But since their dispositions were changed — for the natures of those born of mothers and fathers of flesh and blood were not — and they were born by the second birth that comes from the Lord’s birth, through Spirit and fire, he gave them authority to become children of God.

**66,87,4** As, then, here they were born of flesh and of blood, and yet the birth is no longer reckoned to be of flesh and blood, because of the change wrought by righteousness — although it is in flesh and blood, as he puts it, “For though walking in the flesh we do not make war according to the flesh” — it is therefore still flesh,

**66,87,5** but not making war according to the flesh; and for this reason he says that flesh and blood do not inherit the kingdom of heaven, speaking not of this flesh that has laboured, that has been sanctified, that has been well-pleasing to God, but of the flesh that has been found in sins.

**66,87,6** Otherwise how would the saying be fulfilled, “For this perishable thing must be clothed with imperishability, and this mortal thing be clothed with immortality”?

**66,87,7** And the same apostle, indicating this more clearly, so that some might not be led astray and, in place of the base works, give up hope for the fashioning of the body from the resurrection, says, “Put to death the members that are on the earth,” which are fornication, adultery, licentiousness and the rest.

**66,87,8a** [...] but also those who appeared to the Galileans and said, “This Jesus, whom you have seen taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him taken up.”

**66,87,8b** From all that has been said, those of good sense can apply their mind to all the words of the truth, and to those spoken out of the falsehood of the Manichaean mentioned before, so that, even if I have not recalled some testimony, all his teachings may be detected as false from the two or three testimonies which we have cited.

**66,87,8c** But we, having with difficulty travelled a long, rough road and the perilous haunts of this amphisbaena and deadly beast, the kenchritis, which is variegated with many likenesses to deceive those who look at it, but keeps hidden beneath the stinging and venomous source of one that takes its rise from every quarter.

**66,87,8d** For since he is a Greek with the Greeks, worshipping the sun and moon and the stars and demons — the man is a Greek, beloved, and his heresy teaches the doctrines of the Greeks, is versed in the lore of the magi and wallows in it, praises astronomers, busying itself with their arts, and prides itself on the name of Christ in word only, just as the kenchritis itself hides its venom and deceives by its varied colouring, lying amid much brushwood and blending with its surroundings —

**66,88,4** yet by the power of God, by the wood of the truth and the blood of Christ, and by the body from Mary, truly born, and by the rising of the dead and by confessing the one unity, having shattered the dragon’s head on the waters, this many-headed heresy, having turned it back and bruised its head, let us continue in thanksgiving to God, and let us hasten to go on to the heresies that follow, calling on God as the helper of our weakness, so that, having brought to completion what we promised in God, we may give thanks to God perfectly.

### Sect 67: Hieracites

Against the Hieracites, the forty-seventh, but the sixty-seventh in the series.

**67,1,1** After this wicked, reptilian, barbarian beast-bite of Mani’s teaching, venomous beyond every heresy, there arose a man named Hieracas, from whom come the Hieracites.

**67,1,2a** He lived in Leonto in Egypt; he had received no small preliminary education, having been trained in the pursuits of all Greek learning, and had acquired an exact knowledge of medical science and of the other studies of the Egyptians and the Greeks.

**67,1,2b** And perhaps the man had also dabbled in astronomy and magic.

**67,1,3a** For he was most experienced in many kinds of learning, and in exegesis, as his writings show, and he knew the Egyptian language very well.

**67,1,3b** For the man was an Egyptian, but was also articulate in no small degree in the language of the Greeks, being sharp in every way.

**67,1,4a** He was ostensibly a Christian, but he did not abide in the way of life of Christ.

**67,1,4b** For he fell away and, having slipped, ran aground.

**67,1,4c** For this man, who knew the old and the new covenant by heart, to put it plainly, and had written expositions of them, laid down as doctrine on his own authority, out of his own empty babble, whatever seemed good to him and whatever crept into his mind.

**67,1,5a** For he too holds that the flesh does not rise at all, but the soul alone.

**67,1,5b** And he declares that the resurrection is spiritual.

**67,1,5c** And, having gathered whatever there is from the divine scriptures to suit his own sense, he thus heaped up for himself certain base fabrications of absurd notions, contriving them for himself to establish his heresy.

**67,1,6a** And the man was astonishing in his asceticism and able to persuade souls.

**67,1,6b** For instance, many of the Egyptian ascetics were carried away along with him.

**67,1,6c** For I suppose that, concerning the resurrection of the dead, when he denied the resurrection of the flesh, he had taken his pretexts from Origen, or had vomited this up out of his own mind.

**67,1,7a** This man does not accept marriage, declaring that it belongs to the old covenant.

**67,1,7b** For he accepts alike, and regards as prophets, the circle of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and Moses and Aaron and all the saints, Isaiah and Jeremiah;

**67,1,8** and he says that in the old covenant it was permitted to be joined in marriage, but that from the coming of Christ marriage is no longer accepted, nor can it inherit the kingdom of heaven.

**67,1,9a** For what new thing, he says, did the Word come to do?

**67,1,9b** Or what new thing did the Only-begotten come to proclaim and to accomplish?

**67,1,9c** For if it concerned the fear of God, the law possessed that; if marriage, the scriptures have proclaimed it; if envy and greed and injustice, the old covenant contained all these.

**67,1,9d** But he came to accomplish this one thing only: to proclaim continence in the world and to choose for himself purity and continence; and without this one cannot live.

**67,2,1** He gathers these pretexts from every quarter, as when he says, “And your sanctification, without which no one will see God.”

**67,2,2** And if they say to him, “How did the apostle say, ‘Marriage is honourable and the bed undefiled, but God will judge fornicators and adulterers’?”, he at once replies in turn,

**67,2,3** saying: but a little further on he says, “The unmarried woman is concerned with the Lord’s affairs, how she will please the Lord, and so is the virgin; but she who has married is concerned with how she will please her husband, and she is divided.”

**67,2,4a** If, then, there is division, how can there be fellowship in the same thing where there is division?

**67,2,4b** And if it is not God she pleases but her husband, how is she able to obtain the inheritance with God?

**67,2,5a** For “because of fornications let each man have his own wife” — not praising marriage after the coming, he says, but bearing with it, so that they may not fall into further destruction.

**67,2,5b** “For there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.

**67,2,5c** And I wish, he says, all to be as I myself am.”

**67,2,6a** And, “The kingdom of heaven has been likened to ten virgins, five foolish and five wise.”

**67,2,6b** Wise virgins, foolish virgins — but virgins nonetheless — are likened to the kingdom of heaven, and he did not say married women.

**67,2,6c** And he heaps up many such things for himself, in order, supposedly, to cast out marriage.

**67,2,7a** And he does not accept children who die before knowledge, but excludes them from the hope that is held.

**67,2,7b** For he declares that these do not inherit the kingdom of heaven, since, he says, they have not contended.

**67,2,7c** For if anyone competes, he is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules.

**67,2,7d** For if even the one who competes is not crowned unless it is according to the rules, how much the more those never yet called into the contest?

**67,2,8** Again, this man does not believe that paradise is perceptible to the senses — just as Origen of course did not — nor, as I have said, a resurrection of the dead that is in the flesh; he speaks of a resurrection of the dead, but a resurrection of souls, declaring a kind of spiritual mythology.

**67,2,9** And no one assembles with them unless he is a virgin, or a monk, or continent, or a widow.

**67,3,1a** But concerning the Father and Son and Holy Spirit he does not speak as Origen does, but believes the Son to have been truly begotten of the Father.

**67,3,1b** And that the Holy Spirit is from the Father.

**67,3,2a** But this man declares, as I have shown above in the heresy of the Melchizedekians, concerning the Holy Spirit, that he is Melchizedek, because, he says, it has been said that “he intercedes with wordless groanings on our behalf.”

**67,3,2b** And who is this?

**67,3,2c** “But he remains a priest for ever.”

**67,3,2d** And “a priest for ever” because of his interceding.

**67,3,3a** And that this Spirit met Abraham at that time, since indeed it is like the Son.

**67,3,3b** And for this reason the apostle speaks of one “without father, without mother, without genealogy.”

**67,3,3c** Without mother, he says, because it has no mother; without father, he says, because it had no father on earth.

**67,3,3d** “And, made like the Son of God, he remains a priest for ever.”

**67,3,3e** And, talking much nonsense about the Holy Spirit, he went through a lengthy treatment of this subject.

**67,3,4** And he wants to make the full proof of it from the Ascension of Isaiah, as though, in the so-called Ascension, he said there, “The angel walking ahead of me pointed it out to me; he showed me and spoke: ‘Who is the one at the right hand of God?’

**67,3,5a** And I said, ‘You know, lord.’

**67,3,5b** He says, ‘This is the Beloved.’

**67,3,5c** ‘And who is the other, the one like him, who came on the left?’

**67,3,5d** And I said, ‘You know’; that is, the Holy Spirit who speaks in you and in the prophets.

**67,3,5e** And it was, he says, like the Beloved.”

**67,3,5f** From this he wants to establish the saying, “Made like the Son of God, he remains a priest for ever.”

**67,3,6** How many things, then, will our mind be able to discuss on this subject too, in opposition to his badly counterfeit thinking?

**67,3,7a** This man died in old age.

**67,3,7b** He wrote both in Greek and in Egyptian, expounding and composing works on the Six Days, and fabricating certain myths and pompous allegories.

**67,3,7c** And on how many other parts of scripture he composed works; and he fabricated many new-fangled psalms.

**67,3,8a** And many of them, of those who are true to their doctrine, do not partake of animate things.

**67,3,8b** Hieracas himself in reality practised great asceticism, but his disciples after him practise it in hypocrisy.

**67,3,8c** He abstained from all kinds of food and disciplined himself by abstaining from wine too;

**67,3,9a** and it is said by some about him that, having lived over ninety years, he did fine copying until the day of his death; for he was a calligrapher.

**67,3,9b** For his eyesight remained sound.

**67,4,1** Come, let us examine this man’s tares too, and see with what understanding of the divine word we may engage and destroy this venomous reptile, which strikes in front and behind like a scorpion, heaping up for itself from the two covenants what serves for harm, not as the divine words have them, but as his counterfeit notion has them; it understood the things of light darkly.

**67,4,2** For honey is not to blame, nor is it most bitter, nor are the finer foods created by God; but when given to someone in a fever they appear bitter in his mouth — not that the sweet things have become bitter, but that the fevered man’s taste has made bitter what is given to him.

**67,4,3** So too everyone who has fallen from the truth has not been deceived by the truth, but has tasted the truth through bitter thoughts, and for him it has turned to bitterness.

**67,4,4a** And concerning the children, let us see what we are to say about those who were killed straightaway in Bethlehem of Judaea because of Christ.

**67,4,4b** Are such as these without a share in heaven’s kingdom, or do they share in it?

**67,4,4c** They do indeed share in it, being blameless.

**67,4,5a** For if they have no share in it, then the Lord has become to blame for them; for it was because of him that they were killed.

**67,4,5b** And if they were killed because of him, before they had had time to contend or to receive the prize, then his coming has turned out rather to the harm of the world, since it has become the cause of the infants’ departing this life before their time, punished and fallen under a king’s threat, so that they did not reach the contest in order to win the prizes.

**67,4,6a** But let us look at other considerations too.

**67,4,6b** Call me the blessed and most wise Solomon for the refutation of this Hieracas.

**67,4,6c** Come, most blessed of prophets, you who received from the Lord breadth of heart and wisdom like the sand on the shore of the sea, what would you think about the children?

**67,4,7a** And he says, “For honourable old age is not that of length of time, nor is it measured by number of years.

**67,4,7b** But understanding is grey hair for men, and an unspotted life is the age of old age; having become blameless to God he was loved, and while living among sinners he was translated.

**67,4,7c** He was snatched away, lest wickedness alter his understanding or deceit beguile his soul.

**67,4,7d** For the bewitching of baseness darkens what is noble, and desire’s roaming undermines an innocent mind.”

**67,4,8a** And that he is speaking about children he goes on to show, adding, “Made perfect in a short time, he fulfilled,” meaning: having died young, he fulfilled long times.

**67,4,8b** “For his soul was virtue before the Lord; therefore he hastened out of the midst of wickedness.”

**67,4,9** And the Lord says to Jeremiah, “Before I formed you in the belly, I know you, and before you came forth from the womb, I have sanctified you.”

**67,5,1** And let us look at the Saviour himself, the mouth that does not lie, that knows all things: come, Lord, help our understanding, and refute Hieracas and his rashness.

**67,5,2a** “The children came to him,” it says, “that he might lay his hands on them and bless them.

**67,5,2b** But the disciples were pushing them away and hindering them.

**67,5,2c** But he said to them, ‘Let the children be, and do not prevent them from coming to me; for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.’”

**67,5,3** And so that the kingdom of heaven might not be thought to belong to little children only, and not to every age, he makes his beginning from them, but has granted to those who are like them to have the inheritance with them.

**67,5,4a** For if those who are like them are to reign, how much more those who are the originals of those who are like them?

**67,5,4b** And his fabulous argument has fallen.

**67,5,5a** For the Lord has mercy on all.

**67,5,5b** “For the Lord guards the little ones.”

**67,5,5c** And, “Praise the Lord, you children.”

**67,5,5d** And the children proclaimed, “Hosanna in the highest, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

**67,5,5e** And, “Out of the mouth of infants and sucklings you have perfected praise.”

**67,5,5f** And how many such sayings there are!

**67,6,1a** And concerning the resurrection of the flesh: how will there not be a resurrection of the flesh, you self-made sage, Hieracas?

**67,6,1b** For the very name of the expression shows its meaning.

**67,6,1c** For one does not speak of the rising again of what has not fallen.

**67,6,2a** And what is it that fell?

**67,6,2b** What is it that was buried?

**67,6,2c** What is it that was dissolved, if not the body, and not the soul?

**67,6,2d** The soul, then, does not fall, nor is it buried.

**67,6,2e** And how many things might be said on this subject?

**67,6,2f** For one does not speak of a resurrection of the soul; rather, what is raised is the body.

**67,6,3** And concerning the selection — that the Saviour came to select virginity and continence and purity: to whom is it not clear that this is a choice and the boast of the holy catholic and apostolic church, and that he saves those in honourable marriage too, since he is wont to save each according to his own order?

**67,6,4a** For how shall marriage not be honourable and possess in God the kingdom of heaven, seeing that the Saviour was invited to a wedding to bless marriage?

**67,6,4b** For if he had declined to go to a wedding, then he would have been a destroyer of marriage, and one who does not accept each person with allowance for his weakness.

**67,6,4c** Marriage, then, is honourable, because he himself ordained it.

**67,6,5a** That is why he attends a wedding — to shut the mouths of those who talk against the truth.

**67,6,5b** For there, in Cana of Galilee, Jesus performed his first sign, making the water wine.

**67,6,6** For as he rose from a virgin, to show the light rising from a virgin upon the world, so too he performed his first sign at a wedding in Cana of Galilee, so that he might honour virginity through his birth and the beam of light that rose through her, and honour honourable marriage through the divine signs, performing the first of them at the wedding, when he changed the water into unmixed wine.

**67,6,7a** Likewise, if marriage was alien, how does the teacher of the Gentiles give command?

**67,6,7b** As he says, “Refuse younger widows.

**67,6,7c** For when they have grown wanton against Christ they want to marry, incurring judgement because they have set aside their first faith.”

**67,6,8a** What, then, does he say?

**67,6,8b** “But let them marry, bear children, manage their households.”

**67,6,8c** If, then, he accepts these things, how is marriage, in your view, Hieracas, cast out after Christ’s coming in the flesh?

**67,7,1a** And as to Melchizedek, since you declare that he is the Spirit: then the Spirit came and took flesh.

**67,7,1b** So it is no longer the Only-begotten alone who has been born according to the flesh, but the Spirit too.

**67,7,1c** But if the Spirit has been born according to the flesh — see, there is Mary, who bore the Saviour; let Hieracas say where she is who bore the Spirit.

**67,7,2** And in the saying, “Made like the Son of God, he remains a priest for ever,” the word is no longer about the Holy Spirit.

**67,7,3a** For it is not “like the Son of God” that he said, but “made like”.

**67,7,3b** And “made like” has its process afterwards.

**67,7,3c** But if it is after Abraham’s time that the Spirit is made like Christ, then there was a time when it was not, and that is why it is made like God’s Son; and in what way can it be without father?

**67,7,4a** For if the Spirit exists of itself, and is not from the proper essence of the Godhead, it might reasonably be shown to be without father.

**67,7,4b** And indeed the Son is in truth only-begotten and without a brother, yet he is Son of God.

**67,7,5a** But even if we do not call the Spirit begotten, since the Son is only-begotten, yet it is the Spirit who goes forth from the Father and who takes of what is mine, says Christ.

**67,7,5b** At any rate, that which proceeds from the Father and receives of what is mine cannot be without father.

**67,7,6a** And even if he should say “without mother in heaven and without father on earth”, this can be said of the Saviour too.

**67,7,6b** How, then, does the apostle explain at the end, saying, “But he whose descent is not reckoned from them has taken tithes of Abraham the patriarch”?

**67,7,7a** For “from them” indicates precision.

**67,7,7b** For since his descent was not reckoned from the sons of Israel, he certainly had his descent from other nations.

**67,7,7c** But because his mother or father has not been recorded, those who slander the truth fancy one thing instead of another.

**67,7,8a** But we have discovered in traditions both his mother and his father.

**67,7,8b** For he was of the families of Sidon and of the Canaanites.

**67,7,8c** His fabulous argument has therefore fallen through, and his way of life too is in vain.

**67,7,8d** For to practise asceticism on inanimate things with a false faith — this is not a school of life and of hope and salvation.

**67,7,8e** For, it says, “Let everything be done for God’s glory.”

**67,8,1a** But on these matters I think it enough, in his case too.

**67,8,1b** For we have shattered the wings of the scorpion and dragged down its powers.

**67,8,1c** For this is a winged serpent and a scorpion, having wings in many ways, and flying, and imitating the virginity of the church, but not having a pure conscience.

**67,8,2a** For in him and in those like him is fulfilled the saying, “of men seared in their conscience, forbidding to marry, to abstain from foods which God made to be partaken of.”

**67,8,2b** It is sanctified through the living God’s word and through prayer, because everything is good and pleasant and nothing is to be cast away with God;

**67,8,3** but they are utterly ridiculed because of the women whom each of them keeps living in with him, whom they are accustomed to pride themselves on having for their service.

**67,8,4** But having pulled down this one’s wings too, as I have said, and crushed its head with the tree of life — that is, with the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ — on to those that follow let us go, calling on God himself as our helper for the refutation of the remaining heresies and the overthrow of what they vainly put forward to the world.

### Sect 68: Melitians

Against the schism of Melitius the Egyptian, the forty-eighth, but the sixty-eighth in the series.

**68,1,1a** There is a body of Melitians in the country of the Egyptians, derived from one Melitius, who had been a bishop in the Thebaid of the catholic church and of the orthodox faith.

**68,1,1b** For in no respect did his faith at any time depart from the holy catholic church’s faith.

**68,1,2** This Melitius was a contemporary of the aforementioned Hieracas and flourished at the same time, and came next after him in succession; he was also a contemporary of Saint Peter, the bishop of Alexandria.

**68,1,3a** And all these lived at the time of the persecution that took place under Diocletian and Maximian.

**68,1,3b** And the affair of Melitius came about in this way.

**68,1,4a** He made a schism, but he did not become altered in faith.

**68,1,4b** At the time of the persecution this man, together with Peter, the holy bishop and martyr, and the other martyrs, was arrested by the governors of Alexandria and Egypt at that time, who had been appointed by the emperor for this purpose — the prefect of the Thebaid being Culcianus, and of Alexandria Hierocles —

**68,1,5a** and Melitius was shut up in prison, he and the aforementioned martyrs, together with the aforementioned Peter, the archbishop of Alexandria.

**68,1,5b** And Melitius was reckoned foremost among those throughout Egypt,

**68,1,6** holding second place to Peter in the archiepiscopal office, as though for the sake of assisting him, but being under him and referring church affairs to him.

**68,1,7** For it is the custom that the archbishop in Alexandria holds the church’s administration over all Egypt and the Thebaid, Mareotes and Libya, Ammoniaca, Mareotis and Pentapolis.

**68,1,8a** Since, then, all these had been arrested for the sake of martyrdom and were in custody, they remained shut up for a considerable time.

**68,1,8b** But others, handed over before them, bore their witness, received the consummation of the prize, and fell asleep.

**68,1,8c** But these, as leading men and greater, were being kept for later.

**68,2,1a** And since some had borne witness to death, while others had fallen away from martyrdom and committed the lawless deed of the worship of idols — those who under compulsion even partook of sacrifice.

**68,2,1b** So, having fallen away and sacrificed and transgressed, they approached the confessors and martyrs in order to obtain mercy through repentance, some of them being soldiers, others clergy of various ranks, of the presbyterate and the diaconate and others;

**68,2,2a** and a stir arose among the martyrs, and no ordinary turmoil, some saying that those who had once fallen away and denied, and had not held out with courage nor contended, ought not to be admitted to repentance, lest those still remaining should also care less about the penalty because of such a pardon granted them too quickly, and turn aside and arrive at denial of God and the lawless deeds of Hellenism.

**68,2,2b** And what the confessors themselves were saying was reasonable.

**68,2,3a** The ones saying this were Melitius and Peleus and a number of others of the martyrs and confessors along with them.

**68,2,3b** Having displayed their zeal on God’s behalf, then, they evidently spoke these words out of strong feeling.

**68,2,3c** And they declared that, after the persecution had ceased and a considerable time had passed, repentance might be granted to the persons mentioned, once peace had come, if they repented in truth and showed the fruit of their repentance; not, however, that each should be received back in his own clerical rank, but that after an interval of time they should assemble in the church and in the communion, in the ranks, and not among the clergy.

**68,2,3d** And this was truth-loving and full of zeal.

**68,3,1** But the most holy Peter, being compassionate and being as a father of all, begged and pleaded, saying, “Let us receive them as they repent and set them a penance, so that they may sit beside the church; and let us not drive them away, nor their clerical rank” – as the account that has reached us records – “lest at some time, from shame and through the drawing-out of the time, those once shaken and unsettled by the devil through cowardice and weakness should turn aside altogether and not be healed, according to what is written, ‘that the lame be not turned aside, but rather be healed’”;

**68,3,2a** and Peter’s plea stood for mercy and kindness, while the plea of Melitius and his companions stood for truth and zeal.

**68,3,2b** From this, under the guise of a position that seemed pious on both sides, the schism came about, the one party asserting this, the other that.

**68,3,3** For when the archbishop Peter saw that Melitius’ party, carried along all too far by a godly zeal, had set themselves against the counsel of his kindness, Peter himself hung a curtain across the middle of the prison, spreading out a garment, that is, a blanket, or rather a cloak, and had a deacon proclaim: “Whoever are of my mind, let them come over to me; and whoever are of Melitius’ mind, to Melitius.”

**68,3,4a** And the greater number went apart with Melitius, bishops and monks and presbyters and those of other orders.

**68,3,4b** But very few indeed went with Peter the archbishop, bishops and a few others.

**68,3,4c** And from then on these prayed by themselves and those by themselves, and each likewise performed the other sacred rites apart.

**68,3,5a** Now it came about that Peter suffered martyrdom, and the blessed man was made perfect, leaving Alexander behind him in Alexandria as his successor.

**68,3,5b** For he succeeded to the throne after the Peter already mentioned.

**68,3,6a** But Melitius and many others fell under banishment, being sent off into exile in the mines of Phaeno.

**68,3,6b** And then at last the confessors who were being dragged along with Melitius – and Melitius himself, in custody – on the journey, passing through each region and each place, appointed clergy, bishops and presbyters and deacons, and built churches of their own; and neither did these communicate with those, nor those with these.

**68,3,7a** And each party wrote an inscription on its own church: those who had succeeded from Peter, who held the ancient churches that existed, “Catholic Church”;

**68,3,7b** those from Melitius, “Church of the Martyrs”.

**68,3,8** Hence the same Melitius, passing through Eleutheropolis, and Gaza, and Aelia as well, ordained many in this way.

**68,3,9a** And it came about that he spent a long time in the mines already mentioned; but in the meantime the confessors are released from the mines, both those on Peter’s side (for many of them still remained) and those of Melitius.

**68,3,9b** For not even in the mines did they communicate with one another or pray together.

**68,3,9c** And it came about that Melitius still spent a time in the world, so that he flourished alongside Alexander, Peter’s successor, as well, and was on friendly terms with him, and gave his care to the affairs of the church and of the faith.

**68,3,9d** For I have often said that he held nothing at variance.

**68,4,1a** For this same Melitius, being in Alexandria and spending time there, holding his own congregation with his own people, detected Arius and reported him to Alexander.

**68,4,1b** Now he had been informed that Arius, in his expositions, had stepped outside the set standard of the faith.

**68,4,2a** For he was presbyter in the church of Alexandria called Baucalis.

**68,4,2b** For over each church one presbyter is assigned.

**68,4,2c** For there were many churches, and now there are more, and this church had been placed in his charge, though another was with him too; on which matters we shall speak in detail when we reach the place, when there is need of it.

**68,4,2d** So when Alexander had diligently detected Arius, he called together bishops and a synod and conducted an inquiry, requiring an account concerning the faith, and calling Arius to answer for the corruption of false doctrine that had twined itself like ivy within him.

**68,4,3** But Arius did not deny it at all; rather, with a brazen face, just as he was, so he answered; and Alexander drives him out of the church, and with him is driven out a great multitude, those who had been tainted by him, of virgins and of other clergy.

**68,4,4a** And Arius, running away, sets out on the road to the country of the Palestinians.

**68,4,4b** And going up to Nicomedia, and writing letters from there to Alexander, he did not get beyond the frenzied mind of his false doctrine.

**68,4,5** But within a short time, when the same Alexander, the holy bishop of Alexandria, had taken the matter in hand and had stirred the blessed Constantine, he convened a synod in the city of Nicaea.

**68,4,6a** And the heresy of Arius is anathematized, after his death.

**68,4,6b** For at first he denied it to the face of the blessed emperor Constantine, and with oaths he feigned, in pretence, the words of orthodoxy.

**68,4,7a** And the emperor told him: “If your sworn denial is most just, may your oath be made good, and you shall be guiltless.

**68,4,7b** But if deceitfully, may he by whom you have sworn bring vengeance upon you.”

**68,4,7c** Which befell him not long afterwards, as we shall tell later.

**68,4,8a** So this Arius, acting in concert with Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, a man of like mind with him, was presented to the same emperor as one who, forsooth, was renouncing and anathematizing his own heresy.

**68,4,8b** Hence the emperor commands and permits Eusebius to bring him into communion at Constantinople under Alexander, a bishop of the same name as the bishop in Alexandria, who was bishop of Constantinople.

**68,5,1a** Now already the late Alexander of Alexandria, after the death of Melitius, the confessor already mentioned, having taken up zeal against the schism in the church, resolved to harass and constrain in every way those who were assembling separately, the ones left behind by Melitius, and to put pressure on them so that they should not break away from the one church.

**68,5,1b** But they, being unwilling, made trouble and stirred up disturbances.

**68,5,2** Pressed and constrained on this account by the blessed Alexander, some of them who were in their prime and who carried off the first place both in piety and in manner of life take the matter in hand and set off for the court to make petition, to petition and to obtain leave to assemble separately and not be hindered.

**68,5,3** Now there was a certain Paphnutius, a great man, an anchorite, himself the son of a woman confessor, who had himself also had some share in confession; and John, a bishop of theirs, himself also a most honoured man; and Callinicus, the bishop in Pelusium; and some others who undertook this;

**68,5,4** and when they went off and came to petition the emperor, they were turned back and thrown out.

**68,5,5** For those in the palace, hearing the name of Melitians and not knowing what such a thing might be, would not allow them to petition the emperor.

**68,6,1a** And meanwhile it came about that Paphnutius and John and their party, and the rest, spent time in the regions of Constantinople and Nicomedia.

**68,6,1b** And then they make friends with Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, and lay before him the matters concerning this same business.

**68,6,1c** For they knew that he had freedom of speech with the emperor Constantine, and they ask him that through him they might be made known to the emperor.

**68,6,2** But he, after promising them that he would bring their case before the emperor and accomplish for them the business of their petition, asks of them this request: that they receive Arius into communion with them, as one who was repenting, forsooth, in feigned fashion and in pretence.

**68,6,3** And they promise him, and from there he presents them to the emperor, and Eusebius informs him of their affairs, and leave is granted to the Melitians from then on to assemble by themselves and not to be troubled by anyone.

**68,6,4** Would that these same Melitians, who had taken upon themselves the strictest righteousness of the truth, had rather communicated with those who had lapsed, after their repentance, than with Arius and his followers.

**68,6,5a** For this befell them according to the proverb, that fleeing the smoke they fell into the fire.

**68,6,5b** For neither could Arius have had a footing and freedom of speech except through such a circumstance, which has become for them an evil association even to this day.

**68,6,5c** For the Melitians, who were once pure and strict in righteousness in the faith, became mingled with the disciples of Arius.

**68,6,6a** And most of them have already been defiled by the false belief of Arius, having turned aside from the faith in these times.

**68,6,6b** And some, even if they have remained holding the true faith – they do hold it, yet they are not free of the miry filth, through their fellowship with Arius and the Arians.

**68,6,6c** And it was from the circumstance already described that the alliance hitherto of Melitius and the Arians took its pretexts.

**68,6,7** But within a short time (for, as I promised to tell the story, I shall relate it here), while Alexander the bishop of Constantinople was being compelled to receive Arius into communion, and was praying and groaning and bending his knees about the ninth hour on the Sabbath before the altar, Eusebius saying, “If you will not consent to receive this man into communion willingly, he will come in with me tomorrow, whether you wish it or not” – and the Lord’s day was about to break.

**68,6,8** And, as I said, when Alexander had made his prayer, entreating our Lord either to take him up, lest he be defiled together with Arius, who had blasphemed against the Lord, or to work some marvel, as he is wont to work marvels in generation after generation, the holy man’s prayer was fulfilled before long.

**68,6,9a** During the night Arius, going into a privy to attend to his needs, burst asunder, just as Judas also once did.

**68,6,9b** And so his end came about in a foul-smelling place of uncleanness.

**68,7,1a** After this time, then, the schemes against the church were stitched together by his disciples.

**68,7,1b** And Alexander of Alexandria died after the synod at Nicaea.

**68,7,2a** And Athanasius was not present after the death of Arius.

**68,7,2b** For at that time he was a deacon under Alexander, and had been sent by him to the court.
