**68,7,3a** And though Alexander had given charge that no one should be appointed except Athanasius, as both he himself and those on the church’s roll testified, and the whole church, the followers of Melitius, the bishop in Egypt, seized the opportunity, while no bishop of Alexandria was present; for Alexandria has never had two bishops, as the other cities have.

**68,7,3b** So they appoint in Alexander’s place a certain man named Theonas, who died after serving three months.

**68,7,4a** And Athanasius arrived not long afterwards, after the death of Theonas.

**68,7,4b** And a synod of the orthodox was convened from every quarter.

**68,7,4c** And so he was installed, and the throne was rendered to him as the worthy man, the one for whom it stood prepared according to the will of God and according to both the testimony and the charge of the blessed Alexander.

**68,7,5a** From then on Athanasius begins to be hard pressed and to be grieved over the division of the church, between the Melitians and the catholic church.

**68,7,5b** He persuaded, he exhorted, and they would not bear it.

**68,7,5c** He compelled, he used force.

**68,7,5d** And he often went about visiting the churches nearby, especially those in the Mareotis.

**68,7,6** And once, when the Melitians were assembling, it came about that a deacon from the multitude that was with Athanasius burst in and, together with some of the people, smashed a lamp, so the account runs, and that a fight broke out.

**68,7,7** From this the plot against Athanasius came about, the Melitians accusing and slandering him with one charge after another, and the Arians joining in the scheme and lending themselves to it, because of their envy towards the holy faith of God and orthodoxy.

**68,7,8a** And they lay the matter before the emperor Constantine.

**68,7,8b** And it was Eusebius of Nicomedia, already mentioned, who was the agent of their whole combination and the contriver of the harm against the church and against Pope Athanasius.

**68,7,8c** So the accusers came before the emperor, saying that it was a vessel of the mysteries – which some called a lamp – the one I spoke of before.

**68,7,9a** And they brought certain other accusations too, asserting that a certain Arsenius, a presbyter of the Mareotis, had been beaten, and his hand severed with a knife by Athanasius’ people, or rather by Athanasius himself.

**68,7,9b** For they even carried a hand about at the court, and displayed it, which was in a box.

**68,8,1a** On hearing this the emperor is roused to anger.

**68,8,1b** For the late emperor had a godly zeal; but he did not know that they were slanderers, on account of the jealousy of the Arians against orthodoxy which I spoke of before.

**68,8,1c** And he commands that a synod be assembled at the city of Tyre in Phoenicia.

**68,8,2a** And he gave orders that Eusebius of Caesarea and some others should act as judges.

**68,8,2b** Now these were inclined somewhat more towards the vulgar babble of the Arians; and there were summoned bishops of catholic Egypt, and, under Athanasius, certain men in their prime and of greater standing, whose life in God was conspicuous.

**68,8,2c** Among them was the late Potamon the great, the bishop of Heraclea and a confessor; but also those of the Melitians, especially those who were accusing Athanasius.

**68,8,3** Now the late Potamon already mentioned, being a zealot for truth and orthodoxy and speaking freely – a man who never respected anyone’s person; for he had been blinded in one eye in the persecution for the truth’s sake – on seeing Eusebius sitting and judging, and Athanasius standing, overcome with grief and weeping, as happens with those who are true, cried out with a loud voice to Eusebius, saying, “Do you sit, Eusebius, and is Athanasius, who is guiltless, judged by you?

**68,8,4a** Who could bear such things?

**68,8,4b** But tell me, were you not with me in prison during the persecution?

**68,8,4c** And for my part I gave up an eye on behalf of the truth, while you neither appear to have any part of your body maimed, nor did you suffer martyrdom, but you stand here alive, mutilated in nothing.

**68,8,4d** How did you get out of the prison, unless you promised those who brought the constraint of the persecution upon us that you would do the unlawful thing, or did it?”

**68,8,5a** On hearing this Eusebius is roused to indignation, and rising up he dissolved the court, saying, “If you have come here and speak against us in such terms, then your accusers are telling the truth.

**68,8,5b** For if you play the tyrant here, much more so in your own country.”

**68,9,1** Then Eusebius and those with him set to work, and they send two of the bishops from Pannonia who held the views of Arius, Ursacius and Valens, to Alexandria and the Mareotis, where they said the things already mentioned had taken place, the matter of the vessel and the other matters of the fight.

**68,9,2** But when they had gone, they did not report the things that were true; rather, shifting one thing for another, they lied, and slandered the late Pope Athanasius.

**68,9,3** And having fabricated those things as though they were true, they brought them in writing and laid them before the synod of Eusebius’ party and the others, as Ursacius and Valens showed later when they repented, coming with petitions to the late Julius, the bishop of Rome, and making their defence for their error: “We slandered Pope Athanasius; but receive us into communion and to penance.”

**68,9,4a** And to Athanasius himself, too, they addressed written overtures of their own by way of repentance.

**68,9,4b** But Pope Athanasius, being in Tyre and seeing that the plot of that time was heavy from every quarter, before he entered the court or before the matters alleged in slander could be dealt with face to face in confrontation, withdrew by night and goes up to Constantine at the court, and lays before him the matters concerning himself, informing him.

**68,9,5a** But he, still carried along by vexation, and thinking that perhaps the accusers were telling the truth and that the one defending himself was lying, was still angry.

**68,9,5b** And as he was angry, Pope Athanasius pressed a heavy word upon the emperor: “The Lord will judge between me and you, since you yourself also agree with those who slander our lowliness.”

**68,9,6a** From this it comes about that he falls under exile, as a result of what had been written by the synod to the emperor.

**68,9,6b** For they pass a deposition on him in his absence, and as a result of this the emperor, provoked against him, was vexed, and he remains in the parts of Italy upwards of twelve or fourteen years.

**68,10,1** And afterwards a great story is noised abroad: how Arsenius, who had long been reported by slanderers as among the dead and was said to have had his hand cut off, was found in the regions of Arabia; and how Arsenius made himself fully known to Pope Athanasius while he was in exile; and how, when Pope Athanasius had sent for him secretly, as the report that has come to us contains, and Arsenius himself had come to the same late Athanasius, and they had appeared together before Constans and Constantius, the sons of Constantine, Athanasius showed Arsenius alive and having two hands, and the accusers were thenceforth found guilty not only of slander but also of tomb-robbing, because of the dead hand that had once been carried about.

**68,10,2** From this the whole affair became laughable, and there was astonishment at so strange and so great a piece of stagecraft, and perplexity as to what one might say about the accusers, and about the accused, and about all the other matters, to tell which in detail I should spend much time.

**68,10,3** And when Constantine had died, Pope Athanasius enjoying great freedom of speech and high repute, and a warm welcome from Rome and from the whole of Italy, and standing well with the emperor himself and with his sons Constantius and Constans, he is sent back by the two emperors after the death of the great Constantine, Constantius being at Antioch and giving his consent (we have learned of letters, both personal and in writing, sent by the three emperors to the people of Alexandria and to Pope Athanasius in person);

**68,10,4** and he takes his seat once more upon the throne after Gregory, who had succeeded him, the man the Arians had sent at the time when Athanasius was in exile.

**68,11,1a** And again a plot was got up against him before Constantius by Stephen and his party, and he was driven out.

**68,11,1b** And afterwards a plot was got up against him again by Leontius the eunuch and those with them.

**68,11,1c** From then on it came about that he was driven out and brought back again.

**68,11,1d** For George is sent by Constantius, and Athanasius withdraws, hiding for some time, until George was done away with, at which time Julian reigned and turned to Hellenism after the death of Constantius.

**68,11,2** For the Alexandrians, nursing their wrath against George, killed him, and burning him and reducing him to ashes, they scattered him to the winds.

**68,11,3** And when Julian had died in Persia and the late Jovian had succeeded to the empire, and had written to Bishop Athanasius with great honour and in trustworthy letters, and had sent for him and embraced him and sent him back to his own throne, the holy church receiving its bishop again and being comforted for a little while, then, when Jovian died, the blessed Athanasius was carried along once more in the same persecutions and rumours and disturbances.

**68,11,4** Yet he was not removed from the church and the throne; but, the Alexandrians having sent envoys on his behalf and the whole city having pleaded for him, after Lucius, the Arian of the present day, had been appointed abroad – at Antioch, perhaps – and had many times entreated the emperor Valens to be sent to the see of Alexandria, the emperor, because of the turmoil of the people, would not drive him out.

**68,11,5** At any rate, in the end, when Pope Athanasius died, Lucius was sent, who displayed many evils towards the church and towards the city, towards the peoples, towards the bishops, towards the clergy who were under Athanasius, and towards those who had succeeded him in each church, and towards Peter, who after Athanasius was appointed his successor in Alexandria.

**68,11,6** These things have been done up to the present: some bishops, presbyters and deacons were sent into exile, while others underwent capital punishment in Alexandria, others fought with wild beasts, virgins were killed, and many others perished.

**68,11,7** In these things the church of God is still carried along up to now, as a result of the circumstance already described of the Melitians and of the Arians, who obtained their standing by such means, and of the strengthening of that same combination of false doctrine – I mean that of the Arians.

**68,11,8a** But in the refutation against Arius we shall relate everything in detail.

**68,11,8b** And I shall pass beyond this circumstance too, and go on to the heresy of the Arians itself, calling on God as my helper as I proceed to come to close quarters in battle with this fearsome and many-headed serpent.

### Sect 69: Arians

Against the Ariomanites, the forty-ninth, but the sixty-ninth in the series.

**69,1,1a** Following in order upon these times of Melitius and of the holy Peter, bishop of Alexandria, comes Arius, with the Arians who derive from him, having flourished in the times of Alexander the holy bishop, Peter’s successor, who deposed this same Arius through much exertion and a great synod.

**69,1,1b** For he dislodged him and expelled him from the church and from the city alike, as a mighty evil that had found its way into the world.

**69,1,2a** They say that he was a Libyan by race, and had become a presbyter in Alexandria, presiding over the church called Baucalis.

**69,1,2b** For all the churches of the catholic church in Alexandria are subject to a single archbishop, and over each of them separately presbyters are placed, for the church needs of the inhabitants who live near each of their churches, and of the districts, or “lanes”, as the people who dwell in the city of the Alexandrians call them in the local way.

**69,1,3** Now this Arius lived in the times of Constantine, the great and late emperor, the son of Constantius the elder, who was the son of the emperor Valerian; and these reigned together with Diocletian and Maximian and the others.

**69,1,4a** And all know that Constantine, the father of Constantius and Constans and Crispus, was devoted with godly reverence to Christianity and to the faith of the fathers, the apostolic and prophetic faith in the churches, which until Arius himself had not been adulterated.

**69,1,4b** And it came about that this man split off a multitude.

**69,2,1** Now into this Arius, who was a presbyter of the Alexander already mentioned, there entered a spirit of Satan, and it stirred him up, according to what is written, to raise dust against the church, and a fire was kindled from him, no ordinary one, which has seized almost the whole Roman world, especially the regions of the east, so that even to this day his heresy has not ceased warring against the true faith and the church.

**69,2,2a** Now at that time Arius was accounted a presbyter, and he had many fellow presbyters, one in each church.

**69,2,2b** So there are several in number in Alexandria, along with the one now built, called the Caesareum, which was formerly the Hadrianum and later became the gymnasium of Licinius, or rather a palace.

**69,2,3** And afterwards, in the times of Constantius, it was resolved that it be built into a church, Gregory, the Melitian and Arian, having begun it, and the blessed Athanasius, father of orthodoxy, having completed it; and it was burned under Julian and rebuilt again by the late bishop Athanasius himself.

**69,2,4** And there are several others, as I said: the church called that of Dionysius, and that of Theonas, and that of Pierius and Serapion, and that of Persaea, and that of Dizya, and that of Mendidius, and that of Annianus, and that of Baucalis, and others.

**69,2,5** In one of these was a certain Colluthus, in another Carpones, in another Sarmatas, and this Arius already mentioned held one of the churches already mentioned.

**69,2,6a** And each of these, evidently, teaching at the customary assembly the people entrusted to him, they cast a certain strife among the people in their expositions; and some inclined towards Arius, others towards Colluthus, others towards Carpones, and others towards Sarmatas.

**69,2,6b** So as each expounded in his own church, one saying one thing and another another, from their partiality and the praise they gave, some named themselves Colluthians and others Arians.

**69,2,7** For Colluthus too taught some perverted things, but his heresy did not last, but was at once scattered; would that the thunderstruck faith of Arius had been so too – or rather his unbelief, or rather still, his false belief.

**69,3,1a** For the old man, lifted up with conceit, departed from the set standard.

**69,3,1b** He was very tall in stature, downcast in appearance, got up like a crafty serpent, able to steal away every guileless heart through that cunning outward show of his.

**69,3,1c** For this man, always wearing a short cloak and a sleeveless tunic, was sweet in his address, always persuading and flattering souls.

**69,3,2a** So straightaway – for what else? – did he not draw away from the church at one stroke virgins to the number of seven hundred?

**69,3,2b** And the story has it that he also drew away seven presbyters and twelve deacons.

**69,3,2c** And his poison straightaway reached even as far as bishops.

**69,3,2d** For he persuaded Secundus of the Pentapolis and others to be carried off together with him.

**69,3,3** These things were going on in the church while the blessed bishop Alexander knew nothing of them, until Melitius, the one of Egypt, who was reputed to come from the Thebaid and was himself an archbishop, whom I have already mentioned – for the affairs of Melitius had not yet run on to hostility and absurdity – Melitius,

**69,3,4a** then, carried along by zeal – for he differed in nothing in the faith, but only in a show of self-chosen righteousness, which he too wrought as something terrible in the world, as we have already said about him as well.

**69,3,4b** So Melitius, the archbishop in Egypt, brought it to the ears of the archbishop Alexander – he was reckoned to be under Alexander’s hand; and this Melitius was a contemporary of Peter, the late bishop and martyr, as I said.

**69,3,5** So when he had made known everything concerning Arius – how he had stepped outside the truth, and how he had defiled and destroyed many, corrupting from the right faith those who had been persuaded by him – then the bishop summoned Arius in person and questioned him about what had been reported, whether these things were so.

**69,3,6** But he neither hesitated nor shrank back, but from the very beginning, with a brazen brow, spewed out all his false doctrine, as his letters show, and the examination held concerning him at that time.

**69,3,7a** So Alexander calls together the presbyterate, and certain other bishops who were present, and holds an examination and inquiry of him.

**69,3,7b** And when he was not persuaded by the truth, he drives him out of the church and has him publicly proclaimed an outcast in the city.

**69,3,7c** And with him were drawn away the virgins already mentioned, and the clergy already mentioned, and a great crowd of others.

**69,4,1a** And while Arius was spending a long time in the city, Melitius, the confessor and martyr, presently dies.

**69,4,1b** So this same Arius, making schisms and stealing each one away, destroyed many.

**69,4,1c** And later, when he had been detected and brought to refutation in the city and had been publicly proclaimed an outcast, he runs away from the city of the Alexandrians and sets out on the road to Palestine.

**69,4,2a** When he came there, he approached each of the bishops with fawning and flattery, so as to make many his fellow workers.

**69,4,2b** And some receive him, while others thrust him away.

**69,4,3** And afterwards it comes to the ears of Bishop Alexander, and he writes encyclical letters, which are still preserved among lovers of learning, some seventy in number, to each of the bishops: to Eusebius in Caesarea first, for he was then living, and to Macarius of Jerusalem, to Asclepius at Gaza, to Longinus at Ascalon, to Macrinus at Jamnia, and to others; and also in Phoenicia to one Zeno, an aged man, at Tyre, and to others, and in Coele-Syria as well.

**69,4,4** So when the letters had been sent, finding fault with those who had received him, each wrote back to the blessed Alexander in his own defence.

**69,4,5a** And some wrote in pretence, others in truth: some saying that they were not receiving him, others that they had taken him in without knowing, and still others pleading in their defence that by receiving him they had sought to win him over.

**69,4,5b** And the story concerning these matters is a long one.

**69,5,1** And afterwards, when Arius learned that letters had been carried to the bishops everywhere, and that from then on he was being driven away from every side, and that no one any longer received him except his fellow workers.

**69,5,2** For Eusebius, the aged old man of Nicomedia, was wholly his, having lived together with Lucian in Nicomedia; and Leontius the eunuch at Antioch as well, not yet entrusted with the bishopric, and some others besides.

**69,5,3a** So since all these were of the same faction of poison, Eusebius receives him for a considerable time; and it was from there that this same Arius carried on his business at that time, having written to Eusebius in Nicomedia, before he had yet reached him in Nicomedia, letters filled with every kind of nonsense and containing all his heterodox faith, setting down in them nothing more than the very things he also thought; and since one of these has come into our hands, I have thought it necessary to set it out here, so that readers may see that we have not said, nor do we say, anything in slander against anyone.

**69,5,3b** And it is as follows.

**69,5,3c** Letter of Arius.

**69,6,1** “To my lord, most longed-for, a faithful man of God, the orthodox Eusebius, Arius, who is wrongfully persecuted by Pope Alexander on account of the truth that conquers all things, which you also defend, sends greeting in the Lord.

**69,6,2** As my father Ammonius was coming to Nicomedia, it seemed to me reasonable and fitting to address you through him, and at the same time to put your inborn love and disposition, which you bear towards the brothers on account of God and of his Christ, in mind of this: that the bishop greatly ravages and persecutes us and sets every evil in motion against us,

**69,6,3** so as to drive us out of the city as godless men, since we do not agree with him when he says publicly: ‘Always God, always Son; at once Father, at once Son; the Son coexists with God unbegottenly; ever-begotten, unbegotten-begotten; neither in thought nor by any single instant does God precede the Son; always God, always Son; the Son is from God himself.’

**69,6,4** And since Eusebius your brother in Caesarea, and Theodosius, and Paulinus, and Athanasius, and Gregory, and Aetius, and all those in the east say that God pre-exists the Son without beginning, they have been made anathema – except Philogonius and Hellanicus and Macarius, heretical and uninstructed men, who say of the Son, some that he is an eructation, others that he is an unbegotten projection.

**69,6,5** And we cannot even listen to these impieties, even if the heretics threaten us with ten thousand deaths.

**69,6,6a** But what do we say and think, and what have we taught and do we teach?

**69,6,6b** That the Son is not unbegotten, nor a part of the unbegotten in any way, nor yet from any substratum, but that by will and counsel he came into existence before times and before ages, full God, only-begotten, unalterable, and that before he was begotten, or created, or defined, or founded, he was not.

**69,6,6c** For he was not unbegotten.

**69,6,7a** And we are persecuted for having said, ‘The Son has a beginning, whereas God is without beginning.’

**69,6,7b** For this we are persecuted, and because we said, ‘He is from things that are not.’

**69,6,7c** And we said this inasmuch as he is neither a part of God nor from any substratum.

**69,6,7d** For this we are persecuted; the rest you know.

**69,6,7e** I pray that you fare well in the Lord, remembering our afflictions, fellow Lucianist, truly Eusebius.”

**69,7,1a** But we have also appended another letter, written from Nicomedia to the most holy Pope Alexander, ostensibly by way of defence, and, worse again, filled without omission with the blasphemous words of his venom, and sent by him to Alexandria.

**69,7,1b** And it is as follows.

**69,7,2** “To our blessed Pope and bishop Alexander, the presbyters and the deacons send greeting in the Lord.

**69,7,3a** Our faith from our forefathers, which we have also learned from you, blessed Pope, is this.

**69,7,3b** We know one God, alone unbegotten, alone everlasting, alone without beginning, alone true, alone having immortality, alone wise, alone good, alone sovereign, alone judge, governor of all, steward, unchangeable and unalterable, just and good, God of the Law and the Prophets and the New Covenant; this God begot an only-begotten Son before eternal times,

**69,7,4** through whom he made both the ages and all else; and he begot him not in seeming but in reality, and gave him existence by his own will, unchangeable and unalterable,

**69,7,5** a perfect creature of God, but not as one of the creatures; an offspring, but not as one of the things begotten;

**69,7,6** nor, as Valentinus taught, is the offspring of the Father a projection; nor, as the Manichaean introduced, is the offspring a consubstantial part of the Father; nor, as Sabellius, who divides the monad, said, a Son-Father; nor, as Hieracas, a lamp from a lamp, or as a torch divided into two.

**69,7,7** Nor is he one who existed before and was later begotten or created anew into a Son – as you yourself too, blessed Pope, have very often forbidden those who introduced these things, in the midst of the church and in council – but, as we say, he was created by the will of God before times and before ages, and received life and being from the Father, and the glories, the Father giving them existence together with him; for the Father, in giving him the inheritance of all things, did not deprive himself of what he holds unbegottenly within himself; for he is the fount of all things.

**69,8,1a** So there are three hypostases, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

**69,8,1b** And God, being the cause of all things, is without beginning and most alone; but the Son, begotten timelessly by the Father and created and founded before the ages, was not before he was begotten, but, begotten timelessly before all things, he alone was brought into existence by the Father alone.

**69,8,2a** For he is not everlasting, or co-everlasting, or co-unbegotten with the Father; nor does he have his being together with the Father, as some speak of things relative, introducing two unbegotten principles; but as monad and principle of all things, so God is before all things.

**69,8,2b** Therefore he is before Christ too, as we learned from you, who preached it in the midst of the church.

**69,8,3a** Inasmuch, then, as he has from God his being and his life and his glories, God having granted him all things, in this respect God is his beginning.

**69,8,3b** For he rules over him as his God, and has his being before him, because the Son is from him.

**69,8,4a** And if ‘from the womb’ and ‘I went forth from the Father, and I am here’ are understood by some as a part of the consubstantial and as a projection, the Father will be compound and divisible and changeable, and a body, according to them, and, so far as it rests with them, the incorporeal God would suffer what follows upon a body.

**69,8,4b** I pray that you fare well in the Lord, blessed Pope.

**69,8,5** Arius, Aeithales, Achillas, Carpones, Sarmatas, Arius, presbyters; deacons, Euzoius, Lucius, Julius, Menas, Helladius, Gaius; bishops, Secundus of the Pentapolis, Theonas the Libyan, Pistus” – whom the Arians appointed for Alexandria.

**69,9,1a** So when matters were stirred up in this way, Alexander writes to the emperor Constantine.

**69,9,1b** And the late emperor called together Arius and certain bishops and examined them.

**69,9,2a** But he, having his fellow initiates, at first denied it to the emperor’s face, while inwardly he was working the plot against the church.

**69,9,2b** So when the blessed Constantine had called him in, inspired as he also was in part by the Holy Spirit, he addressed a word to him, saying, “I have trusted in God: if you deceitfully keep something hidden and deny it, the Master of all will very soon convict you, especially he by whom you have sworn.”

**69,9,2c** Hence he was indeed detected holding the same views, and was convicted to the emperor’s face.

**69,9,3a** But again he denied it in the same way, and many champions of his made entreaty on his behalf through Eusebius of Nicomedia.

**69,9,3b** And at the same time the emperor, roused by zeal, also wrote a great encyclical letter to the whole Roman world against Arius and his faith, full of all wisdom and of true words;

**69,9,4** and this letter too is preserved to this day among lovers of learning, having this beginning: “Constantine, the most great Augustus, to Arius and the Arians: An evil interpreter is in very truth an image and statue of the devil.”

**69,9,5** Then, after other things, and after setting out against him a long refutation from the divine oracles, he also set down a verse from the poems of Homer, addressing it to him by way of reproach,

**69,9,6a** which I too have thought it necessary to set down here; and it is: “Come now, ‘Ares Arius’, there is need of shields; do not, we beseech you, do this; but let at least the company of Aphrodite restrain you.”

**69,9,6b** So when Arius wished to be received into communion at Constantinople as well – Eusebius compelling it, wielding great power with the emperor and harassing the bishop at Constantinople at that time, while that bishop did not wish to assemble with him nor to come into communion with him, and was hard pressed and groaning – Eusebius said, “If you do not wish it of your own choice, tomorrow, as the Lord’s day dawns, he will go in with me; and what can you do?”

**69,10,2** But the most reverent and God-fearing bishop Alexander, the bishop of that same most excellent city (for he too bore the same name as the one in Alexandria), from the moment he heard it, spent the whole day and the night in prayer, groaning and downcast, and imploring God either to receive his soul, lest he be defiled by sharing communion with Arius, or to perform some marvel; which indeed happened to this man.

**69,10,3a** For Arius, being pressed during the night to go out to relieve himself, goes through as far as the privy, and sitting within, in the secluded place, he was found burst asunder and with the breath gone out of him.

**69,10,3b** So he was overtaken in the foul-smelling place, meeting his end, just as he had also spewed out an unclean false belief.

**69,11,1** So when these things had been accomplished, the emperor, contributing his own care to the church, because many had by now often quarrelled with each other and schisms were numerous, convened an ecumenical synod of three hundred and eighteen bishops, whose names are preserved to this day; and they anathematize the faith of Arius in the city of the Nicaeans, and confess the orthodox and unwavering faith of the fathers, handed down from the apostles and prophets.

**69,11,2a** And when the bishops had subscribed to it and had anathematized the Ariomanite heresy, so it was done.

**69,11,2b** And at the same time, at the same synod, they also laid down certain ecclesiastical canons; and together with these they also determined concerning the Passover that there should be one union and concord on the holy and all-excellent day of God, since it was kept differently among some.

**69,11,2c** For some anticipated it, others kept it in the middle, and others celebrated it afterwards.

**69,11,3a** And, in short, there was much talk at that time.

**69,11,3b** And God awarded the setting right of these matters through the late Constantine, for the sake of peace.

**69,11,4a** So when Arius had been anathematized and these things had been done in this way, in the same year Alexander departs this life, and Achillas succeeds him.

**69,11,4b** And there was also Theonas, appointed by the Melitians.

**69,11,4c** Then the late Athanasius succeeds Bishop Achillas, who had served three months; Athanasius was at that time Alexander’s deacon and had been sent by him to the court, and it was to him that Alexander, when about to die, gave charge that the episcopate be handed over.

**69,11,5** And it is the custom in Alexandria that, when a bishop dies, the appointment of those installed is not put off, but takes place at once for the sake of peace, so that there be no friction among the people, some wanting this man and others that.

**69,11,6a** And they appointed Achillas out of necessity, since Athanasius was not present.

**69,11,6b** But the throne and the priesthood were being made ready for him who had been called by God and designated by the late Alexander.

**69,11,7** So since, when Athanasius had come and been installed – a man exceedingly zealous for the faith and suffering greatly for the church – assemblies were already being held everywhere and the people were being drawn away by those called Melitians, for the reason I have explained before in the account of Melitius, and since he wished to bring about the reunion of the church, he reproached and threatened and admonished, and no one would bear it.

**69,11,8** Hence everything set in motion against him was done and contrived as a result of the surpassing zeal from God that was in him, so that he even endured exiles, and the most unjust exclusion from communion under the later dominance of the Arians.

**69,11,9a** But concerning the late Athanasius let this be enough for now.

**69,11,9b** For the matters concerning him were told in the fullest detail above, in the account of Melitius.

**69,12,1a** This Arius, then, was inspired by diabolical working, and, carried along shamelessly with an unbridled tongue, he lifted up his tongue against his own Master, wishing, forsooth, from the outset to interpret the passage in the Proverbs of Solomon: “As the beginning of his ways the Lord created me; before the age he established me.

**69,12,1b** In the beginning, before the making of the earth and before the making of the abysses, before the fountains of the waters went forth, before the mountains were firmly fixed, and before all the hills, he begets me.”

**69,12,2a** From this the introduction of his error came about.

**69,12,2b** And he was not ashamed, nor were his disciples, to call him a creature who created all things – the Word, timelessly and without beginning begotten of the Father.

**69,12,3** And thereafter, starting from this one passage and driving his own perverse mind into many evil paths, he and his successors after him undertook to utter countless blasphemies, and more besides, against the Son of God and against the Holy Spirit.

**69,12,4a** And they broke up, so to speak, the close array and the concord of the holy and orthodox faith and church, not through their own power or wisdom.

**69,12,4b** For few are those who inclined to them through being deceived, but many those who slip in by hypocrisy.

**69,12,4c** And many, too, who do not hold these views, are in communion with them under force.

**69,12,4d** And none of these was the agent of it, but first the testing of the faithful, and then the championship of emperors.

**69,12,5** The beginning was the emperor Constantius, in all other respects gentle and good, being the son of Constantine the great and perfect, the God-fearing, who truly kept the right faith – and Constantius himself too was God-fearing and good in many ways;

**69,12,6** but in this alone, in not having walked according to his father’s faith, he erred, not through any cause of his own, but because of those who will have to give account at the day of judgement, those called bishops in appearance, who have corrupted the true faith of God;

**69,12,7** who must render account for the faith and for the persecutions of the church, and for so many evils and murders that have taken place in the churches on their account, and for the peoples, so many myriads, who to this day endure affliction in the open air, and for the late Constantius himself, who was led astray by them and was ignorant of the faith of orthodoxy, and yielded to them as priests in his ignorance, not knowing the error of blindness and false belief in them, which came about through the devil’s contrivance.

**69,13,1a** In the second place, their serpentine workshop grew strong again through Eusebius, who slipped in and corrupted, in turn, the hearing of Valens, the God-fearing, most reverent and God-loving emperor.

**69,13,1b** For since he received the washing from him, through such a circumstance these men were able to stand.

**69,13,2** For otherwise they would long ago have been driven out, refuted from the ancients even by women and children – I do not speak of the more perfect, who know the whole exactness of godliness and of the right faith, but even by those who know something in part, however little, of the truth – as blasphemers of the Master, and second Lord-slayers, as it were, and rejecters of the divine perfection of our Lord Jesus –

**69,13,3** through the patronage of the emperor, that is, their protection, for attempting all the evils that have been done and are still done through them in Alexandria and in Nicomedia, in Mesopotamia, in Palestine, by the patronage of their present emperor.

**69,14,1** So from this passage written in the Proverbialist, “The Lord created me as a beginning of his ways towards his works”, everything is then devised by them that can be consonant with the saying and balances with it and can agree with it, though neither the saying itself nor the other words about the Godhead of the Son of God assert anything of the kind.

**69,14,2a** But then whatever is like these: what is written in the Apostle, “to receive the high priest of your confession, who was faithful to him who made him”.

**69,14,2b** And what is written in the Gospel according to John: “This is he of whom I said to you, ‘He who comes after me has come to be before me.’”

**69,14,2c** And what is written in the Acts: “Let all the house of Israel know that God has made this Jesus whom you crucified both Lord and Christ.”

**69,14,2d** And other things like these.

**69,14,2e** For wherever it is a matter of watching, it is for the warding off of enemies.

**69,14,2f** For they are in very truth enemies and plotters.

**69,14,3a** For perhaps it is about them, and about those like them, that it is written, “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered.”

**69,14,3b** And they seem to be of the household as well.

**69,14,3c** And none is worse than enemies of one’s own household.

**69,14,3d** For “a man’s enemies are all the men of his own house”.

**69,14,3e** And this too is perhaps fulfilled in the case of these men.

**69,15,1a** For they leap up like rabid dogs to ward off enemies.

**69,15,1b** And they say, “How do you speak of the Son of God?”

**69,15,1c** For such are the tricks by which they bring their poison in among the simple.

**69,15,1d** And what is there beyond this, after saying “Son of God”?

**69,15,1e** O you who are wise in yourselves, and discerning in your own sight, and who seem to be knowledgeable!

**69,15,1f** What more could one add to the name of Jesus, unless one should say that he is a true-born Son, being from the Father, and unaltered?

**69,15,1g** Then straightaway they leap up mockingly, saying, “How can he be from God?”

**69,15,2a** And when they are asked, “Do you mean that he is not a Son?”

**69,15,2b** They confess the word “Son” in name, but deny it in meaning and intent, wishing to call him wholly a bastard, and not true.

**69,15,2c** “For if,” they say, “he is from God, and God begot him from himself – from his own hypostasis by nature, so to speak, or from his own essence – then he swelled, or underwent a cutting, or was broadened in begetting, or was contracted, or underwent something of the bodily passions.”

**69,15,2d** And they make themselves a mockery in everything, measuring God by analogy with their own conditions, and wishing to picture God from themselves.

**69,15,4** For in God there is nothing of the kind; for God is spirit, and from himself he begot the Only-begotten ineffably and incomprehensibly and without defilement.

**69,15,5a** “How then,” says he, “if he is from his essence, does he not know the day, as he says, and the hour?

**69,15,5b** ‘But of that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels nor the Son, but the Father alone.’

**69,15,5c** And how did he come into flesh, if he is from the Father?

**69,15,5d** And how could that uncontainable nature put on flesh, if he was from the Father by nature?”

**69,16,1a** And they do not know how they gather these reasonings together to their own shame.

**69,16,1b** For if it was because he had been altered from the Father’s essence that he put on flesh, and suffered in it, and was crucified, let them show us which of the other spiritual creatures – and such there certainly are – put on flesh.

**69,16,1c** For one cannot but confess that the Son is above all things.

**69,16,1d** And though they may speak of him as a creature, they confess him to be above all his creatures.

**69,16,2a** But they also wish, as though doing him a favour, to pay him court in word, like men striking with one hand and anointing with the other.

**69,16,2b** For this is what they want: to bestow a favour on him, as it were, of their own free choice.

**69,16,2c** And they say, “A creature, we say, yet not as one of the creatures; and a thing made, and not as one of the things made; and an offspring, and not as one of the offspring” – so that in saying “not as one of the offspring” they may deprive him of the begetting by nature, and in saying “not as one of the creatures”, that they may declare him a true creature.

**69,16,3a** For whatever sort of creature a thing may be, it is a creature; and even if it should have a name ten thousand times higher, it is the same thing, put on a level with all the creatures.

**69,16,3b** For it is not because the sun is brighter than the others that it can fail to be a creature, just as the stone is.

**69,16,3c** Nor, because the moon excels the stars, does it on that account cease to be one of the creatures.

**69,16,4a** For see, “all things are your servants”.

**69,16,4b** For all things that are have been created by him and are servants.

**69,16,4c** The Only-begotten, however, is the truth, and his word is a true word, as he said: “If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.”

**69,16,4d** And if his word is truth and makes free those who are made free, how much more indeed is he himself free, being truth and making free those who obey him, though they were servants?

**69,16,4e** For all things are servants of him, and of his Father, and of his Holy Spirit.

**69,17,1a** Then again they say: How did he come to dwell in flesh, if he was from the Father’s essence?

**69,17,1b** Let them tell us, then, how it is that angels did not take flesh, though they are his servants?

**69,17,1c** How is it with the archangels?

**69,17,1d** How with the hosts?

**69,17,1e** How with all the other spiritual beings?

**69,17,2a** But such people also say that the Spirit is inferior, and a creature of a creature – that is, of the Word himself.

**69,17,2b** How then did the Spirit not take flesh, since by their own account it could have a changeable person more than the Son?

**69,17,2c** But since he was the Wisdom of the Father, he was pleased, through his own perfection, to take up our weakness, so that all salvation might come to the world through himself.

**69,17,3a** But turning good things into evil, they are ungrateful – ungrateful and unfeeling men, insolent towards their own Master, and blasphemers.

**69,17,3b** And as for the rest, whatever they say, they think of him in a diminished way.

**69,17,3c** And how did he hunger, if he was of the Father’s essence?

**69,17,3d** For of God it is written, “He shall not hunger, nor thirst, nor is there any searching out of his understanding.”

**69,17,3e** But this one both hungered and thirsted.

**69,17,3f** How did he grow weary from the journey and sit down? – and there is the saying that “God will not grow weary”.

**69,17,4a** And how, he says, did he say, “He who sent me, my Father, is greater than I”?

**69,17,4b** For the one who sends is one, and the one who is sent is another.

**69,17,4c** And plainly the Father is not the Son, nor is the Son the Father.

**69,17,4d** For we do not speak according to Sabellius, who says that he is a Son-Father.

**69,17,5a** For had he not said, “It is another who sent me”, and, “I go away to my God and your God” – “to my Father and your Father” he said, and the disciples were not begotten by nature from the essence of God.

**69,17,5b** And he said to them, “your Father”.

**69,17,6a** But great is the derangement of those who say such things.

**69,17,6b** For if he is called so by name only, and is not so in nature, he differs in nothing from all the rest of the creatures, though he may stand pre-eminent in rank.

**69,17,6c** For it is not because the emperor is above the prefects and generals that he is on that account not of like passions with the others and a fellow servant of the same creation, being a mortal man, just as those who are ruled by him are.

**69,17,7** And it is not because the sun is above the other stars, and the moon in its turn, that they are on that account not subordinate elements, yielding to the ordinance of the one Craftsman and Creator, Father and Son and Holy Spirit.

**69,17,8** And it is not because angels stand above the visible things and, in the order of the others, are greater than all – created, as they were, invisible, and reaping the first privilege of the service of God in unceasing hymns, and created immortal by him by grace and not by nature, and immortal as having been deemed worthy to become so by nature from the Immortal himself, who is in himself life and immortality – that they are on that account not held in servitude under fear and trembling, and under accountability, and examination, and command, and injunction of the holy Godhead.

**69,18,1a** For hence comes the exactness of the truth that is sought: to speak of the Son, and to speak of and hold not merely some name, but a Son, a Son by nature.

**69,18,1b** For among us too many are called sons who are not our sons by nature.

**69,18,1c** But the true sons are called true-born, those begotten by us by nature.

**69,18,2a** And so, if he were only called Son, as all were called sons of God, then he differs in nothing from the others.

**69,18,2b** And how is he worshipped as God?

**69,18,2c** Then all the others too, upon whom the name of adoption has been called, would have to be worshipped as he is, since they are addressed as sons of God.

**69,18,3** But the truth does not stand so; it ever knows a single only-begotten Son of God, to whom all things render service and worship, “and every knee will bow, of beings in heaven and on earth and beneath the earth, and every tongue will openly acknowledge that Jesus Christ is Lord, unto the glory of God the Father.”

**69,18,4a** Nor, again, is the Holy Spirit made equal to the rest of the spirits, since God’s Spirit is one, a Spirit going forth from the Father and taking from the Son.

**69,18,4b** But these men want it to be a creature of a creature.

**69,18,4c** For they say that “all things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being”.

**69,18,5a** “Therefore,” they say, “the Spirit too is among the things made, since all things came into being through him.”

**69,18,5b** And they do not know, these men who have vainly lost their own souls, that the creatures are one thing and the creating ones another – Father and Son and Holy Spirit, one God, a Trinity in truth and a Monad in unity.

**69,18,6a** For this is why there is one God: because there are not two Fathers, nor two Sons, nor two Holy Spirits; and because the Son is no stranger to the Father but has been begotten from him, and the Holy Spirit is no stranger either; but the Son is only-begotten, begotten without beginning, while the Holy Spirit – as is known to the Father himself and to the Only-begotten – is not begotten, not created, not foreign to Father and Son, but proceeding from the Father and receiving from the Son.

**69,18,6b** For “my Spirit”, he says, “stands in your midst”.

**69,18,6c** And he anointed Christ in the Holy Spirit.

**69,18,6d** If the Only-begotten himself is anointed in the Spirit, who will bring a charge against the Holy Trinity?

**69,19,1a** Then again the frenzied Arius says: How did the Lord say, “Why do you call me good?

**69,19,1b** One is good, God.”

**69,19,1c** As though he were denying his goodness.

**69,19,1d** And who else is so good as the Only-begotten?

**69,19,1e** He who gave himself as a ransom for our souls.

**69,19,2** And they do not know the power of God and his goodness, nor the dispensation of God’s wisdom, being natural and fleshly men, judged by the Holy Spirit, being empty of him, not having the gift of the Holy Spirit, which makes every man wise.

**69,19,3a** And again, he says, the sons of Zebedee ask him, through their mother, that in his kingdom one may be seated on his right hand and one on his left.

**69,19,3b** And he said to them, “You do not know what you are asking.

**69,19,3c** Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink?

**69,19,3d** And when they said, ‘Yes’, he said to them, ‘My cup you shall drink; but to sit on my right and on my left is not for me to give, but it is theirs for whom it has been made ready by the Father.’”

**69,19,4a** Then again the apostle declares, “God raised him from the dead”, as if he had need of the one who raised him.

**69,19,4b** And, he says, “an angel of the Lord appeared strengthening him, because he was in agony, and sweated, and his sweat became for him like clots of blood”, in the Gospel according to Luke, when he went away and prayed as he was about to be betrayed.

**69,19,5a** And again on the cross, he says, he was saying, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani”, which is, “My God, my God, to what end have you forsaken me?”

**69,19,5b** And do you see, he says, how he stands in need of help?

**69,19,6a** But as to his saying, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”, and that “we two are one, so that they too may be one”.

**69,19,6b** So then he speaks of being one not by nature at all, but by concord.

**69,19,7a** And not only this, but they also deny that he took a human soul, preparing this very point in advance.

**69,19,7b** For they confess that he had true flesh from Mary, and everything that is in man, except a soul; so that when you hear of hunger or thirst, or weariness, or journeying, or sweat, or sleep, or deep indignation, and say that it was because of his becoming man that he was subject to these, they will tell you afterwards that flesh by itself does not do these things unless it has the soul.

**69,19,8a** And in fact it is indeed so.

**69,19,8b** “What else is it, then,” he says, “but that his Godhead was in need?” – so that, when they say that his Godhead was in need, they may declare him foreign and alien to the essence and true nature of the Father.

**69,19,9a** And I think that, for one who possesses understanding, when one or two testimonies, or five, of those wrongly devised by them have been refuted and overturned, and the whole truth has been proclaimed and clearly confirmed in the faith of orthodoxy, they will stand refuted before those already mentioned, who possess a godly mind, even if after these solutions they bring forward ten thousand other passages of their devising.

**69,19,9b** For from the few the greater number will be resolved, since they carry the same force.

**69,20,1** And I shall begin first by speaking of the place from which they undertook wickedly to plant the root of their bitterness: the saying spoken by Solomon, “The Lord created me as a beginning of his ways towards his works”.

**69,20,2a** And nowhere at all has Scripture confirmed it, nor has any of the apostles made mention of this passage so as to bring it to bear on the name of Christ.

**69,20,2b** So then it is not of the Son of God at all that he speaks, though he does say, “I, Wisdom, have made counsel and knowledge my dwelling, and I have called upon understanding”.

**69,20,3a** For how many wisdoms of God are there, so called in a loose sense?

**69,20,3b** But the Only-begotten is one, so called not in a loose sense but in truth.

**69,20,3c** For all things are wisdom of God.

**69,20,3d** And whatever is from God is wisdom.

**69,20,4a** But there is another, a peculiar one, which is above all things, that is, the Only-begotten, who is wisdom not in a loose sense but in truth, who is ever with the Father, who is the power of God and wisdom, according to what is written, “But for us Christ is God’s power and God’s wisdom”.

**69,20,4b** And there is “the wisdom of the poor man, despised.

**69,20,4c** And since the world, in the wisdom of God, did not know God, it pleased him to save those who believe through the foolishness of the gospel.

**69,20,4d** And God turned the wisdom of this world into folly; and God bestowed on Solomon a heart like the outpouring of the sea, and he became wise above the sons of Anak.

**69,20,4e** And God gave wisdom to Bezalel, and God filled Uri with wisdom.”

**69,20,5a** And there is much to say about wisdom.

**69,20,5b** And “what is the place of understanding, and where was wisdom found?”

**69,20,5c** So even if this celebrated Wisdom says, “I, Wisdom, have made counsel and knowledge my dwelling; I have called upon understanding.

**69,20,5d** Through me kings reign, and through me great men are magnified, and rulers write righteousness, and princes hold sway over the earth.

**69,20,6a** I love those who love me, and those who seek me shall find me.

**69,20,6b** Riches and glory are mine, and possession of many things, and righteousness; in the path of righteousness I walk, and amid the paths of justice I go about, so that I may share out substance to those who love me and fill their treasuries with good things.

**69,20,7a** If I tell you the things that happen day by day, I shall be mindful to number the things from of old.

**69,20,7b** The Lord created me as a beginning of his ways towards his works; he founded me before the age, in the beginning, before the making of the earth and before the making of the abysses, before the fountains of the waters went forth, and before the mountains were firmly fixed, and before all the hills, he begets me”, and what follows.

**69,20,8a** It is clear that, when some wish to speak against the passage, those on the opposing side make use of a counter-objection, because of the name of Wisdom and the sequence of the text which says, “The Lord created me”.

**69,20,8b** And because of its saying, “I, Wisdom, have made counsel my dwelling”.

**69,20,8c** Namely, that, see, Wisdom, having named herself at the outset and proceeding in order, refers to herself when she says, “The Lord created me”.

**69,20,9a** For see, above she says, “I, Wisdom”.

**69,20,9b** And further down she says, “If I declare to you the things that happen day by day, I shall be mindful to number the things from of old”.

**69,20,9c** And what is it that she says: “The Lord created me as a beginning of his ways”?

**69,21,1a** Now we have said that there are a good many wisdoms, so called in a loose sense, given by God from time to time, because God accomplishes all things in wisdom.

**69,21,1b** But there is one Wisdom of the Father that truly is, the subsistent God the Word.

**69,21,1c** For the text itself in no way obliges me to say that it concerns the Son of God; for it did not declare it, and no apostle made mention of it, nor indeed did the gospel.

**69,21,2a** But if, after all, this were understood as concerning the Son of God, the saying is not the same as it sounds, nor is it set down for straightforward judgement.

**69,21,2b** For the whole book is proverbs.

**69,21,2c** And everything spoken in proverb is not the same in its meaning, but it narrates in one form of words and is allegorized in another meaning.

**69,21,3** If, then, it says this, and some dare to apply this to the Son of God – far be it! – this saying is not applied to his Godhead.

**69,21,4a** But if it can be fulfilled in his coming in the flesh.

**69,21,4b** For since Wisdom herself built herself the house; and if indeed it were said piously from the person of his becoming man, as his coming in the flesh speaks concerning his Godhead, “The Lord created me” – that is, built me in the womb of Mary – “as a beginning of his ways towards his works”.

**69,21,5a** For the body taken from Mary was the beginning of the ways of Christ’s coming down into the world, in his work of righteousness and salvation.

**69,21,5b** But surely he whose heart is damaged, and who has been struck with this dreadful blow, holding in his mind his enmity concerning the Son of God, would leap forward:

**69,21,6a** “Because,” he says, “she said, ‘If I tell you the things that happen day by day, I shall be mindful [also] to number the things from of old.’”

**69,21,6b** And you see that it says “from of old”; but the coming of God in the flesh took place after sixty-two generations, according to Matthew; how then can the things from the beginning of the age be said of this?

**69,22,1** And those who have strayed from the whole way of the truth do not know that the divine Scripture, in all that it wishes to teach, always begins its narration not by setting out at once upon what is most ancient and, so to speak, upon the chief point, but begins from the things nearest at hand, so that it may indicate last what was before.

**69,22,2a** For this is why it also said, “If I tell you the things that happen day by day”, and from these I call to mind “also the things from of old”.

**69,22,2b** So too God showed Moses first the burning fire, and at the outset the vision took place in the fire of a bush.

**69,22,2c** An angel spoke to him at once, and afterwards the Lord from the bush.

**69,22,3a** And straightway, in speaking to him, he does not seek the things that are seen, but asks about the things from the beginning.

**69,22,3b** “Come,” he says, “let me send you to the children of Israel, and you shall say to them, ‘The God of our fathers has sent me, Abraham’s God and Isaac’s God and Jacob’s God’”, naming Abraham and those with him, five or six generations before Moses.

**69,22,3c** And since he said “God of the fathers”, he declared what was ancient.

**69,22,4a** But Moses, graced by God with understanding, asked not about these things but about what was higher still: “If I go away to them, and they put it to me, ‘What is his name?’

**69,22,4b** what shall I say to them?”

**69,22,5a** And he then reveals, “I am he who is.”

**69,22,5b** And at first he began from the things nearest at hand, but at the last he made known what is highest.

**69,22,5c** But Luke too begins from the things below and nearest at hand: “Jesus himself, when he began, was about thirty years old, being the son, as was supposed, of Joseph, of Heli, of Matthan, of Nathan, of David, of Judah, of Jacob, of Abraham, of Nahor, of Noah, of Lamech, of Enoch, of Seth, of Adam, of God.”

**69,22,5d** And you see how he showed first the coming in the flesh, and then what is last.

**69,22,6** That is why Matthew too, in the genealogy according to the flesh, wishing to bring Christ’s coming down to the understanding of men, did not say at once, “The origin of Jesus Christ, son of Abraham”, but first “son of David”, and then “son of Abraham”, so that, pointing out what had lately been done and what was most nearly joined together, and what was higher still, he might indicate what is still above all creation and cannot be taken away.

**69,23,1** That is why the blessed John, when he came, found people occupied with Christ’s coming here below; the Ebionites had gone astray because of Christ’s genealogy according to the flesh, traced down from Abraham and carried back by Luke as far as Adam; and he found the Cerinthians and Merinthians claiming that he was simply a man, conceived by intercourse, and the Nazoraeans, and many other sects;

**69,23,2a** and so, coming last, for he is the fourth to write the gospel, he begins, so to speak, to call back those who had gone astray and were occupied with Christ’s coming here below, and to say to them, like one who comes behind and sees some turned aside onto rough roads, having left the straight and true one: “Where are you being carried?

**69,23,2b** Where are you walking?

**69,23,2c** You who walk the rough road that causes stumbling and leads to a chasm, turn back.

**69,23,3a** It is not so: God the Word, begotten from the Father on high, is not from Mary only; he is not from the times of Joseph her betrothed, nor from the times of Salathiel and Zerubbabel and David and Abraham and Jacob and Noah and Adam; but in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

**69,23,3b** This “was” and “was” and “was” does not admit that he ever was not.

**69,23,4a** And you see how he at once indicates first the things nearest at hand.

**69,23,4b** How Matthew showed the way through the genealogy, and even he did not set it out in exact detail, though he did carry the genealogy down from above.

**69,23,4c** How Mark wrote of the things done in the world and of “a voice crying in the wilderness,” concerning the Lord foretold by the prophets and the law.

**69,23,4d** How Luke, coming later, led upward from the things below to the things above.

**69,23,4e** John, the fourth, made known last the crown and the pure essence of the order on high and of the Godhead that always is,

**69,23,5a** as Solomon too says in a proverb, “the beginning of the ways,” supposing that some should wish to speak devoutly of the incarnate dispensation, as though the text said of Christ’s Godhead that the Godhead itself built the house, that the Godhead itself wrought the flesh and the becoming man, a beginning of his ways toward his works of the salvation and goodness of mankind.

**69,23,5b** Then immediately afterward, as the matter advances, it says, “He established me in the beginning.”

**69,23,6a** Was the Son of God, then, created according to his Godhead and afterward established?

**69,23,6b** Let the engineers tell us, those surveyors of the things above, by what craft wisdom was created, by what tool it was established.

**69,23,6c** But if one must reason at all, let one flee from so great a depth of blasphemy and not lay a hand on the Godhead of the only-begotten, which always exists with the Father and is begotten from him.

**69,23,7a** For the Word was ever with the Father, ever Wisdom, ever Lord, God from God.

**69,23,7b** Ever true Light and not counterfeit, ever having his being from him, being Truth and existing as Life.

**69,24,1a** And why should I say a great deal about this?

**69,24,1b** Then it says, “He established me in the beginning.”

**69,24,2a** So it is possible to see a devout sense: that here it indicates the human soul.

**69,24,2b** For “The Lord created me” is spoken by the incarnate becoming man, if indeed it is to be understood in this way.

**69,24,2c** And “he established” means that he was established in the soul.

**69,24,2d** And “before all the hills he begets me” is said to show the begetting from above.

**69,24,2e** And we have said this not as laying it down as altogether so, but rather as having devoutly understood it of the coming in the flesh.

**69,24,3a** Even if one ought to speak in this way, still no one could compel us to say that this saying is by all means about Christ.

**69,24,3b** But if it is to be said of Christ, it has its own force too, spoken not by way of divination but according to the devoutness of reasoning, so as not to reckon anything of deficiency against God by supposing that he has a Godhead lower than the essence of the Father.

**69,24,4a** For indeed some of our fathers, orthodox men, assigned this to the coming in the flesh, having so understood it, if indeed one should speak thus, the passage about “The Lord created me, and established me.”

**69,24,4b** And this is the devout reasoning, as great fathers have explained it.

**69,24,5a** And if any of the orthodox should not wish to accept it, he will not be compelled.

**69,24,5b** And with regard to those who are strangers and aliens to the faith, the harm comes to nothing.

**69,24,5c** For this will not bring down on us anything of deficiency, since the Godhead is free and is ever with the Father.

**69,24,6a** And whatever Christ suffered, he suffered; but he was not changed in his nature, and his Godhead remained in its own impassibility.

**69,24,6b** Therefore, having willed to suffer by his own good pleasure for the human race, since the Godhead could not suffer, being in itself impassible, he, being Wisdom, took our passible body, so that in it he might consent to suffer and take upon himself our sufferings, the Godhead being present together in the flesh.

**69,24,6c** For indeed the Godhead does not suffer.

**69,24,7a** For how will he who says, “I am the life,” be able to die?

**69,24,7b** No, God remains impassible.

**69,24,7c** But he suffers together with the flesh, so that the suffering may be reckoned to the Godhead, the Godhead suffering, to the end that our salvation may be in God.

**69,24,7d** But the suffering is in the flesh, so that we may not have a passible God but an impassible one, who reckons the suffering to himself by choice and not by necessity.

**69,25,1** Yet these people too, without having either handled or understood the Hebrew words, or how their meaning stands, have rashly and headlong sprung up as dreadful enemies, seeking a pretext by which to maim the faith, or rather themselves, for it is not the truth they maim; and since they came upon “The Lord created me”, they recklessly fall to dreaming, like men seeing visions, bringing into life things of no use and throwing the world into confusion.

**69,25,2a** But the Hebrew does not read so; hence Aquila says, “The Lord acquired me.”

**69,25,2b** And those who beget children always say, “I have acquired a son.”

**69,25,2c** Yet not even Aquila rendered the meaning.

**69,25,2d** For indeed “I have acquired a son” is said as of something recent.

**69,25,2e** But in God there is nothing recent.

**69,25,3a** And should anyone acknowledge that the Son has been begotten from the Father, then he is not created.

**69,25,3b** And he has been begotten timelessly and without beginning.

**69,25,4a** For there is no time between Son and Father, lest some time should come to exceed the Son.

**69,25,4b** For if all things are through him, then the times are too.

**69,25,5a** But if there exists a time that is before all things, how will this be?

**69,25,5b** Unless, then, another son is to be sought, through whom time came into being before the Son.

**69,25,5c** And there are many matters which the notions of men who busy themselves with curiosities and do nothing good lead into endless perplexity.

**69,25,6a** But the Hebrew has adonai, which is rendered “Lord”, and kanani, which can mean both “brought me forth as his young” and “acquired me”.

**69,25,6b** But the most exact rendering is “brought me forth as his young”.

**69,25,6c** And what young one is not born of the nature of the one who begot it?

**69,25,6d** And here, among bodily formed creatures, the young that are brought forth come about through the pairing of male and female, from man to beast and birds and the rest.

**69,25,7** Therefore the only-begotten, being in all things the Wisdom of the Father, and wishing to do all things for correction, so that no one might reckon to him what is not so and fall away from the truth, when he came to dwell among the race of men, and was born by nature of a woman, and lay in a virgin’s womb for the time of pregnancy, was not conceived of the seed of a man, so that pairing and intertwining might not take place in the birth in the flesh as well; but he took the flesh from a mother alone, and fulfilled in himself his own becoming man as complete, not deficient but true.

**69,25,8** And it is not that, because he was not from the seed of a man, he had anything lacking; for he had all things completely, having everything, flesh and sinews and veins and all the other things there are, and a soul truly and not in appearance, and a mind and all that belongs to the becoming man, without sin, as it is written, “tempted in all things as a man,

**69,25,9** without sin,” so that by being born here completely and not deficiently from a mother alone according to the flesh, he might show those who wish to see the truth and not to blind their own minds that above too he has been begotten completely from the Father, timelessly and without beginning, and below he has been born from a mother only, without stain and without defilement.

**69,26,1a** Let us also interpret the expression adonai kanani, which is “The Lord brought me forth as his young.”

**69,26,1b** For everything that begets will beget something like itself.

**69,26,1c** Man begets man, and God begets God; and man begets according to the flesh, but God according to the spirit.

**69,26,2a** And as the man who begets is, such too is the one begotten by him.

**69,26,2b** The man who has begotten his own son did so held within passions; and the impassible God begot the Son begotten by him impassibly, truly and not in appearance, from himself and not from outside himself, being impassible Spirit and begetting Spirit impassibly, being impassible God and having begotten true God impassibly.

**69,26,3** For if he himself created all things, and you confess, Arius, that God has created all things, he himself also begot the Son.

**69,26,4a** And should you say, “If he begot, then in begetting he suffered,” we in turn shall say to you, “If he suffered in begetting, he grew weary in creating.”

**69,26,4b** But all that he wills is at once; he has all things in himself in perfection; and neither will passion fall upon the Son in his creating, nor will the divine be thought to be held by passion because of the undefiled begetting of the Son.

**69,26,4c** For the Father is unchangeable, the Son unchangeable, the Holy Spirit unchangeable: one essence, one Godhead.

**69,26,5a** But you will surely say to me, “Did he beget willing it, or not willing it?”

**69,26,5b** And I am not like you, contentious man, so as to conceive any such thing of God.

**69,26,5c** For if he begot without willing it, he begot unwillingly.

**69,26,5d** And if he begot willing it, then the will was before the Son, and even a moment of time will intervene between him and the Son because of the will.

**69,26,6a** But in God there is no time for counsel, no willing for deliberation.

**69,26,6b** So he begot neither willing nor not willing, but in the nature that is above will.

**69,26,6c** For his is a nature of Godhead, neither needing will nor doing anything without will, but having all things at once from itself and lacking nothing of the things that are.

**69,27,1a** Yet again the same Arius hunts for words, ever roaming over everything and contriving wicked things for himself, not as the divine writing has it, but as one himself sick over questions and disputes about words; and to no useful end, but to the ruin of himself and of those led astray by him, he seizes upon the saying in which the Lord, blessing the disciples, spoke the words, “Father, give them to have life within themselves.

**69,27,1b** And this is eternal life, that they may know you, who alone are true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.”

**69,27,2** But I have already treated all these matters in the great discourse on the faith, in which, once again, constrained according to our modest ability and weakness by the urging exhortation of the brethren, we wrote on the faith, a discourse to which we gave the name Ancoratus.

**69,27,3** For indeed, as far as our poor mind was able by the help of God, gathering from all Scripture the true things of God’s teaching, we plainly set forth, like an anchor for those who wish it, the holy faith of the fathers, apostolic and prophetic, proclaimed from the beginning until now in the holy church of God, so that the understanding may be held fast and made secure, and not be tossed about by the devices of the devil nor harmed by the surge of the sects that has been stirred up in the world in so many gushing streams.

**69,27,4** For so too the Lord taught his own disciples, saying, “If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, [and if what you heard from the beginning abides in you,] you will remain in me, and I in you; I also am in the Father, and you are in me.”

**69,27,5** So then the true things of the faith heard from the beginning from the Lord abide in the holy church of God;

**69,27,6** and for this reason the holy church of God and the orthodox faith remain in the Lord, and the only-begotten Lord remains within the Father, and the Father within the Son, and we abide in him through the Holy Spirit, if we become temples that have room for his Holy Spirit;

**69,27,7a** as the holy apostle of God said, “You are God’s temple, and God’s Spirit dwells in you.”

**69,27,7b** So then the Spirit is God from God, the Holy Spirit through whom we are called temples, if we make his Spirit dwell in us.

**69,27,7c** For it is the Spirit of Christ, a Spirit proceeding from the Father and receiving from the Son, as the Only-begotten himself acknowledges.

**69,28,1a** All these things, then, we have explained in the discourse on the faith mentioned before, the one which, as I said, was written to the regions of Pamphylia and Pisidia.

**69,28,1b** But here, since we have come to the words that are next in question, we have been eager of necessity to recall the same things again, so to speak, because of the heresiarch Arius now before us and the Arians who follow him, so that we may undo their wickedness, which turns sweet into bitter, and good into evil, and light into darkness.

**69,28,2a** For upon such people the woe is laid down in full by the Lord through the holy Isaiah, upon those who turn good things into evil.

**69,28,2b** And God is nowhere the cause of such things; but each of these, whether through vainglory, or through prejudice, or through self-chosen wisdom, or through demonic conceit, fell away from the truth and brought affliction into the world, their own wickedness.

**69,28,3** Come then, let us examine this passage, so that we may know the things spoken by the Lord, as the holy apostle says, “We too possess God’s Spirit, so that we may know the things graciously given us by God, which things we also speak,” and so on.

**69,28,4a** The Lord, then, says, “Give them to have life within themselves.

**69,28,4b** And this is eternal life, that they may know you, who alone are true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.”

**69,29,1a** But this Arius and those who follow him leap up, stirring up confusion, and say, of the fact that he prayed to God at all and said, “Father, give them to have life within themselves”: “He is not equal to the one who provides life.

**69,29,1b** For if he were of the essence of the Father, he would himself bestow life, and would not ask the Father to give, through petitions, to those who receive the things given by him.”

**69,29,2** And those who have perverted their understanding against themselves do not know that the only-begotten came in all things to become for you a pattern and salvation, standing in the midst of the world as in a theatre, like an athlete who undoes all that has risen up against the truth from the unbelief and slander and error of the devil, here through idolatry, there through Jewish conceit, there through unbelief, and there through the exaltation of men’s opinion, so that he might teach men to be humble-minded, so that no one, being a man, should think himself to be anything, but should refer the whole to the Father of all.

**69,29,3** And for this reason, though he is life, as his words “I am the life” declare, and has power to provide life, he does not wish to disturb what is right, but came to gather into one principle, into one Godhead, into one truth, into one concord, into one doxology, both the salvation and the understanding of men; and in the presence of the disciples he asks the Father.

**69,29,4a** For what son does not ask of his father?

**69,29,4b** And what father does not give to his son?

**69,29,4c** And what son turns out to be of another kind than his father’s nature?

**69,29,4d** And for this reason the only-begotten Son from the Father, full of grace and truth, was not in need of the fullness, not lacking in the truth, but full of grace and truth.

**69,29,5a** And being full, he both gives and has the power to give.

**69,29,5b** But he wishes to refer everything back to the Father.

**69,29,5c** For the Son glorifies the Father; the Father glorifies the Only-begotten.

**69,29,5d** “For I glorified you on earth,” the Son said to the Father.

**69,29,5e** And to the Son the Father said, “I have glorified you, and will glorify again.”

**69,29,6a** For there is no separation, there is no envy, in the Godhead.

**69,29,6b** “Give them, then, to have life within themselves.”

**69,29,6c** He who is life wishes to receive life from the Father and to give it to the disciples, though he himself is life, so that he may not divide the unity, so that he may not become a stumbling-block to the Jews, so that the Jews may hear him asking of the Father and giving to their disciples.

**69,30,1a** How then does the Son ask the Father?

**69,30,1b** As one who does not have, and so asks?

**69,30,1c** No; but he is indicating the unity of the Trinity, which completely provides worthy gifts to the one who receives.

**69,30,1d** And to indicate that the Godhead is one, in another place again he gives no longer by asking, but by his own authority, what is his own: as a spring from a spring, and God from God, he breathed into their face and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit”; and at another time, raising his hands, he said, “Receive the Holy Spirit.”

**69,30,2a** And he has life in himself, so that he may give it to whom he wishes to give.

**69,30,2b** “For as the Father has life in himself, so the Son too has life in himself.”

**69,30,3** And you see that, for honour’s sake towards the Father, and for the sake of a single unity and a single doxology, and so that the disciples should not think that the Only-begotten had come to lead the minds of believers away from the God of the Law and of the prophets – for this reason, being God and knowing beforehand the malice of men, he addresses his word as though to the Father, and grants the Father a glory that cannot be taken from him, so that the Manichaean may be shamed for denying the Father, so that the disciples may learn that the Godhead in the Old and in the New Testament is the same, so that the Jews may be abashed because the Only-begotten came not to teach of another God but to disclose his own Godhead and that of his heavenly Father.

**69,30,5a** “Give them, then, to have life within themselves,” though he himself was preaching this life.

**69,30,5b** How then did he request of the Father that he give them that which he himself was teaching and bestowing?

**69,30,5c** For afterwards he made plain what the life is, saying, “This,” he says, “is the life, that they may know you, the only true God.”

**69,31,1a** Then Arius and those who follow him leap up because of the phrase, as though they had found something against the truth: “He said,” he says, “‘the only true God’.

**69,31,1b** You see, then, that the Father alone is the true one.”

**69,31,2a** But we too ask you: what then do you say?

**69,31,2b** “The Father alone is the true one.”

**69,31,2c** Then what will the Son be?

**69,31,2d** Is the Son not true?

**69,31,2e** If the Son is not true, our faith is vain, the preaching among us is vain;
