**69,62,4a** Do we supply strength to God if we say, Yours is the strength, yours is the power, yours is the blessing?

**69,62,4b** Have we given him power?

**69,62,4c** Have we, then, bestowed blessing on God?

**69,62,4d** No: in ascribing strength and power we have acknowledged God’s power, and have given the strength back to God.

**69,62,5** So too the angel at that hour, marvelling and astounded at the surpassing love for mankind of his own Master — that, being God, and worshipped with the Father in heaven, and served by his own angels, he endured so far as to come of his own will, freely, and put on flesh.

**69,62,6** And not only that, but even to suffer for the human nature that he himself had fashioned; he endures even to be delivered up to the cross, tasting death, and death on a cross, so that through him humanity might receive a trophy over death, and he might abolish him who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and triumph over every principality and authority.

**69,62,7** Therefore the angel too, marvelling and astounded, said to him, glorifying and praising his own Master as he stood in such a contest and such a working of wonders: Yours is the worship, yours is the might, yours is the power, yours is the strength — so that he might fulfil what was written by Moses, “Let every angel of God strengthen him.”

**69,62,8a** And see, servants of Christ, sons of the holy church of God and of the orthodox faith, that nothing in the divine scripture is crooked or twisted, but all things have been written and accomplished wonderfully for our salvation.

**69,62,8b** But those mentioned above, being at enmity with the only-begotten Son of God and with the Holy Spirit, think and reason sophistically about everything as enemies.

**69,62,9a** But God forbid that we should give heed to human sophistries; rather may we keep our own mind strong, so that we may glorify our Master and conceive nothing whatever inferior in him.

**69,62,9b** For if he who came to save all things has something of inferiority in himself, how will creation be saved from its own inferiorities?

**69,63,1** But again they lay hold like adversaries (for indeed they are intent on a Jewish way of thinking, and differ from them in nothing but the name alone) — these new Jews who again spring up against us, seeking certain expressions against the Saviour so as to ensnare him in a word, as the holy gospel said —

**69,63,2a** and they say: he said on the cross, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani,” meaning, “My God, my God, for what reason have you forsaken me?”

**69,63,2b** And do you see, they say, how he pitifully pleads and laments, and says, Why have you forsaken me?

**69,63,3** And those whose heads are heavy from this poison of Arius’ madness, and who come short in their understanding of the knowledge of God, are unaware that every human passion must be confessed in the Lord in his true coming in the flesh.

**69,63,4a** And first, leaping from one thing to another, they forget what they hold about him, having no one settled position.

**69,63,4b** For how could those who are not sound in their understanding?

**69,63,4c** For at one time they wish to call him Saviour and Lord and Christ, and before all ages, and the Master of the angels and the archangels, through whom the universe came into being — principalities and authorities, angels and archangels, heavens and all things, the earth and all men, and all things on earth, the sea and what is in it.

**69,63,5** And O the great folly of those who hold such views about him, and do not understand here that he who is before the ages in his Godhead, through whom heaven and earth came into being, angels and archangels and, in a word, the universe, things visible and invisible, cannot speak this utterance in the person of his Godhead: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

**69,63,6a** For at what time was the Son abandoned by the Father, and at what time was the Son not within the Father, and the Father within the Son?

**69,63,6b** For the Son and God the Word had set foot on earth, yet he touched heaven, and all enemies were filled with his glory.

**69,63,6c** And he was in Mary, and became man, but by his power he filled the universe.

**69,63,7a** How then could one so great and of such a kind in his Godhead say pitifully, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani,” meaning, “My God, my God, for what reason have you forsaken me?”

**69,63,7b** And yet he says, “Again I go away, and I will not leave you orphans, but I come to you.”

**69,63,7c** And again in another place he says, “Truly I tell you, on this night all of you will take offence at me, and all of you will leave me alone; but I am not alone: with me is the Father who begot me.”

**69,63,7d** And again: “I go away, and I will send you the Holy Spirit, which proceeds from the Father and receives of what is mine.”

**69,63,7e** And again in another place: “I knock, and if anyone opens to me, we shall go in to him, my Father and I, and make an abode with him,” since he is not forsaken by the Father, since the Father too is ever with the Son, since the Holy Spirit is with the Father and the Son.

**69,64,1a** What then, they say, is this saying which he spoke: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

**69,64,1b** But to whom would it not be clear that the utterance is put forth in human fashion from the person of his becoming man?

**69,64,2a** For his becoming man was not some separate thing on its own.

**69,64,2b** For he did not speak as though there were one and another, with the Godhead separated off and the becoming man existing apart; but with the becoming man united to the Godhead — since there was one holy being, which already knew in itself the most perfect things, as being united in God and joined into one Godhead — seeing already that the Godhead was moving, together with the soul, to leave the holy body: from the person of the Lord’s man himself, that is, of his becoming man.

**69,64,3a** For the Godhead was about to complete all things belonging to the mystery of the passion, and to go down with the soul to the regions under the earth, to work there the salvation of those who had fallen asleep before — I mean the holy patriarchs.

**69,64,3b** So when the movement took place in this way, from the person of the becoming man the voice said to its own Godhead, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

**69,65,4** But this had to happen, so that the divine scriptures, proclaimed beforehand concerning him through his own prophets, might be fulfilled through him; so that he might also fulfil what was against Hades, in the form of the man, before Hades; so that the ruler Hades and death, wishing to overpower a man, in ignorance, not knowing the Godhead in the holy soul — so that rather Hades himself might be overpowered, and death destroyed, and the saying fulfilled, “You will not leave my soul in Hades, nor will you let your holy one see corruption.”

**69,65,5a** For neither did the holy God the Word leave the soul, nor was his soul left in Hades.

**69,65,5b** For the Trinity — the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit — dispenses all that belongs to so great a mystery without omission, the Son being in flesh and the Father bodiless; and by the good pleasure and will proper to the Holy Spirit, who is bodiless, the Son became embodied, yet unchanged.

**69,65,5c** And the whole was dispensed by the Trinity for the salvation of men.

**69,66,3a** For this reason again he says in another place — since he had said, “Why have you forsaken me?”

**69,66,3b** — here he says, “I will not let you go, nor will I forsake you.”

**69,66,3c** For the body had to spend three days in the tomb, so that the saying might be fulfilled, “And I became one free among the dead”; and “They flung me away, the beloved one, like a loathsome corpse.”

**69,66,3d** And so that “You will not let your holy one see corruption” might be fulfilled, to show the holiness through the body, and to show that neither was the soul left in Hades.

**69,66,3e** For God the Word was in it in Hades, holding it fast, so that he might fulfil the saying of the apostles, “For it was impossible for him to be held by Hades.”

**69,66,3f** And why does it say “impossible”, except that death and Hades hastened to hold down a soul, but his soul could not possibly be held down, because of the Godhead?

**69,66,3g** But if it was impossible for it to be held down because of the Godhead, how then could “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” be spoken from the person of his Godhead?

**69,66,4** But this saying was shown in human fashion from the person of his becoming man, so that we might learn that the coming in the flesh is real, and was not carried out by him in appearance or phantom.

**69,66,5a** And what rose from the earth, if not what had fallen asleep?

**69,66,5b** “For he has risen,” it says, “he is not here.”

**69,66,6a** And what was it that rose, if not the body?

**69,66,6b** The body, then, was what lay in the tomb, while the soul came up together with God the Word.

**69,66,6c** And again he brought the perfect resurrection to completion all together, in his Godhead, in the same soul, in the same holy body, uniting at last the whole dispensation into one spiritual union, into one union of Godhead, into one dispensation, into one perfection, as he says in the 92nd Psalm, “The Lord has reigned, he has put on beauty,” to show the entrance of God the Word from the heavenly places into the world, putting on beauty, that is, the flesh born of the virgin.

**69,66,6d** For since he seemed a person of no account to the unbelievers who saw him, while it was reckoned to him as beauty, so that he might show his strength through the seeming weakness of the flesh, abolishing him who had the might — having loosed the bonds of sin — that is, death; having accomplished in beauty the whole dispensation of our salvation, and made corruption vanish, and blotted out the curse and the bond that stood against us, and dissolved the covenant with Hades, and dispensed all things for men unto salvation.

**69,66,7** For immediately after saying, “The Lord has reigned, he has put on beauty,” he adds again, “and repeats”, saying, “The Lord has put on power and girded himself,” to show the first garment, from Mary, and the second clothing, repeated again, from the resurrection of the dead.

**69,66,8a** For indeed he is the firstborn from the dead, as the divine scripture said.

**69,66,8b** For this reason he adds to this second clothing a certain greater security, saying, “The Lord has put on power and girded himself.”

**69,67,1** For just as one who girds himself about the loins binds the garment tight upon the loins, making its shape firmer and uniting it to his own skin, so first he put on beauty on account of his sojourn in the flesh here, and the second time, it says, he put on power, having risen from the dead; his becoming man no longer goes to suffering, no longer to scourges, no more is he crucified, just as the apostle said about him, “He has risen; he no longer dies; death is lord over him no more.”

**69,67,2** That is why it says “he girded himself”, having united his flesh into one Godhead, into one unity, into the divine and bodily spirit, into one spiritual whole, brought to perfection and having no dissolution, so that thereafter he entered through closed doors — the gross made subtle, the passible impassible, having suffered in the flesh yet remaining in impassibility;

**69,67,3a** though after entering he showed bones and flesh, the mark of the spear and the mark of the nails, being touched by Thomas, being seen by the disciples.

**69,67,3b** But he entered through closed doors to show that he had dispensed the whole of his salvation toward us men into one spiritual union.

**69,67,4a** And why should I wear myself out over so long a discussion?

**69,67,4b** For repeating the same things many times is no burden to us, and for the security of our readers we have taken care to set them out often, so that, having made our way through the wild-beast volleys of Arius’ opinions and words and thoughts,

**69,68,1** and having likewise treated this expression sufficiently, we may go on to what follows, so that, by making plain on every side most of the things that fall under our understanding through their quibbling, we may show from a few or even more that in the divine scripture, for one who possesses the Holy Spirit and has received from the Lord a wakeful mind, there is nothing crooked to be suspected, nor any form of passion as regards the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit;

**69,68,2** but all things are most perfect, and have been spoken in the divine scriptures by way of the dispensation for each need, and in each place in accordance with the subject in truth, by the Lord himself and his apostles and the holy prophets sent by him.

**69,68,3** For indeed he prophesied concerning this, saying in the Hebrew tongue, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani”; and this the Lord fulfilled in due sequence on the cross, uttering the things foretold of him — “Eli, Eli” in the Hebrew word, as it had been written beforehand — and, completing the paired phrase no longer in Hebrew but in the Syriac tongue, he said “lema sabachthani,” so that he might use the beginning in the form written about him, yet change the account of what remained of the text into another language;

**69,68,4** and he did this for a good dispensation, so that the text should be confessed as spoken of him by the prophet, through his saying “Eli, Eli”, but the remainder no longer in the Hebrew word but in Syriac, so that he might bring down those who boast of Hebrew, and honour other languages too with the fulfilment of the texts concerning him.

**69,68,5** For he was already about to spread his knowledge to all the nations, and not to the Hebrews only, as this whole sequence has it in the twenty-first Psalm, setting forth all his human passions from the person of his coming in the flesh.

**69,68,6** And he himself, when he came, fulfilled it, as there are things in sequence throughout the whole psalm pointing to the coming of Christ in the flesh which this exposition concerns — a most perfect account — as it says, “And they divided my garments,” and “They dug my hands and my feet, and they themselves considered and looked upon me,” and all such sayings, which cannot be fulfilled in respect of the Godhead, but in flesh, the Godhead dispensing all things in impassibility and in truth.

**69,69,1a** But they leap up again, like raving dogs seized by some madness, not recognizing their own master because of the madness, and attacking him first.

**69,69,1b** And again they say, when they hear from us how the truth stands — the Lord saying in the gospel concerning his disciples, “Those whom you have given me, Father, I guarded in the world.”

**69,69,2** And again: “Make them to be in me, as I and you are one”; and they say, “Do you see what he says, ‘I am within the Father and the Father within me, and we two are one’?” — that he speaks not of equality but of concord?

**69,69,3** For how were the disciples able to be in him through equality, and not through concord — and at once the truth of God refutes them on every side, since neither could the disciples fulfil this nor could it be said of them, unless the Word had come and shared their flesh, and joined them in himself unto adoption.

**69,69,4** For this is why in the Song of Songs too he everywhere calls his holy church his near one, addressing her with his holy voice that rouses and exhorts, saying, “Arise, come, my near one, my fair one, my dove.”

**69,69,5a** And do you observe that he names her his near one?

**69,69,5b** Yet it was impossible for the church to be called Christ’s near one unless he had come from on high and drawn close to her through the flesh of like passions which he took, so that, gathering humanity which had drawn near to him, he might call those who came to be in obedience near to himself — the holy and spotless bride.

**69,69,6** And for this reason here the Word, our Lord, the Only-begotten, asks the Father concerning the disciples, that they may be in himself, so that he may join the kinship with him that came about through the flesh — the disciples having been sanctified by the Father’s good pleasure — into a unity of good pleasure and adoption; so that they may have, in the Firstborn of the Father, the enrolment of the firstborn in heaven;

**69,69,7** and so that none may think the Son estranged from the Father’s glory because he wore flesh, making secure the faith and the knowledge of his truth, lest it fall under some suspicion among his servants and such a one fall away from hope, he says, “That they may be as I and you are one, so these too may be one.

**69,69,8a** For I and you are one,” because he is God from God and of one essence in Godhead.

**69,69,8b** And “we are one” does not signify a singular.

**69,69,8c** For what he said was not “I am one” but “I and you”; and “we are one”, so as to refute Sabellius and his school — Sabellius, who supposes the Son and the Father to be a fusion, and the Father likewise with the Holy Spirit.

**69,69,8d** For this reason he says “we are one”, rather than saying “I am one”.

**69,69,8e** For there are two perfect ones, Father and Son, but one because of the equality, because of the Godhead and one power and one likeness.

**69,69,10a** So in the Godhead the Father and the Son are one; in the becoming man the Son and the disciples are one, those of the disciples being brought, through being deemed worthy of the calling, to his indescribable love for mankind, into one unity of adoption, through the good pleasure of Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

**69,69,10b** And once again the error of the vain men who think wickedly about their own Master has been refuted.

**69,70,1a** And passing over this expression too, I shall examine the next ones.

**69,70,1b** But the sophists leap forward, inventing certain expressions for themselves — men who have spent their leisure on syllogisms and the reasonings of vain-mindedness, men who, being human, try to reason God out by syllogism, as the prophet too refutes them, saying, “Will anyone trip up God, that you trip me up?”

**69,70,2a** For what do these noble fellows say again?

**69,70,2b** As we set down the other expression too, interpreted above, which they had stretched out to us for inquiry, “Did he beget the Son willing, or not willing?” — as we showed that in God there is nothing pending for him, but all things in him are perfect at once.

**69,70,3** And he does not first will before he makes, nor does he make without counsel; and he does not take counsel in order to prepare something, nor does his preparation need counsel.

**69,70,4a** So that with him the offspring has always been begotten, and did not begin in time, but exists ever begotten with the Father, and never ceases; as here too, repeating the expression, I set it down again: that he begot neither willing nor unwilling, but in the nature that is above will.

**69,70,4b** For God is of a nature above will and above every conception and supposition.

**69,71,1a** But the new Aristotelians, as I said, invent for us another expression similar to this one.

**69,71,1b** For they have taken the impress of that man’s venom-spitting, and have forsaken the Holy Spirit’s guilelessness and gentleness, as the Lord says, “Learn from me that I am gentle and humble in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls.”

**69,71,2** But these men, having abandoned gentleness, have rather given themselves over to cleverness, putting on Aristotle and the other dialecticians of the world, whose fruits they also pursue, knowing no fruit of righteousness, nor deemed worthy to have the gift of the Spirit in themselves — these contentious men.

**69,71,3a** They say to us, at any rate, whenever we tell them that the Son, the one who is, was with the Father, the one who is, since the Father told Moses, “You shall say to them, He who is has sent me.”

**69,71,3b** And again the gospel declares of the Son, “The Word was in the beginning, and the Word was in God’s presence, and God was the Word.”

**69,71,3c** Should we say that the one who is was with the one who is, they reply to us: Was it, then, what is that was begotten, or what is not that was begotten?

**69,71,3d** For if he was, how was he begotten?

**69,71,3e** But if he was begotten, how was he?

**69,71,4** And this belongs to the same vain-mindedness, which busies itself with inquiries and intrudes into things on high, and meddles with what is above, and works nothing good.

**69,71,5a** For we shall say to them: Where did you get this notion, to think these things?

**69,71,5b** And if they say that thought demands such examination, we too say: Well then, tell us, you men, do you reason about your own things, or about the things of God?

**69,71,5c** Then they say: From ourselves, as rational beings, we reason about the things of God.

**69,71,5d** Does God then differ in nothing from your condition, nature and essence?

**69,71,5e** Yes, they say.

**69,71,5f** If, then, the nature of God differs from your nature, first, your nature cannot grasp the incomprehensible things about God; and secondly, it is impious for God to be likened by you to your own essence.

**69,71,6a** For in us what is not is begotten, since we ourselves once were not, but we have been begotten of our fathers, who themselves also once did not exist; and so one must reckon from the beginning back to Adam.

**69,71,6b** And Adam came into being from the earth, not having once existed, and the earth came into being out of things that were not, because it did not always exist; but God the Father always was.

**69,71,7a** And such as he was by nature, such a Son he begot.

**69,71,7b** And he begot him as ever being, not a fellow-brother but begotten of him, like him by nature, Lord from Lord, God from God, true God from true God.

**69,71,7c** And whatever one reasons about the Father, so must one reason about the Son too; whatever one believes about the Son, so must one hold regarding the Father too.

**69,71,8a** For thus it says, “He who does not believe in the Son as he believes in the Father, and honour the Son as he honours the Father, the wrath of God abides on him,” as the divine gospel has it.

**69,71,8b** And again their syllogistic thinking has collapsed.

**69,71,9a** For God, being incomprehensible, begot God incomprehensible before all ages and before times, and between Son and Father there is no interval; but at once you think of Father, at once you think of Son; at once you name Son, at once you point to Father.

**69,71,9b** For from the Father the Son is conceived, and from the Son the Father is known.

**69,71,10a** For whence is there a Son, unless he has a Father?

**69,71,10b** And whence a Father, unless he begot the Only-begotten?

**69,71,10c** For at what time can the Father fail to be called Father, or the Son Son, so that some might picture a Father without a Son who later, as if he had made progress, begot the Son, so that only after the begetting would the Father be named Father of the Son — the perfect one advancing in Godhead, he who never stands in need of perfecting?

**69,72,1a** Again, wishing to cast away from themselves this healing medicine and saving antidote — the firm foundation of the faith held by the holy church of God — they put forward pretexts, saying: Where does the term essence come to us from?

**69,72,1b** Why is the Son said to be homoousios with the Father?

**69,72,1c** What Scripture spoke of sameness of essence?

**69,72,1d** Which of the apostles spoke of an essence of God?

**69,72,2a** But they do not know that hypostasis and essence are the same in meaning.

**69,72,2b** For the Lord is in his hypostasis, and is “the radiance of the glory and the imprint of his hypostasis.”

**69,72,2c** Essence, then, is not superabundance, but that very thing which is, as Moses says when he told the children of Israel, “He who is has sent me.”

**69,72,2d** He who is, then, is that which is, and that which is turns out to be the essence that is.

**69,72,3a** The “homo”, again, does not signify one; rather, from the homoousion it signifies two who are perfect, yet they are not different from one another, nor foreign to their own unity.

**69,72,3b** And if we have used a particular word for piety’s sake, it was because of the bond of the truth; for without confessing the homoousion there can be no refutation of heresies at all.

**69,72,4** For just as the snake hates the smell of bitumen, the breath of the deer, the incense of jet stone and the smoke of storax, so Arius and Sabellius too hate the word of the confession, in truth, of the homoousion; but to them too we shall say:

**69,72,5** even if the word were not in the divine Scriptures (but it is, and it is plainly contained in the Law and in the apostles and the prophets; for “on the evidence of two witnesses or three every word shall stand”), still it would have been permissible for us, for piety’s sake, to use a useful word, making the holy faith secure.

**69,72,6a** But what do you say?

**69,72,6b** Tell us, you people, what do you say about the Father?

**69,72,6c** Is the Father uncreated?

**69,72,6d** Certainly yes.

**69,72,6e** For who is so foolish as to be in doubt about this?

**69,72,6f** And who is so thunderstruck as to reckon that our Lord Jesus Christ’s God and Father is not uncreated?

**69,72,6g** For surely you yourselves also confess that he is unoriginate, uncreated and unbegotten.

**69,72,6h** For before him he has no father, nor “limit of years, nor beginning of days”, as it is written.

**69,72,7a** If, then, he has neither beginning of time nor end, it is confessed that he is uncreated, and this is beyond dispute; yet nowhere has this been written about him.

**69,72,7b** But for piety’s sake we are compelled to think and to say these things piously about him, even if it is not written.

**69,72,8** So too we are compelled to speak of the homoousion, even if it were not written in its own wording, within the narrow strait of words, even though this discoursing about God should seem to be beyond us and beyond our nature.

**69,72,9a** But nevertheless may the Lord himself pardon us, since we wish to make a defence not on behalf of the Godhead, which stands in no need of our support.

**69,72,9b** But we must speak piously and think piously, so that we may not perish.

**69,73,1a** Answer us, then, you disciples of Arius: we all alike call the Father unbegotten and uncreated, and the word is clearly a wonderful one.

**69,73,1b** Where, then, is this written?

**69,73,1c** Show us the passage.

**69,73,1d** For neither the Law has said it, nor the prophets, nor the gospel, nor the apostles.

**69,73,1e** If, then, we piously use a word that is not written, and it is acceptable because it is spoken for the glory of God, who could find fault with us, even if the homoousion were not written,

**69,73,2a** when we have found a term through which we shall be able to confess what is secure for our salvation?

**69,73,2b** But there are testimonies, together with pious reasoning, both those set out above and many others.

**69,73,2c** But I shall pass over this word too, and with God’s help I shall tear apart their other sayings and notions, uttered as bait against the guileless.

**69,74,1** For again these same people, along with all the expressions from the apostle and the gospels which they distort to suit their own mind through wicked misconstruction, speak also of this one, bringing it forward from the apostle, as is said in the Epistle to the Corinthians, within the section about the resurrection of the dead, where he says in sequence,

**69,74,2a** “Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished every rule and every authority and power.

**69,74,2b** For he must reign until he has set all his enemies beneath his feet; the last enemy to be abolished is death.”

**69,74,2c** “But when he says that all things have been subjected to him, it is plain that he is excepted who subjected all things to him.

**69,74,3** And when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself too will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all things in all.”

**69,74,4a** They seize upon the text, then, and from the habit of their enmity towards the Only-begotten they make their case concerning his ineffable and glorious Godhead, carried away by folly, as I have often said, and they say: You see that it says, “When at the end he delivers the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished all authority and power.

**69,74,4b** For he must reign until he has put all the enemies under his feet.”

**69,74,5a** And the “must” and the “until” and the “when he delivers the kingdom” are a fixing of time.

**69,74,5b** And in their blasphemy they say: These words indicate a ceasing and an ending of the one who reigns, until he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father.

**69,74,6** Nor do they grasp the meaning of the truth at all: that because the Only-begotten has partaken of flesh and blood, the human experiences concerning him and his incarnate coming, which involve the receiving of glory, are sung and spoken of; but not apart from his Godhead, which is ever perfect and glorious, which needs to receive no glory, but has the self-glorified and the self-perfect;

**69,74,7** as he himself gives account of the two parts, saying, concerning the recent one, “Glorify me, Father, in the glory that I had beside you before the world came into being”; and the Father, announcing the glory of the two relations, concerning the first, which is according to the Spirit, says, “I have glorified,” to show what is without limit, and concerning the recent one, because of the incarnate coming, “and I will glorify again,” so that here too the clear sense might be shown of what the apostle also has said, setting forth the truth about him in a twofold way.

**69,75,1a** And “until he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father” is said on account of the beginning in time that the incarnate coming had.

**69,75,1b** For the Only-begotten’s Godhead was ever with the Father, which is to say the only-begotten God the Word, who came forth from the Father without beginning and without time.

**69,75,2a** Otherwise how will the word spoken by the angel be fulfilled, “The Spirit of the Lord will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you”?

**69,75,2b** Since he was saying to her, “You will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus,” to show that God the Word had come down from above and had been made flesh in the womb of the same virgin and had become perfectly man,

**69,75,3a** then, so as not to separate the perfection in the flesh from the perfection in the Godhead, he said to her with the addition of the “also”, “Therefore also the holy one that is born will be called Son of God.”

**69,75,3b** Then: “God will give him the throne of David, his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob to the ages, and of his kingdom there will be no end.”

**69,75,4** Since, then, these are set in contrast, the one against the other, the “he must reign until” and the “he will reign over the house of Jacob to the ages” (and he did not say “to the age” only, but “to the ages”), and again the “when he delivers the kingdom to God and the Father” set against the “and of his kingdom there will be no end”, while both have said such things about the Lord and Christ, and all of them are worthy of belief, the angel Gabriel being holy and the holy apostle being a bearer of the Spirit, what would those who are ignorant of the life-giving teaching say?

**69,75,5a** Can it be that Scripture, which always speaks the truth in all things, is contrary to itself?

**69,75,5b** Far from it.

**69,75,5c** But, as we said from the beginning, because of the assumption involved in the incarnation, all things keep to a reasonable sequence.

**69,75,6a** For if he delivers up the kingship at a point in time, then he does not even reign now; and if he does not yet reign, how is he found always worshipped by the angels and archangels before the incarnate coming and in the incarnate coming, as Scripture says of him, “When he brings the firstborn into the world, it says, ‘And let all the angels of God worship him’”?

**69,75,6b** And again, “He took his seat on the Father’s right,” and it says, “To him shall every knee bend, of beings in heaven and on earth and under the earth.”

**69,75,7a** So, then, he who is worshipped by all reigns always.

**69,75,7b** What, then, have we said of the Son, who reigns always, from of old and now and for what follows, since he has not yet delivered the kingdom to the Father?

**69,75,8a** Is the Father, then, outside the reigning?

**69,75,8b** Far from it.

**69,75,8c** For he reigns together with the Father, and the Father together with the Son and the Holy Spirit.

**69,75,8d** But what do they say: that “when he delivers the kingship to God and the Father,” he himself ceases from reigning?

**69,75,8e** Far from it.

**69,75,9a** Otherwise how is “and of his kingdom there will be no end” fulfilled?

**69,75,9b** But it is to show that nothing in the Son has been fulfilled, or is being fulfilled, that breaks away and holds itself apart from union with the Father and from the single will of Father and Son and Holy Spirit.

**69,75,10a** For we see here too that it is said of the Son himself, “when he delivers the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished every rule and authority and power,” as though the Son himself were delivering the kingdom and abolishing every rule, and so on.

**69,75,10b** And the “he must reign until he has put all the enemies under his feet” is said as though the Son were doing all things, exercising rule and authority, and delivering to the Father, together with the kingdom, those who are subjected.

**69,76,1a** Then he passes on again to another person — the Father, who subjects all things to the Son — and says, “All things he subjected beneath his feet; the last enemy to be abolished is death.”

**69,76,1b** No longer from the person of the Father alone, nor from the person of the Son alone, but squarely between the Father’s person and the Son’s, he says, “The last enemy to be abolished is death.”

**69,76,1c** But as for “when he says that all things have been subjected to him”, I should like to ask these same people from whose person it speaks the “he says”.

**69,76,2a** For the depth of the mysteries of God judges the carnal spiritually.

**69,76,2b** For “the carnal man does not receive the things of the Spirit; for it is foolishness to him.”

**69,76,3** For here, when he says that all things have been subjected to him, if the Father is saying it to the Son, the argument is deficient, for the Son subjected all things to the Father; and if “when he says that all things have been subjected to him” is uttered in the Son’s person, the conception falls short, because it reckons that there are some things yet to come in God, whether in the Father or in the Son.

**69,76,4a** But who is it that says that all things have been subjected?

**69,76,4b** For he did not say, “when they say”.

**69,76,4c** For if this “when they say” had been spoken of the Son, it could have been fulfilled either with regard to the angels or with regard to those who were subjected.

**69,76,5** But since he had indicated above the Son subjecting to the Father and handing over, and the Father subjecting everything to the Son, while for the word-hunters the person of the Holy Spirit remained over, for this reason, without naming the speaker, after the Son’s person and the Father’s person he gave a glimpse of the Holy Spirit’s person — the Spirit who ever announces and teaches the things of the Father and the Son — so as not to leave deficient the perfect knowledge concerning the Trinity and concerning the incarnate coming that received glory.

**69,76,6a** Then, he says, “the last enemy to be abolished is death.”

**69,76,6b** And what has been abolished is fettered, no longer working what it works, nor existing any longer; for it has indeed been abolished.

**69,77,1a** What, then, do those who do not know how to understand the Scriptures have to say about this?

**69,77,1b** We would then have to reckon of the Son that he will cease from reigning, if the expression really had this meaning.

**69,77,1c** But we shall commit impiety, above all, by numbering him too among those who are subjected, once he has ceased from working what he worked; but far from it.

**69,77,2a** For none of those who believe and hope in Christ in truth will have it in mind to say or to hear what is unbefitting his glory, as these people vainly suppose.

**69,77,2b** But the divine Scripture teaches all things, when it says, “All things have been subjected to him,” plainly with the exception of him who subjected all things to him, “and when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself also will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him,” so that what was indicated by the angel from the beginning,

**69,77,3** and is here too joined together through the likeness of the word, might set forth the whole expression of the power of the word, consistently and very clearly, just as the angel also said the like, first indicating the Son from above, and then, with an addition concerning the incarnate coming, showing the union: “Therefore also that which is born of you” (with the addition of the “also” and of “holy”) “will be called Son of God.”

**69,77,4** For this reason, then, and for such reasons, since “therefore also that which is born will be called Son of God”, on this account the Son himself will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that what is fleshly may in power be fleshly no more, but joined to the Godhead, the fleshly united into one union, reigning with the Father and the Holy Spirit, of whose kingdom there will be no end.

**69,77,5a** And from the time he rose, the “so that God may be all things in all” has had its beginning; for the fleshly has been united together spiritually into his one Godhead.

**69,77,5b** But since he says, “Do this for my remembrance, until the Son of Man’s coming”, and “You shall see him in the same manner as you saw him being taken up”, then at last, when all things have been brought to perfection and nothing is left of what is needed for fulfilment, it is signified that the “so that God may be all things in all” is to be referred to his Godhead, so that there may be no division.

**69,77,6a** For there is none, lest polytheism be supposed; for the doxology is one.

**69,77,6b** For neither now is the Son not subjected to the Father, as though he were a usurper, nor is he subjected as a slave without authority, since he was begotten from the Father and is of the selfsame nature and the selfsame Godhead; nor then is he subjected to the Father by way of deficiency, or of lowering, or of necessity, or of termination,

**69,77,7** but as the true-born only-begotten Son, reigning always with the Father, and leading the whole creation up into one unity and into one prize of honour, and teaching his church, “so that God may be all things in all”, since the Godhead is one, the lordship one, the doxology one, of Father, Son and Holy Spirit, the Father being fittingly honoured by the Son, as by a true-born Son, and by the Holy Spirit, as one not alien to Father and Son.

**69,77,8a** And let the very words of those who speak blasphemy against God’s Son and the Holy Spirit be shut out, along with the devices of their enmity toward the Son and the Holy Spirit.

**69,77,8b** And once more we shall detect what they wickedly devise and overturn it.

**69,78,1a** Again they quote some expressions from the gospel and say: Why is the Son unable to do anything by himself unless he sees the Father doing it?

**69,78,1b** And they do not understand from the start what is said: that the Father did not, in fact, make things first, and the Son contrive them afterwards.

**69,78,2a** For what heaven did the Father make by himself, so that the Son, taking the likeness from the pattern of the first heaven, might then produce his work?

**69,78,2b** But not one of those who devise this wickedness can show it.

**69,78,2c** For “in the beginning God made the heaven and the earth.”

**69,78,2d** But together with this, at the beginning, in the making of the world, he says, “Let us make man according to our image and according to likeness,” and he did not say, Come, I will make, and show you how you are to work.

**69,78,3a** And then, “And God made man,” and he did not say, He made, and showed the Son how man must be made.

**69,78,3b** For the Son was not in ignorance, so that only after learning a craft he would then produce its works.

**69,78,4** But since our Lord, for his part, came, put on the flesh, became man and lived among us, and was directing his word to the Jews, who supposed that he was overthrowing the things of the Father, wishing to lift their understanding so that they should not fix their attention on his incarnation alone, he said, “The Son does nothing unless he sees the Father doing it,” in order to show that the Son’s work is the Father’s work, and that the Father takes pleasure in his ordering of the whole work.

**69,78,5a** So too, stumbling in turn over the other expressions, like wild beasts, and refuted before the face of the lightning of the Word, the truth, they will be put to flight.

**69,78,5b** “Flash forth lightning, and you will scatter them; send out your arrows, and you will throw them into confusion.”

**69,79,1a** For there is attached to this expression, which they recite in its sequence and cite from the gospel, “For the Father loves the Son, and shows him all that he himself does, and greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel.”

**69,79,1b** And again, “The Father raises the dead and gives them life.

**69,79,1c** Likewise the Son also gives life to whom he will.”

**69,79,1d** And again, “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgement to the Son, that all may honour the Son, even as they honour the Father.”

**69,79,2a** Now look, I pray you, Arius, at the end of my discussion with you, and see where the word has brought it to its conclusion.

**69,79,2b** It did not say some yes and some no, but “that all may honour the Son as they honour the Father.”

**69,79,2c** Do not dishonour the Son, then, so that you may not dishonour the Father; for if you reckon anything in the Son to be inferior, or think of a deficiency in him, then your thought rises to the Father as well.

**69,79,2d** For it belongs to the same audacity on your part to think such things of the Son and not to honour him as you honour the Father.

**69,79,3a** For even granting that the Father gives to him, tell me, my fine fellow, what does it say?

**69,79,3b** “So that the Son may make alive whomever he wishes.”

**69,79,3c** It did not say, to whom he is ordered.

**69,79,4a** It was fitting that the Son should receive all these things from the Father, yet not be less than the Father, especially in two respects: first, to lift our understanding up to one union of Godhead, of Father and Son and Holy Spirit, and not to bring human reasoning down into divisions and polytheism, but to lead it up to one unity.

**69,79,4b** And secondly, with a view to the change into glory of the incarnate coming and its union with his Godhead.

**69,79,5a** For since he had come to bring joy to his disciples through the promise in which he said, “There are some of those who stand here who shall not taste death until they see the Son of Man as he comes in his glory.”

**69,79,5b** And on the eighth day, according to the gospel — or, as the other gospel puts it,

**69,79,6** after six days — not because the evangelists say different things in place of one another, but because their accuracy is one, and always takes care that no pretext should arise for people to stumble in necessary matters, since the mind of man is intently set on evil from his youth.

**69,79,7a** For this reason one evangelist said, on the eighth day.

**69,79,7b** For some part of the day was left when he spoke the word, and he included that day and that hour in his count, if the day had worn on to about the ninth or tenth hour.

**69,79,7c** And again, since the event took place on the eighth day, at about the third or fourth hour, this was called the eighth.

**69,79,8a** But the other evangelist takes care and says, after six days.

**69,79,8b** For he did not count the day on which he spoke the word to the disciples, nor the day on which he accomplished the deed, but the six full days in between.

**69,80,1a** And having come here to the word, he made its expression plain: how, taking Peter and John and James, he brought them up onto the mountain, and was transfigured, and his face shone like the sun, the face in the flesh united in the Godhead.

**69,80,1b** And his garments were white as snow, that is, the flesh which was from Mary and which belongs to our race.

**69,80,2** And it was being transfigured into glory, acquiring the glory of the Godhead, the honour and perfection and the heavenly glory, which the flesh did not have from the beginning, but received here in the union with God the Word.

**69,80,3** Understand in this way what was said before, that he has given all judgement to the Son, that he gave him authority to make alive whomever he wishes: so that he might show, as the first principle, the union of the one Godhead and the one will, bringing the whole of goodness back to the Father, and to the one principle and Godhead of the three hypostases, which are perfect yet of one Godhead, Father and Son and Holy Spirit; and again the incarnate coming receiving, together with the Godhead, the gift of dignity and the authority and the perfection granted to it from Father and Son, and into one spiritual union of Godhead.

**69,81,1** And with great difficulty we have escaped this region of rough seas and all this onslaught of beasts, the wild humps of the waves, the foam and the terrible surges, having burned up the arrows and shields of the adversaries by right reasoning in the mind and having broken the bows of those opposed to us, against this many-headed serpent, the shapeless form of a hydra, we, the incapable, having received from God the power and the grace,

**69,81,2a** so that, made strong by God, we may sing the song of victory that says, “Let us sing to the Lord, for gloriously has he been glorified; horse and rider he has hurled into the sea.”

**69,81,2b** And we have shattered the head of the dragon upon the water that flows quietly, the water in which those new men who have acquired an inheritance with the Jews did not wish to have a share, those to whom the prophet directed his words when he said,

**69,81,3** “Because you do not wish for the water of Siloam that flows gently, but wish to have Rezin as king, and Tabeel, Remaliah’s son, see, the Lord is bringing on you the strong water of the river, the Assyrians’ king,” and so on.

**69,81,4** But we, having received help in the Lord, and the spittle from true flesh cast upon the ground, and the clay kneaded with spittle pressed on to our eyes, so that we, once in ignorance, might now come to know the truth, having gone and washed in Siloam, the Sent, that is, in the incarnate coming and in the Godhead of perfection, and having at last seen, no longer deny the Lord, even if those of the faction of Arius, the successors of the Jews, put us out of the synagogue.

**69,81,5a** For these too, like those, have decreed that everyone who confesses the Lord be put out of their synagogue, so that they might show that the one who has received his sight has become a reproof of those who do not see.

**69,81,5b** For if their whole synagogue were not blind, they would not have put out of the synagogue the man whose eyes had been opened.

**69,81,6** Let us give thanks, then, to the Lord, that we have received our sight, and confess the Lord, and have been healed of our injuries, if we also do the work of his commandments, and have trampled on the serpent and broken the dragon’s head in the power of God: to him be glory, honour and might, to the Father within the Son, to the Son within the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, for the ages of the ages, amen.

**69,81,7** Leaving behind this hydra, now put to death, the seven-headed and many-cleft, let us go on as usual to the next, beloved, calling upon God, our ever-present helper, to show the same care for us and for those who wish to read this work, for the healing of those who have been bitten and for the correction of those not yet proved to be in evil.

## Anacephalaeosis VI

Tome 1. These are the contents also of the first tome of the third book, which is the sixth tome by the count we gave before, in which there are seven heresies, together with the schisms, as follows.

**Anaceph. VI 70a** 1. The defection and schism of the Audians, not, however, a heresy.

**Anaceph. VI 70b** These have a well-ordered conduct and life, and in every respect they hold the faith just as the catholic church does; the majority of them dwell in monasteries.

**Anaceph. VI 70c** They also make excessive use of many apocrypha.

**Anaceph. VI 70d** They do not pray with us, finding fault with our bishops as rich, and with others, but also because they keep the Passover separately, at the time when the Jews keep it.

**Anaceph. VI 70e** They also have something unlearned and contentious about them, interpreting the “in the image” most rigidly.

**Anaceph. VI 71a** 2. Photinians.

**Anaceph. VI 71b** This Photinus, who was from Sirmium, was still going about up to now.

**Anaceph. VI 71c** He held the same views as Paul the Samosatian, but they differ from him in some respect, and they too maintain that Christ exists from Mary onwards.

**Anaceph. VI 72a** 3. Marcellians, those descended from Marcellus of Ancyra in Galatia.

**Anaceph. VI 72b** He was reported at first to have held views like those of Sabellius.

**Anaceph. VI 72c** But though he often came to make his defence and defended himself in writing, many charged him with remaining in the same views.

**Anaceph. VI 72d** But perhaps he changed his mind and corrected himself, or his disciples did.

**Anaceph. VI 72e** For some orthodox people made a moderate defence on his behalf or on behalf of his disciples.

**Anaceph. VI 73a** 4. Semi-Arians, who confess Christ a creature, but call him a creature with dissimulation, not as one of the creatures; but, they say, we call him Son, yet, so as not to attach passion to the Father through his having begotten, we call him created.

**Anaceph. VI 73b** Likewise they define the Holy Spirit too as altogether a creature, rejecting the homoousion of the Son, and they wish to say homoiousios.

**Anaceph. VI 73c** And others of them have rejected the homoiousion too.

**Anaceph. VI 74a** 5. Pneumatomachi.

**Anaceph. VI 74b** These are sound concerning Christ, but they blaspheme the Holy Spirit, defining him as created and not from the Godhead, but rather as created, by a misuse of terms, for the sake of an activity, saying that he is only a sanctifying power.

**Anaceph. VI 75a** 6. Aerians.

**Anaceph. VI 75b** This Aerius came from Pontus.

**Anaceph. VI 75c** And he is still alive to this day, a trial to the world.

**Anaceph. VI 75d** He served as presbyter under Bishop Eustathius, the one denounced as being among the Arians.

**Anaceph. VI 75e** And since Aerius himself was not appointed bishop, he taught many things against the church; in faith he is a most complete Arian, but he teaches something beyond that.

**Anaceph. VI 75f** He says that no offering should be made on behalf of those who have already fallen asleep; he forbids fasting on the fourth day and the day before the sabbath, at the Forty Days and at the Passover; he preaches renunciation, yet makes use of every kind of meat-eating and luxury without scruple.

**Anaceph. VI 75g** And if any of his people should wish to fast, not on appointed days, he says, but when he wishes; for you are not under law.

**Anaceph. VI 75h** And he says that a bishop is in no way different from a presbyter.

**Anaceph. VI 76a** 7. Aetians, who derive from Aetius the Cilician, who had been ordained deacon by George, who was bishop of Alexandria for the Arians; they are known also as Anomoeans, and by some as Eunomians, because of a certain Eunomius who became a disciple of Aetius and is still alive.

**Anaceph. VI 76b** Eudoxius too was with them, but supposedly from fear of the emperor Constantius he separated himself, and indeed had Aetius banished.

**Anaceph. VI 76c** Eudoxius remained an Arian, though not in the manner of Aetius; these Anomoeans, also called Aetians, altogether estrange Christ and the Holy Spirit from God, maintaining that he is created, and they say that he does not even have any likeness.

**Anaceph. VI 76d** For they wish to present God on the basis of syllogisms drawn from Aristotle and from geometry, and Christ, supposedly, as unable by such modes of reasoning to be from God.

**Anaceph. VI 76e** And those who are called Eunomians after him rebaptize all who come over to them, and not only these but also those who come from the Arians, turning the feet of those being baptized upwards and their heads downwards, as the widespread story goes.

**Anaceph. VI 76f** And they say that to fall into some fornication or other sin is nothing.

**Anaceph. VI 76g** For God requires nothing but that a person be in this faith of theirs, which they deem the only one.

**Anaceph. VI 76h** These, likewise, are the seven heresies of the first tome of the third book, which is the sixth in the sequence.

### Sect 70: Audians

Concerning the schism of the Audians, the fiftieth, but the seventieth in the series.

**70,1,1a** 1. The Audians, or Odians, are an order.

**70,1,1b** They have withdrawn and make their dwelling in monasteries, being an order both in desert places and closer to towns, in the outskirts and wherever they keep their own dwellings, or folds.

**70,1,1c** This Audius became their founder in the times of Arius, when the synod of those who deposed Arius was convened against him.

**70,1,2** The man came from Mesopotamia, and was eminent in his own country for the purity of his life and for his zeal and faith towards God; seeing what was done in the churches, he would often set himself against such things to the face of bishops and presbyters by way of reproof, saying, These things ought not to be done so, these things ought not to be practised so, as a man who spoke the truth, and in the way that is usual with men who speak out freely from love of the truth, especially those who live their life at its very highest.

**70,1,3a** And so, seeing such things in the churches, as I said before, he was compelled to speak by way of reproof, and he did not keep silent.

**70,1,3b** For if he saw any of the clergy who loved money, whether a bishop or a presbyter or anyone else of the clerical order, he would always speak out.

**70,1,3c** And if he saw anyone living in luxury and wantonness, or anyone counterfeiting what belongs to the church’s preaching and the church’s ordinance, the man could not bear it and, as I said, brought forward his word.

**70,1,4a** And this was burdensome to those whose life was not of proven worth.

**70,1,4b** On this account he was insulted and contradicted and hated, and he bore it, buffeted, shoved about and dishonoured, while he went on assembling in the churches for a considerable time, until some, taking it badly, drove the man out for this reason.

**70,1,4c** But he would not accept this; rather he strove to speak the truth and yet not to withdraw from the bond of the one union of the holy catholic church.

**70,1,5a** But as he and those with him were often beaten, and he suffered terrible things, he groaned heavily and took as his counsellor the compulsion of the insults.

**70,1,5b** For he cuts himself off from the church, and many break away along with him, and so he brought about the division, though he held nothing altered in the faith, but he and those with him believed most rightly, even if one must certainly say that in some small matter he and those with him were carried away by contentiousness.

**70,2,1** For besides confessing admirably concerning Father and Son and Holy Spirit, as the catholic church holds, and keeping the faith most orthodoxly, all the other things of his life were admirable too.

**70,2,2a** For he himself, and the bishops under his authority, and the presbyters, and all the others, earn their keep by the labour of their own hands.

**70,2,2b** Later, after he had been driven out of the church, he was ordained bishop by another bishop who was engaged in the same dispute and had withdrawn from the church.

**70,2,3** But as for what I set out to speak of, since I have gone into a digression, I shall take it up again and go through the account; I mean the expression from the divine Scripture which is harped upon among them in the most rigid, unlearned and contentious way.

**70,2,4a** For the “in the image”, which God bestowed on Adam, he and those with him harshly wish to define as being fulfilled in the body, on the strength, supposedly, of the text which reads, “Let us make man according to our image and according to likeness.”

**70,2,4b** And then the divine word goes on to say that “God made man, taking dust from the earth.”

**70,2,5a** Since, he says, it spoke of man from the earth, see that it most truly called the whole earthy thing man, and so it foretold that the earthy thing itself would be in the image of God.

**70,2,5b** And it is harsh, as I said, and unlearned, for a man to define in what part of man the “in the image” is placed, if one ought to speak of a part at all, because of the many things in this saying that run counter to human understanding and contain a multitude of questions.

**70,2,6** For either we shall make God visible and bodily, if the “in the image” is fulfilled in the body bodily and in shape, or, in saying this, we shall make man equal to God.

**70,2,7a** Therefore one must not by any means define or insist in what part the “in the image” is fulfilled, but one must confess that the “in the image” is in man, so that we may not set aside the grace of God and disbelieve God.

**70,2,7b** For whatever God says is true, even if in some few words it has escaped our understanding.

**70,2,8a** To deny this “in the image”, then, is not the part of a believer, nor of the holy church of God.

**70,2,8b** For every man is plainly in the image, and none of those who have their hope in God will deny it, unless it be some who fashion myths for themselves, being cast out of the church and of the tradition of the fathers, which comes from the prophets and the Law and the apostles and the evangelists.

**70,3,1** So then those people, being too contentiously disposed in this matter, themselves also step outside the tradition that accords with the church’s teaching, which believes that every man is in the image but does not define where the “in the image” is placed; for neither those who discourse about these matters in a fabulous way, nor those who deny it, are able to show it.

**70,3,2** For some say that the “in the image” is fulfilled in the soul, supposing that only the case of the flesh can be reasoned out by syllogism, and such people do not know that the case of the soul is reasoned out too, if one must give heed to syllogisms and not simply approach God with a simple mind and believe that what has been spoken by God is truth, but known to him alone who knows all truth.

**70,3,3a** Others say that the “in the image” is neither in the soul nor in the body, but is virtue.

**70,3,3b** Others again assert that it is not virtue, but rather baptism and the gracious gift conferred in baptism, supposedly on the strength of the text that says, “Just as we wore the image of the one made of dust, let us wear also the image of the heavenly one.”

**70,3,4a** Others again will not have this, but wish to say that the “in the image” was in Adam then, until he fell into disobedience, ate from the tree and was driven out.

**70,3,4b** But from the time he was driven out, he lost the “in the image”.

**70,3,5a** And there is a great deal of myth-making among men, to whom one must not yield even for an hour, neither to these nor to those who say this or that; but one must believe that the “in the image” is in man, and indeed in every man, and not loosely.

**70,3,5b** But where the “in the image” is, or where it has been fulfilled, is known to God alone, who by grace bestowed the “in the image” upon man.

**70,3,6a** For man has not lost the “in the image”, but at most has debased the “in the image”, having defiled himself with careless deeds and incurable sins.

**70,3,6b** For see, after Adam he says to Noah, “Behold, I have given you all things as the herbs of the field; kill and eat; do not eat flesh in the blood of its soul, for I will require your souls.

**70,3,6c** Whoever sheds the blood of man upon the earth, for his blood his own blood shall be shed, for it was in God’s image that I made man, and from everyone who sheds it upon the face of the earth I will demand your blood.”

**70,3,7a** And do you see that the “in the image” is spoken of in man in the tenth generation after Adam was formed?

**70,3,7b** At the same time David too, after a long time, says by the Holy Spirit, “All things are vanity, every living man.”

**70,3,7c** And next after him the apostle says, “A man ought not to wear his hair long, being God’s image and glory.”

**70,3,8a** And after him James too says of the tongue, “An evil that cannot be restrained, full of deadly poison; with it we bless God and the Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in the image of God; these things ought not to be so, my brethren.”

**70,3,8b** And see how the case of those who claim that Adam lost the “in the image” has collapsed.

**70,4,1a** Again, of those who say that the soul is the “in the image”, the argument and the defence are as follows.

**70,4,1b** Because, one says, just as God is invisible, so is it invisible; it is capable of action, of movement, of thought and of reasoning; and for this reason it is itself the “in the image”, since it imitates God on earth, setting things in motion and acting, and doing everything else that man performs through his reasoning faculty.

**70,4,2a** But these too are found to be refuted by syllogism.

**70,4,2b** For indeed, if for these reasons the soul is called in the image, it can no longer be in the image.

**70,4,2c** For God is ten thousand times beyond the soul, and is still more abundantly incomprehensible and inconceivable, knowing all things, those that were before and those that are present and seen, and those that are not seen, the ends of the earth and the depths of the abyss, the heights of the heavens, and all things that are, himself containing all things, but contained by nothing.

**70,4,3a** But the soul is contained in a body; it does not know the depths of the abyss, it does not understand the breadth of the earth, it does not know the bounds of the inhabited world, it has not grasped the heights of the heavens, nor how many things are going to be, or when they come about, nor how many things have come to be before it.

**70,4,3b** And there is much to say about it and about such matters.

**70,4,3c** And at the same time it has divisions, but God is undivided.

**70,4,4a** For the apostle says, “For God’s word is alive and at work, and keener than every sword with two edges, reaching as far as the dividing of soul and of marrow, and able to judge thoughts and intentions.

**70,4,4b** And there is no creature hidden before him,” and so on.

**70,4,4c** And you see that the argument of these people too has collapsed.

**70,5,1a** And again the case of those who claim that the body is in the image falls apart.

**70,5,1b** For how is it possible for the visible to be similar to the invisible?

**70,5,1c** How can the bodily be like the bodiless?

**70,5,1d** How can what may be touched be like what cannot be grasped?

**70,5,2a** For we see what is in front with the eyes we have, but we do not know what is behind; but in God there is no passion, no defect, far from it; rather he is light on every side, eye on every side, glory on every side, since God is spirit, and spirit beyond spirit, and light beyond all light.

**70,5,2b** For all things that have come into being through him stand below his glory.

**70,5,2c** The Trinity alone is in incomprehensibility, and in glory beyond comparison and beyond comprehension.

**70,5,3a** And again, as for those who say that virtue is the “in the image”: virtue cannot exist without the keeping of the commandments, and many differ greatly from one another in virtue.

**70,5,3b** For virtue has many forms.

**70,5,3c** For we ourselves know some who were among the confessors, who gave up their own body and soul for their Master, persevering in confession and chastity, who acquired a most true faith, who excelled in piety, kindness and reverence, and passed their lives in fastings and in all goodness and in the tokens of virtue.

**70,5,4a** Yet it has happened that they had some defect, being either abusive, or swearing in the name of God, or given to idle tales, or irritable, or possessed of a livelihood in gold and silver and other things, which make the measures of their virtue fall short.

**70,5,4b** What, then, are we to say?

**70,5,4c** That they acquired the “in the image” through their virtue, but that because of their few human defects the image is out of shape?

**70,5,4d** And that the image in them is no longer perfect?

**70,5,5a** Again the argument of these people has collapsed.

**70,5,5b** And again, the case of those who claim baptism to be the “in the image” falls badly apart.

**70,5,5c** For neither Abraham had baptism, nor Isaac, nor Jacob, nor Elijah, nor Moses, nor, before them, Noah and Enoch and those with them, nor the prophets, Isaiah and those who followed.

**70,5,5d** What then?

**70,5,5e** Do those men, then, not have the “in the image”?

**70,5,5f** And there is much to be said against these people, as against Audius and his followers, who contentiously define the “in the image” as being in the body.

**70,6,1a** These same Audians also bring forward certain other testimonies from the divine Scripture, saying, “The Lord’s eyes look towards the poor, and his ears towards their entreaty.”

**70,6,1b** And, “The hand of the Lord has made all these things.”

**70,6,1c** And, “Has not my hand made all these things?

**70,6,1d** Stiff-necked ones!”

**70,6,2a** And, “To me heaven is a throne, and the earth a footstool for my feet,” and all such things as are written about God.

**70,6,2b** And, “I saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, and his head was like white wool, and his robe like snow.”

**70,6,2c** And do you see, he says, in what way the body is in God’s image?

**70,6,2d** And in this too they are in opposition and strain beyond human capacity.

**70,6,3a** And as for “the Lord appeared to the prophets”: he did indeed appear, as he willed, since he is able to do all things.

**70,6,3b** Nor do we deny that God was seen by the prophets — and not by the prophets alone, but by the apostles as well.

**70,6,3c** For the holy Stephen, the first martyr, says, “Look, I see heaven opened wide, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God and the Father.”

**70,6,4** But God, who is all good, by his own power, showing loving-kindness to his own creature, so that none of the unbelievers might suppose that what is said about God is merely in word and not in truth, and that what concerns God stops at words, and does not fulfil what is said by the apostle, that “whoever approaches God must believe that he exists, and that for those who love him he becomes the giver of reward.”

**70,6,5** So, in order to embolden the human being he had moulded, God discloses himself to his saints and to the worthy, so that they may see God by nature and be grounded in their understanding, and hope in truth, and preach him truly, and make faithful man believe, as indeed the sons of the Greeks hold views about God that go only as far as word and imagination.

**70,6,6** But we truly know God, true and truly subsisting King, incomprehensible, Maker of all things, one God, and from him the only-begotten God, differing from the Father in nothing, and his Holy Spirit, differing in nothing from the Father and the Son, as we have treated at length in every heresy concerning the faith that is according to God.

**70,7,1a** And that God appeared to men many times we have said, and we do not deny it.

**70,7,1b** For if we deny the divine Scriptures, we are not truthful, and we are found falling away from the truth; or if we cast out the Old Testament, we no longer belong to the catholic church.

**70,7,2a** But the gospel said, “No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten God himself has made him known.”

**70,7,2b** And again the same divine Scripture: “God was seen by Abraham while he was in Mesopotamia.”

**70,7,2c** And the Lord himself in the gospel: “The angels of these look upon the face of my Father in heaven.”

**70,7,3** But someone will certainly say that the divine Scripture has said that the prophets saw God in the mind, on the strength of the text, “And the angels of these look upon the face of my Father in heaven,” and again on the strength of, “Happy are those pure in heart, since it is they who will see God.”

**70,7,4** And having said this, and having put the expressions side by side according to his own understanding, he might say that each person sees God in the mind.

**70,7,5a** For it is not with the eyes; but the divine word contradicts this, declaring through the prophet Isaiah, “Wretched am I, for I am pierced to the heart, for being a man of unclean lips I dwell among a people of unclean lips, and I have seen the Lord Sabaoth with my eyes.”

**70,7,5b** And he did not say “with the mind”, nor “in thought”, but “with the eyes”, confirming the true and solid things of the faith.

**70,7,6a** What, then, are we to say, when the gospel declares that God has never been seen by anyone, while the prophets and apostles assert it, and the Lord himself?

**70,7,6b** Is there, then, anything in the divine Scripture contrary to itself?

**70,7,6c** Far from it.

**70,7,7a** But the prophets and apostles did see, and it is true.

**70,7,7b** But they saw as far as they themselves were able and as far as was possible, and God appeared to them in the way he wished; for to him everything is possible.

**70,7,7c** And that God is invisible and incomprehensible is plain and confessed.

**70,7,7d** But, again, it is in his power to do whatever he wishes.

**70,7,7e** “For no one resists his will.”

**70,7,7f** He is invisible, then, in his nature, and incomprehensible in his glory.

**70,7,8a** But when he wills to be seen by the man who was made by him, nothing opposes his will.

**70,7,8b** For the divine is not held fast by passion, so as not to do what it wills, or to do what it does not will; for he is able, doing what he wills.

**70,7,8c** But he does what befits his Godhead, with nothing at all opposing his will so as to prevent him from doing what he wishes, as befits his Godhead.

**70,7,9a** And it is impossible to see God, especially for human nature, and the visible cannot behold the invisible; yet God, who is invisible, in loving-kindness and power strengthened what was incapable and by his own power deemed it worthy to see the invisible; and it beheld the invisible and boundless, not as the boundless is, but as far as nature was able to contain it, empowered, from being incapable, to an extension of capability.

**70,7,9b** And nothing in the divine Scripture will be at variance, nor will one expression be found contrary to another.

**70,8,1** The matter is like this, as I have often set out the illustration: as if someone should look at the heaven through a very tiny hole and say, I see the heaven, and such a person would not be lying, for he does in fact see heaven; but someone might say to him with understanding, You have not seen the heaven, and such a person would not be lying either.

**70,8,2a** For the one who says that he has seen is not lying, and the one who tells him that he has not seen is just as truthful.

**70,8,2b** For he did not see its extent, nor its breadth.

**70,8,2c** And the one who has seen spoke the truth, and the one who contradicted him, saying that he has not seen, did not lie, but he too spoke the truth.

**70,8,3a** For often, too, standing on a mountain ridge, we behold the sea, and if we say that we have seen the sea, we have not lied; but if someone contradicts us, saying, You have not seen it, he is not lying either.

**70,8,3b** For how far the breadth reaches, where the length, where the depth, where the recesses of the deep and its farthest limits are, he cannot know, being a man.

**70,8,4a** If, then, matters concerning the creatures are fulfilled in us in this way, how much more in the grace which God has granted to prophets and apostles?

**70,8,4b** They beheld, then, him who is, in reality, and they did not behold him; rather they beheld as far as nature could endure, and this by grace of the power with which he who is mighty in all things strengthened them, out of love for his own man, and for the one who serves him in truth.

**70,8,5** If, then, such people suppose that God has hands in this way, or eyes, or the other things, because he appeared in this way to the prophets and apostles, they are carried away by contentiousness and are refuted by the truth.

**70,8,6a** But whatever it says in the divine Scripture, one must believe that it is so, but how it is so is known to him alone.

**70,8,6b** And that he appeared in reality, yes; but he appeared as he willed, and truly appeared as he appeared.

**70,8,6c** For God is able to do everything, and for him nothing is impossible.

**70,8,6d** But he is incomprehensible, being inconceivable spirit, containing all things, himself contained by nothing.

**70,8,7a** And as the Father is, such is the Son also, and so too the Spirit, in the Godhead.

**70,8,7b** But the Only-begotten alone, when he came, put on flesh, in which he also rose, and which he also united with the Godhead, uniting it into spirit, and he sat down in glory at the right hand of the Father, as it is written.

**70,8,8a** As, then, he is incomprehensible and inconceivable, so all that is said about him is true and real.

**70,8,8b** And as God is incomprehensible, so everything that is said about him is indeed incomprehensible, but incomprehensible in the way that the things of God are, and as he is, in incomprehensible glory.

**70,8,9a** And these things we have spoken with a human mouth, as far as we were capable, for the glorifying of God.

**70,8,9b** For we have the use of no other speech beyond what has been given us by God in measure, even if in the mind we conceive more about God.

**70,8,9c** But the mouth cannot say as much as the mind holds, being shut in by measure and constrained by the bodily organs.

**70,8,10** Therefore God also pardons us, accepting from us the knowledge and glorifying of him, which reaches out beyond our capacity, not so as to bestow anything on God, but so as to glorify the divine as far as we are able, in order to think piously and not to fall away from his grace and truth.

**70,8,11** In treating these matters concerning this same Audius and the Audians, we have set out what they say, matters which they themselves expound in their unlearned way and to which they cling contentiously, insisting on them in an unbecoming manner.

**70,9,1** They also have certain other matters, on account of which above all they hold their ground, having made the division from the church all the wider, a division through which they often frighten others too and draw them away from the church, enticing both men and women.

**70,9,2a** For they wish to keep the Passover together with the Jews — that is, at the season when the Jews hold their own Unleavened Bread, then they contentiously insist on keeping the Passover.

**70,9,2b** And, supposedly, this was the way the church used to proceed, if indeed they also put forward a slanderous argument to the church’s members on this point,

**70,9,3** saying: From the time of Constantine, out of partiality, he says, towards the emperor, you have abandoned the sequence of the fathers for the feast of the Passover, and you have changed the day to suit the emperor.

**70,9,4** And some again, according to their particular contentiousness, maintain: When Constantine’s birthday fell, he says, then you shifted the Passover.

**70,9,5a** And if the Passover were kept on the same day every year, and the synod convened under Constantine had decreed that it be kept on that same day, what they say would have been plausible; but since the sequence cannot keep to the same reckoning every year, their argument has collapsed.

**70,9,5b** For it was not on account of his birthday that the emperor took the matter in hand, but on account of the unity of the church.

**70,9,6** For in truth God accomplished two very great things for us through the aforementioned Constantine, most beloved of God and ever blessed: the convening of an ecumenical synod and the setting forth of the faith set forth at Nicaea and confessed with the signatures of the bishops who had assembled, so that Arius was deposed and the purity of the faith proclaimed to all; and the matter of the Passover set right by them for our unity.

**70,9,7** For long ago, and from early times, it had been kept in the church in different ways and was a cause of division, giving rise to mockery every year, some keeping it a week earlier and contending with one another, others a week later, some anticipating, some keeping it in between, and others celebrating it afterwards.

**70,9,8** And there was, in short, much confusion and toil, as is not unknown to many learned people, at how many times an uproar was stirred up in the church’s preaching about the question of this feast: in the times of Polycarp and Victor, when the East, being at variance with the West, would not accept letters of peace from each other;

**70,9,9a** and at how many other times, in the times of Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, and of Crescentius, when each of them is found writing to the other and contending, down to our own times; ever since it was thrown into confusion after the time of the circumcised bishops, so it continued.

**70,9,9b** Therefore those who came together from every quarter at that time, having examined the matter precisely, decreed that it should be kept in concord, according to what befits the reckoning and the sequence.

**70,10,1a** For this purpose these same Audians adduce the Ordinance of the Apostles, which is disputed by many, yet is not unworthy of acceptance.
