**70,10,1b** For every canonical order is contained in it, and nothing of the faith has been counterfeited, neither of the confession nor of the church’s administration, rule and faith.

**70,10,2a** But the text which the people I have mentioned take up concerning the Passover they wickedly misinterpret, and in their ignorance they understand it otherwise.

**70,10,2b** For in this same Ordinance the apostles lay down: “Do not compute it yourselves, but keep it when your brethren who are of the circumcision do; keep it together with them.”

**70,10,2c** And they did not say, “when your brethren who are in the circumcision”, but “who are of the circumcision”, in order to show that the people who had crossed over from the circumcision into the church were the leaders after that time, and so that the others should agree with them, in order that different people should not keep it at different times.

**70,10,3a** For they gathered this whole concern for the sake of the one unity, so that there might be no schisms nor divisions.

**70,10,3b** But these people, not understanding the mind of the apostles and of the word contained in the Ordinance, supposed that the Passover must, it seems, be celebrated with the Jews;

**70,10,4** but at the same time fifteen bishops had come from the circumcision, and at that time, since the bishops established in Jerusalem were of the circumcision, the whole world had to follow them and celebrate with them, so that there might be one concord and one confession, one feast celebrated.

**70,10,5** Therefore their care, which gathered the minds of men into the unity of the church, but could not be brought to completion during so long a time, came about by the good pleasure of God under Constantine, for the sake of concord.

**70,10,6a** With the apostles the text is included for the sake of concord, as they testify when they say, “Even if they err, let it be no concern of yours.”

**70,10,6b** But from the very texts that are stated there the contradiction will be seen.

**70,10,6c** For they say that the vigil is to be kept in the middle of the Unleavened Bread.

**70,10,6d** But this cannot always happen in the church’s reckoning.

**70,11,1** For the combination that makes up the Passover consists of three things: from the sun’s course on account of the Lord’s day and the month, and from the moon’s course on account of what the Law requires, that the Passover is to be sacrificed on the fourteenth of the moon, as the Law said.

**70,11,2a** So it cannot be kept unless the equinox has passed, which is not observed among the Jews, nor do they wish to carry out so precise a reckoning.

**70,11,2b** For among them everything has fallen apart and gone astray; except that, even if such precision requires so much inquiry, it was not for the sake of this inquiry and precision that it was said by the apostles; but if, for the sake of concord, the apostles commanded that it be kept even with the enemies of Christ, as these people insist, how much more, for the sake of concord, must it be kept with the church, so that we may not scar the concord of the church?

**70,11,3a** How, then, can this be carried out?

**70,11,3b** For the same apostles say, “When they feast, you are to fast and mourn for them, because on the day of the feast they crucified Christ; and when they mourn, eating the unleavened bread with bitterness, you are to feast.”

**70,11,4a** But it happens that they take the unleavened bread on the Lord’s day.

**70,11,4b** For they are able to sacrifice the Passover on the evening when the Lord’s day is dawning.

**70,11,4c** For until the sabbath has passed, after evening, they cannot perform work.

**70,11,4d** If, then, when they have sacrificed, they rise up feasting, how shall we mourn and fast on the Lord’s day, when we hear them say again in the Ordinance, “He who afflicts his soul on the Lord’s day is accursed before God”?

**70,11,5a** And do you see how great the precision is, and the contradiction, since the matter cannot be carried out according to the letter of the text?

**70,11,5b** But the whole truth of the preaching stands upon the sense, and upon the Ordinance of the apostles itself, that it was for the sake of concord that the bond of the saying was put together: if we celebrate, or they also celebrate, after the equinox, as they too often keep it, and we as well; but again before the equinox has been completed, as they keep it, when they keep it alone.

**70,11,6a** If, then, we too celebrate, it would come about that in one year we celebrate two Passovers, after the equinox and before the equinox, while in the following year we shall not celebrate the Passover at all, and the whole thing will be found to be the work of error rather than truth.

**70,11,6b** For before the equinox the year will not be completed, nor is the year of the cycle of the course ordained for men by God completed unless the equinox has passed.

**70,12,1a** And there would be much to say about this: how the fathers did well, or rather how God through them accomplished for the church the whole precise determination of the truth of this most venerable and all-holy feast, that it is to be kept after the equinox, when the reckoning of the fourteenth day of the moon falls, not so that we should celebrate it on the fourteenth itself.

**70,12,1b** For among them one day is sought, but among us not one but six, a full week.

**70,12,2** Therefore the Law itself also says, widening the matter, “You shall take for yourselves a yearling sheep, unblemished, perfect, from the month’s tenth day, and it shall be kept in store for you until the fourteenth, and you shall sacrifice it toward evening on the month’s fourteenth day,” that is, of the moon.

**70,12,3a** And the church takes care to keep the feast of the Passover, that is, the week that has been appointed, also by the apostles themselves in the Ordinance, from the second day of the week, which is the purchase of the sheep.

**70,12,3b** And if the fourteenth of the moon is on the second day of the week, the sacrifice of the sheep is brought into the middle, and so too if it falls on the third day of the week, or the fourth day of the week, or the fifth day of the week, or the day before the sabbath, or the sabbath, since the six days hold the arrangement for such a purpose.

**70,12,4** For we can begin the week of dry eating, which is called the holy week of the Passover, neither from the sixteenth of the moon nor from the ninth of the moon, but from the tenth until the dawning of the fifteenth, the night and the day being in the middle of the two courses.

**70,12,5** And their number being reckoned together, the fourteen days of the moon, even if it should reach into the dawning of the fifteenth, because of the necessary precision of the sun’s course after the equinox, and of the moon’s course on account of the fourteenth, and of a complete week on account of the Lord’s day, and the count from the tenth day of the moon, which is the taking of the sheep and the first letter of Jesus’ name, since the sheep that was his antitype was taken by his name, being thus fixed from the tenth; but we can no longer have the beginning or the end at the dawning of the sixteenth, nor from the ninth of the moon.

**70,12,6** For the years, falling behind in alternation because of the courses of sun and moon, which differ from one another, produce this inequality; not a stumbling-block appointed by God, but because this precision has been ordained by God according to his all-wise ordering, which he granted to his own age, having set the bounds of the luminaries and of seasons and months and years and solstices, and of his providential care for men, out of his loving-kindness.

**70,13,1** For since the year according to the course of the sun is completed in three hundred and sixty-five days and three hours, it comes about, because the moon makes up its year in three hundred and fifty-four days, that the course according to the moon falls short by eleven days and 3 hours.

**70,13,2** And in the first year the so-called epacts come to eleven and three hours, in the second year to twenty-two days and six hours, in the third year to thirty-three days and 9 hours, and the one month called intercalary is cut off.

**70,13,3a** For the thirty days are intercalated, and three days and 9 hours remain, which, when added to the fourth year’s eleven days and three hours, make 14 days and 12 hours.

**70,13,3b** When another eleven and three hours are added, the epacts come to 25, and 15 hours.

**70,13,3c** And in the sixth year, when another 11 of the year and 3 hours are added, they come to 36 days and 18 hours, which produce one intercalary month; and so, by three-year periods, two months have been intercalated.

**70,13,4a** In the first three years one month, and in the other three years another month.

**70,13,4b** And six days and 18 hours of the epacts are left over.

**70,13,4c** And when in the seventh year these are added to the 11 days of the year and the three hours, the epacts amount to 18, and 21 hours.

**70,13,4d** And in the eighth year, when the 11 days and 3 hours are added again, they come to 28 days of epacts and 24 hours, which make 2 days.

**70,13,5** When these hours are added to the 28 days, they come to 30 together, and it comes about that in the eighth year the 30 days are intercalated, the one month for the two years.

**70,13,6a** And so in the period of the eight-year cycle there are ninety days, which are three full intercalary months, which come to one month for each three years and one month for the last two years.

**70,13,6b** In these three intercalations of the three periods the Passover is at variance among the Jews and the Christians and the others.

**70,14,1** It is in these that the divergence arises among the Audians mentioned above, and they lead men and women astray, priding themselves in this matter on following the tradition kept from the beginning and the Ordinance of the Apostles, while they pay no attention to exactness and do not understand the plain intent of the care which the apostles took in the Ordinance — care taken not in order that the Jews should by all means be followed with exactness, but in order to cut away the contentiousness of those who wished each to keep the feast by themselves and not in concord.

**70,14,2** For Christ wills one Passover, and this is what he reckons, and he accepts the one who keeps it without contention — that is, together with those who keep it with exactness, with the whole holy church, which keeps the feast in many ways.

**70,14,3** And if the Passover had been divided from the time of Constantine, the charge would have been plausible for those who bring this false accusation; but since the schisms existed before Constantine, and there was mockery, the pagans talking about and ridiculing the disagreement in the church, while under Constantine, through the zeal of the bishops, the schism was instead united into one concord,

**70,14,4a** what then is more profitable and more pleasing than this: that a people from the ends of the earth should on one day be set free for God, should be of one accord and keep vigil together, and should observe the same days alike, in vigils and supplications, in concord and worship, in fasting and dry fare, in purity and in the other good works pleasing to God that belong to this all-venerable day?

**70,14,4b** But I think that enough has been said about the disagreement concerning this order of the Audians.

**70,14,5a** The old man Audius himself also underwent exile, banished by the emperor to the regions of Scythia for making the people unruly; and it was the bishops who had referred his case to the emperor.

**70,14,5b** Spending a very long time there — how many years I cannot say — and going on further, into the innermost parts of Gothia, he instructed many of the Goths, and from that time monasteries came into being in that same Gothia, together with a way of life, and virginity, and asceticism of no ordinary kind.

**70,14,6** For this order truly lives in a wholly admirable manner, and everything they have in their monasteries is well conducted, apart from these contentions: their alteration of the Passover, and their unlearned insistence on their confession concerning the “according to the image”.

**70,15,1a** But the most dreadful and fearful thing of all is that they do not pray with anyone — even if he is plainly one of the approved, who have nothing to be accused of and no reproach of fornication or adultery or greed — and their reason is that such a person assembles in the church.

**70,15,1b** And this is the fearful thing: to change the name of Christians belonging to the holy church — which has no added name, but only the name of Christ and of Christians — so as to be called by the name of Audius, and to agree upon and require a watchword of human origin, even though the order should pride itself on purity of life and on all righteousness.

**70,15,2a** After his death, moreover, there have been many bishops of his order, both along with them and after him: one Uranius of the land between the rivers; and he had some from Gothia as well, and appointed them bishops; and also one Silvanus, and certain others, some of whom have happened to depart this life, Uranius in particular.

**70,15,2b** For this man held a place of honour in the midst of such an order.

**70,15,3** After the death of these bishops of theirs, Uranius and Silvanus of Gothia, many were scattered, and their community dwindled to a few, both in the regions of Chalcis near Antioch and in the regions of the Euphrates.

**70,15,4a** For most of them were driven out of Gothia — and not they alone, but our own Christians there as well — when a great persecution arose under a pagan king, which became fierce, in rivalry with the Romans, because the emperors of the Romans were Christians, so that the whole race of the Christians was driven out from among them.

**70,15,4b** Yet the root of wisdom does not fail, nor the planting of faith; and even if all seem to have been driven out, there are certainly people of that land still there.

**70,15,4c** For the spring of the faith cannot fail.

**70,15,5** Many, then, of these same Audians withdrew from Gothia and came here to our regions, and they have been dwelling here for four years up to this time; and moreover the monasteries of these same Audians have withdrawn again from the Taurus mountain, and from Palestine and Arabia; for they had already been spread abroad, but now they are few, with few monasteries, perhaps in two villages as well, in the regions mentioned before, on the outer side of Chalcis; and beyond Damascus and the regions of Mesopotamia the order exists to this day, reduced to a few, as I have said.

**70,15,6a** But thus far I consider that enough has been said about these too; and passing them by, I shall go on again to examine what follows, so that I may leave out none of the divisions and cuttings-off, the separations and schisms, that have occurred in the world.

**70,15,6b** For even if they should not differ in faith, nor so very much in manner of life, nevertheless everything that has been divided off and goes by a name in the world will not, as far as is possible, be passed over by us.

### Sect 71: Photinians

Against the Photinians, the fifty-first, but the seventy-first in the series.

**71,1,1** Photinus, from whom the Photinians come, flourished at this time; he had been a bishop of the holy catholic church, but he was carried away by no slight madness and became more thunderstruck than all who went before him, holding views about the Son of God like those of Paul the Samosatian and going beyond them, and vomiting forth incoherent words of blasphemy.

**71,1,2a** He came from Sirmium.

**71,1,2b** And when he introduced this tare into the world, it was then, at that time, the time of the emperor Constantius; and he was still living until lately, having been deposed by the western synod assembled at Sardica on account of the blasphemy which he vomited forth.

**71,1,3a** He asserts that Christ did not exist from the beginning, but that he exists from Mary onward, from the time when, he says, the Holy Spirit came upon him and he was born of the Holy Spirit.

**71,1,3b** And the Holy Spirit, he says — like a daring master-builder, and like a measurer of the heavens in matters beyond telling — he considers to be Christ’s.

**71,1,4a** This Photinus was talkative in character and sharp of tongue, and able to deceive many by his delivery and readiness of speech.

**71,1,4b** For he was often refuted by many, even after the defence he made at Sardica on that occasion, at the time the bishops called on him to render account for the false belief he had put forward.

**71,1,4c** For he petitioned the emperor Constantius, as one deposed without cause, that he might be granted hearers again, in order to prove that he had been deposed without cause.

**71,1,5** So the emperor at that time sent out judges and hearers of the defence he was about to make — Thalassius, Datianus, Cerealius, Taurus, Marcellinus, Evanthius, Olympius and Leontius — while Basil of Ancyra put his questions and spoke against what Photinus was going to say in his defence, or else accepted it.

**71,1,6** He held no short debate with this same Basil; but like the painted complexion of a worthless woman, through his words he brought forward in the debate texts that did not hold together with the meaning of the truth, though they were understood in his mind in a counterfeit sense.

**71,1,7** And being equipped, through his deceptive voice and readiness of speech, to build up both himself and his hearers through their tongue, the fine fellow even promised, with boasting, to bring a hundred testimonies on the subject.

**71,1,8** For those who opposed him were constantly disputing with him, many times over, as we have found also in the debate with Basil, in which they ordered shorthand writers to take it down — Anysius, the emperor’s deacon; Callicrates, exceptor of Rufinus the prefect; Olympius, Nicetas and Basil, memorialists; and Eutyches and Theodulus, notaries of Basil — and one sealed volume was sent to the emperor Constantius, while one remained in the synod around Basil, and another volume with the counts, likewise sealed, as the record set down of his opinion.

**71,2,1** For whenever Basil asked how it is that the divine Scriptures teach, concerning the Lord, God the Word, that the Only-begotten is before the ages and with the Father, Photinus accepted the Word, but made a division, attaching some things to Christ and referring others on high to the Word.

**71,2,2a** For the Father, he says, spoke to his own Word the words, “Let us make man according to our image and according to likeness.”

**71,2,2b** What then?

**71,2,2c** The Word, he says, existed in the Father, yet he was no Son.

**71,2,2d** And “The Lord rained from the Lord” — the Word being in the Father.

**71,2,3** And “I saw,” it says, “one coming down upon the clouds like a son of man”: this, he says, it said by way of advance announcement, not as though the Son existed, but because he was going to be called Son after Mary, and to ascend in place of the flesh; Christ having been born of the Holy Spirit and from Mary, all things, he says, are referred to him by anticipation from the beginning.

**71,2,4a** But he did not yet exist; there was a word, just as the word is in me.

**71,2,4b** I have already said that he holds in part ideas like those of Paul the Samosatian, but in other respects has gone still further than he in his thinking.

**71,3,1a** And this man too will be overthrown, having come to the utmost denial of God and to a notion in every respect foreign to eternal life.

**71,3,1b** For if the Son of God is recent as to his Godhead, then David holds the first place, or rather is even to be ranked before the one who made him.

**71,3,2** For this is how he himself thought, or rather he even overstepped the divine Scripture, asserting according to his own erring notion that the apostle too said, “The first man is out of the earth, made of dust, and the second from heaven.”

**71,3,3a** But the word of truth at once stands against him and refutes his darkened understanding.

**71,3,3b** For the holy apostle spoke of a man and of a man, and said that the first man, Adam, was out of the earth, made of dust, but the second from heaven.

**71,3,4a** And yet, though he says “man”, the flesh did not come down from heaven; rather, it is acknowledged from this very passage too that it is from Mary.

**71,3,4b** And it is not the flesh that he calls “from heaven” by an extended use of the term, but the second man, from the time when the Word came from above and dwelt among us, as it is written.

**71,3,5a** If, then, the Lord pre-existed and is present, he who found out every way of understanding, then he exists, as the divine Scripture does not doubt.

**71,3,5b** For “after these things” signifies one who already existed, as does his having found out every way of understanding; then “he was seen on earth”, the incarnate coming that was to be.

**71,3,6** And the apostle does not say, as they claim, that he brought the man from heaven; but because of the union of the incarnate coming he calls him “man”, on account of the time between Adam and the incarnate coming, and he calls him

**71,3,7** “from heaven” because God the Word came from above, and flesh too, as it says — the Word having become flesh — not, as Photinus supposes, a word that went forth from the Father and was changed into flesh; for this is how, in his deluded notion, he expounded the definition.

**71,3,8a** But if Adam exists before the Word exists, through whom then was this same Adam created, and all the creatures of God before him?

**71,3,8b** Or to whom was the Father speaking when he said, “Let us make man”?

**71,3,9** For no one ever directs deliberation to his own inner word, or to his uttered word; but to his own innate and holy Word he sets out, with all wisdom, the fashioning of man that was to come, so that we may learn that the Child was from the beginning with his Father, so that we may not think our Creator recent, but existing always with the Father before the ages, as John too testifies, saying, “The Word was in the beginning, and the Word was with God.”

**71,4,1a** As the charlatan himself says, “I too say that the Word was from the beginning, but not a Son of God begotten.”

**71,4,1b** And if he is not the Son of God, his labour is vain, and vain too are his purpose, his hope and his understanding.

**71,4,1c** For this man says nothing more than the Jews who denied him.

**71,4,2** For the gospel does not say of him, “The Word was in the beginning, and the Word was in God,” but rather, “the Word was with God.”

**71,4,3a** And it does not say only that he was in God, but “the Word was God.”

**71,4,3b** But in a man, the word which is always within him and is uttered cannot be termed a man; it is the word of a man.

**71,4,4a** But if the offspring did not yet exist, as he says, and if God the Word was not yet Son of God, through whom have all things come into being?

**71,4,4b** Since the gospel says, “All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being.”

**71,4,5** “But,” he says, “just as a man does what he wishes through a word, so the Father made all things through his own word, through the word that is in him.”

**71,4,6a** How then does the Lord say through the gospel, “The Father works until now, and I work”?

**71,4,6b** But “The Father works, and I work” is not said as though the Father did not work in the Son’s working, nor as though the Son were a stranger and did not work in the Father’s creation.

**71,4,7a** For all the works that exist have come into being together from Father and Son and Holy Spirit.

**71,4,7b** For through him all things have come into being from the Father, and he himself, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, accomplished everything.

**71,4,7c** “For by the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all his power.”

**71,4,8a** Therefore the Lord too spoke with certainty in the gospel — knowing the notions of those who go astray, since as God he knows beforehand, and how each was going to cast himself out of the truth — and said to the Jews, “The Son does nothing of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it.”

**71,4,8b** And this is not that he first sees and then acts, but he has all things in himself and does what he wills.

**71,5,1a** How then shall these things be, Photinus?

**71,5,1b** Or who is it that, in you, puts forth this tare against us once again?

**71,5,1c** Who is it that prepared this poison for the world?

**71,5,1d** Where did you get the wickedness to devise against your Lord, to take up a blasphemous notion?

**71,5,2a** Did not Abraham persuade you, when he addressed him and said, “You who judge all the earth, will you not execute judgment?”

**71,5,2b** Be convicted, then, that the Son sojourned with him, and not as some utterance, but as God the Word, subsisting in his own being.

**71,5,3** And so that you may know, you would-be philosopher, the conclusion of what was transacted in this matter, how in the divine Scripture he set his seal on it and declared its completion to us, saying, “The Lord rained fire and brimstone from heaven upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord” —

**71,5,4a** and it did not say “the word of the Lord”, but “the Lord from the Lord” — as David too says, “The Lord said to my Lord.”

**71,5,4b** And so that you may know that the Son is not found only after the incarnate coming, it tells also of his being from the beginning: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.”

**71,5,5a** And concerning the Holy Spirit, you idle talker, ranked among the idle and the meddlesome, no one will accept your word.

**71,5,5b** For the Spirit is neither greater nor smaller.

**71,5,5c** “For who has required these things,” it says, “at your hands?”

**71,5,6a** And the same holy word refutes you, where the Lord speaks concerning the Holy Spirit.

**71,5,6b** Confessing it to be true-born of his own Godhead, he says, “He who proceeds from the Father will also receive of what is mine.”

**71,6,1a** And how many other testimonies are there?

**71,6,1b** But since your trifling is plain to all, being a thing of error and not of truth.

**71,6,1c** Not only the intelligent will detect it, but also those who know even a little of the sequence of the divine Scripture, and for this reason I shall not need many witnesses or a lengthy refutation; for your account and your false belief are easily caught;

**71,6,2** therefore what has been said to you should suffice, and having crushed it with the foot of reason and with the truth of God the Word, like a feeble and powerless creature sprung up from the earth, or like a worm — that is, an earthworm — I shall leave it behind.

**71,6,3a** For the sect of this deluded man has already been scattered within a short time.

**71,6,3b** And calling upon God, as is my custom, I shall go on to those that follow.

### Sect 72: Marcellians

Against the Marcellians, the fifty-second, but the seventy-second in the series.

**72,1,1a** At the same time again (for all these men belonged to one period) Marcellus arose in Ancyra.

**72,1,1b** For he died only lately, about two years before this year, more or less.

**72,1,2a** He too caused a certain division in the church from the beginning of his period, but this man disclosed only some slight notion, being likened to Sabellius and Novatus because of the Arians’ exasperation against him — ostensibly on account of the reasoning of his opposition to the Arians.

**72,1,2b** Hence he is also reviled by some as having held in part, as I said, the trifling of the Sabellians.

**72,1,2c** But some made a defence on his behalf, saying that it was not so, but that he had lived rightly, and they maintained that he was right in his thinking.

**72,1,2d** Hence there has been much inquiry about him.

**72,1,3** The hidden things of his mind are known to God; but those who came from him and were instructed by him — who do not know his thought, who do not relate his true views — would not confess the three hypostases as the truth holds: that the Godhead is one, the doxology one, the Trinity being consubstantial and differing in nothing from its own glory, being a perfect Trinity and a single Godhead, a single power, a single essence, being neither some kind of merging nor ranked lower.

**72,1,4a** But this man, wishing for the most part to say certain things in the company of some, showed that in his thinking he stood under Sabellius.

**72,1,4b** That is why this too has been spoken of and numbered as a sect.

**72,1,5a** And I shall set out next the statement of his position which this same Marcellus made to Julius of blessed memory, the bishop of the Romans, ostensibly in his own defence.

**72,1,5b** From the defence and the petition it will appear that he held views other than the faith of the truth.

**72,1,5c** For if he did not hold other views, on behalf of what was he coming to a defence — unless indeed words that were not right had been put forth by him and, by troubling some, had brought him down to this defence?

**72,1,5d** Now this is the copy.

**72,1,5e** Copy of the letter of Marcellus, removed from office by the synod on account of heterodoxy.

**72,2,1a** “To the most blessed fellow-minister Julius, Marcellus sends greeting in Christ.

**72,2,1b** Since some of those who were formerly condemned for not believing rightly, whom I refuted at the synod of Nicaea, have dared to write against me to your Godliness, as though I did not think rightly or in accordance with the church, being eager to transfer their own charge onto me,

**72,2,2** for this reason I thought it necessary to come to Rome and remind you to summon those who wrote against me, so that when they came they might be refuted by me on both counts: both that the things they have written against me are untrue, and that even now they continue in their earlier error and have ventured on dreadful things against the churches of God and against us who preside over them.

**72,2,3** Since, then, they would not come, though you sent presbyters to them, and that although I have spent a whole year and three months in Rome, I thought it necessary, as I am about to leave this place, to hand you my own faith in writing, written with all truth in my own hand, the faith which I learned and was taught from the divine Scriptures, and to remind you of the things wrongly said by them, so that you may know with what words they wish to hide the truth, using them to deceive their hearers.

**72,2,4a** For they say that the Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, is not the proper and true Word of God the Almighty, but that his Word is another, and his Wisdom and Power another.

**72,2,4b** That this one, having been made by him, has been named Word and Wisdom and Power; and because they think this way, they say that he is another hypostasis, standing apart from the Father.

**72,2,5a** Moreover, by writing that the Father pre-exists the Son, they declare that he is not truly a Son from God; and even if they say ‘from God’, they say it in the way that applies to all things.

**72,2,5b** Further, they dare to say that there was once when he was not, and that he is something created and something made, marking him off from the Father.

**72,2,5c** I am persuaded, then, that people who talk like this are alien to the catholic church.

**72,2,6** But in following the divine Scriptures my belief is that there is one God, and the only-begotten Son of this God, the Word, ever coexisting with the Father, who has at no time had a beginning of being, existing truly from God, not created, not made, but ever being, ever reigning together with God the Father, of whose kingdom, according to the apostle’s testimony, there will be no end.

**72,2,7a** This is the Son, this the Power, this the Wisdom, this the proper and true Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, the indivisible Power of God, through whom all things that have come into being came into being, as the gospel testifies, saying, ‘The Word was in the beginning, and the Word was in God’s presence, and the Word was God.

**72,2,7b** All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being.’

**72,2,8a** This is the Word to whom Luke the evangelist also bears witness, saying, ‘just as those who were eyewitnesses from the first and became servants of the Word handed them down to us.’

**72,2,8b** Of him David too said, ‘My heart has poured forth a good word.’

**72,2,9a** So too our Lord Jesus Christ teaches us through the gospel, saying, ‘It is from the Father that I came forth, and I am here.’

**72,2,9b** He, having come down in the last days for our salvation and having been born of the Virgin Mary, took up the man.”

**72,3,1** “I believe, then, in God Almighty, and in his only-begotten Son, Christ Jesus, our Lord, begotten of the Holy Spirit and of Mary the Virgin, who under Pontius Pilate was crucified and buried, and rose from among the dead on the third day, went up into the heavens and sits at the Father’s right hand, from where he comes to judge living and dead; and in the Holy Spirit, a holy church, remission of sins, resurrection of flesh, life everlasting.

**72,3,2a** We have learned from the divine Scriptures that the Godhead of Father and Son admits no division.

**72,3,2b** For if anyone separates the Son, that is, the Word of God the Almighty, he must necessarily either think that two gods exist, which has been held to be foreign to the divine teaching, or acknowledge that the Word is not God, which is itself plainly alien to the right faith as well, as the evangelist declares, ‘and the Word was God.’

**72,3,3a** But I have learned exactly that the Power of the Father, the Son, is undivided and inseparable.

**72,3,3b** For our Lord Jesus Christ, the Saviour himself, declares, ‘In me is the Father, and I am in the Father.’

**72,3,3c** And, ‘I and the Father are one.’

**72,3,3d** And, ‘He who has seen me has seen the Father.’

**72,3,4** This faith, which I have received from the divine Scriptures and have been taught by my forebears in God, I both preach in the church of God and have now written to you, keeping a copy of it by me.

**72,3,5a** And I request that you insert a transcript of it in the letter you send to the bishops, lest any who lack exact knowledge both of us and of them should heed what those men wrote and be led astray.

**72,3,5b** Farewell.”

**72,3,5c** Here it ends.

**72,4,1a** If, then, this petition is sound, let those who are able read it, and those who are able examine closely what is said in it; and if it is unsound, let them judge for themselves.

**72,4,1b** For we do not wish to speak beyond what we know and what has come to us.

**72,4,2** For even if the petition is sound in its content, those who read and hear it will reflect, again, that it was neither in vain nor idly nor against him that the matter of a defence arose for him — unless it was that he had vomited forth certain words which caused trouble and compelled him to come to a defence concerning what he had said.

**72,4,3a** For it may be either that, after he had erred, he made his defence through the petition and corrected himself, or else that he adorned his words with the petition in order to conceal what he had said, so that he might not be cast out through deposition from the common assembly of the bishops and from the canon.

**72,4,3b** At any rate, this is what has come to us about Marcellus.

**72,4,5a** I myself once asked the blessed Pope Athanasius about this Marcellus, what his view of him was.

**72,4,5b** He offered no defence of him, nor again did he bear himself with any hostility towards him; he only smiled, and by his face indicated that Marcellus was not far from depravity, but that he regarded him as having cleared himself.

**72,5,1** I shall set out what some found in the treatises of Marcellus himself, things which seemed to them blameworthy, and against him they too directed themselves and composed counter-treatises.

**72,5,2** And again by others — because those who had composed the counter-treatises later turned to another position — for the sake of refutation the counter-treatises they had composed were put forward and displayed; and they did this in their own treatises, at the time of the divisions that arose between the party of Acacius and Basil the Galatian and George of Laodicea, in order to refute this same Acacius.

**72,5,3a** For he it was who spoke against Marcellus from Marcellus’ own treatises — so that we, leaving out nothing of the truth in any respect, may show that we neither disavow what serves for correction nor wish to agree with those who attempt anything contrary to the truth.

**72,5,3b** And these are the passages from Acacius’ reply against Marcellus.

**72,5,3c** These things concerning Marcellus.

**72,6,1** “These things, then, and the like Marcellus has written after his misinterpretation of the texts in Proverbs, uttering injustice against God and exalting his own horn on high; and when he has got beyond the middle of the book, he again sets down the statements of Asterius,

**72,6,2** which run: ‘For other is the Father, who begot from himself the only-begotten Word and firstborn of all creation — alone begetting one alone, perfect begetting one perfect, a king begetting a king, a lord begetting a lord, God begetting God — the unvarying image of essence and will and power and glory.’

**72,6,3** Having set these down, then, and being vexed at the unvarying image — that is, the exact and clear impression of the essence of God — and at what follows, he calls this notion worthless and adds his own displeasure, writing as follows.

**72,6,4a** ‘These words plainly expose his worthless opinion about the Godhead.

**72,6,4b** For how can the Lord and God who was begotten, as he himself said earlier, still be the image of God?

**72,6,4c** For God’s image is one thing and God is another.

**72,6,4d** Hence, should he be an image, he is neither Lord nor God, but an image of Lord and God; while if he is in truth Lord and in truth God, then as Lord and God he can no longer be an image of Lord and God.’

**72,6,5a** And next: ‘So he wants him to be none of the things he mentioned before; for he says absolutely that he is the image of these.

**72,6,5b** So if he is the image of essence, he cannot be essence itself; and if he is the image of will, he can no longer be will itself; and if the image of power, no longer power; and if the image of glory, no longer glory.

**72,6,5c** For the image is not of itself, but of something else.’”

**72,7,1** “But you, Marcellus, who earlier, in the opening part of your book, praised these words, and have now denied that the Son is the Word, God from God, alone from alone and perfect from perfect, have plainly exposed your own worthless opinion about the Godhead.

**72,7,2** For since you took the image of the great King as lifelessness and godlessness, as want of will, want of power and want of glory, and as a thing without essence, you ought to have had your unholy tongue cut out, having spoken a word against the Lord and having come at last to a soul so impious.

**72,7,3a** For having circumscribed the image of God with lifelessness, you hold that it is neither Lord nor God, not essence, not will, not power, not glory.

**72,7,3b** You want it to be a motionless image of these, making it, as it were, soulless and lifeless, set up outside, and, as you yourself say, soulless and composed by human art alone; but you do not want the image of God to be the living image of the Living One, nor essence as the image of essence, nor will, power and glory as the unvarying image of will, power and glory.

**72,7,4** To say “unvaryingly” is not to say something like “ingenerately”, but that it has been made like, exactly and precisely, to the Father’s goodness and Godhead and every activity.

**72,7,5** And after other things: ‘Your deceitful lips ought to have been struck dumb, which speak unrighteousness against God in pride and contempt.’

**72,7,6a** For indeed the Father, being alone, begot the Only-begotten as alone, even if you do not wish it, now that you wish something else — the Son not having taken his entrance by cause of the aeons of Valentinus, but having his begetting from the Father alone.

**72,7,6b** And perfect begot perfect.

**72,7,6c** For there is nothing imperfect in the Father, and therefore nothing in the Son either; but the perfection of the Son is a true-born offspring of the perfection and surpassing perfection of the Father.

**72,7,7a** And king begot king.

**72,7,7b** For it is a pious thing that God should reign, the Son having been begotten before the ages, a King who is himself reigned over, through whom the rest also are ruled, and who gratefully acknowledges his subjection.

**72,7,7c** For the Father has begotten not a private person but a king, whose kingdom has neither beginning of days nor end of life.

**72,7,7d** For the dignity is not from outside; it belongs to his essence, as it does to the Father who begot him.

**72,7,7e** That is why it is written, ‘And his kingdom shall have no end.’

**72,7,8a** So too it is confessed by us that Lord begets Lord and God begets God.

**72,7,8b** And, to put it simply, we speak of an image of essence and will and power and glory, not soulless and dead, but having essence, will, power and glory.

**72,7,9a** For power does not beget powerlessness but power itself, and glory does not beget inglory but glory itself, and will does not beget want of will but will itself, and essence begets not the consubstantial but essence itself.

**72,7,9b** The Word, then, is an image: God, living Wisdom, subsisting, an active Word, and Son — this Wisdom endowed with essence.

**72,7,9c** For this is she in whom God rejoiced daily, when he was glad at having completed the world.

**72,7,10** But you, Marcellus, denying these things before men, will be denied by that very Wisdom before the Father who is in the heavens, and you will be denied also before the church under heaven, which writes of you everywhere on the earth: ‘Hear the word of the Lord: write down this man as a man proscribed, for no ruler shall any more grow up from his seed, sitting on the throne of David in Judah.’”

**72,8,1** And after other things, when Marcellus has mentioned the sayings of Asterius, he adds, saying, “Having set these down, then, and proceeding to the denial of our Saviour’s image and essence, and of his only-begotten sonship from the Father, and of his being firstborn of all creation, and of the singleness that is from the Only-begotten, and of the perfection that is from the perfect, and of the kingship that is from the king, and of the lordship that is from the lord, and of the Godhead that is from God, and, in a word, of the unvarying image of the essence and will and power and glory of God,

**72,8,2a** denying it before men in no few words, and for that reason destined to be denied before his Father, you write these things openly.

**72,8,2b** ‘These words plainly display his worthless opinion about the Godhead of Father and Son.’

**72,8,2c** But the denial of these has plainly exposed your perverse and worthless heterodoxy concerning the Godhead and essence of Christ.”

**72,9,1a** And after other things he brings in Marcellus’ words: “Stale, then, is what he adds next, writing: ‘He wants him to be none of the things he mentioned before.

**72,9,1b** For you say that he is the image of all these.

**72,9,1c** So if he is the image of essence, he can no longer be essence itself.

**72,9,1d** And if he is the image of will, he can no longer be will itself.

**72,9,1e** And if of power, no longer power.

**72,9,1f** And if of glory, no longer glory.

**72,9,1g** For the image is not the image of itself, but of something else.’

**72,9,1h** But these things, Marcellus, are stale and false.

**72,9,2** For Asterius wants him to be all the things mentioned before, saying, ‘a king begetting a king, a lord begetting a lord, God begetting God’, and he undoes your soulless image, which according to you is composed by human art alone.

**72,9,3** For he speaks of a living image of all these, which is the impression of the image of the living one who begot him; and he calls the image of essence essence itself, and of will will itself, and of power power itself, and of glory glory itself, and an image not of itself but of another.

**72,9,4a** But you, not confessing the Son as God from God, nor light from light, nor power from power, want the Son to be neither God, nor light, nor power, nor essence, nor will, nor glory.

**72,9,4b** But these things impiously do away with the body at the consummation, along with them.

**72,9,5a** And you deny ‘the Word was God’, yet you call him Son of God either in name only or in the manner of men, so that God would be begetting something of another kind, a Son begotten by adoption, according to ‘I have begotten sons and exalted them.’

**72,9,5b** And according to ‘You have received a spirit of adoption.’

**72,9,5c** And ‘Bring to the Lord, you sons of God.’

**72,9,6** When Asterius, then, calls the Son the unvarying image of the Father’s essence and power and will and glory, he is surely saying that the Father’s features, as it were, reside within the Son, and that the attributes conceived of in the Father have been impressed upon, or given to, the Son, not being other things beside him.

**72,9,7a** So he wants him to be all the things he mentioned before.

**72,9,7b** For he does not mean the image in colours, nor does he bring in a third, a painter, to paint elsewhere in colours the qualities of one at variance with the Father, and call this a Son.

**72,9,8a** For that is how you have conceived it, and you speak without understanding.

**72,9,8b** ‘So if he is the image of essence, he cannot be essence itself; and if of will, no longer will itself.’

**72,9,8c** For according to us, if he is a living image of essence, he can be essence itself, and he is.

**72,9,8d** And so we call him essence that is the image of essence, because of a most close imitation of life and activity.

**72,9,8e** And so too we call him will that is the image of will, the Angel of great counsel, and power and glory that are the image of power and glory.

**72,9,9a** And demonstrative of these is the text, ‘For as the Father has life in himself, so he has given to the Son also to have life in himself.’

**72,9,9b** And, ‘As the Father raises the dead and gives them life.’

**72,9,9c** For the words ‘as’ and ‘so’ are the exact impression of the imitation and likeness proper to an image.”

**72,10,1** And after a few other things: “For God the Word, [but] Jesus, who furnishes life and beauty and form, is not himself lifeless, without beauty and without form, conceived of in deadness or in not being; but he has been formed with the Father’s features — not as being himself one thing while having the features of his form as something other, but the features are in his being, and his being is in the features.

**72,10,2a** But the image, being the image of another and not of itself, as you too would have it, and bearing in itself the features of the original, presents otherness — but otherness as likeness.

**72,10,2b** For he is the image not of himself but of another, being the one who is ‘the image of the invisible God’.

**72,10,3a** The Son, then, is the image of the Father, the living image of the Living One, in motion and activity, in power and will and glory; not soulless, nor motionless — having its being in another and being painted, while not itself in motion, in itself and through itself.

**72,10,3b** And he is an unvarying image, the unvaryingness making him not Father but a Son exactly wrought.”

**72,10,3c** Here end the passages of Acacius.

**72,10,4a** But now our orthodox brethren and confessors say that they have received, from certain disciples left behind by Marcellus, a statement of confession making a defence concerning the faith; and since I myself have not grasped its subtleties, I have set it out here.

**72,10,4b** And this is the copy.

**72,10,4c** The superscription of the faith of Marcellus.

**72,11,1** “To the most reverend and most holy bishops exiled at Diocaesarea for the orthodox faith in our Saviour Jesus Christ — Eulogius, Adelphius, Alexander, Ammonius, Harpocration, Isaac, Isidore, Annubion, Pitimus, Euphratius and Aaron — the presbyters from Ancyra of Galatia, Photinus, Eustathius, another Photinus and Sigerius, and the deacon Hyginus, and the subdeacon Heraclides, and the reader Elpidius, and the warden Cyriacus, send greeting in the Lord.”

**72,11,2** “Having come to visit your Godliness from our homeland mentioned above, paying the visit that was fitting, and having been asked by your Holiness about our faith, how we hold, and having welcomed this caring inquiry of yours which you made — above all because of those who wish idly to spread false stories about us —

**72,11,3** we thought it necessary to give you full assurance on this, not only from the letters of communion written to us by the thrice-blessed Pope Athanasius, which we showed to your Holiness, but also from the present confession we have put in writing,

**72,11,4** namely that we neither think nor have ever thought anything outside the ecumenical and ecclesiastical faith defined at Nicaea, which we confess that we hold in its full force;

**72,11,5** anathematizing those who dare to call the Holy Spirit a creature, and the Arian heresy, and that of Sabellius and of Photinus and of Paul the Samosatian, and those who do not say that the holy Trinity is three Persons, uncircumscribed, subsisting, consubstantial, co-eternal and complete in themselves;

**72,11,6** and anathematizing also those who call the Son an expansion, or a contraction, or an operation of the Father, as well as those who do not acknowledge God the Word, the Son of God, as before the ages, co-eternal with the Father, subsisting and complete in himself, Son and God.”

**72,12,1a** “If anyone says that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are identical, let him be anathema.

**72,12,1b** If anyone ascribes a beginning or an end to God’s Son and Word, or else to his kingdom, let him be anathema.

**72,12,1c** If anyone calls the Son, or the Holy Spirit, a portion of the Father, and fails to acknowledge that God’s Son was begotten from the essence of the Father before all conception, let him be anathema.

**72,12,2** As to the incarnation of God the Word, God’s only-begotten Son, we acknowledge that the Son of God became man as well, without sin, by assuming human nature in its entirety — that is, a soul endowed with reason and intellect, and human flesh.

**72,12,3** Our belief is in one God, the Father, the Almighty, the maker of all that is seen and unseen; and in one Lord, Jesus Christ, God’s Son, who was begotten from the Father as only-begotten, that is, from the essence of the Father, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things came into being, both those in heaven and those upon the earth; who because of us human beings and because of our salvation descended and was made flesh and became man, suffered, and rose again on the third day, went up into the heavens, and is coming to judge living and dead; and in the Holy Spirit.

**72,12,4** But those who say, ‘There was once when he was not’, and ‘Before he was begotten he was not’, and that he came into being from things that are not, or who assert that the Son of God is from another hypostasis or essence, or is changeable or alterable — these the catholic and apostolic church anathematizes.

**72,12,5a** I, Photinus, a presbyter of the catholic church in Ancyra, so believe and think, as is written above.

**72,12,5b** I, Sigerius, presbyter of the same church, so believe and think, as is written above.

**72,12,5c** I, Hyginus, deacon of the same church, so believe and think, as is written above.

**72,12,5d** I, Heraclides, subdeacon of the same church, so believe and think, as is written above.

**72,12,5e** I, Elpidius, reader of this church, so believe and think, as is written above.

**72,12,5f** I, Cyriacus, warden of the same church, so believe and think, as is written above.”

**72,12,6a** This is what was written by them to the confessors and fathers.

**72,12,6b** If, then, it can be judged by men of understanding to stand on a better footing, let it indeed be so ranked.

**72,12,6c** But if there too, again, through the reasoning in this very defence, some things have gone astray that are not right, let it again likewise be set before those who love learning.

**72,12,6d** Since, then, we have gone through the account of all that has been said above concerning this Marcellus, I shall pass him by as well, and examine those that follow.

### Sect 73: Semi-Arians

Against the Semi-Arians, the fifty-third, but the seventy-third in the series.

**73,1,1a** Having, by the power of God, torn apart the wretched doctrines of Arius and of those after him — I mean Photinus, and Marcellus too, in the little in which he seemed to have been shaken — the things which he vomited forth from the beginning, the man being overtaken as if in drunkenness.

**73,1,1b** May it come about that his followers are corrected, if indeed they would be corrected.

**73,1,1c** But having cut out, through the divine Word that is sharper than any two-edged sword, the tares too of those who sprang from Arius himself, let us examine, out of the wild overgrowth that has sprung from Arius himself, how some are half-Arian: they deny his name, but are clothed in him and in his false doctrine,

**73,1,2** feignedly moulding upon themselves, under some pretext, an altered face, as the play-acting of those on the stage is contrived, so that they hide their own faces with other masks and, from behind the mask, recite the shameful things of comedy, things full of drunkenness, either carried along in some other way or giving shape to the myths of the ancients, their poets having done this.

**73,1,3** So too these men, wishing to lead the innocent astray, are themselves, in face and character and false doctrine, of the same sort as Arius and the Ariomaniacs.

**73,1,4a** And wishing, supposedly for the sake of deceitful flattery, to adorn the perverse teaching confessed among those men, they speak of the Son of God as a creature, but so as, supposedly, to deceive and to grant the Son of God something, they add with fawning, like charlatans, for those who are startled by this statement: “We do not say a creature as one of the creatures, nor an offspring as one of the offsprings.”

**73,1,4b** And they cast out the “consubstantial” entirely, supposedly as being foreign to the divine Scripture.

**73,1,5a** But we have discussed these matters most thoroughly in the treatise against Arius.

**73,1,5b** And so that they might put forward a term like this one, the party of Basil, I mean, and of George, the leaders of this sect of the Semi-Arians, say, “We do not say ‘consubstantial’, but ‘of like essence’.”

**73,1,6** These were the men who separated from the synod of the Ariomaniac sect itself, this same Basil of Ancyra being their leader, and George of Laodicea near Daphne of Antioch, that is, of Coele-Syria.

**73,1,7a** These same men also hold views concerning the Holy Spirit equal to those of the Pneumatomachi.

**73,1,7b** For it is no longer with embarrassment, or with any hesitant word, as about the Son, when they are ashamed to call him outright a creature — which is in fact what they hold.

**73,1,7c** But through fear of men they add the “of like essence” and the “a creature, not as one of the creatures”.

**73,1,7d** But concerning the Holy Spirit, as I said, they rush on without hesitation, and like rabid dogs they unsparingly define it as altogether a creature, and so they firmly maintain, and as being foreign to the Father and the Son.

**73,1,8a** And so that no one may say that we speak against anyone by way of false accusation, I shall set out here how each of them wrote a letter: Basil one, and George of Laodicea, together with Basil and those with him, another.

**73,1,8b** And they are these.

**73,2,1** “The holy synod at Ancyra, assembled from various provinces as the Passover drew near, to our most honoured lords and like-minded fellow-ministers in Phoenicia, and to the rest who think as we do, greeting in the Lord.

**73,2,2** We had prayed that — after the testing of the church’s faith, as in fire, by the trials that arose in the meantime on behalf of the faith, and after what happened at Constantinople on account of Marcellus, and after the statement of the faith in the synod assembled for the dedication of the church of Antioch, and after this at Sardica and the faith which flourished there once more, and further after what happened at Sirmium in the matter of Photinus —

**73,2,3** we might, if only through the reasonings which we set out on each article of the faith when we were questioned about those at Sardica who had separated towards the east, be at rest henceforth, and, the church from east to west having been united in the pious reign of our master Constantius and the stumbling-blocks having been cast out, be at peace and devote ourselves to the worship of God.

**73,2,4** But since, it seems, the devil does not cease to busy himself, through his own vessels, on his own behalf, so that he may by all means bring to the point of apostasy what was foretold by the Lord and, in agreement with it, proclaimed through the holy apostle as a safeguard for the faithful —

**73,2,5** devising innovations against the church’s faith, and now winning over some to himself in a form of godliness, and through them devising profane novelties of speech against the pious legitimacy of God’s only-begotten Son — having heard earlier that some were running about Antioch, and Alexandria too, and also Lydia, or Asia, and casting sparks of impiety into the souls of the simpler,

**73,2,6** we hoped that, through the audacity of the impiety and their great shamelessness, and with our lords and fellow-ministers in each place also fighting in defence, the heresy that had been devised would wither and the wickedness be quenched.

**73,2,7** But since, one after another, both those who have come from the places mentioned and those from the regions of Illyricum report that the inventors of this evil are making it their business, and daring to harm more people and to leaven them towards wickedness, we could no longer bear to put it off;

**73,2,8** and having also read the letters of our like-minded fellow-minister George of the church of Laodicea, copies of which we have appended, together with the testimonies of those who solemnly testified to us before God,

**73,2,9** we took care, as the occasion allowed, the holy day of the Passover being at hand; and assembled — as many of us as could [also] assemble, since the winter too had been a hindrance to many, as they indicated in their letters — we were eager to set out,

**73,2,10** with regard to this form of error, the distinctive character of the faith: as for the rest, keeping to the faith set out at Antioch at the dedication, as we said before, and also to that at Sardica, which the synod at Sirmium took up, and to the reasonings from there, we resolved to articulate exactly the faith of the catholic church in the holy Trinity, and in addition, as we said before, dictating only the form of the innovation, as the Spirit granted.

**73,2,11** And we urge you, most honoured lords and fellow-ministers, when you have read this — since you have loved the faith handed down from the fathers, and since we think in agreement with you — to subscribe as we have believed, so that those who dare to bring in this same impiety, being fully assured that we guard, as a kind of inheritance, the faith received from apostolic times through the fathers in between down to us,

**73,2,12** may either be ashamed and corrected, or, if they persist, be expelled from the church — they who by their own doing are already preparing the apostasy for the son of lawlessness, who threatens to dare even to sit in the temple of God.”

**73,3,1a** “Our faith is in Father and Son and Holy Spirit.

**73,3,1b** For thus did our Lord Jesus Christ teach his own disciples, when he said, ‘Go and make disciples of all the Gentiles, baptizing them into the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.’

**73,3,2a** We, then, who are born again into this faith ought to understand piously the notions that come from the names.

**73,3,2b** For he did not say, ‘baptizing them into the name of the fleshless and the enfleshed’, or ‘of the immortal and the one who tasted death’, or ‘of the ungenerate and the generate’, but into that of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit,

**73,3,3** in order that, hearing names drawn from natural things, we might understand the Father as the cause of an essence like his own, and, hearing the name of the Son, might think of the Son as like the Father whose Son he is.

**73,3,4a** We have believed, then, in Father and Son and Holy Spirit, not in creator and creature.

**73,3,4b** For creator and creature is one thing, Father and Son another, because each of these is distinct in its notion.

**73,3,5a** For when I say ‘creature’ I first say ‘creator’; and the word ‘son’, taken over as from bodily things, and through the passions and effluxes of bodily fathers and sons, establishes in a pure sense the notion of the existence of an incorporeal Son from an incorporeal Father.

**73,3,5b** For this reason he also wove in the notion of the creature, drawn from what is bodily.

**73,3,6** And since ‘creature’ alone does not make a son, he took from ‘creator’ and ‘creature’ the impassibility of the one who creates, as regards the creature, and, of the creature, the stability of what subsists from an impassible creator, creating; he wished it to be perfect; and from the bodily father and son, and from the bodily creator and creature, he taught us purely the notion concerning Father and Son.

**73,3,7** For when there is removed from ‘creature’ both its subsisting outside and its being material and the other things which the name of a bodily creature contains, there remains from ‘creature’ only the notion — I mean the notion of the creature as impassibly made, and of what is created as perfect, and as created such as the creator wished what is created to be.

**73,3,8a** If, then, casting out the other things again from ‘creator’ and ‘creature’, we take only the notion of the creature as being from an impassible creator, and as perfect and stable and such as he wished it to be, it follows that we do likewise from the names ‘Father’ and ‘Son’, especially since we have been taught to believe in Father and Son.

**73,3,8b** We must, then, piously take a single notion.”

**73,4,1** “Therefore in this case too, when there is cast out the notion that the Father is thought of as Father of the Son by way of passion or efflux, and when it is held that the Son is not sown as seed and brought to perfection by the bodily processes of nature, which are always moving towards growth and decay, so as to have the characteristics of bodily things, only the notion of the like will be retained.

**73,4,2** For just as — we shall say it again — when everything had been cast out from ‘creature’, there was retained the notion of the creator’s impassible making, perfect and such as he wished, and that of the creature’s stability, so too in the case of Father and Son, when everything bodily has been cast out, there will be retained only the generation of a living being like him, and like him in essence, since every father is thought of as father of an essence like his own.

**73,4,3a** But if, along with all the rest, when the bodily notions are cast out of the names Father and Son, there should be cast out also the notion that allows us to think of a living being like the Father in essence, then it will no longer be Father and Son that is believed in, but creator and creature, and the names will be superfluous, contributing nothing of themselves.

**73,4,3b** And thus he will be creator, as God, but in no way at all Father.

**73,4,4a** For that the Father is not called Father of an activity but rather of an essence resembling himself, which subsists through such an activity, has been made plain from natural reasonings.

**73,4,4b** For God, having many activities, is thought of as creator by one activity, in that he is creator of heaven and earth and of all things in them, and of the invisible things too.

**73,4,4c** But being Father of the Only-begotten, he is thought of not as creator, but as a father who has begotten.

**73,4,5** But if, because of the suspicion attaching to bodily fathers and sons — fearing the passions, lest the incorporeal one should suffer something in begetting, unless what is begotten were imperfect, and being wary of all that happens in the case of a bodily father and son — someone should take away the true notion in the case of Father and Son, he would be speaking of some other kind of thing made, and will never call the Son a Son.

**73,4,6** For whether he should say that he excels in magnitude, as heaven excels a mountain or a hill, he will prove him to be of the class of things made, even if he is thought of as surpassing in greatness; or whether in usefulness, as having come into being first, or as having served in the fashioning of other things, not even so will he put him outside the notion of things made.

**73,4,7a** For just as it makes no difference that the coal is taken from the altar with the tongs and not with the hand itself, and that by means of the tongs the smith’s craft may beat out the iron (for both the tongs and the iron beaten out by means of them will be of the class of things made), so he through whom all things are will differ in no way from the things made, if he is not a Son in the way the natural notion suggests.

**73,4,7b** But if he was made, he will be the first of the things made, and an instrument coming into being for the maker, through which the creator works all things.

**73,5,1a** And no one could cleverly derive the notion of the Father in the proper sense and of the Son in the proper sense from those who are called sons in a more common sense, since in that way the sons of God will be many, when it says, ‘I have begotten sons and exalted them, but they have rejected me.’

**73,5,1b** And, ‘Is there not one Father of you all?’

**73,5,1c** And, ‘To all who received him he gave authority to become God’s children — who were born,’ it says, ‘not of the flesh’s will, nor of a man’s will, but of God.’

**73,5,1d** And besides these, of soulless things, ‘as the one who has begotten the drops of dew.’

**73,5,2** For through these, from the common appellation, it will be the more established that he is not a Son, as these are not, but, being a thing made as these are, shares only in the name of son.

**73,5,3** The church, however, has believed that God is not merely the creator of creatures (for this the Jews and the Greeks know too), but that he is also Father of an Only-begotten, having not only the creative activity, from which he is thought of as creator, but also the activity of begetting, in a proper and only-begotten manner, according to which he is thought of by us as Father of the Only-begotten.

**73,5,4a** For teaching us this, the blessed Paul writes, ‘For this reason I bow my knees to the Father, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named’ — those who have their sons according to the likeness of their own essences.

**73,5,4b** So too there is named a Father in the heavens, from whom the fathers on earth have been named according to essence, he who surely has the Son begotten from him according to the likeness of his own essence.

**73,5,5a** And the notion that applies to those called sons by extension and homonymously cannot fit the Only-begotten.

**73,5,5b** For just as a ‘box’ properly means one made of boxwood, but in a more common sense and by extension from that, what is made of lead or bronze or some other material is also called a ‘box’.

**73,5,6** So the Only-begotten will be conceived neither as in ‘the one who has begotten the drops of dew’, that is, in the sense of essence — for here the word for begetting has been applied by extension to a thing made — nor as in ‘I have begotten sons and exalted them’ — for here too the name has been applied by extension, from goodwill and honour —

**73,5,7** nor as in ‘he gave them power to become children of God’ — for this too has been taken from the making that comes by virtue and imitation; but properly, as alone from alone, like in essence, from the Father, of whom he has both been named and been conceived as the begotten Son.

**73,6,1** But if, because reasonings cannot reach it, someone cannot grasp in knowledge the reasoning of how a Father could be conceived in this way, the Father undergoing passion or division or efflux, and, thrusting aside the faith which establishes the pious notion concerning Father and Son,

**73,6,2** should demand reasonings, he must be required to give reasonings for how God is crucified, and how what is more foolish in the gospel proclamation — because it is beyond syllogism in the eyes of those who are reckoned wise in the world — is wiser than men; men whom the blessed Paul does not even deem worthy of an argument, because by the power that is beyond syllogism he made foolish the wisdom of those able to reason by syllogism.

**73,6,3a** For he has said, ‘I came proclaiming to you the mystery of God, not in wisdom of word, so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied.’

**73,6,3b** Let him, then, who demands the mystery in wisdom of word, having his portion with the wisdom that was made foolish, disbelieve the mystery, since in the matter of wisdom of word even Paul himself is disbelieved, so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied.

**73,6,4** But if he answers in these matters not in wisdom of word, but by exposing all syllogistic wisdom as foolishness through the power that is beyond syllogism, then it is faith alone that he accepts for the salvation of those who welcome the proclamation.

**73,6,5** Nor does he answer how the Father begets the Son impassibly, so that the mystery of the Only-begotten’s sonship from the Father may not be emptied; but, exposing the wisdom of the prudent as made foolish — as it is written, ‘Where is the wise man, where is the scribe, where is the debater of this age?’ — not in wisdom of word, so that the pious notion, I mean, concerning Father and Son may not be emptied through what is suspected from reasonings, he will proclaim Father and Son impassibly — the Father as having begotten the Son from himself without efflux and passion, and the Son as like, and like in essence, from the Father, perfect from perfect, subsisting as only-begotten — to the faithful, or as things beheld beyond syllogism.

**73,6,7** For it is absurd, when one hears of Wisdom subsisting from the wise God — how wisely he knows to become Father of the Wisdom begotten from himself — to conceive that passion is incurred in respect of the Wisdom, if the Wisdom is to subsist from him like the wise one in essence.

**73,6,8a** For if the wise God is not conceived by us as wise compositely, by participation in wisdom, but is himself wise without composition — he is of essence — and if the Wisdom, which is the Son, is not so either, it is conceived accordingly.

**73,6,8b** But Wisdom is essence from the essence of the wise one, and the Son, which is Wisdom, having subsisted as essence, will be like also in essence to the wise Father, from whom the Son subsisted as Wisdom.

**73,7,1** Therefore the blessed Paul too, being well instructed in the things of the Hebrews, and accustomed to draw the same notions from the selfsame Spirit, who spoke in the Old Testament and in the New — as from the two psalms, the one that says, ‘Your judgements are a great deep,’ and the one, ‘Your paths are in many waters, and your footsteps shall not be known’ — transformed the saying about the judgements of God: instead of ‘a great deep’, ‘O the depth of the riches’; instead of ‘Your paths are in many waters and your footsteps shall not be known’, ‘untraceable’; and instead of ‘Your judgements are a great deep’, ‘unsearchable are your judgements.’

**73,7,2** So too, having learned from Wisdom herself the notion concerning herself and the Father, and her relation to the things that have come into being, he sets before us in his own writings the notion concerning Father and Son and the things that have come into being from the Father through the Son.

**73,7,3** For when Wisdom had said, ‘I, Wisdom, have made counsel my dwelling,’ and what follows, and had passed on to the language of ‘through whom’ (for she said, ‘Through me kings’, and, ‘If I declare to you the things done through me, I shall remember to number the things from of old’), and had said, ‘The Lord created me as beginning of his ways, unto his works; before the age he founded me; and before all things he begets me’,

**73,7,4** the apostle took ‘first’ instead of ‘beginning’; instead of ‘he begets me’, ‘born’; instead of the whole together, ‘he created me a beginning of his ways and begets me’, ‘firstborn of all creation’; instead of ‘he founded’, ‘in him all things were created’; and instead of ‘through me’, ‘the things from of old, whether thrones or lordships, whether principalities or authorities, all things have been created through him and for him.’

**73,7,5** Since, then, all the apostle’s terms correspond word for word to those of Wisdom — that is, ‘beginning’ to ‘first’, and ‘begets’ to ‘firstborn’, and ‘he created me a beginning of his ways for his works’ to ‘firstborn of all creation’, and instead of ‘he founded me’, ‘in him were created’, and instead of ‘through me’, as corresponding to ‘through him’ — it is plain that the image too is not in passion.

**73,7,6a** But it has been taken over instead of ‘I, Wisdom’; and as the Wisdom of the wise one is a Son, essence of essence, so too the image resembles the essence.

**73,7,6b** That is why he was conceived as the image of the invisible God, he who is the Son.

**73,7,7** And we have all the terms corresponding: instead of ‘wise’, ‘God’; instead of ‘Wisdom’, ‘image’; instead of ‘beginning’, ‘first’; instead of ‘begets’, ‘born’; and instead of the whole together — we say, instead of ‘a beginning of his ways he created me for his works and begets me’ — ‘firstborn of all creation’; instead of ‘he founded me’, ‘in him were created’; instead of ‘through me’, ‘all things through him and for him.’

**73,7,8** It is plain that, when people hear of the Son as the image of the invisible God and yet attempt so shamelessly to argue away the Son’s likeness in essence to the Father, it is not Paul alone who convicts them of having fallen away in every respect, but before him John too, truly a son of thunder, who with his own loud voice, as if from certain clouds of the riddles of Wisdom, sent forth to us the pious notion of the Son in like manner.

**73,8,1** For see how he too has handed down, in the gospel proclaimed to us by him, the things he was taught by Wisdom.

**73,8,2a** For when Wisdom said, ‘He created me a beginning of his ways’, he set out the ‘in the beginning’, saying, ‘In the beginning was the Word.’

**73,8,2b** And instead of ‘he created me’, ‘and was God’, so that we should conceive of God the Word not as one in utterance, but as one in stable subsistence, impassibly from the Father.

**73,8,2c** And instead of ‘I was with him’, ‘with God’.

**73,8,3a** And instead of ‘through me’, ‘[from of old, the] all things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being.’

**73,8,3b** And instead of ‘he founded’, ‘what has come into being. In him was life’, to which ‘in him all things were created’ is equal.

**73,8,4a** And instead of ‘the Word became flesh’, ‘Wisdom built herself a house.’

**73,8,4b** And instead of ‘I was beside him, fitting things together’, ‘The Son can do nothing of himself, unless he sees the Father doing something; for whatever he does, these things the Son also does likewise’ — so that we have the testimony at the mouth of two and three witnesses for the proof of the Son’s likeness in essence to the Father.

**73,8,5** For one calls the Wisdom of the wise one a Son, another calls the Word of God only-begotten God, another calls the Son of God an image, so that the Word of God, the Wisdom and the image is proclaimed to all as like in every respect, as has been said before, and as Son in essence of God the Father.

**73,8,6** And still more, the Word of God brings us, like Thomas, to the touching of the activity of the likeness in essence, saying, ‘As the Father has life in himself, so he has given to the Son also to have life in himself.’

**73,8,7a** For if the ‘as the Father has’ is not understood as in something else — for it is not that the Father is one thing and the life that is in him another, so that the one should be thought of as having and the other as had.

**73,8,7b** But the Father himself is life without composition, and as he himself has it, so he has given it also to the Son, that is, without composition, as the Father has it.

**73,8,7c** It is plain that, having it thus — since he does not have it ungenerately, nor does he have it compositely — he has all things alike, in essence and without composition, as the Father does,

**73,8,8a** it being clear that the like can never be the same as that to which it is like; as proof of this, the Son of God, having come in the likeness of men, became man, yet did not become in every respect the same as a man; and having come in the likeness of sinful flesh, he came to be in the passions that are the causes of sin in the flesh — hunger, I mean, and thirst and the rest — but did not come to be in the identity of sinful flesh.

**73,8,8b** So that from the apostolic testimonies too the Son’s likeness in essence to the Father is proclaimed.

**73,9,1** For just as, having come to be in the likeness of men, he was both man and not man in all respects – man in that he took on human flesh, since the Word became flesh, but not man, since he was not born as men are (for he was not born of seed and coupling) –

**73,9,2a** so also the Son who is before the ages is God inasmuch as he is Son of God, just as he is man inasmuch as he is Son of Man.

**73,9,2b** Yet he is not identical with the God and Father who begot him, even as he is not identical with man: inasmuch as he is without emanation and passion, inasmuch as he is without seed and pleasure.

**73,9,3a** And he was in the likeness of sinful flesh inasmuch as he endured hunger and thirst and sleep in the flesh, the passions by which bodies are moved sinfully.

**73,9,3b** But though he underwent the fleshly passions already mentioned, he was not moved by them in a sinful way.
