**73,9,4** So also he who is Son of God, existing in the form of God and being equal to God, had the properties of the Godhead, being incorporeal in essence and like the Father in Godhead, in incorporeality and in activities, just as he was like the flesh by being flesh and by enduring the passions of the flesh – yet without being the same; for, being God, he is not the form of God but God, nor equal to God but God, nor is he such with original authority, as the Father is.

**73,9,5a** For just as he was man not in a sinful way, but like a man in activity.

**73,9,5b** For “whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does likewise.”

**73,9,6a** As then here he was moved not sinfully but like those who are in the flesh; for it is absurd that he should come from what accords with nature into what is contrary to nature – that is, having become son of man from God, should become like those who are so by nature, that is, those who are men by nature, in what was contrary to his own nature – and yet in what accords with his own nature should not be like his Father by nature, having been begotten God from God.

**73,9,6b** And it is plain that those who do not call the Son like the Father in essence call him neither Son, but only a creature, nor the Father Father, but Creator, since the notion of “like” leads the Son not to sameness with the Father, but to likeness in essence and to the ineffable true-born sonship that is from him without passion.

**73,9,7** For just as – I will say it again – “in the likeness of human beings” and “in the likeness of sinful flesh” he was not brought to sameness with man but to likeness with the essence of the flesh, for the reasons stated, so too the Son, having come to be in essence like the Father who begot him, will bring his own essence not into sameness with the Father but into likeness.

**73,10,1** And if anyone, giving heed to the world’s wisdom, which God made foolish, should not give heed to the preaching of the word in wisdom and confess with faith the Son’s likeness to the Father, in essence as well, as one who calls them Father and Son falsely, speaking truly neither of a Father nor of a Son, but of a Creator and a creature, and who makes the notion of the Father and of the Son common to the rest of the things made, and wishes to argue cleverly, either from need – as the first of the things made through him – or from the surpassing of his greatness, and in no way confesses the church’s faith in Father and Son, as one who wishes to proclaim a gospel other than that which the apostles proclaimed to us, let him be anathema.

**73,10,2** And, as the blessed Paul says, “We have said before, and now I say again”; taking it up again, we also say of necessity: if anyone, on hearing that the Father alone is wise and that his only-begotten Son is wisdom, should say that the wisdom is identical with the only wise one, doing away with his being Son, let him be anathema.

**73,10,3** And if anyone, hearing that the Father is wise and that his Son is wisdom, should call the wisdom unlike the wise God, even in essence, as one who does not say that the wise one is in truth the wisdom’s father, let him be anathema.

**73,10,4** And if anyone, understanding the Father to be God, should say that the Word and God who was in the beginning with God is the same as the very God with whom the Word and God was, as one who does not truly call him Son, let him be anathema.

**73,10,5** And if anyone, hearing that the only-begotten God the Word is Son of the God in whose presence the Word and God was, should say that God the Word is unlike the Father, even in essence – the God unlike the God and Father with whom the only-begotten God the Word was in the beginning – as one who does not truly call him Son, let him be anathema.

**73,10,6** And if anyone, hearing that the Son is image of the invisible God, should call the image identical with the invisible God, as one who does not truly confess a Son, let him be anathema.

**73,10,7** And if anyone, hearing that the only-begotten Son is image of the invisible God, should say that the Son, being image of the invisible God, is unlike him, even in essence – him of whom he is understood to be the image in essence too – as one who does not truly call him Son, let him be anathema.

**73,10,8** And if anyone, hearing the Son say, “For as the Father has life in himself, so also he has given the Son to possess life in himself,” says that he who received life from the Father, and who confesses, “I too live because of the Father,” is the same as the one who gave it, let him be anathema.

**73,10,9a** And if anyone, hearing “For as the Father has life in himself, so also he gave the Son to possess life in himself,” should call the Son unlike the Father in essence, though he solemnly testifies that it is so as he has said, let him be anathema.

**73,10,9b** For it is plain that, since the life understood to be in the Father signifies essence, and the life of the Only-begotten, begotten from the Father, is understood as essence, the word “so” signifies the likeness of essence to essence.

**73,11,1** And if anyone, hearing from him “he created me” and also “he begets me”, fails to understand “he begets me” of the same one and in respect of essence, but should say that “he begets me” is the same as “he created me”, as one who does not speak of the Son who is impassibly perfect from the two names, “he created me” and “he begets me”, but confesses only a creature and no longer a Son, as Wisdom has reverently handed down the meaning from the two, let him be anathema.

**73,11,2** And if anyone – while the Son makes known to us how he is like his own Father in essence, by the words, “For as the Father has life in himself, so also he gave the Son to possess life in himself,” and his likeness in activity by the teaching, “For whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does likewise” – granting only the likeness in activity, should rob the Son of the likeness in essence, which is the most fundamental point of our faith, as one who robs himself of the eternal life that lies in knowing Father and Son, let him be anathema.

**73,11,3** And if anyone, professing to believe in Father and Son, should say that the Father is father not of an essence like his own but of an activity, as one who dares to voice profane novelties of speech against the Son of God’s essence and abolishes his being truly Son, let him be anathema.

**73,11,4** And if anyone, while understanding the Son as like in essence to the one of whom he is also understood as Son, should call the Son either identical with the Father, or a portion of the Father, or should say that the bodiless Son, who came to subsist from the bodiless Father, did so by emanation and by passion, as bodily sons do, let him be anathema.

**73,11,5** And if anyone, because the Father is never understood as Son and the Son is never understood as Father, calling the Son other than the Father because the Father is one and the Son another – as it is said, “It is another who bears witness about me,” and “for the Father who sent me,” he says, “bears witness” – should, on account of this distinctness of the persons, of Father and of Son, which is reverently understood in the church, and fearing lest the Son should ever be understood as the same as the Father, call the Son unlike the Father in his essence, let him be anathema.

**73,11,6** And if anyone thinks of the Father as Father of the only-begotten Son within time, and does not believe the only-begotten Son to have come to subsist from the Father impassibly, beyond times and beyond all human conceptions, as one who transgresses the apostolic preaching, which set times aside in the case of Father and Son and taught us faithfully, “The Word was in the beginning, and the Word was in God’s presence, and God was the Word,” let him be anathema.

**73,11,7** And if anyone should say that the Father is older in time than the only-begotten Son who is from him, and that the Son is younger in time than his Father, let him be anathema.

**73,11,8** And if anyone attributes the timelessness of the only-begotten Christ’s hypostasis from the Father to God’s unbegotten essence, as one who calls him a Son-Father, let him be anathema.

**73,11,9** And if anyone should say that the Father is the only-begotten Son’s Father by authority alone, and not the only-begotten Son’s Father by authority and essence together, as one who takes only the authority and makes him common with the rest of the things made, and does not say that he is truly a true-born Son from the Father, let him be anathema.

**73,11,10** And if anyone, saying that the Father is Father of the Son by authority and by essence, should say that the Son is consubstantial with the Father or identical with him in essence, let him be anathema.

**73,11,11a** And the signatories are Basil, Eustathius, Hyperechius, Letoius, Heorticus, Gymnasius, Memnonius, Eutyches, Severinus, Eutychius, Alcimides, Alexander: I believe thus, as has been written above, and I confess it by my signature.

**73,11,11b** Here the memorandum of Basil and George and their party is completed.

**73,12,1a** The term essence does not stand in plain words in the Old and New Scripture, but its sense is carried everywhere.

**73,12,1b** And first, from the words God spoke when sending Moses, “Thus you shall say to the sons of Israel: He Who Is,” as said of the Father, who is understood first, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, who is from no one and is cause of the things that are.

**73,12,2** But since the Son too is He Who Is – and he took from the Gospel according to John him who says, “In the beginning was the Word” – Paul the Samosatian, and Marcellus, found a pretext: no longer wishing to call the Son of God truly Son, but taking a pretext from the name Word, they wished, I say, to call the Son of God an utterance and a sound from the mouth;

**73,12,3** and so the fathers who judged Paul the Samosatian were compelled, in the face of such questioning, in order to show that the Son has hypostasis, and is existent, and is a being, and is not an utterance, to call the Son also essence, showing by the name of essence the difference between what has no existence of its own and what exists.

**73,12,4a** For an utterance, taken by itself, lacks existence and is incapable of being a Son of God, since in that way many would be sons of God.

**73,12,4b** For the Father is acknowledged to say many things to the Son, when he says, “Let a firmament come to be, let lights come to be; let the earth produce,” and “Let us make man.”

**73,12,5** So the Father speaks to the Son, and the words of God which he speaks to the Son are not sons; but the Son, to whom the Father speaks, is reverently called, among other names, bread and life and resurrection, and is further named Word, because he interprets the purposes of God.

**73,12,6a** Therefore, so that the heretics might not deceive the simpler sort and call the Son identical with the words spoken by God, the fathers, pointing out the difference of the Son of God as compared with the words of God, called the Son, I say, essence – thus presenting the difference, that God is He Who Is, and that the words he utters do exist, but are not essences of God, rather activities of speech.

**73,12,6b** But the Son, being Word, is not an activity of speech of God, but, being Son, is essence.

**73,12,6c** For if the Father is One who is and the Son is one who is – and the Son is so as having his being from God as a true-born Son – the Son will be understood as Word not in the way of the words spoken by God.

**73,12,7** For those have their being in the one who speaks them.

**73,12,8a** But he has his being by having been begotten from the Father and by hearing the Father and ministering to the Father.

**73,12,8b** This hypostasis, then, the fathers called essence.

**73,13,1** We therefore understand the Son to be like the Father in all things, contending also against the heresy that is now growing upon the church.

**73,13,2** For the present heresy declares the Son to be like the Father in will and in activity, but, as to being, that the Son is unlike the Father,

**73,13,3a** so that it is maintained by the new heretics of the present day that the Son’s will and the Son’s activity resemble the Father’s will and the Father’s activity, whereas the Son himself is unlike the Father.

**73,13,3b** And for this reason they want the will and the activity of the Son to be like the will and the activity of the Father, but do not want the Son to be like the Father, since they firmly maintain that the Son was not begotten from God, but that he is only a creature, and that he differs from the rest of the creatures both by excelling in magnitude and in that he came to subsist first of all, and in that God used him as an assistant for the making of the rest.

**73,13,4** Since, say the heretics, God made the other things through the Son, but him not through anyone – rather he himself wrought him by his own hand, and made him surpassing all things in greatness and power – for this reason he called him only-begotten Son.

**73,14,1** But we of the catholic church, having received the confession of the faith from the divine Scriptures, hold thus: that the Father is Father of a Son resembling himself, and the Son resembles the Father, from which Father he is understood to be Son.

**73,14,2** We add this further definition and so clear the understanding, as against the Sabellians and the rest: that neither can the Son be Father nor can the Father be Son, but the Son is Son and the Father is Father, and not Son.

**73,14,3a** For in these lies the precision of the knowledge of the persons: that the Father, being always Father, is without flesh and immortal, while the Son is always Son and never Father.

**73,14,3b** And we say “always” because of the timeless and incomprehensible character of the hypostasis; and we say that, in accordance with the Father’s will, he assumed flesh and underwent death on our behalf.

**73,14,4** When these things have been clearly distinguished, these admirable men, the allies of the heresy, hasten to contrive two things: one, not to say Father and Son, but Unbegotten and Begotten, thinking by this means to bring the sophistry of the heresy into the church.

**73,14,5a** For these men, wise in the things of God, are well aware that “unbegotten” is less than the name Father.

**73,14,5b** For by “unbegotten” it is understood that he was not begotten, but it does not yet signify whether he is also Father; whereas “Father” is more than the name unbegotten.

**73,14,6** For in “unbegotten”, I say, the power of the Father is not displayed, but in the name Father it is displayed at once that the Father is not Son, if the Father is understood in the proper sense, and that he is cause of a Son like himself.

**73,14,7a** This, then, is the one thing; the other, that they had been the first to put in writing that the Son is, in essence, unlike the Father.

**73,14,7b** Indeed, they thought to pass sentence on the church by means of the writing they had hunted out from the venerable bishop Hosius, in which “unlike in essence” appears.

**73,14,8** But since those from the East, having gone up to Sirmium, gathered up the villainy too of this heretical scheme, they, so as not to be called to account for what they had dared against the faith of the East, were eager to remove from the teaching of the church the term essence, which was in use among the fathers for the reasons already stated, so that in this respect too they might seem to strengthen their heresy.

**73,15,1** For they supposed that, if the term essence were thrown out, by declaring the Son to resemble the Father in will alone and in activity, they would have licence, since essence was not named, thereafter to call the Son unlike the Father in being and in existence.

**73,15,2** But nevertheless God, the avenger of the truth, who catches the wise in their craftiness, [...] who openly declared, before the pious emperor, the kinship of his Only-begotten, namely that the Son resembles the Father in all things.

**73,15,3** For he too thought so, being devout on behalf of the only-begotten Son of God, his champion, and, so thinking, he determined with a pious mouth that the Son is in all things like the Father, as we catholics have believed; and through him the scheme against the faith of the church did not advance, which wished to abolish the term essence, so that, essence not being spoken with the mouth, the heresy might thereafter lurk in hearts and spread.

**73,15,4** But let us forestall them, who write “like in will, but unlike in essence”: if they confess “like in all things” without reservation and purely, the scheme of those who were eager to remove the term essence will be exposed to them as stale.

**73,15,5** For they gained nothing when they were compelled to confess the Son like the Father in all things; for if he is like in all things, as they confessed – just as indeed the Son does resemble the Father – then he resembles him not in will and activity only, as they themselves define, but in existence and in hypostasis and in being, as Son; and, once for all,

**73,15,6** “in all things” embraces all things and admits no difference, it being agreed that neither is the Father like himself nor is the Son like himself, but that the Son is like the Father, and that in being like the Father in all things he is Son and not Father,

**73,15,7** begotten from that Father perfectly, perfect from perfect, before every conception and all reasonings and times and ages, from the Father in likeness, as only the Father knows, who begot him impassibly from himself, and the Son who holds his being from him, and whoever it is to whom he will reveal it, granting us in the contemplation proper to him to understand his own Father worthily.

**73,16,1** And let not the term hypostases trouble anyone; for those of the East speak of hypostases for this reason, to make known the properties of the persons as subsisting and existing.

**73,16,2a** For even if the Father is spirit, and the Son is spirit as well, and the Holy Spirit is spirit too, the Son is not understood as Father.

**73,16,2b** And the Spirit too subsists, which is not understood as Son, which it also is not (the Spirit is not understood as Son, but the Holy Spirit too subsists.)

**73,16,2c** And the Holy Spirit is no longer the Father, nor the Son, but Holy Spirit from the Father, given to the faithful through the Son; since, then, Father and Son and Holy Spirit subsist and exist, those of the East fittingly name the properties of the subsisting persons, as we have said before, hypostases, without calling the three hypostases three principles or three gods.

**73,16,2d** For they anathematize anyone who says three gods.

**73,16,3** But neither do they call Father and Son two gods.

**73,16,4** For they confess that there is one Godhead, embracing the universe through the Son in the Holy Spirit; they confess one Godhead and one kingdom and one principle, yet they reverently recognize the persons in the properties of the hypostases, understanding the Father as subsisting in the fatherly authority, and confessing that the Son, being no portion of the Father, has been begotten purely from the Father, perfect from perfect, and subsists, and recognizing the Holy Spirit, whom the divine Scripture names Paraclete, as subsisting from the Father through the Son,

**73,16,5a** inasmuch as the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, instructs us in the truth, and the truth is the Son.

**73,16,5b** For “no one says ‘Lord Jesus’ except in the Holy Spirit.”

**73,16,5c** So also the Son, who is truth, will teach us reverently to know the true God, his own Father, as he says, “He who has seen me has seen the Father.”

**73,16,6a** Therefore in the Holy Spirit we worthily understand the Son, and in the only-begotten Son we reverently and worthily glorify the Father.

**73,16,6b** This is the faith’s seal, in which seal the Saviour and Lord Jesus Christ commanded that people be baptized, saying, “Go and make disciples of all the Gentiles, baptizing them into the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.”

**73,17,1** For concerning the Son’s resemblance to the Father in every respect, it has been said at greater length elsewhere; but we shall not hesitate likewise to note briefly now as well that the apostle, having called the Son image of the invisible God and having taught in this that the Son is like the Father, elsewhere handed down how one must understand the Son.

**73,17,2** For he says in the Epistle to the Philippians, “Who, existing in God’s form, did not count being equal to God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, having come to be in the likeness of men.”

**73,17,3a** And in that to the Romans: “For the thing impossible to the law, in that it was weak by reason of the flesh – God, having sent his own Son in a likeness of flesh, and concerning sin, condemned sin in the flesh.”

**73,17,3b** So that, from the two testimonies of the two epistles, we might be reverently taught the meaning drawn from what is bodily, and concerning “like”, in the case of the incorporeal Father and Son as well.

**73,17,4a** For “taking the form of a servant and having come to be in the likeness of men” shows that he took flesh from the virgin.

**73,17,4b** Accordingly the flesh that God’s Son assumed is identical with the flesh of men, yet exists in the likeness of men, inasmuch as he was not born of seed as men are,

**73,17,5a** nor of the bed of a man; and so, in the like manner, the Son too, being spirit and having been begotten spirit from the Father, is the same in respect of being spirit from spirit, just as in respect of being flesh from the flesh of Mary.

**73,17,5b** But in respect of having been begotten from the Father without emanation and passion and division, he resembles the Father and is not identical with him; the Son according to the flesh is in the likeness of men, and is not that very thing, a man in all respects.

**73,18,1** Therefore through the Epistle to the Philippians he showed us how the Son’s hypostasis resembles the Father’s hypostasis; for he is spirit from the Father, and in respect of the notion of the Father the same, as in respect of the notion of the flesh the same; yet not the same, but like, because the spirit which is the Son is not the Father, and the flesh which the Word took is not from seed and pleasure, but is as the gospel has taught us.

**73,18,2** Through these words, then, as has been said before, the Son taught us how the Son, in respect of his own being and in respect of his own subsisting being, is like the Father in all things;

**73,18,3a** and how he is like in will and in activity and in works, through the Epistle to the Romans, from his words, “In the likeness of sinful flesh he condemned sin in the flesh.”

**73,18,3b** For the flesh assumed by the Son of God, though identical with the flesh of sin and moved in the same way to hunger and thirst and sleep as all flesh is, was not moved by these sinfully.

**73,18,4a** Therefore it is said, “in the likeness of sinful flesh”, which is like the saying, “For whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does likewise.”

**73,18,4b** For the Father, being spirit, acts with original authority, while the Son, being spirit, does not act with original authority as the Father does, but likewise.

**73,18,5a** Therefore, inasmuch as it is flesh and flesh, it is the same, just as, inasmuch as it is spirit and spirit, it is the same; but inasmuch as it is without seed, it is not the same but like, just as, inasmuch as the Son is without emanation and passion, he is not the same but like.

**73,18,5b** And in so far as he exists in the likeness of sinful flesh, to that extent he resembles the movements of the flesh and is not the same.

**73,18,5c** So then the Son is in the likeness of movement as one who ministers, and not the same as the Father, who acts with original authority.

**73,18,5d** For what the Father does, these things the Son also does, not in that same way himself, but likewise.

**73,18,6a** And it is plain from these things that in all things the Son resembles the Father, as Son to Father, having been begotten from him as a true-born Son.

**73,18,6b** For it is absurd that the Son of God, who existed before the ages and is by nature God from God the Father, when, contrary to his own nature, he became man from Mary, should become like those who are men by nature in what was contrary to his own nature.

**73,18,6c** For it was contrary to nature for him, being God, to become man – and yet in what accords with his own nature he should not be like the Father who begot him.

**73,18,7a** For if in what is contrary to his own nature he is like those who are so by nature, much more is he like, in what accords with his own nature, the Father who by nature begot him as a true-born Son; so that it is established, according to the Scriptures, that in all things the Son resembles the Father.

**73,18,7b** And he was understood to be like in the way that the apostle taught us the notion of “like” through the passages cited above.

**73,18,8a** For he is like also inasmuch as he is life from life, light from light, and true from true, and wisdom from wise.

**73,18,8b** And, once for all, according to the Scriptures he is like not only in activity and will, but in his very being and subsisting and existing he is like in all things the Father who begot him, as Son to Father.

**73,19,1a** If the new heretics, in disputing with us, speak of Unbegotten and Begotten, we shall say to them: since, having dealt villainously with the term essence, which was in use among the fathers, you do not accept it as unscriptural, neither shall we accept “unbegotten”, which is unscriptural.

**73,19,1b** The apostle calls him incorruptible and invisible and immortal, but Scripture has never named him unbegotten.

**73,19,2a** Next, because, as has been said before, “the Unbegotten” does not yet signify the notion of Father, and because “the Begotten” will not yet signify the Son in the proper sense, but makes the notion common to all begotten things.

**73,19,2b** For he who said “begotten” signified that he has come into being, but nowhere indicated what is understood eternally as Son.

**73,19,3a** Therefore, since we understand a Son of God eternally, we shall not accept this; and, in addition to these reasons, because the name of Father and Son signifies relation to another.

**73,19,3b** Therefore, even if we name only the Father, we have the notion of the Son understood together with the name of the Father; for a father is called father of a son.

**73,19,3c** And even if we name only the Son, the notion of the Father is present to us, because a son is called son of a father.

**73,19,4** For the one is bound to the other, and the relation is not broken off; rather each, even when spoken alone, brings in with it the notion of the other, and not the name only, but with the name also the kinship of nature.

**73,19,5a** For when we understand God as Father, we understand him as Father of God, and when we understand a Son of God, we understand as God him who is called Son of God, and as like in nature to the one of whom he is understood to be Son.

**73,19,5b** But the unbegotten is not called unbegotten of a begotten, nor is the begotten called begotten of an unbegotten.

**73,20,1** Since, then, the terms unbegotten and begotten neither have the relation to one another nor convey the nature along with them, but make the distinctive character of the Son common with the rest of the things made, we shall not accept these names, because of the scheme that aims at impiety, but shall always reverently use the name of Father and Son.

**73,20,2** First, then, because we who were called out of the Gentiles were baptized not into Unbegotten and Begotten, but into Father and Son; next, because nowhere is the Son found calling his own Father unbegotten, but always calling God Father, and always himself Son of God –

**73,20,3a** a few instances must be noted – as we hear him saying, “If you loved me, you would have rejoiced that I am going to my Father.”

**73,20,3b** And, “Whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world – you are angry with me because I said, ‘I am Son of God.’”

**73,20,3c** And, “It is from the Father that I came forth, and I am here.”

**73,20,3d** “I came forth from the Father and have come into the world; once more I am leaving the world and going to the Father.”

**73,20,3e** And Peter’s confession too: “You are the Christ, the Son of God.”

**73,20,3f** And the Father from above: “This is my beloved Son.”

**73,20,4** And for this reason, since the Father thus makes mention of the Son and the Son of the Father, and in these names – I will say it again – we were sealed, we shall always use these, repelling the profane empty chatter directed against the apostolic faith.

**73,20,5** For the word spoken by the Father, “In the splendours of the saints, from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you,” was spoken of necessity, and will lead the Son of the Father away from any commonality with the things made, since by the term womb it teaches that the Son is true-born from him and begotten in his own proper way;

**73,20,6** just as likewise the Son too, having said, “The Lord created me,” lest we should suspect his nature of being made common with the rest of the creatures, of necessity added, “But before all the hills he begets me,” presenting to us a reverent and impassible notion of his sonship from God the Father.

**73,20,7a** But the Father once and the Son once set forth for us the word “begotten”, because of the reverent true-born sonship of God spoken of above.

**73,20,7b** But the whole New Testament is full of the names of Father and Son.

**73,21,1** But so that those who are making the heresy new may be made known from their own words, from the many writings of theirs on the subject we have noted a few, because of the length, from which the catholics, having learned the whole sense of the heresy, will of necessity, I think, judge that those who wrote these things must anathematize them, and must themselves cast their own writings out of the apostolic faith, and must also anathematize those who think and teach the same as they do.

**73,21,2a** For they write in these very words: “For I have been eager to impart to you briefly the chief of the finest words that are in God.”

**73,21,2b** “All who suppose that the Son preserves likeness in essence to the Father have gone outside the truth, bringing a charge against the ‘like in essence’ by means of the appellation unbegotten.”

**73,21,3a** And again they will say: “But the Son both is, and is confessed to be, inferior by reason of generation.”

**73,21,3b** “Therefore he does not preserve likeness in essence to the Unbegotten, but he does preserve it by bearing the will of God unmixed in his own hypostasis.”

**73,21,3c** “He therefore preserves a likeness, not in essence, but in the principle of the will, because he brought him into subsistence such as he willed.”

**73,21,3d** And again: “How is it that you yourself do not also concede to me that in essence the Son bears no likeness to the Father?”

**73,21,4** And again: “When indeed the Son is confessed to be without end, having life not from his own nature but from the authority of the Unbegotten, while the unbegotten nature is endlessly superior to all authority, how are the impious plain to see, who exchange the ‘other in essence’ of the preaching of piety for likeness of essence?”

**73,21,5** And again: “Because the name Father is indicative not of essence but of authority, which brought the Son into subsistence before the ages as God the Word, with the essence and authority bestowed in him, which he continues to hold without end.”

**73,21,6** And again: “They want ‘Father’ to be indicative of essence and not of authority; then let them also call the hypostasis of the Only-begotten by the name Father.”

**73,22,1a** We shall now say to the present heretics: You wrote “like in will, unlike in essence”.

**73,22,1b** Therefore we wrote in reply that he is like not by imitation only, but also in essence.

**73,22,2** Since, then, you were the first to mention essence, saying “unlike in essence”, and for this reason are eager to have the term essence removed, so that you may say that the Son is like only in will,

**73,22,3** if you truly agree that in all things the Son resembles the Father, anathematize those who speak of a difference of likeness, and write thus: If anyone should not call the Son like the Father in all things, as Son to Father, but should say that he is like in will but unlike in essence, let him be anathema.

**73,22,4** And after this, if they wish to make mention of the term essence – and they are also setting aside their own signatures, in which they mentioned essence everywhere – let them also confess the teaching of the fathers, that the Son is, once for all, like the Father in all things, not only in will, but in being and in subsisting and in existing, as Son to Father, as the divine Scriptures say.

**73,22,5a** To the faith set forth concerning the Son’s being like the Father in all things they signed thus: Mark, the bishop of Arethusa: I believe thus and am of one mind with what is written above; and those present likewise.

**73,22,5b** And Valens thus: How we signed the subscription written above, on the night when Pentecost was dawning, those present know, and the pious emperor, to whom I also bore witness, both without writing and in writing.

**73,22,6** After this, when Valens had signed according to his own custom, and had added to his signature the words “the Son like the Father” without adding “in all things”, and had shown how he agreed to what was written above, or how he understands the consubstantial, and when the pious emperor had noted this and compelled him to add “in all things” – which Basil also added, suspecting that he had likewise added the “in all things” with a private meaning of his own – Valens and his party were eager to take the document in order to carry it to the council at Ariminum; he signed thus:

**73,22,7a** Basil, bishop of Ancyra: I believe and agree with what is written above, confessing the Son like the Father in all things.

**73,22,7b** And “in all things” not only in will, but in hypostasis and in existence and in being, as Son according to the divine Scriptures, spirit from spirit, life from life, light from light, God from God, true Son from true, Son who is wisdom from the wise God and Father, and, once for all, the Son like the Father in all things, as Son to Father.

**73,22,8a** And if anyone says that he is like in some particular respect, as has been written above, he is alien to the catholic church, as one who does not call the Son like the Father in accordance with the divine Scriptures.

**73,22,8b** The signature was read out and handed to Valens; there were present Mark, George, Ursacius, Germanus and Hypatianus, bishops, and a number of presbyters and deacons.

**73,23,1** These letters have been placed here so that every lover of learning who searches out the truths of the faith may know that we are not carried along idly in speaking against certain people, but make it our aim to set out from true evidence.

**73,23,2** These same men, then, fell out again with their own associates, through hatred of certain persons and human jealousy, each wrangling with the other and loving pre-eminence; and the faction of these Semi-Arians then gained strength – I mean Basil and George and Silvanus and the rest – having with them a right hand of flesh, the emperor Constantius, [...] the party of Eudoxius and George of Alexandria and Euzoius of Antioch.

**73,23,3** And Basil and George of Laodicea, with their followers, were brought low, although they had been very powerful; and from them others again were divided off from the same heresy and council, and the body of the Arians came to be in three factions.

**73,23,4** For Acacius the Palestinian, of Caesarea, together with Meletius and Uranius of Tyre and Eutychius of Eleutheropolis, because of his jealousy and hatred toward Cyril of Jerusalem, opposed Basil and George of Laodicea with their followers, and Silvanus of Tarsus, and also Eleusius of Cyzicus, Macedonius the Constantinopolitan, Eustathius of Sebaste, and Anianus the Antiochene, who had then been appointed; marshalling himself against them, the same Acacius produced great confusion.

**73,23,5** And they came to stand against one another, holding an opinion of the same doctrine, but, as each of them confessed it differently, at variance with one another; and being split, they were torn apart into the three factions already mentioned.

**73,23,6** For Acacius and those with him confessed neither the consubstantial nor a creature, one of the creatures, though they were the same; but having for the time being secretly passed over in silence the word creature, they were themselves wholly such as the Arians are, yet they hid themselves at that time, holding no other view but this, on account of those mixed in with them, who were orthodox by nature but were hypocrites, playing a part because of the emperor’s right hand and being afraid, and having enmity toward one another, wishing to keep their footing.

**73,23,7** For Eutychius of Eleutheropolis, inasmuch as he held from the blessed Maximonas, the confessor bishop of Jerusalem, the clear faith of orthodoxy, because of his enmity toward Cyril did not blend with the party of Acacius, holding orthodox views for a time, but playing a part for the sake of his own see.

**73,23,8** And many others of Palestine, on whose account Acacius and those with him, who had the same madness and frenzied false belief, for the time being made no move about these matters, neither to confess nor to deny, but, assembling at the Seleucia called Tracheia in Isauria, by order of the emperor Constantius, set forth, forsooth, another creed – not in accordance with the one drawn up by the fathers in the city of Nicaea, the orthodox and well-ordered one, but feignedly, as though speaking in simplicity.

**73,24,1a** “We believe in one God, Father almighty,” and so on.

**73,24,1b** And “in the Son of God”, in plain terms, saying nothing forceful.

**73,24,1c** Afterwards, in order to put their play-acting on display, they said, “We reject the consubstantial as foreign to the divine Scripture, but we anathematize the unlike of the Son to the Father.”

**73,24,2a** And this was the bait of crafty hunters.

**73,24,2b** For when they were among themselves, they used to say and teach that, while the Son of God is a creature, he is like the Father, in the sense of likeness that is current among men.

**73,24,3a** For sculptors too fashion statues and model likenesses, either of gold and silver and other material, or with colours on wood, and these have the likeness, but nothing by way of equality with the things portrayed.

**73,24,3b** So the craft among them lay in this: to confess him like the Father, but to have nothing whatever of the Father’s Godhead.

**73,24,4a** But some of those with them accepted it as well, because of the calamity of the times that had so befallen, and most of them were at the same time in the secret, while some were also ignorant, as was shown later.

**73,24,4b** For with them was Patrophilus of Scythopolis, and with these Philip, who was appointed there as successor of the aforesaid, and many others, who by nature held this heresy.

**73,24,5** But now, after their death, when their false belief has spread abroad, and they enjoy freedom of speech because of the right hand of flesh, and are no longer hindered, they openly proclaim their design, no longer restrained by any shame nor putting on appearances because of any decree;

**73,24,6a** but so that no one may think that I am being carried along at random, I shall set out here the creed set forth there by the very men of Acacius’ party, with the signatures of those who were at that council.

**73,24,6b** And it is as follows.

**73,25,1** The bishops who assembled from various provinces at Seleucia in Isauria by order of the piety of Constantius, our most God-fearing emperor – we who were gathered at Seleucia in Isauria by the imperial will have declared the following.

**73,25,2** Yesterday, which was the fifth day before the Kalends of October, we applied every effort, with all good order, to preserve peace for the church and to treat the matters of the faith soundly, as our most God-beloved emperor Constantius commanded, in accordance with the prophetic words, and to introduce nothing into the faith of the church contrary to the divine Scriptures.

**73,25,3** But since at the council certain persons insulted some of us, silenced others, not allowing them to speak, and shut out others against their will, and had with them those who had been deposed from various provinces, and brought with them those who had been appointed contrary to the canon, so that the assembly was full of uproar from every quarter, as the most illustrious count Leonas, and Lauricius, the province’s most illustrious governor, saw for themselves, for this reason we declare that we do not shun the authentic creed of the Dedication at Antioch, and we bring it forward – the creed in which our fathers themselves especially concurred at that time with regard to the subject under inquiry.

**73,25,4** Since the “consubstantial” and the “like in essence” have troubled many in times past and up to now, and moreover the “unlike” of the Son to the Father is said to be introduced as a novelty by some even until the present, for this reason we reject the “consubstantial” as foreign to the Scriptures, but anathematize the “unlike”, and regard all who are such as aliens from the church.

**73,25,5a** But we clearly acknowledge the Son’s likeness to the Father, in accordance with the apostle, who says of the Son, “who is the image of the invisible God.”

**73,25,5b** And we confess and believe in one God, Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of things visible and invisible.

**73,25,7** And we believe also in our Lord Jesus Christ, God’s Son, who was begotten from him impassibly before all ages, God the Word, God from God, only-begotten, light, life, truth, wisdom, power, through whom all things came to be, those in the heavens and those on the earth, whether visible or invisible.

**73,25,8** We believe that he, at the consummation of the ages, for the abolition of sin, took flesh from the holy virgin and became man, suffered for our sins and rose again and was taken up into the heavens, to sit at the right hand of the Father, coming again in glory to judge the living and the dead.

**73,25,9a** We believe, moreover, in one Holy Spirit as well, whom our Saviour and Lord Jesus Christ also named Paraclete, having promised after his ascension to send him to the disciples, whom he also sent, through whom he also sanctifies those in the church who believe and are baptized in the name of Father and Son and Holy Spirit.

**73,25,9b** Those who preach anything other than this faith the catholic church knows to be aliens.

**73,25,10a** And that the creed lately set forth at Sirmium, under the piety of our emperor, is of equal force with this faith, those who read the creed recognize.

**73,25,10b** Those present signed: Basil, Mark and George, the bishop of Alexandria, Pancratius and Hypatianus, and the majority of the western bishops.

**73,25,10c** George, bishop of Alexandria: I have set forth the faith thus; I confess that I think as is set out above.

**73,25,10d** Acacius, bishop of Caesarea: I have set forth the faith thus; I confess that I think as is set out above.

**73,25,10e** Uranius, the bishop of Tyre; Eutychius, the bishop of Eleutheropolis.

**73,25,10f** Zoilus, the bishop of Larissa in Syria; Seras, the bishop from Paraetonium in Libya; Paul, the bishop of Emesa; Eustathius, the bishop of Epiphania; Irenaeus, the bishop of Tripolis in Phoenicia; Eusebius, the bishop of Seleucia in Syria; Eutychianus, the bishop of Patara in Lycia; Eustathius, the bishop of Pinara and Sidyma; Basil, the bishop of the Caunians in Lydia; Peter, the bishop of Hippos in Palestine; Stephen, the bishop of Ptolemais in Libya; Eudoxius, bishop; Apollonius, the bishop of Oxyrhynchus; Theoctistus, the bishop of Ostracine; Leontius, the bishop of Lydia; Theodosius, the bishop of Philadelphia, Lydia; Phoebus, the bishop of Polychalandus in Lydia; Magnus, the bishop of Themisa in Phrygia; Evagrius, the bishop of Mitylene in the Islands; Cyrion, the bishop of Doliche; Augustus, the bishop of Euphrates; [Magnus, the bishop of Themisa in Phrygia;] Polydeuces, the bishop of the province of Second Libya; Pancratius, the bishop of Pelusium; Philicadus, the bishop of Augustada in the Phrygian province; Serapion, the bishop of Antipyrgus in Libya; Eusebius, the bishop of Sebaste in Palestine; Heliodorus, the bishop of Sozusa in the Pentapolis; Ptolemy, the bishop of Thmuis in Augustonice; Augarus, the bishop of Cyrus in Euphrasia; Exeresius, the bishop of Gerasa; Arabion, the bishop of Adraa; Charisius, the bishop of Azotus; Elissaeus, the bishop of Diocletianopolis.

**73,25,10g** Germanus, the bishop of Petra; Barochius, the bishop of Arabia.

**73,25,10h** In all, forty-three bishops.

**73,25,10i** The statement of the aforesaid Semi-Arians and Arians is completed up to this point.

**73,27,1** You who are sensible, having gone through this statement and the others, recognize how unscrupulous is the scheme of one of their two bodies, and that there is nothing right in it, nothing that shares even a little in the confession that accords with God.

**73,27,2a** For the Lord declares, saying, “What you heard in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops.”

**73,27,2b** And as the holy apostle says, “Let each one speak truth with his neighbour.”

**73,27,2c** And the prophet, refuting their malice, brings it to light, saying, “He speaks peaceably with his neighbour, but in his heart he holds enmity,” that is to say, wickedness.

**73,27,3** So also these men of Acacius’ party, divided off from Basil’s party, wishing to loose the bond of the true confession, set forth a bastard statement, easily caught out from every side and loose, so that from these words, if they wished to deceive some, they could confess what is right, but if they wished to bring out the poison of their false belief,

**73,27,4** this statement would serve them as one that plays both ways between the two positions and can make the confession of either of their constructions.

**73,27,5** But since, in this council of Acacius, which was divided off from the other two councils – for we have said how the order of the Arians was divided into three factions: how Eudoxius and Germanus, and George of Alexandria and Euzoius of Antioch broke off into one faction;

**73,27,6** Basil and Eleusius, Eustathius and George of Laodicea, Silvanus of Tarsus, Macedonius the Constantinopolitan and a good many others were likewise divided off into one faction.

**73,27,7** And Acacius again, as I said before, and Meletius and Eutychius and certain others – another faction: these too came into being, and the whole business was full of trickery.

**73,27,8a** For what each one thought, that the other also held; but they were divided into schisms against one another, or by some hatred toward one another, because Cyril of Jerusalem bore a grudge against Eutychius and Eutychius against Cyril.

**73,27,8b** And Cyril was with Basil the Galatian and Anianus, who had been appointed over Antioch, and George of Laodicea.

**73,27,9a** But why do I wear myself out dividing and recounting the factions?

**73,27,9b** I shall come to the refutations of these men and the overthrow of the craftiness of each of them.

**73,27,9c** But first I must speak about what happened later.

**73,27,9d** For this turned out for some to goodness, but for others to wickedness.

**73,28,1a** For Meletius, who was appointed in Antioch by Acacius’ party – for this is the origin of Acacius’ stance, so as to turn aside even a little from their heterodox opinion, and he shows himself, forsooth, among the orthodox, in order to confirm the aforesaid Meletius in his appointment.

**73,28,1b** For this Meletius, having been appointed by these very men of Acacius’ party, was thought by them to be of their own opinion, but he was not found to be so, as many report about him.

**73,28,2** For now those who are attached to him and to his faction, from the time when he was persecuted and driven from his own see, advancing with time and with the long duration of his persecution, and attaching themselves to it for God’s sake, are orthodox.

**73,28,3** For the greater part of the laity belonged to this faction, the one of the council; and they, having appointed bishops for themselves, confess admirably concerning the Son and do not reject the consubstantial, but say that they hold it in readiness, should a full council take place, to confess it and not deny it.

**73,28,4a** For it came about that this same most honourable Meletius, appointed by the Arians of Acacius’ party, gave an exposition, as a first-fruit, at his first address in the church of the Antiochenes; and, as most say, in orthodox fashion.

**73,28,4b** I shall set out his exposition here, and it is as follows.

**73,28,4c** Copy of a homily of Meletius.

**73,29,1a** The most wise Preacher says that the end of a discourse is good beyond its beginning.

**73,29,1b** Inasmuch as it is better and safer to cease from the contest of speaking than to begin it, especially when the same Preacher says, “This wisdom of the poor man is despised, and his words are not heard.”

**73,29,2a** Since the body is not a single member but many, and all the members take thought for one another, so that there may be no division within the body, and the head cannot tell the feet, “Of you I have no need,” but “God has blended the body together, giving greater honour to the part that lacks.”

**73,29,2b** That, when the whole body is moved, one cannot excuse oneself from being moved along with it, is self-evident.

**73,29,3a** But what beginning might one make of the discourse before us?

**73,29,3b** Or is it plain that, at the beginning of every word and deed, it is fitting to make peace the beginning and the end, and, beginning from it, to end in it?

**73,29,3c** For this, the apostle says, will turn out for salvation by means of your prayer and the Spirit’s supply, whom Jesus bestows on all who believe in him.

**73,29,4** And whether one speaks edification, or exhortation, or the consolation of love, or the fellowship of the Spirit, it comes about through the peace that is according to God, not indeed to all without distinction, but to the lovers of the law, as the prophet puts it: the law, not the bodily one, which has an image and shadow of the things to come, but the spiritual one, which wisely unveils the outcome of what was proclaimed beforehand.

**73,29,5a** “For great peace,” he says, “is for those who love you, and for them there is no stumbling-block,” so that it is plain that the stumbling-block remains for those who have hated peace, and that those who long to be freed from these should hold up love toward the Lord before them as a kind of shield.

**73,29,5b** “For he is our peace, who made both one and broke down the dividing wall of the fence, abolishing in his flesh the enmity, the law of commandments in ordinances.”

**73,29,6a** And neither can the Lord’s commandment be kept unless the love of God goes first.

**73,29,6b** “For if you love me,” he says, “you will keep my commandments”; nor is it possible for the eyes or the heart to be enlightened, unless the commandment enlightens them.

**73,29,6c** “For the commandment of the Lord,” he says, “is far-shining, enlightening the eyes”; but neither is it possible to put forth a word of truth unless one has Christ speaking within him, according to him who says, “If you seek a proof of the Christ who speaks in me,” or rather, who not only speaks but also shows mercy.

**73,29,7a** “For let your mercy and your salvation come upon me,” he says, “and I shall give an answer to those who reproach me.”

**73,29,7b** This would not come to be unless one seeks out the statutes.

**73,29,7c** For with those who are not so disposed, the shame that lies in reproaches rests on their outward bearing, so that they cannot say, “Remove from me reproach and contempt.”

**73,29,7d** And the word of truth is removed from the mouth, so that it is of no further avail to the one who prays, “Do not take the word of truth out of my mouth.”

**73,30,1a** And when does this happen?

**73,30,1b** When one does not keep the law continually; when one does not walk in a broad place.

**73,30,1c** The heart must be enlarged if anyone means to make room for Christ walking within – Christ whose glory is told not by men but by the heavens; for “the heavens tell the glory of God” – or rather by the Father himself, who says, “This is my Son, the beloved, in whom I am well pleased.”

**73,30,2** Him it is not possible to confess “if one speaks unrighteousness on high to his neighbour”, if one should call himself into the rank and name of the antichrists, having forsaken the Christians’ rank and name, concerning whom it is said, “Do not touch my anointed ones.”

**73,30,3a** “For who,” he says, “is the liar, but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ?”

**73,30,3b** “This,” he says, “is the antichrist.”

**73,30,3c** “For he who denies the Son does not have the Father either, but he who confesses the Son confesses the Father also.”

**73,30,3d** “What then,” he says, “you heard from the beginning, let it remain in you.”

**73,30,3e** “And if,” he says, “what you heard from the beginning remains in you, you too will remain in the Son and in the Father.”

**73,30,4a** And we shall remain when we make our confession in the presence of God and of the elect angels, and also before kings, and are not ashamed.

**73,30,4b** “For I spoke,” he says, “of your testimonies before kings, and I was not ashamed.”

**73,30,4c** That he is Son of God, God from God, One from One, Only-begotten from the Unbegotten, the choice offspring of him who begot him, and a Son worthy of him who is without beginning, the inexpressible interpreter of the inexpressible, Word and Wisdom and Power of him who is beyond wisdom and power, beyond what a tongue can utter, beyond what thought can move toward.

**73,30,5** An offspring perfect and abiding, from one perfect and abiding in sameness, not flowing out from the Father, nor cut off and divided, but come forth impassibly and entire from him who has lost nothing of what he had.

**73,30,6a** And that the Son is and is called Word, yet is not understood as a voice of the Father, nor as an utterance.

**73,30,6b** For he subsists of himself and acts, and through him are all things and in him are all things, just as also, being himself Wisdom, he is not understood as a thought of the Father, nor as a movement and activity of the ruling faculty, but as an offspring like the Father and reproducing exactly the stamp of the Father.

**73,30,7a** For “him has God the Father sealed”; and it is not that he exists in another while not subsisting of himself, but he is an active offspring, which has made this universe and always preserves it.

**73,30,7b** These things are sufficient to free us both from the error of the Greeks and from the self-made worship of the Jews and from the false belief of the heretics.

**73,31,1a** But since certain persons, perverting the sense of the words that stand in the Scriptures and interpreting them otherwise than is fitting, and understanding neither the force of the terms nor the nature of the things, dare to set aside the Godhead of the Son, stumbling at the word of creating that occurs in the Proverbs, “For the Lord created me as beginning of his ways, unto his works” – men who ought to follow the life-giving Spirit, and not the letter that kills.

**73,31,1b** For the Spirit gives life.

**73,31,2** Come then, let us too venture to treat these matters a little, not because it has not been said fully by those who have spoken before us – for one would be mad to say this – nor because you need a teacher – for you yourselves are taught by God – but that we may be made manifest in our consciences as being among those who desire to impart some spiritual gift to you.

**73,31,3** Believe, then, that neither elsewhere in Scripture nor in the present passage are the words of Scripture contrary to one another, even if they seem to conflict in the eyes of those who are not sound in the faith, or who are weak in judgement, and that none of the examples found in the world can be discovered which suffices of itself to present clearly the nature of the Only-begotten.

**73,31,4** And for this reason Scripture has used many conceptions and names concerning the Only-begotten, if somehow through what is on our level we might be able to grasp what is above us, and through what is known to form an image of what is unknown, being led on gently and little by little from the manifest to the hidden.

**73,31,5a** Since, then, it was needful that those who believe should believe in Christ, that the Son is like the Father, being indeed the image of him who is over all, he who is through all, through whom all things have been fashioned, both those in the heavens and those on earth.

**73,31,5b** But an image, not as a lifeless thing is of a living one, nor as the working of an art, nor as the product of an activity, but an offspring of him who begot him.

**73,31,6** And that it is not right for the Only-begotten’s generation, which is before the ages, to be characterized by bodily human generation; and that, after the pattern of wisdom, which comprehends human thoughts – the Father’s wisdom, however, being not without hypostasis or existence – Scripture used both words, that of creating and that of begetting, both “he created” and “he begot”, not so that contrary things should seem to be said of the same things in the same respect, but so that through “he created” it might present what is subsistent and abiding, and through “he begot” what is special and distinctive to the Only-begotten.

**73,31,7a** “I,” he says, “came forth from the Father, and I am come.”

**73,31,7b** And the name of wisdom too is sufficient to shut out every notion of passion.

**73,32,1** But where are we being carried off to, forgetful of the one who said, “O depth of riches and of wisdom of the knowledge of God! How beyond searching are his judgements, and how untraceable his ways”?

**73,32,2a** For we have as our teacher the Spirit of truth, whom the Lord gave us after his taking up into the heavens, “that we may see the things freely given to us by God, in which we also speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in those taught by the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual”, in whom we serve and worship.

**73,32,2b** Therefore we are dishonoured in him in whom the prophets prophesied, in whom the righteous were guided, through whom we are brought to the Son.

**73,32,2c** But why are we busying ourselves with the matters of the nature?

**73,32,2d** For are we, then, conversing as with people of the flesh, and not as with spiritual people?

**73,32,3a** For it was said in the case of others, “We cannot speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to people of the flesh.”

**73,32,3b** For there is cause to fear lest, through contentiousness over things incomprehensible and through the search into things unattainable, we fall into an abyss of impiety.

**73,32,3c** “And I said, I will become wise; and it went far from me, beyond what it was, and a deep depth: who shall find it?”

**73,32,4a** For let us remember the one who said, “In part we know and in part we were prophesying; but when the perfect has come, then what is partial will be abolished.

**73,32,4b** If anyone thinks he knows, he has not yet known as he ought to know.”

**73,32,4c** And for this reason there is cause to fear lest perhaps we be forcing ourselves to speak about things of which we are not able to speak.

**73,32,4d** For one must speak from faith, not believe from what is spoken.

**73,32,4e** For “I believed,” it says, “therefore I spoke.”

**73,32,5** When, then, unable as we are to declare anything about our own birth, we busy ourselves with curiosities and set about contending over the begetting of God, how is there not cause to fear lest he who grants not merely an instructed tongue but also the knowing of when a word ought to be spoken should condemn our rashness in speaking to silence?

**73,32,6** This is what was done in the case of the blessed Zacharias, who, since he did not believe the one who brought him the good news of the child’s birth, but put the grace and power of God to the test with human calculations, and debated with himself whether an old man has it in his nature to beget a child by a woman advanced in years — what does he say?

**73,32,7a** “How shall I know this, that it will be?

**73,32,7b** For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days.”

**73,32,7c** Accordingly, when he heard, “Behold, you shall be silent and unable to speak”, he did not speak when he came out.

**73,33,1a** Therefore, ceasing to contend over things disputed and over things beyond us, we hold fast to what we have received.

**73,33,1b** For who is it that dares to be puffed up with knowledge, when the very man who was counted worthy of the revelations, “he who was taken up into the third heaven, he who heard words not to be uttered”, was chastened into sobriety by the thorn in respect of the flesh, lest he be lifted up above measure?

**73,33,2a** And the very prophet who said, “I believed, therefore I spoke; I was humbled”, says, “not merely, but exceedingly.”

**73,33,2b** For the nearer anyone seems to be to knowledge, the more he ought to reckon within himself that he is a man.

**73,33,2c** On this, hear what he says: “But I said in my ecstasy, Every man is a liar.”

**73,33,3a** Since, then, we have the teacher of truth, let us no longer make use of human teachers, but, taking thought, let us busy ourselves neither about modes nor about anything else.

**73,33,3b** For just as it is not possible to tell the begetting of the Son, so neither is it possible to declare the manner of the begetting from the Father; but one must consider this sufficient for teaching, that “all things came into being through him, and without him not even one thing came into being.”

**73,33,4** May the Lord grant that we, minded like Abraham, the one who says, “I have now begun to speak to my Lord, and I am earth and ashes”, and not exalting ourselves like the cedars of Lebanon — since it is not in words taught by human wisdom but in those taught by faith that the smooth and peaceable wisdom is attained — may not be in perplexity,

**73,33,5a** but, whatever we do, may be well-pleasing to God and the Father, and with him also to the Son together with him in the Holy Spirit, to whom be the glory, the might, the honour and the power, now and always and to the ages of ages.

**73,33,5b** Amen.

**73,33,5c** The confession of Meletius is concluded.

**73,34,1a** It seemed good to these people, the greater part of the Arians, to transfer him from the Pontic country, not to their joy nor for their relief, but to their vexation.

**73,34,1b** Thereupon they stir up the emperor and plot against the man, on the ground that he had not confessed him a perfect creature, and they thrust him out of his see.

**73,34,2** And the man is driven by night into an exile that lasts up to these present times; he is still in his own homeland, a man honoured and much loved, above all because of what we now hear he has accomplished, and because of what those under him in Antioch now confess, no longer making any mention at all, not even in passing, of the word ‘creature’, but confessing Father and Son and Holy Spirit consubstantial, three hypostases, one essence, one Godhead;

**73,34,3a** as is the true faith, the faith from of old, prophetic, evangelical and apostolic, which our fathers and bishops who assembled at the council of Nicaea confessed, in the time of Constantine, the great and most blessed emperor.

**73,34,3b** May it come about that the most honoured Meletius himself also confesses thus, like those under him in Antioch and those in certain other places who confess thus.

**73,34,4** For there are also some among those who appear to be in communion with him and with his synod who blaspheme the Holy Spirit, speaking rightly about the Son but holding the Spirit to be created and wholly alien to God; about these we shall later, in the refutation of their heresy, say everything precisely, as far as we are able.

**73,35,1a** The man, then, is held in honour by us, as I said, because of such reports about him.

**73,35,1b** For in other respects too his life is dignified and his character good, and he is beloved by the people in every way, since his life is extolled as godlike by all.

**73,35,2** But some — whether carried away by hatred or by envy, or wishing to magnify their own cause, I cannot say — have put about certain accounts concerning him too, to the effect that the movement against him came about not because of orthodoxy, but, they say, because of canonical matters and a squabble between him and his own clergy, and because he had admitted some whom he had long before expelled and anathematised.

**73,35,3a** But we have not at all taken these things to heart, chiefly because of what was afterwards corrected day by day in his synod and confessed in the faith, as I have already shown above.

**73,35,3b** For in this part one must speak the truth as far as one can, according to our weakness in all things.

**73,35,4a** For whether it escaped the man in the rush of his exposition of the words, I cannot say; whether the expression was brought out by him in simplicity, is known to God.

**73,35,4b** Except that in one part two or three blameworthy expressions are found in the same exposition: in his taking up the term ‘creature’ at all concerning the Son of God in his Godhead, even if only as far as the name, and in his saying ‘beyond wisdom’, and whatever else there may be.

**73,36,1a** After saying a few things in answer to what they have put forward, we shall pass over this account too.

**73,36,1b** Tell us, you people: what pained you about calling the ‘homoiousios’ ‘homoousios’?

**73,36,1c** Confess it to us plainly, so that we may recognise you too as our own and not as strangers.

**73,36,1d** For bronze too can be ‘homoiousios’ with gold, tin with silver, lead with iron.

**73,36,1e** But your contrived and finely turned myth-making will not deceive us.

**73,36,2** For if, wishing to deceive some, you choose to put forward false pretexts, saying that one must not say ‘homoousios’, lest we make a fusion of the Son with the Father, or of the Spirit with Son and Father, then in this too your contrived argument has fallen to pieces.

**73,36,3** For we did not say ‘hamaousios’ but ‘homoousios’, so that we might confess nothing differing from the Father, but God truly begotten of God, and not from elsewhere, nor from things that are not, but come forth from the Father, begotten timelessly, without beginning and indescribably, ever being with the Father and never ceasing to be, but begotten — not a brother, not a forefather.

**73,36,4a** For ‘homou’ signifies two hypostases that are not alien in nature; therefore the bond of truth in this word was arranged by the Holy Spirit in the mouth of those who set it forth, and you observe that no pretext will be left to you, nor can you speak against orthodoxy and frighten those who accept from you what they hear of your counterfeit doctrine, saying that if anyone says ‘homoousios’ he has confessed a fusion.

**73,36,4b** For this will no longer hold.

**73,36,5** For from ‘homoousios’ two will be signified, and from ‘homoousios’ it will be made plain that the offspring is not alien to the Father.

**73,36,6** But you, who have fabricated ‘homoiousios’, will be convicted by the term ‘essence’, and condemned by your altered confession, as not thinking what you say, but teaching in counterfeit form what you think; for if he is not from him at all, but is like him, you have strayed far from the truth.

**73,36,7a** For with whatever materials anyone might wish to adorn the one being portrayed, he would not produce something equal to the one portrayed; for the work, too, is a matter of craftsmanship.

**73,36,7b** But what is begotten of someone preserves, in relation to its kind, the like and equal form of legitimate birth.

**73,36,8** If, then, the Son has not been begotten of the Father himself, but should be outside him, and is to be called ‘homoiousios’ by you by grace, you have given him nothing, but have fallen from the grace that comes from him.

**73,36,9a** “For he who does not honour the Son as he honours the Father, the wrath of God abides on him,” says the holy apostle.

**73,36,9b** And again: “From the Father I came forth, and I am come.”

**73,36,9c** He who declared, “I am within the Father, and the Father within me”; he who says, “Philip, he who has seen me has seen the Father.”

**73,37,1** Having often given an account of these matters too, we think we are sufficiently provided here with the same refutations that were given above against the root which put forth these people’s wrong belief, since they are able here too to refute these Semi-Arians already mentioned, and those who split off from them,

**73,37,2** Acacius and his party and the others who set forth at Seleucia in Isauria another creed contrary to that of the truth; and this creed too, set forth by them and written in the name of them all, we have placed above in its entirety, likewise after Basil of Ancyra’s and George of Laodicea’s, wishing to bring it into the open.

**73,37,3** But so that I may not seem to have done this through forgetfulness, by treating as secondary this creed too, which works its mischief in secret but has taken a muzzle upon its mouth, as with a bridle, because of the season of hypocrisy, I shall also say a few things against it and against those who set it forth, the aforementioned party of Acacius, Euzoius, Eutychius and the others.

**73,37,4a** Now it is evident that the creed set out above has changed the confession of the truth.

**73,37,4b** But so that some may not say that we have spoken against these men by way of slander, let us show what, as time went on, was seen and detected in the aforementioned synod of these same men;

**73,37,5a** for from among them is Euzoius of Caesarea, being their disciple, even though he succeeded Acacius after the installation of Philumenus, who was installed by Cyril of Jerusalem, and after the installation of Cyril the elder, who was installed by Eutychius’ party, and after the installation of Gelasius, who was installed in turn by Cyril of Jerusalem; for he was his sister’s son.

**73,37,5b** For when the three had been installed and had been left idle because of their strife with one another, the aforementioned Euzoius was installed in turn.

**73,37,6a** From among them, then, was Gemellinus as well; from among them Philip of Scythopolis; from among them Athanasius of Scythopolis.

**73,37,6b** These men, not in secret but openly, as men without experience of the good, not only teach the doctrines of Arius but fight hard for their heresy, and persecute those who teach the truth, no longer wishing to refute them with words, but handing over those who believe rightly to hostilities, wars and swords.

**73,37,6c** For they have wrought ruin not on one city and country, but on many.

**73,38,1a** This is the Lucius who did so many things in Alexandria against those who confess the Son of God in truth.

**73,38,1b** And to which of those who have understanding of God is their faction not evident day by day?

**73,38,1c** For they proclaim publicly that the Son of God is created, and that the Holy Spirit too is created and wholly alien to the essence of God.

**73,38,2a** For as to Eudoxius and his party: ever since George of Alexandria shamefully met his end, he also received the first place, and friendship with the authority that is pre-eminent.

**73,38,2b** Eudoxius, who was of the party of Hypatius and Eunomius, appeared through a kind of flattery as one under reproof, yet did not cease to hold the views of the Anomoeans,

**73,38,3** while concealing those whom they had once exiled for such an exposition of the pit; he himself advanced Demophilus, Hypatius and Eunomius, the pupils of Aetius — the man once banished to the regions of the Taurus, whom George of Alexandria had installed as deacon — from whom the root of the Anomoeans sprang;

**73,38,4** and just as, though the thorny wood is one and the root the same, the branchings differ as on each thorn, so too the malice of these people, with the misinterpretations of their heterodox sect advancing for the worse, in one way at one time and in another way at another, has spewed out its ruin upon the world, as we shall again say later concerning this Anomoean.

**73,38,5** For the present, thinking it well to stop here, and having, as it were, overturned and thrust aside a dreadful reptile — we have indeed overturned it — let us trample it and leave it dead, and, turning aside, hasten on to those that follow, calling on God to help us likewise to fulfil our promise.

### Sect 74: Pneumatomachi

Against the Pneumatomachi, the fifty-fourth, but the seventy-fourth in the series.

**74,1,1** From these Semi-Arians and from some of the orthodox, men have risen up against us, born to some, so to speak, as a monstrosity, double-natured and half-formed, like the Centaurs, or Pans, or Sirens of those who wrote down the myths:

**74,1,2** some of them, being from Arius and professing to define the Son not as a perfect creature but as a Son timelessly begotten — though they speak of him who is from heaven and hither with a suggestion of time, not being freed from the expression first spewed out by Arius, which says that there was once when he was not — saying that he is before all times, he through whom all things came into being, blaspheme the Holy Spirit.

**74,1,3a** Others hold orthodox views concerning the Son also as to nature: that he always was with the Father and never ceased to be.

**74,1,3b** But though they hold that he was begotten of the Father without beginning and timelessly, against the Holy Spirit all these blaspheme, since they do not count him together with Father and Son within the Godhead.

**74,1,4a** We have often discussed this at length, and in each heresy we have set out in no small measure the true account concerning him, how he is properly spoken of together with the Father and the Son.

**74,1,4b** For “the Spirit of the Lord has filled the inhabited earth”: the Spirit of the truth, the Spirit of God.

**74,1,4c** For he is named Spirit of the Lord, both as going forth from the Father and as taking from the Son, bestowing the gifts in various ways as he wills, searching even the depths of God, being with the Father and the Son, baptising, sealing, perfecting the one who has been sealed.

**74,1,5a** But so as not to take on labour here, I shall set down what I have already said in the great treatise on the faith written to the regions of the Pamphylians, as a rebuttal of those who blaspheme the Holy Spirit, for the instruction of those who read it, and for the delight of those counted worthy of the Holy Spirit.

**74,1,5b** And it is as follows.

**74,1,5c** Discourse from the Ancoratus.

**74,2,1** “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ has been made manifest, instructing us that, renouncing ungodliness and the desires of the world, we should live with self-control, with piety and with uprightness in this present age, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ; who gave himself on our behalf, to ransom us from every lawless deed and to cleanse for himself a people peculiarly his own, eager for good works;

**74,2,2** having wiped out the bond written against us in its decrees, which stood opposed to us, he has removed it from our midst, nailing it to the cross; having stripped the principalities and the authorities, he exposed them publicly, leading them in triumph in it; having smashed the doors of bronze and crushed the bars of iron”, he showed once more the light of life, holding out his hands, making a road, pointing out the stairway to the heavens, deeming us worthy to dwell once again in paradise.

**74,2,3** Accordingly he dwelt among us, and, giving us the just requirement of the law of the Spirit, so that we might know him or the things concerning him — which is the beginning and end of life — he has become for us a law of righteousness, a law of faith, a law of the Spirit, set free of the law of the flesh of sin.

**74,2,4a** Hence “I rejoice in God’s law according to the inward man.”

**74,2,4b** And let Christ be ours, if indeed he dwells in us.

**74,2,5a** But he himself, by dying, has become a way of life for us, “that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for us and rose again”, the cause of life, having remembered the oath sworn many generations before, as David says.

**74,2,5b** “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning their trespasses to them.

**74,2,6** For in him the whole fullness was pleased to make its dwelling, and through him to reconcile all things to him, making peace by the blood of the cross.”

**74,2,7** He has come, therefore, for a dispensation of the fullness of the seasons, just as had been promised to Abraham and to the rest of the saints, to gather up all things under one head in himself, both what is in the heavens and what is upon the earth.

**74,2,8a** There was estrangement and enmity in the time of God’s forbearance, but he brought reconciliation in his body of flesh, through himself making the two into one.

**74,2,8b** “For our peace came, and, having broken down the middle wall of the partition, the enmity, in his flesh, having abolished the law of commandments in ordinances, that he might create the two in himself into one new man.”

**74,2,8c** And he commanded that the Gentiles be fellow members of the body, sharers and joint heirs of the promise, saying, “Come to me, all who toil and are weighed down with burdens, and I will refresh you.”

**74,2,9** Accordingly, in that I was weak through the flesh, the Saviour was sent to me in a likeness of the flesh of sin, fulfilling such a dispensation, that he might redeem me from slavery, that he might redeem me from corruption, that he might redeem me from death.

**74,2,10a** And he became for me righteousness and sanctification and redemption: righteousness, by having loosed sin through faith in him; sanctification, by having freed me by means of water and Spirit and in his word; and redemption, his blood.
