**77,33,5a** Now, this being so, our brothers want to bring before us as proof, “But we have the mind of Christ.”

**77,33,5b** But by their argument, as it is expressed on this understanding, they bring us to suspect that perhaps they have conceived of the mind as something other than Christ.

**77,33,6a** But if they do not reckon the Godhead to be outside the incarnation, but the dispensation to be one, what more, then, will the so-called mind of Christ be?

**77,33,6b** Is it, then, that God the Word exists by himself, without a human mind in the coming in the flesh, as they say, while Christ has another mind besides his own subsistence of Godhead — or is it customary for every exalted expression to be used of us by extension, to set forth the things accomplished in us?

**77,34,1a** For in reality every godly person conducts his life not according to the human mind but according to that of Christ — the mind filled with understanding by Christ, reasoning in righteousness according to Christ, living in Christ by its confession, saved through Christ in doing right.

**77,34,1b** For it is this that is Christ’s mind, able to be in us without confining Christ in a place that encloses him.

**77,34,2** For Father, Son and Holy Spirit are present everywhere, and he dwells within us in a spiritual manner, should we become worthy of him, with no place shutting in either him or his Father or his Holy Spirit; rather, through the might of his Godhead he is found in all things, while unmixed with all things, by reason of his essence, which admits no sharing and no comparison, and his unalloyed and incomprehensible Godhead.

**77,34,3a** But when the apostle says, “But we have the mind of Christ,” what, pray, shall we reckon?

**77,34,3b** Did he have his own human mind, or, being filled with the mind of Christ, did he throw away his own and possess Christ’s mind in place of his own?

**77,34,3c** Not at all.

**77,34,3d** For each one of those listening would grant that he had his own mind, but was filled with Christ’s — Christ, who had adorned him with godliness and knowledge and a heavenly manner of life in God.

**77,34,4** If, then, having his own mind, he was filled with the mind of Christ, then Christ himself, the Word, was also mind — if indeed one must speak so, since to some it has seemed good to call God mind.

**77,34,5a** But I do not regard our mind as a subsistent being, nor does any of the sons of the church, but as a certain activity given us by God and existing in us.

**77,34,5b** But Christ I call a subsistent being, as all the faithful also confess; and I confess him God, and Lord, begotten of the Father, perfect from perfect, and light from light, and God from God.

**77,34,6a** Yet even so, by their own argument, there is the one who in himself is mind, just as the holy apostle teaches concerning him, “But we have the mind of Christ”; and he had — he and those to whom he bears witness — his own mind.

**77,34,6b** And again they were thus filled with the mind of Christ, his grace being able to be brought to perfection in them.

**77,35,1** So, then, on the exactly corresponding comparison, it will make no difference to take this of Christ as well: that Christ, being God in himself, even if he partook of a human mind, as he also shared in flesh and blood and possessed the human soul, was in no way taken captive by the mind.

**77,35,2** For if the apostle, who possessed by nature his own human mind, and the mind that comes from sharing in gift and endowment and grace, no longer conducted his life according to his own mind but was adorned with the mind of Christ by a guidance surpassing nature, how much more did God the Word, having in himself all perfection, being perfection itself, being God himself, power itself, mind itself, light itself, become the one who filled both the mind and the entire body — or rather who perfected them — and in all things work out salvation for us through his coming in the flesh?

**77,35,3a** Such an argument, then, must be set aside, since it has no bearing on such a subject; and the refusal to confess everything complete in Christ, without sin, must be set aside.

**77,35,3b** For the Word, when he came, did all things truly, fulfilling what had been written of him beforehand, as it is written, “Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb,” and what follows: carried in the womb in truth and not in appearance, conceived in the womb in truth, dwelling in flesh in truth, having flesh and soul in truth and mind in truth, and all that a man is, in truth, without sin;

**77,35,4** and born of a virgin womb and of a holy virgin in truth, not of the seed of a man, but having in truth flesh and soul and mind, as I have said; and coming forth through the passages of birth in truth, and wrapped in swaddling clothes in a manger in truth, carried by Mary, and going down into Egypt, and brought back from Egypt, and returning to Nazareth,

**77,35,5** and coming to the Jordan, and baptised by John, and tempted by the devil, and choosing disciples in truth, and having preached the kingdom of heaven, as all things are found to be in truth; betrayed by Judas, and seized by the Jews, presented to Pontius Pilate and by him sentenced to death, handed over to the cross, saying, “I thirst, give me to drink,” receiving in truth, tasting vinegar with gall and accepting no further drink, fastened to the cross, crying out in truth, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani,” bowing his head in truth and breathing his last, the body in truth taken down and received in truth, and wrapped by Joseph, and laid in a tomb in truth, made secure with a stone;

**77,35,6** going down in his Godhead with his soul into Hades, and freeing those in bonds with valour and with power, coming up again, God the Word with his holy soul, with which he delivered them from captivity, raised on the third day in truth with body and soul and the whole instrument in truth, found with the disciples for the forty days, and blessing them on the Mount of Olives in truth, going up into heaven in truth, while the disciples watched him being taken up as far as the clouds in truth, seated and sitting at the right hand of the Father in truth, in the very body and in the Godhead, in the very perfect incarnation,

**77,35,7a** in which he united all things into one and into one spiritual perfection, being God, sitting in glory, coming in truth to judge the living and the dead.

**77,35,7b** And nothing is altered, but all things have been wrought in him perfect, perfectly, in perfection.

**77,36,1a** Judging this to be sufficient on these matters, we have thought it right that what is said about them should go thus far.

**77,36,1b** But concerning the further idle talk of those who say such things, which has reached our ears, it is necessary to point this out as well.

**77,36,1c** Yet we do not altogether believe that this is what is repeated among them.

**77,36,2a** Nevertheless we shall not keep silent about what has reached our ears.

**77,36,2b** For some have even ventured to say that, again, some of them say of Mary that after she had given birth to Christ she was joined in union with her husband, Joseph.

**77,36,3a** But I wonder whether they too say this.

**77,36,3b** But those who say this are people whom we have also numbered among the schisms, when, at a request, we wrote a letter to some persons in Arabia directed against those who say this.

**77,36,4a** And we have said much about this there, in the treatment directed against them.

**77,36,4b** And next in order, with God’s help, I shall subjoin this too as a sect of its own.

**77,36,5a** And others said that the old man had said that in the first resurrection we are to complete a kind of thousand-year period, living by the same ways as now, keeping the law as well as other things, and partaking of everything in use in the world, marriage and circumcision and the rest — which we have not altogether believed about him.

**77,36,5b** But as some have firmly maintained, they said that he had said this.

**77,36,6a** Now that this thousand-year period is written of in the Revelation of John, and that the book is believed by very many, the godly among them, is plain.

**77,36,6b** But most readers of the book, and the devout, knowing about spiritual things and taking what is in it to have a spiritual sense, have believed these things to be true, but set forth with depth.

**77,36,6c** For not only this is said there with depth, but many other things as well.

**77,37,1** But at the present time, for brevity’s sake, I have only made mention of the matter in my account, so that the godly may know that with everyone who wishes to overstep the boundaries of God’s holy church and the hope of the tradition of the prophetic and apostolic faith and teaching, from the one premise of a small and brief argument, his reasoning — straying in an instant, as chance will have it, into a digression of thought —

**77,37,2** will thereafter turn to many empty babblings and dangerous suspicions, and to unsuitable and strange inquiries and endless genealogies, according to what was said by the apostle.

**77,37,3** For that this is very foolish and needs no interpretation is clear to everyone who possesses understanding, since such wisdom and such a premise of argument does not even call for inquiry.

**77,37,4a** For if we are to rise again so as to be circumcised, why have we not undergone circumcision in advance?

**77,37,4b** On this reckoning, then, those who from here on have recognised what is perfect, and have taken it up beforehand so as to be perfected in the perfection that is then to come, are of more importance than we.

**77,37,5a** Where, then, is what was said by the apostle, “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing,” and “You who are justified by the law have fallen from grace”?

**77,37,5b** And how stands what was said by the Lord, “For in the resurrection they do not marry and are not given in marriage; rather they are the equals of angels”?

**77,37,6** But the sayings, “You will sit at the table of my Father, eating and drinking,” and “Whenever I drink it new along with you in the kingdom of heaven,” together with the addition of “new,” and the “at the table of the kingdom,” signify another meaning.

**77,37,7** For we ourselves too, having learned it from the divine words, speak of a certain partaking of ambrosial drink and food, concerning which it is said, “What eye has not seen and ear has not heard, and has not entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him.”

**77,38,1** But, he says, first, in the thousand-year period, we partake of natural pleasures, without toil and grief, and after the thousand-year period we then partake of the things spoken of, as it is written, “Which eye has not seen and ear has not heard.”

**77,38,2a** But the argument is opposed to the whole understanding of Scripture.

**77,38,2b** For if the law brought no one to perfection, yet we are commanded to keep the law after the resurrection; and since the holy law given by the Lord through Moses has become our tutor to bring us to Christ,

**77,38,3** as lesser than the things that are perfected and entrusted with bringing us to the greater and most perfect; and since Christ, the perfect one and Master, has come, and has received from the hand of the tutor the one being brought in, that is, the holy virgin and church of the faithful, and since we have come to know through the law, the tutor, the greater one and perfecter, Jesus — how will the argument of those who say such things not rather be shown to be of short understanding and of foolishness,

**77,38,4** that after the perfecting of Christ there is again need of a tutor, so that we should turn back to the first principles of the elements, of teaching and of laying on of hands, according to what is written, though the apostle plainly tells us that “Everything that is growing old and ageing is near to vanishing,” as of the old covenant and legislation?

**77,38,5a** “For when the priesthood is changed,” he says, “there takes place of necessity a change of law as well.”

**77,38,5b** But if the old has been changed and the new has been made new, who would boldly bring the old back into use for us, turning the new into the old, causing us to fall from grace and trying to turn us aside from the benefit of Christ?

**77,38,6** Having discussed these things briefly in our account, and judging it sufficient because of the length of the treatise, let us proceed to what comes next, beloved, calling on God as our helper, as is our custom, for the subject and exposition of the rest and their refutation.

### Sect 78: Antidicomarians

Against the Antidicomarians, the fifty-eighth, but the seventy-eighth in the series.

**78,1,1** From this sect, called by some that of the Dimoerites, or named that of Christ’s coming in the flesh without a mind, certain other matters have sprung up, especially in Arabia, and a report about them has been brought to our humble self by certain devout persons.

**78,1,2a** And first we have written a letter on this subject.

**78,1,2b** Nevertheless, for the sake of the order of the numbering, here too we shall set out the letter itself in full against the heresy, together with what has reasonably been added to it or taken out of it.

**78,1,3** For some of the Antidicomarians, as though bearing enmity towards the virgin and wishing to belittle her glory, carried away by some envy or error, and wishing to defile the minds of men, have ventured to say that holy Mary, after the birth of Christ, was joined to a husband — I mean to Joseph himself.

**78,1,4a** And they say, as I have stated above, that the teaching was sounded forth by the old man Apollinarius himself, or by some of those who have been his disciples; and I am in doubt.

**78,1,4b** But about those who say these things I am under necessity to speak.

**78,1,4c** But so that I do not put myself to a second labour, I shall subjoin next the letter which I mentioned before, written to the country of the Agabi.

**78,1,4d** And it is as follows.

**78,2,1** To my most honoured lords and most beloved children and true-born brothers, orthodox and of one faith with me, from priest to layman, and to the catechumens in Arabia, Epiphanius, least of bishops, greeting.

**78,2,2a** At the present time there is cause both to wonder and not to wonder: to wonder, because in our generation everything is being fulfilled; and not to wonder, for it must be fulfilled.

**78,2,2b** For day by day now, by design, there arises among us, out of human reasonings and notions, a sophistical supposition that advances for the worse and abandons the apostolic teaching, as the most holy apostle foretold: “Some will depart from sound teaching, giving heed to myths and teachings of demons,” and what follows.

**78,2,3** For if there is any way to search out and devise evil ways, men are more eager for these than to fulfil the commandment which tells us to seek what is good and acceptable, and “Let the word be seasoned with salt, so that it may impart grace to its hearers.”

**78,2,4a** And if we should ponder these things — from where it comes about that evils are renewed among us every day — we ourselves shall be as people untaught and not attending to the divine and prophetic words.

**78,2,4b** For these things must be fulfilled.

**78,2,4c** For in all parts of the faith the saying must be accomplished, “When the Son of Man comes, will he then find faith on the earth?”

**78,2,5a** For how far has the mind of men gone, bent upon evil from youth?

**78,2,5b** What parts of the faith has it not destroyed?

**78,2,5c** And in what doctrines has ill will not confounded what is profitable?

**78,2,5d** And what of the most seemly matters, even in the condition of a rational nature, whose fitting part was rather to ponder what is reverent and to strive to add to it, even if it had to be beyond nature, and not rather to twist what is true into what is irreverent, forcing their way towards the worse?

**78,3,1** For now, since everything has been fulfilled in our generation, both the blasphemies and the things outside the Holy Spirit, they turn again to other novelties.

**78,3,2** For some — those called the Gnostics — blaspheme the Father, God and Maker of the universe; and others again, called Marcionites and Archontics, and the Manichaeans who follow them, who have most justly received their name by a just dispensation of God, the name of madness — all these, with many more heresies,

**78,3,3** Cainites, I mean, and Sethians, Melchizedekians, Colorbasians, Cerdonians, and the others, blaspheme against the Father of the universe, in that they deny that he is God — he who gave utterance in the law and in the prophets and who is justly worshipped by all creatures as Creator and Maker;

**78,3,4** these try to abolish his lordship together with the worship, denying the one who truly is and imagining another, who is not, by their fabulous supposition, so that they fall away from the one who is and do not find the one they suppose.

**78,3,5** For thus the drivel and the devil’s sowing of words are accustomed to produce such confusion and muddying, rousing through blasphemous reasonings the mind of created men to wage war concerning their own Master with evil suppositions and denials of God.

**78,3,6** But again, turning aside from this, some have ventured to walk in other paths, denying the only Master who bought them — Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Child, Son of the living God — who truly is, begotten of the Father without beginning and without time, who always is from the Father and is together with the Father, yet begotten beyond comprehension and without stain, consubstantial with the Father and not other than the Father;

**78,3,7** these, again, gone mad like rabid dogs, bark at their own Master, just as from the beginning the Jews, who failed to recognise him, have been called dumb dogs, fittingly deemed worthy of this title by the prophet, the name of their shameless assault on the Lord and his coming, as one may truly see.

**78,3,8** For they say that rabid dogs are called dumb because they are rendered toothless by the understanding that deserts them.

**78,4,1** For such is the nature of dogs when it turns to madness: those who once knew their master and his sons, his household and all the others who truly belong to the master of the house, when the frenzy seizes them, have the look of their faces changed, and rise up against those very members of the household whom once, honouring them, they fawned on with their tails and submitted to in their behaviour.

**78,4,2a** So it was, for instance, with those who were awaiting Christ’s coming, who were preparing to receive the bridegroom, who prayed to see prophets, who promised to obey the divine words, who had entered into a covenant with Moses — “Be you for us in the things towards the Lord,” and “All that the Lord shall say to you we will hear and do” — when they saw their Master arrive, not recognising the form and the figures of the truth, which the prophets, before he came in the flesh, had outlined, engraved, announced and signified.

**78,4,2b** First, then, they said to him, “Who is this who speaks blasphemies?”

**78,4,3a** At another time they ventured, unashamed, to say that he had a demon.

**78,4,3b** And they did not even blush to call him a Samaritan.

**78,4,4** In the end, then, as I have already shown, they rose up like mad dogs and fastened his hands — as the dog in its frenzy always comes on, raising its paws, and is not ashamed to tear the faces of its own masters.

**78,4,5** They handed over their own Lord to be crucified; and of the prophets, the household servants of their Master, one they sawed asunder, another they stoned, and another they slew with the sword.

**78,4,6** And after them, in the same way, the new Jews now have followed the same course, one after another: the Jews by nature denied him according to the flesh, while those who now deny the perfect true-born relation of the Son of God to the Father unceasingly insist, utterly mad and thunderstruck, that he is a creature and a thing made and alien to the Father.

**78,5,1** And from these again others, leaving the blasphemous teachings already mentioned, as though, so to speak, they had beheld the very heavenly vision as it is by nature, and had trespassed into the things above and busied themselves with them, as men who had come from above, announce with arrogance and stoutly insist, casting the Holy Spirit out of the Godhead.

**78,5,2** And they have not denied the Father, nor the Son’s true-born relation to him, but they walk again on another road, so that on every side the saying might be fulfilled, “Faith has failed from their mouth.”

**78,5,3a** For what else do they intend but to turn now against the Holy Spirit, who is no stranger to Father and Son, who belongs to the same Godhead and cannot be alien to the Godhead, as though they themselves had authority to command God rather than to be commanded?

**78,5,3b** For without shame they call the Spirit alien, and a servant, and a creature, and recent, and made, and whatever other shameful thing they rather devise to procure for themselves as a supposition about him.

**78,5,4** Since, then, the world has now been struck all the more with an incurable wound of unbelief, so that the lawlessness which destroys men by ill will and unbelief and ignorance might leave nothing out, the original and malicious design has, as it were, dragged off into other things again those who escaped the blasphemy concerning the Holy Trinity, so that no one might escape sinning.

**78,5,5** For I hear that some are thinking an empty thing about holy Mary, the ever-virgin, and are venturing to hurl a blasphemous supposition at her, so that our time is, on every side, like an evil serpent and venomous beast lurking in the dark and trying everyone with its bites — one about the face, another about the heel, another about the hand —

**78,5,6** so that the bite of unbelief may pass no one by, but he who thinks he has escaped on this point may not escape the venom in another way, and he who holds the faith sound in one matter may bring harm on himself somehow in another.

**78,6,1a** Where does this ill will come from?

**78,6,1b** Where does such daring come from?

**78,6,1c** Does not the name itself bear witness, does it not persuade you, you lover of strife?

**78,6,1d** Who ever, or in what generation, has ventured to speak the name of holy Mary and, when asked, has not at once added “the virgin”?

**78,6,2a** For from the very titles added to the names it shows the tokens of virtue as well.

**78,6,2b** For the righteous have received dignities of names, each fittingly and as was suitable.

**78,6,2c** And to Abraham was added “friend of God,” and it will not be dissolved; to Jacob, to be called “Israel,” and it will not be altered; to the apostles “Boanerges,” that is, “sons of thunder,” and it will not be abandoned; and to holy Mary “virgin,” and it will not be changed; for the holy one remained undefiled.

**78,6,2d** Does not nature itself teach you?

**78,6,2e** O new madness, O new state of affairs!

**78,6,3** And there are many other things which in the old times were not ventured by the fathers; but now one blasphemes against Christ’s coming in the flesh, saying other things against the Godhead itself, another makes the whole work of the coming in the flesh deficient in his own mind, another is vexed at the resurrection of the dead, and another at a part of it.

**78,6,4** And, in a word, alas for our muddied generation, whose life lies in danger, flooded on every side by the devil with evil sowings of notions and reasonings of false belief!

**78,6,5** How dare they so speak of the undefiled virgin — her who was deemed worthy to become the dwelling of the Son, who was chosen for this very purpose out of the myriads of Israel — as though, a vessel and dwelling deemed worthy, she existed only to be a sign of births?

**78,7,1a** For I have been told by someone that some people venture to say of her that after she had given birth to the Saviour she was joined to a husband.

**78,7,1b** And I am not surprised.

**78,7,1c** For the ignorance of those who have not learned the divine Scriptures accurately, nor come near to the histories, always turns and drags from one thing to another anyone who wishes to track out something about the truth from his own mind.

**78,7,2** For, first, when the virgin was handed over to Joseph, the lots compelling her to come to this, she was not handed over to him for union, if the truth must be told, since he was a widower.

**78,7,3** Yet by the law he is called her husband; but from the tradition of the Jews it is shown in due order that the virgin was entrusted to him not in order to be joined to him,

**78,7,4** but so that she might be kept as a witness of what was to come: that the dispensation of the coming in the flesh did not arrive as something spurious, but was attested in truth, accomplished in truth in the Holy Spirit apart from any man’s seed.

**78,7,5a** For how could so old a man, a widower for so many years after his first wife, have a virgin as his wife?

**78,7,5b** For this Joseph was the brother of Clopas; he was a son of Jacob, who was surnamed Panther.

**78,7,5c** Both of them are born of the man surnamed Panther.

**78,7,6** His first wife this Joseph took from the tribe of Judah, and she conceived and bore him six children, four male and two female, as the Gospel according to Mark and that according to John have made plain.

**78,7,7** His firstborn was James, who was surnamed Oblias, interpreted “wall,” and surnamed the Just, being a Nazoraean, which is interpreted “holy.”

**78,7,8** And he was the first to receive the chair of the episcopate, the one to whom first the Lord entrusted his throne upon the earth;

**78,7,9a** he was also called the brother of the Lord, as the apostle too agrees, saying somewhere, “But I saw none other of the apostles except James the brother of the Lord,” and so on.

**78,7,9b** He is called the brother of the Lord because he was brought up with him, not by nature but by grace.

**78,7,10a** For Mary, betrothed to Joseph, seemed to be the man’s wife, though she had no bodily union with him.

**78,7,10b** On this ground the close kinship of Joseph’s sons to the Saviour came to be called, or rather reckoned, that of brothers.

**78,7,11** For just as Joseph himself, having no part in the Saviour’s birth according to the flesh, is reckoned in the place of a father by dispensation, as Luke the evangelist says of the Saviour himself that he was the son, as was supposed, of Joseph, and as Mary herself said to him in the Gospel according to Luke, “Behold, your father and I have been seeking you in sorrow.”

**78,7,12a** Who, then, would call Joseph the father of the Lord, when he had no causal part in him, especially as the coming in the flesh took place apart from a man’s seed?

**78,7,12b** But by the dispensation the course of events gave him this lot.

**78,8,1a** He begets this James when he was somewhere near about forty years old, more or less.

**78,8,1b** After him is born a son called Joses.

**78,8,1c** Then after him Simeon, then Judas, and two daughters, the one called Mary and the one called Salome; and his wife died.

**78,8,2a** And many years later he takes Mary, a widower, the man being somewhere about eighty years of age or beyond.

**78,8,2b** And after this he takes Mary, as the gospel also says; for it says, “When Mary had been betrothed,” and it did not say “married.”

**78,8,3** And again elsewhere, “He did not know her”; but one may wonder at all the matters in which evil pretexts are hunted for, and at the matters whose causes there is no need to search out, and at seeking what is not to be sought, and at turning from what is necessary to foolish inquiries, so that from every side destruction through unbelief and blasphemy may somehow be fastened upon us because of the dishonour shown to the saints.

**78,8,4a** And first, then, the sequence of events refutes them on every side: first, that an old man past eighty years did not take a virgin for use, but rather she was entrusted to him by dispensation for him to guard.

**78,8,4b** And second, they themselves too were surely righteous.

**78,8,4c** And he who had heard that what was within her came from the Holy Spirit did not dare, after such a dispensation, to go on to make use of the vessel deemed worthy to contain him whom heaven and earth could not contain because of the surpassing greatness of his glory.

**78,8,5a** For if even now people strive in his name to remain virgins and to be pure and continent, how was Joseph not much more faithful, and Mary herself, pondering all things in her heart, as it is written?

**78,8,5b** But that after so great, so remarkable and so mighty a dispensation an old man should again be joined to a pure and honoured virgin, a vessel that contained the one who cannot be contained and had welcomed so great a mystery, that of a heavenly sign and of the life of men?

**78,9,1a** For from what source shall we not show that the virgin remained pure?

**78,9,1b** Let them show us at once that after the bearing of our Saviour Mary gave birth to any.

**78,9,1c** Let the fabricators and stitchers of deceit and mischief invent the names and tell them; and they cannot show it.

**78,9,1d** For the virgin was not joined in union afterwards — God forbid!

**78,9,2a** For if she had given birth, since she was always with the Saviour, they would have said that her children were with him as well.

**78,9,2b** But the saying leads them astray, “Behold, your mother and your brothers stand outside seeking you.”

**78,9,3a** And they do not know what had been written before this, that his brothers did not believe in him.

**78,9,3b** For we too, advancing in years and wondering at things in the divine Scriptures as though written in a slight manner, now, behold, coming to perceive them in every respect, give thanks to God, who made sure beforehand, through what seem to be small words in the divine Scripture, to establish the truth of all Scripture.

**78,9,4a** For always, hearing of James that he was called the brother of the Lord, we wondered and said, “What need is there of this?”

**78,9,4b** But now we have learned for what reason the divine Scripture said this beforehand: surely so that, when we hear, “Behold, your mother and your brothers stand outside seeking you,” we may learn that it is speaking about James and Joseph’s other sons,

**78,9,5a** and not about sons of Mary, who never existed.

**78,9,5b** For it was plain that James was the older in age with respect to the Lord’s coming in the flesh; and Scripture, setting the matter out in proof,

**78,9,6a** calls them brothers and names them — James and Joses and Simeon and Judas and Salome and Mary — so that they may learn, then, whose son James is and of what mother, and may perceive by age which is the older.

**78,9,6b** For the crucifixion of Jesus takes place in the thirty-third year of his coming in the flesh; and at that time it was the twentieth year of Herod, Archelaus’ son.

**78,10,1** For it is in the first Herod’s thirty-third year — Herod son of Antipater — that the Saviour is born in Bethlehem of Judaea, which was the forty-second year of the emperor Augustus.

**78,10,2a** And when he had reached two years, he is taken by Joseph to Egypt, because of what had been said to Herod by the magi, since Herod was seeking the child.

**78,10,2b** And he goes down into Egypt and spends another two years there.

**78,10,3a** And Herod the king dies in the thirty-seventh year.

**78,10,3b** And Archelaus his son succeeds him for nine years.

**78,10,4** And so the work is completed, and he is handed over to the cross in the eighteenth year of Tiberius Caesar; and it was the twentieth year of Agrippa, surnamed the Great, the younger Herod, the son of Archelaus.

**78,10,5a** But nowhere have we heard of Joseph having begotten sons.

**78,10,5b** Nor indeed did he live many years after coming from Egypt; for it was the Saviour’s fourth year, and Joseph’s more than eighty-fourth, when he arrived from the land of Egypt.

**78,10,6** And Joseph remained alive another eight years; and in the twelfth year, when they were going up to Jerusalem, he was sought, when he was not to be found on the journey, as the Gospel according to Luke has it.

**78,10,7a** And in the course of these years Joseph dies, and he was brought up no longer under Joseph, but in the house of Joseph.

**78,10,7b** Hence the gospel no longer says that his father and his mother and his brothers came, but, “Behold, your mother and your brothers stand outside.”

**78,10,8** Nor indeed, when they said to him in Idumaea, “No one who does these things wishes to be in secret; if you do these things, show yourself,” did it say that his father and his brothers said it to him, but his brothers, since Joseph was no longer living in the body.

**78,10,9** Then at the very consummation, when the Saviour stood on the cross, as the Gospel according to John has it, “Turning,” it says, “he saw the disciple whom the Lord loved,” and he said to him concerning Mary, “Behold, your mother,” and to her he says, “Behold, your son.”

**78,10,10a** But if Mary had children, and if she had a husband, for what reason did he hand Mary over to John, and John to Mary?

**78,10,10b** And for what reason does he not rather hand her over to Peter?

**78,10,10c** And for what reason not to Andrew, or to Matthew and Bartholomew?

**78,10,11a** But it is plain that it was to John because of his virginity: “For behold your mother.”

**78,10,11b** And yet she was not the mother of John himself according to the flesh; but it was to show her as mother and source of virginity, since from her came the Life;

**78,10,12** and he spoke to John, though he was a stranger according to the flesh, to teach him to honour his own mother — because in reality the Lord himself was born of her according to the flesh — so that no one might think that the work was an appearance and not truth.

**78,10,13a** For had she not truly been his mother according to the flesh, having carried him in her womb, he would not have been concerned to hand her over — her who had become the ever-virgin mother through the dispensation, and remained undefiled because of the honour due to him and because she was the wondrous vessel.

**78,10,13b** And the gospel says, “And from that day onward he took her to himself.”

**78,10,13c** But if she had a husband, if she had a home, if she had children, she would have withdrawn to her own, and not to a stranger.

**78,11,1a** But let this not turn to harm for some, and let them not think to find in it a pretext for devising for themselves women brought in to live with them, called “beloved,” out of a mischievous notion.

**78,11,1b** For in that case the matters were accomplished by dispensation, the matters being set apart from all the other strictness which ought to be kept in accordance with God.

**78,11,1c** For indeed, when this had taken place and he had taken her to himself, she did not stay with him any longer.

**78,11,2** But even if some think there has been a mistake, let them search the traces of the Scriptures, and they will find neither Mary’s death, nor whether she died or did not die, nor whether she was buried or was not buried, although John made his journey through Asia; and nowhere does it state that he brought the holy virgin along with him, but Scripture simply kept silent, because of the surpassing greatness of the wonder, so as not to throw the minds of men into amazement.

**78,11,3a** For I do not venture to speak, but I ponder and keep silence.

**78,11,3b** For perhaps we have found traces of that holy and blessed one too, showing that her death is not even to be found.

**78,11,4a** For in one place Simeon says concerning her, “And through your own soul too a sword will pass, so that thoughts out of many hearts may be revealed”; and in another the Revelation of John says that the dragon hastened against the woman who had borne the male child, and there were given to her the wings of an eagle, and she was taken into the wilderness, so that the dragon might not seize her.

**78,11,4b** And perhaps this can be fulfilled in her; but I do not define this absolutely, and I do not say that she remained immortal; but neither do I affirm whether she died.

**78,11,5a** For Scripture went beyond the human mind and left the matter in suspense, because of the precious and most excellent vessel, so that no one might come to suspect her of carnal things.

**78,11,5b** So even if she died, we do not know it; and if she was buried, she was not joined in fleshly union — God forbid!

**78,11,6** And who, gathering madness to himself, will wish to hurl a blasphemous suspicion, and to lift up his mouth, and loose his tongue, and part his lips out of an evil mind, and, instead of hymns and glory, to devise insults and behave like a drunkard towards the holy virgin, and not to honour the honoured vessel?

**78,12,1a** And if the matter must also be taken from some other point of view, let us feel our way through the observations of the natural philosophers as well.

**78,12,1b** They say that the lioness does not give birth except from a single pregnancy only, and that the cause is as follows: the animal is very tightly knit, fierce-eyed in appearance, most weighty in strength, the most kingly kind, so to speak, among the other animals.

**78,12,2** And it conceives from one mate, and carries the seed implanted for twenty-six months in the womb, so that the whelp is brought to completeness within because of the length of time, to the point of already having all its teeth before it comes out of the womb, and its claws at their settled growth, both the so-called peg-teeth and the canines and the molars, and all the other things that belong to the animal.

**78,12,3a** So while it is in the belly, in its leapings and movements and in its other ways, it tears with its claws and scrapes the pregnant womb and uterus.

**78,12,3b** So when the mother comes to give birth, on that day her belly becomes a stranger to everything painful in the nature of bearing young.

**78,12,4** For the natural philosophers say that together with the birth both the uterus and the womb are expelled at the same time, so that the female no longer has desire, unless some force should be applied, nor indeed, even if she should happen to be forced into some union, can she conceive any more, since there is no womb, or uterus.

**78,12,5** So, then, this train of reasoning too has given us a means of procuring, for the matter under inquiry, some notion of the relation, tending to what is profitable rather than to what is harmful.

**78,12,6** For if Jacob, saying “Judah is a lion’s whelp,” speaks of Christ in a riddle, and in the Revelation of John it says, “Behold, the lion has conquered, he who is of the tribe of Judah and of the seed of David,” then, since the Lord has been likened to a lion — not according to nature, but for the sake of the riddle, and because the animal is kingly, the boldest and strongest of all animals, and most graceful in all other respects — I might surely call the one who bore him a lioness too.

**78,12,7a** For from where is a lion born at all, unless the mother is to be called a lioness?

**78,12,7b** But a lioness has no second pregnancy; therefore Mary knows no further pregnancy, the holy virgin no further union of bodies.

**78,13,1a** But let us look at other considerations as well.

**78,13,1b** She was a follower of Jesus, being always with him.

**78,13,1c** Jesus was invited to a wedding, and his mother was there, and his brothers, and Joseph nowhere.

**78,13,1d** “What have I to do with you, woman?

**78,13,1e** My hour has not yet come.”

**78,13,1f** And he did not say, “What have I to do with you, people?”

**78,13,2a** Standing by were Mary Magdalene and Mary of Clopas and Mary, Rufus’ mother, and the other Mary, and Salome, and others.

**78,13,2b** And it did not say that Joseph was there, or James the brother of the Lord, who dies at ninety-six years of age, having remained a virgin;

**78,13,3** on whose head no iron came up, who did not use a bath-house, who partook of nothing that had life; who did not put on a second tunic; who used only a single worn cloak of linen, as is said in the gospel, “The young man ran off, leaving behind the linen cloth he had wrapped around himself.”

**78,13,4** For John and James and James — these three have had this manner of life: the two sons of Zebedee, and James the son of Joseph, brother of the Lord because of their sharing a way of life, because of their being brought up together, because the Lord had him in the rank of a brother on account of the lawful bond alone that Joseph had with Mary, from her betrothal to him.

**78,13,5a** To this James alone it was allowed to go into the Holy of Holies once in the year, because he was a Nazoraean and connected with the priesthood.

**78,13,5b** For it is from this that Mary was a kinswoman of Elizabeth in two ways, and that James was distinguished in the priesthood, since the two tribes alone were joined with one another, the royal joined to the priestly and the priestly to the royal, as earlier too, at the exodus, Nahshon, the chief of the tribe of Judah, takes Elizabeth, the daughter of Aaron of old, as his wife.

**78,13,6** Hence many of the heresies are ignorant of the Saviour’s genealogy according to the flesh, and, being at a loss, disbelieve, and think to contradict the truth, saying, “How can she who comes from the tribe of David and of Judah be a kinswoman of Elizabeth, who is from Levi?”

**78,14,1a** This James also wore the plate upon his head; and once, when there was a drought, he lifted up his hands to heaven and prayed, and at once heaven gave rain.

**78,14,1b** He never put on a woollen garment.

**78,14,1c** His knees grew hard like those of camels, from always bending them before the Lord out of the abundance of his piety.

**78,14,2a** So they no longer called him by name; “the Just” was his name.

**78,14,2b** He never bathed in a bath-house; he partook of nothing that had life, as I have shown above; he never put on a sandal.

**78,14,2c** And there would be much to say about the man and his virtuous way of life.

**78,14,3a** Do you see, then, that the house was altogether most worthy of note?

**78,14,3b** For if the sons of Joseph knew the rule of virginity and the practice of the Nazoraeans, how much more did that aged and honoured man know how to guard a pure virgin and to honour the vessel in which, so to speak, the salvation of mankind took up its dwelling?

**78,14,4a** Does not nature itself teach us that he was an old man, far advanced in age, great among men, faithful in character, devout in bearing?

**78,14,4b** For the gospel says that, being a man who feared God, he sought to put her away secretly.

**78,14,5** This James, the brother of the Lord and son of Joseph, died at Jerusalem, having lived twenty-four years, more or less, after the Saviour’s ascension, at ninety-six years of age, struck on the head with a fuller’s club; he had been thrown from the pinnacle of the temple,

**78,14,6a** had come down without any injury, and had bent his knees and prayed for those who threw him, saying, “Pardon them, for they do not know what they are doing,” so that Simeon also, his cousin, the son of Clopas, standing far off, cried, “Cease! Why do you stone the Just?

**78,14,6b** See, he is praying the best of prayers for you.”

**78,14,6c** And so his martyrdom came about.

**78,15,1** If, then, his son was of such great age, how could his father — seeing awe-inspiring things, angels attending the birth of the Son as a guard, singing praise from heaven and saying, “Glory in the highest to God, and on earth peace, among men good pleasure,” and the shepherds coming to the cave where he was born and announcing these things, and the old man Joseph hearing them, and when the time of so many signs and wonders had gone by — how could he venture to behave like a drunkard towards and insult the holy body in which God took up his dwelling?

**78,15,2** From this very body the dispensation of the coming in the flesh was gathered together for us.

**78,15,3** From it the holy, undefiled flesh was built up for us in the Godhead of the Saviour, as the angel Gabriel said there, “The Spirit of the Lord will come upon you, and power of the Most High will overshadow you; for that reason the holy thing born of you will also be called Son of God.”

**78,15,4a** How, then, could he venture to be joined to so great and so holy a virgin, Mary?

**78,15,4b** And what has it profited us to inquire about it, even if he had been joined to her — which God forbid?

**78,15,4c** And which is the more to be chosen: to hand the matter over to God, or to force the worse upon ourselves?

**78,15,4d** That it was not written for us that, unless we believe that Mary was joined in union again, we do not have eternal life but come into judgement, is plain.

**78,15,5a** But what was written — things that are good, or rather things that are just, things that are reverent?

**78,15,5b** So that we may give grace to those who hear as well.

**78,15,5c** But men have left aside the necessary things concerning the faith of truth, the things that belong to the glorifying of God, and from wherever they may find it they procure for themselves, to their harm, what it is grievous even to think of, especially when Scripture does not say it.

**78,16,1a** For if Scripture had said it, we would have rendered the truth and thought nothing amiss.

**78,16,1b** For is marriage unseemly?

**78,16,1c** Is the marriage bed profane?

**78,16,1d** Is the bed not undefiled?

**78,16,1e** Is marriage counterfeit?

**78,16,1f** But it is withheld from prophets and high priests because of their service to the greater thing.

**78,16,2a** For after Moses had prophesied, such a man no longer has union with a wife, no longer conceives children, no longer begets.

**78,16,2b** For he had his life more at leisure for the Master.

**78,16,2c** For how could he have remained on Mount Sinai forty nights and forty days if he were devoted to marriage?

**78,16,2d** Or how could he have been ready for forty years in the wilderness for God’s dispensation, and have given himself to the priesthood?

**78,16,2e** And how could he have recounted the mysteries, and continued in converse with God, while bound in marriage?

**78,16,3a** For if the holy apostle speaks expressly about us and says, “For a season, that they may give themselves to prayer,” how much more truly will this word hold of the prophets?

**78,16,3b** Now Mary too is a prophetess.

**78,16,4a** “For he went in,” it says, “to the prophetess, and she conceived in the womb and bore a son.

**78,16,4b** And the Lord said to me, Call his name ‘Spoil quickly, plunder speedily,’” and what follows.

**78,16,5** And here it signifies Gabriel’s entry to Mary, when he set out to announce to her the good news that she was to bear the Son of God as Saviour for the world, not of a man’s seed but by the Holy Spirit.

**78,16,6** But Philip the evangelist too had four daughters who prophesied; and they prophesied, then, because of the virginity which they were deemed worthy to have.

**78,16,7** And Thecla meets the holy Paul and breaks off her marriage, though she had a betrothed who was most handsome, foremost in the city, very rich, most nobly born and most distinguished in his station; and the holy woman despises earthly things in order to gain possession of heavenly ones.

**78,16,8a** If, then, these did so, how much more Mary, upon whom the whole wondrous dispensation came about?

**78,16,8b** From where, then, shall I gather minds to what is good, and turn aside the gloom of those who have conceived a craving for dreadful things, as it is written, “He conceived toil and brought forth lawlessness”?

**78,16,8c** For these truly conceive a toil of notions and bring forth a lawlessness of blasphemies.

**78,17,1a** But let no one suspect those things, and, trying to sow them in himself in another way, say:

**78,17,1b** How, then, did the gospel say that Mary was found to be pregnant by the Holy Spirit before they came together?

**78,17,1c** Was the coming together, then, expected, and is it for this reason that it said “before they came together”?

**78,17,2** But again, in another place, the same gospel says again, “And she was found with child before they came in,” or again, “She gave birth, and he did not know her,” or again, “She bore her firstborn son, and he did not know her,” and “He did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son.”

**78,17,3** And those who profess to distinguish the senses of the Scriptures, and undertake to busy themselves with lofty and deepest things, do not know that the meaning is of this kind.

**78,17,4a** For if Mary had given birth again, it would have had to state the names of the other brothers as well.

**78,17,4b** But if it is because the Only-begotten is the firstborn of all creation, do not be disturbed.

**78,17,4c** For it did not say that she bore her firstborn, but, “He did not know her until she bore her son.”

**78,17,4d** And it did not say “her firstborn,” but “the firstborn.”

**78,17,5a** For with “her son” it signified that he was born of her according to the flesh, but with the title “firstborn” it no longer put “her,” but only “firstborn.”

**78,17,5b** For this is the one spoken of by the apostle as the firstborn of all creation, not joined to creation, but begotten before creation.

**78,17,6a** For he did not say “first-created,” but “firstborn,” the reading being divided for the better and safer sense: first to say “firstborn,” and then to speak of creation as coming after.

**78,17,6b** For “firstborn” is taken of the Son, while creation came through the Son.

**78,17,7a** So she bore her son, the firstborn — not her firstborn, as though she were going to conceive another — and he did not know her.

**78,17,7b** For how did he know that a woman would receive such great grace?

**78,17,7c** Or how did he know that a virgin would be glorified with such glory?

**78,17,8** He knew her as a woman in her formation and female in her nature, born of her mother Anna and her father Joachim, a kinswoman of Elizabeth, of David’s house and family; but he did not know that anyone upon the earth would be honoured with such glory, and a woman above all.

**78,17,9a** So he did not know her until he saw the wonder; he did not know her wonder until he saw what had been born of her.

**78,17,9b** But when she had given birth, he knew also the honour from God, that she was the one who had heard, “Hail, you who are favoured with grace; the Lord is with you.”

**78,18,1a** She it is who is signified in Eve, who received by way of a riddle the title of mother of the living.

**78,18,1b** For there she is called mother of the living even after hearing, “Earth you are, and to earth you shall depart,” after the transgression.

**78,18,1c** And it was a wonder that after the transgression she had this great title.

**78,18,2a** And as regards what is perceptible, the whole race of men on earth has been born of that Eve.

**78,18,2b** But here, in truth, the Life itself has come to be for the world from Mary, so that she might bear the Living One and Mary might become mother of the living.

**78,18,3a** So it is by way of a riddle that Mary is called mother of the living.

**78,18,3b** For it was said concerning the two women, “Who has given a woman wisdom, or skill in embroidery?”

**78,18,3c** Since Eve, the first wise woman, wove perceptible garments because of Adam, whom she had stripped bare; for this labour was given to her.

**78,18,4** For since the nakedness came about through her, to her it was given to clothe the perceptible body because of the perceptible nakedness; but to Mary it was given by God to bear for us a lamb and a sheep, so that out of the glory of that same lamb and sheep, as from a fleece, a garment of incorruption might be made for us in wisdom through his virtue.

**78,18,5a** But there is another wonderful thing to consider about these, about Eve and about Mary.

**78,18,5b** For Eve became the occasion of death for men, for through her death entered into the world; but Mary is the occasion of life, through whom life was born for us.

**78,18,6a** And it was for this reason that the Son of God arrived in the world.

**78,18,6b** And “where sin abounded, grace overflowed all the more”; and whence death came, there life took the lead, so that life might come in place of death, barring the death that sprang from a woman — he who through a woman has again become life for us.

**78,18,7** And since there Eve, while still a virgin, fell into the transgression of disobedience, again through the virgin came the obedience of grace, when the descent from heaven, the coming in the flesh, and life eternal were announced as good news.

**78,18,8a** “For there,” he says to the serpent, “I will also put enmity between you and her, and between your seed and her seed.”

**78,18,8b** But nowhere is a seed of woman found; except that, by way of riddle, the enmity is taken in the case of Eve towards those born of her — the enmity of the serpent, and of the devil and envy that came to be in the serpent.

**78,19,1a** Yet in its most complete sense the whole cannot be fulfilled in her.

**78,19,1b** But it will be fulfilled in very truth in the holy seed, the chosen, the one and only, which was found to be from Mary alone, not from the conjugal union of a man.

**78,19,1c** For he came to do away with the power of the dragon, the crooked, fleeing serpent, who says he has seized the whole world.

**78,19,2** For this reason the Only-begotten arrived from a woman, to do away with the serpent — that is, with false teaching and corruption and deceit, with error and lawlessness.

**78,19,3a** He it is who truly opens a mother’s womb.

**78,19,3b** For all the firstborn who have been born — to speak more reverently — could not fulfil this, but only the Only-begotten, who opened a virgin womb; for in him alone it has been fulfilled, and in no other.

**78,19,4a** But one may see it from the subject itself as well.

**78,19,4b** For the saying is taken from Mary, and I may say this of the church too: “On this account a man will forsake his father and his mother and will be joined fast to his wife, and the two will be one flesh.”

**78,19,5** And the holy apostle says, “This mystery is great; but I speak of Christ and the church.”

**78,19,6a** And observe for me the precision of the Scriptures: that of Adam it says “he formed,” but of Eve it no longer says that she was formed, but that she was built.

**78,19,6b** “For he took,” it says, “one of his ribs and built it up for him into a woman,” to show that the Lord formed for himself a body from Mary, and that from his very side the church was built up, in the piercing of his side, when the mysteries of the blood and the water became a ransom among us.

**78,20,1a** Nevertheless Joseph did know Mary — not in the sense of any knowledge of conjugal use, not in the sense of a knowledge of intercourse; rather he knew her by honouring her who had been honoured by God.

**78,20,1b** For he did not know that she was of such glory until he saw the Lord born of a woman.

**78,20,2a** And “before they had come together, she was found having a child in her womb” — so that the argument of those who suppose that the mystery dispensed by God came from intercourse with a man might never prevail.

**78,20,2b** For it meant: before that which was expected took place.

**78,20,2c** But this thing did not take place.

**78,20,3** For even if the virgin was expected to come to Joseph for union — which he would not even have accepted, because of his old age — yet Scripture anticipates, and suggests to us, and makes our understanding secure, since the circumstance, in keeping with the divine birth, is able to carry conviction that the virgin should no longer come near a man for union, just as the angel too persuaded Joseph that the suspicion which he himself was entertaining was not so.

**78,20,4** For like the phrase spoken earlier, “before they came together”, as of a thing expected but not done, is the phrase “being a just man, he sought not to make an example of her, but to put her away secretly”, as of something base that would have come about from making an example of her, but which did not come about, as the angel teaches when he says, “Do not fear to take Mary your wife” — her who had not yet become so — and even if she is under suspicion of a fault in your eyes, yet she is not such as you think, and so on.

**78,20,5** For directly in sequence he says, “for that which is begotten in her”, as of something already begotten, and again, “she will bear a son”, as of something still to come; for so it was.

**78,20,6a** The statement in advance is made because the thing had been believed, as is also “before they came together”; and we rest content that it never took place at all.

**78,20,6b** “Until she bore her firstborn son” is to be interpreted in the same terms, because of the wonder of the knowledge concerning the virgin, honoured as it is before God.

**78,21,1** Let no one suppose, from its saying “before they came together”, that they came together afterwards; for no one can show or indicate this; rather, Scripture affirmed it in order to show that the Saviour’s conception was undefiled.

**78,21,2** So “he did not know her” is said because of her glory; and “firstborn”, because he is firstborn before created things existed, and firstborn among many brethren, according to the apostle — not in the sense of the one from Mary, as though there were other sons from her, but among those who have been counted worthy to receive adoption through him, when he truly became her son according to the flesh, so that it might not be supposed to be a mere appearance.

**78,21,3a** But he is both firstborn and son of the virgin herself, not because she had other sons, as I have said.

**78,21,3b** For this is like the first instance, before his sojourn among us.

**78,21,3c** For he who is truly the Father’s firstborn on high, prior to all creation, is not called firstborn on the ground that others were begotten of the Father after him.

**78,21,3d** For he has no second brother, because he is only-begotten.

**78,21,4a** So too in his coming in the flesh he is always Mary’s firstborn, and yet he is Mary’s only-begotten, having no second brother from her; and those will cease who have contrived against themselves what is harmful rather than what makes for benefit.

**78,21,4b** Do not, do not, I beseech you!

**78,21,5a** He who honours the Lord honours a holy one too, and he who dishonours a holy one dishonours his own Master as well.

**78,21,5b** Let Mary be left to herself, the holy virgin, the holy vessel.

**78,21,5c** For these harmful things do us no good; but we ought to think more reverently, so that we do not acquire arrogance, or dissension, or idle talk.

**78,21,6** For of every idle word we shall render an account, as it is written; let us take care for ourselves, let us look into our own affairs, let us not throw our own things onto the saints, let us not examine the things of the saints by our own standard.

**78,22,1a** For certainly some people, forcing the matter and turning towards what is more lustful, and harbouring a corrupt notion within themselves, want to stain the saints as well, to make a plausible defence for their own evil and feeble notion; it is to such that the apostle says, “I would wish everyone to be as myself.”

**78,22,1b** And in what sense, then, does he say “myself”, if not because of his chastity?

**78,22,2a** “But because of fornications let each man have his own wife.”

**78,22,2b** But the pronoun was taken out.

**78,22,2c** For it would have been reproving and too pointed.

**78,22,2d** For he could have said, “because of your fornications.”

**78,22,2e** So he removed the “your”, so that he might not seem to have said this to insult anyone.

**78,22,3** It was said to condemn some who are unwilling to devote themselves to God after living according to the law and rightly coming to know their own vessel for the begetting of children, as our ancient fathers too made use of this form; as we have also found Scripture saying somewhere, “And Rebecca, having conceived by one.”

**78,22,4a** By saying “by one” it told the matter more decorously, and showed that the conception was righteous.

**78,22,4b** For it shows that after he had had children he was no longer joined to his wife;

**78,22,5** but since it is easy and simple for the mind to turn to base things rather than to necessary ones — our human reasoning being slippery, and not quick to direct its impulse onto the straight way of the Lord, but leaning now to the right and now to the left, and fulfilling only with difficulty what was said in Solomon, “Do not swerve to the right, nor yet to the left” — vice turns about in us once more in another way over the same reasonings, and pushes our sobriety to walk again on other roads.

**78,22,6** Let us therefore be on our guard, lest the praising of the virgin beyond measure should somehow become for anyone another stumbling-block of fancy.

**78,23,1** For those who blaspheme against the Son, as I have shown above, made it their ambition to estrange him by nature from the Godhead of the Father; while others again, thinking otherwise and led on, as they suppose, to honour him the more, said that the same one is Father, and the same Son, and the same Holy Spirit; and for both parties the wound is incurable.

**78,23,2a** So too concerning this holy and blessed ever-virgin, some have dared to insult her, as though she had been joined in the flesh after that very great and pure dispensation of the Lord, his coming in the flesh.

**78,23,2b** And this is the most impious of all wickedness.

**78,23,3** And as we say that word reached us of some who had dared so far, giving themselves over very readily to sin, so too we were astonished again on hearing the other report: for others again, raving in their notion about this same holy ever-virgin, have been eager, and are eager, to bring her in in place of God, carried away by a kind of stupefaction and derangement of mind.

**78,23,4** For they relate that certain women there in Arabia have brought this empty babble from the parts of Thrace: that they offer a kind of small loaf in the ever-virgin’s name and assemble together, and in the name of the holy virgin attempt, beyond all measure, to undertake an unlawful and blasphemous act, and to perform priestly rites in her name through women; the whole of which is impious and unlawful, altered from the preaching of the Holy Spirit; so that the whole thing is a devilish working and the teaching of an unclean spirit.

**78,23,5a** For in their case too is fulfilled the saying, “Some shall depart from sound teaching, giving heed to fables and teachings of demons.”

**78,23,5b** “For they shall be,” it says, “worshippers of the dead, as they also worshipped in Israel.”

**78,23,5c** And the glory which the saints had before God, each in his own time, has turned into a cause of error for others, who fail to perceive the truth.

**78,23,6** For in Shechem, that is, in Neapolis, the inhabitants perform sacrifices in the name of the Maiden — supposedly on the pretext of Jephthah’s daughter, offered up long ago to God as a sacrifice; and to those deceived by it this has turned into the harm of idolatry and of vain worship.

**78,23,7a** And the Egyptians too, honouring beyond what was proper, in place of God, Pharaoh’s daughter, who honoured God’s servant Moses, taking him up and rearing him because of the child’s renown at that time, handed this on as well to the foolish as an evil tradition for worship.

**78,23,7b** And they worship Thermuthis, the daughter of Amenoph, who was Pharaoh at that time, because, as I said before, she reared Moses.

**78,23,8** And many similar things of this sort have happened in the world to the error of the deceived — not that the saints are to blame for anyone’s stumbling, but because the mind of men is not at rest, but turns aside to evil things.

**78,23,9a** For either the holy virgin died and was buried — her falling asleep in honour, her end in chastity, and her crown in virginity — or else she was slain, as it is written, “And a sword shall pass through her soul”; her renown lies among the martyrs, her holy body among the blessed, she through whom light dawned on the world.

**78,23,9b** Or else she remained; for God is not without power to do all things whatever he wills.

**78,23,9c** For no one has known her end.

**78,23,9d** One must not honour the saints beyond what is due, but must honour their Master.

**78,23,10a** Let the error of the deluded come to an end, then.

**78,23,10b** For Mary is neither God nor one who has her body from heaven, but she was brought into being from the conception of a man and a woman, though by promise, like Isaac.

**78,23,11a** And let no one make offerings in her name.

**78,23,11b** For he destroys his own soul; and on the other side let no one rave like a drunkard, insulting the holy virgin.

**78,23,11c** For far from it: she was not joined in the flesh after the childbearing, nor before her bearing of the Saviour.

**78,24,1** These few things, then, we have written after considering them among ourselves, for those who wish to learn the truth of Scripture and not to rave to no purpose in their words and arm themselves with a blasphemous tongue.

**78,24,2** But if some wish to resist, and not to accept what is beneficial but rather the opposite, then from us too, humble as we are, must be said, “He who hears, let him hear, and he who disobeys, let him disobey”; let him not cause any trouble to the apostles, nor to us any longer.

**78,24,3a** For what we knew to be more reverent and beneficial to the church, that we have said about the holy virgin, pleading the cause of her who is in all things highly favoured, as Gabriel said, “Hail, highly favoured one, the Lord is with you.”

**78,24,3b** Now if the Lord is with her, in what way will she be in another union?

**78,24,3c** And how, if she draws near to flesh, will she be guarded by the Lord?

**78,24,4a** The saints are in honour: their rest is in glory, their departure hence in perfection, their lot in blessedness, in holy mansions, their choir in the company of angels, their abode in heaven, their way of life in the divine Scriptures, their renown in incomparable and everlasting honour, their prizes in our Lord Christ Jesus; through him and with him be glory to the Father together with the Holy Spirit to the ages.

**78,24,4b** Amen.

**78,24,5** All the brethren greet you; and do you yourselves greet all the brethren with you, faithful and orthodox, who loathe pride, who hate fellowship with the Arians and the frivolity of the Sabellians, who honour the Trinity as consubstantial — Father and Son and Holy Spirit, three hypostases, one essence and one Godhead, and in a word one glorification — and who do not err concerning the saving dispensation and coming in the flesh of our Saviour,

**78,24,6a** but believe perfectly in the incarnation of Christ: perfect God, and the same perfect man, without sin, who received from Mary the very body, and received a soul, and a mind, and everything whatever man is, without sin; who is not two, but a single Lord, a single God, a single King, a single High Priest, both God and man, man and God, being not two but one, united, not unto confusion nor unto non-existence, but unto a great dispensation of grace.

**78,24,6b** Farewell.

**78,24,7** Being content with the copy of the letter, which serves well for the refutation of these people, and judging that it suffices up to this point, and having passed beyond this sect as well in God — having refuted it, like a reptile peeping out of a hole, through the wise teaching and power of God, which like storax breathes forth a sweet fragrance in the world, for the excellence also of the holy children of virginity, which had its beginning from holy Mary through him who dawned from her as light for the world — and having exposed the evil venom of their reptilian wickedness, let us go on again to the others, to the completion of the whole work in God.

### Sect 79: Collyridians

Against the Collyridians, who make offerings to Mary, the fifty-ninth, but the seventy-ninth in the series.

**79,1,1** Next after this a heresy has come to public notice, of which we have already made brief mention in the one before this, through the letter written to Arabia, the one that deals with Mary.

**79,1,2** And this heresy too, again, appeared in Arabia, coming from Thrace and the upper parts of Scythia, and was brought to our hearing; and it too is laughable and is found by the intelligent to be full of matter for mockery.

**79,1,3a** We shall begin to search it out and to relate what concerns it.

**79,1,3b** For it will be judged a thing of silliness rather than of intelligence, as others like it were too.

**79,1,4** For just as above, through their gross insult towards Mary, those who saw fit to hold these notions sow harmful notions in the reasonings of men, so these too, leaning to the other side, are caught in an extreme of harm, so that that saying chanted among some of the outside philosophers will be fulfilled in them as well, where it says, “Extremes are equal.”

**79,1,5** For the harm is equal in both these heresies, the one party belittling the holy virgin and the other, again, glorifying her beyond what is due.

**79,1,6a** For who are these who teach this, if not women?

**79,1,6b** For the female sex is easily made to slip, and is unsteady and low in its thinking.

**79,1,7a** For this too the devil has seen fit to vomit forth through women; as above, with Quintilla and Maximilla and Priscilla, the teachings were laughable, so here too.

**79,1,7b** For certain women deck out a kind of barber’s chair, that is, a four-cornered seat, and spread a linen cloth over it, and on a certain appointed day of the year, on certain days, they set out bread and offer it up in the name of Mary, and all of them partake of the bread, as we discussed this in part when writing in the very letter to Arabia.

**79,1,7c** But now we shall state clearly what concerns it, and, having asked God, we shall set out the refutations of it as far as we are able, so that by cutting out the roots of this idol-making heresy we may be able, in God, to put an end to such madness in certain people.

**79,2,1a** Come then, servants of God, let us put on a manly mind and scatter the madness of these women.

**79,2,1b** For the notion is wholly a woman’s, and once more the sickness of Eve who was deceived — or rather, still more, the promise of error of the serpent, the provoking beast that spoke in her, a promise that brings nothing into the open and fulfils nothing of what it promises, but only works death, calling things that are not as though they were, and through the sight of the tree working disobedience and a turning away from the truth itself and a turning towards many things.

**79,2,2** One may consider that, just like what the deceiver sowed when he said, “You shall be as gods,” so too the mind of these women is befooled by the exaltation of the beast mentioned before, by which by its nature it works death once more, as I have often said.

**79,2,3a** For first, to examine at once from the beginning of time until now, to whom is it not plain that the teaching and the practice are of demons, and the undertaking a perversion?

**79,2,3b** From the beginning of time no woman ever served God as priest —

**79,2,4** not Eve herself, who, although she had lapsed into transgression, still did not dare to carry out so impious an undertaking besides; not one of her daughters, although Abel at once performed sacred service to God, and Cain offered sacrifices before the Lord, though they were not accepted, and Enoch was well-pleasing and was translated, and Noah offered to the Lord thank-offerings from what was left over from the ark, showing a proof of a grateful disposition and confessing his thanks to the one who had saved him.

**79,2,5a** Abraham the righteous performs sacred service to God, as does Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, and Isaac is found well-pleasing to God, and Jacob, as far as he was able, made an offering on the stone, pouring oil on it from his flask.

**79,2,5b** And of his sons, Levi is found to have received the priesthood in succession; and from his own line came those who received the priestly order — I mean Moses the prophet and hierophant, as well as Aaron and the children of Aaron, Eleazar and Phinehas and Ithamar, his offspring.

**79,2,6a** And why should I tell of the multitudes of those who performed sacred service to God in the old covenant?

**79,2,6b** How Ahitub is found performing sacred service, and the Korahites and the Gershonites and Merarites, who were entrusted with the Levitical order, and the house of Eli, and those after him from his kindred in the house of Abimelech and Abiathar, and Hilkiah and Buzi, down to Joshua the great priest, and Ezra the priest, and the others.

**79,2,6c** And nowhere did a woman serve as priest.

**79,3,1a** I shall come to the new covenant as well.

**79,3,1b** If women were appointed to serve God as priests, or to perform any canonical function in the church, then Mary herself ought rather to have exercised a priesthood in the new covenant, she who was counted worthy to receive in her own bosom the heavenly God, the King of all, the Son of God, whose womb became a temple and dwelling-place and was made ready for the Lord’s dispensation in the flesh, by the love of God for mankind and an astounding mystery.

**79,3,2a** But he was not pleased to have it so.

**79,3,2b** Nor was she even entrusted with giving baptism, since Christ could have been baptised by her rather than by John.

**79,3,2c** But John, the son of Zacharias, carried on in the wilderness, entrusted with the baptism of remission of sins, and his father served God as priest and saw a vision at the hour of incense.

**79,3,3** Peter and Andrew, James and John, Philip as well as Bartholomew, Thomas, Thaddaeus, and James son of Alphaeus, and Judas son of James, and Simon the Cananaean, and Matthias, elected to fill up the number of the Twelve — these were all chosen as apostles, performing the sacred service of the gospel throughout the earth, together with Paul and Barnabas and the rest, and as leaders of the mysteries, with James the brother of the Lord and first bishop of Jerusalem.

**79,3,4** From this bishop and the apostles mentioned before, successions of bishops and presbyters were established in the house of God, and nowhere among these was a woman appointed.

**79,3,5a** “Philip the evangelist,” it says, “had four daughters who prophesied” — yet they did not perform sacred service.

**79,3,5b** And there was Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, but she was not entrusted with the priesthood.

**79,3,5c** For it had to be fulfilled: “Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and shall dream in dreams, and your youths shall see visions.”

**79,3,6a** And that an order of deaconesses exists in the church is true, yet not for serving as priests, nor for being permitted to undertake anything of the kind, but for the sake of the modesty of the female sex, whether at the time of the bath, or of visiting the sick or the suffering, and whenever a woman’s body is uncovered, so that it may not be seen by the men who perform sacred service but by the woman who ministers, who is directed by the priest to look after the woman in need, for the occasion, at the moment when her body is uncovered; the order of good discipline and church rule having been very securely and skilfully established within the measure of the canon.

**79,3,6b** That is why the divine word does not permit a woman either to speak in church or to have authority over a man.

**79,3,6c** And there is much that could be said about this.

**79,4,1a** It must be observed that the church’s order required women only as far as deaconesses, and it named widows, and among these called the still older ones elder women, but nowhere did it appoint female presbyters or priestesses.

**79,4,1b** For not even deacons in the church’s order were entrusted with celebrating any mystery, but only with ministering at what is celebrated.

**79,4,2a** From where, again, has this new fable risen up among us?

**79,4,2b** From where comes the conceit of women and a madness of the women’s quarters?

**79,4,2c** From where does vice, nourished once more through the female, pouring the womanishness of its notion into our minds and working its own self-indulgence, attempt to force the wretched nature of men to step outside what has been laid down?

**79,4,3** But let us take on the firm mind of Job, the athlete; let us arm ourselves, taking up his righteous answer on our lips; let us too say, “You have spoken as one of the foolish women.”

**79,4,4a** For how will such a thing not appear crazed to everyone who has understanding and has acquired it in God?

**79,4,4b** How is the practice not idol-making and the undertaking devilish?

**79,4,4c** For the devil, always slipping into the mind of men under the pretext of what is right, made mortal nature into gods and portrayed before the eyes of men statues in human likeness through a variety of arts.

**79,4,5** And those who are worshipped are dead, while their statues, which never lived (for things that never lived cannot even become dead), they bring in as objects of worship, through a mind that has gone whoring away from the one and only God, like the harlot common to many, stirred up to the great absurdity of promiscuity, who has rubbed off the chastity of lawful union with one husband.

**79,4,6** Yes indeed, Mary’s body was holy, yet she was not God; truly, the virgin was a virgin and was honoured, but she was not given to us for worship; rather she herself worshipped him who was born of her in the flesh, but who came from heaven, from the Father’s bosom.

**79,4,7a** And for this reason the gospel makes us secure when it says — the Lord himself having declared it — “Woman, what have I to do with you?”

**79,4,7b** “My hour has not yet come.”

**79,4,7c** So that no one, from “Woman, what have I to do with you?”, might suppose the holy virgin to be something more, he called her “woman”, as though prophesying, because of the schisms and heresies that were going to arise on the earth, so that no one, admiring the holy one to excess, might fall into this nonsense of the heresy.

**79,5,1a** For the whole thing is a matter for mockery, and the account given by the heresy is, so to speak, an old wives’ tale.

**79,5,1b** What scripture has given any account of this?

**79,5,1c** Which of the prophets permitted a man to be worshipped, not to speak of a woman?
