**79,5,2** For the vessel is choice, but she is a woman, and in no way altered in nature, though honoured with honour in her mind and her senses, like the bodies of the saints, and whatever more I might say for her glorification — like Elijah, a virgin from his mother’s womb, and remaining so for ever, and taken up, without having seen death; like John, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast, the one whom Jesus loved; like Thecla the saint; and Mary is still more honoured than she, because of the dispensation of which she was counted worthy.

**79,5,3a** But neither is Elijah to be worshipped, though he is among the living, nor is John to be worshipped, though by his own prayer he made his falling asleep a thing of astonishment — or rather received the grace from God — and neither Thecla nor any of the saints is worshipped.

**79,5,3b** For the ancient error shall not master us, so that we forsake the living one and worship the things made by him.

**79,5,4a** “For they served and worshipped the creature rather than the creator, and became fools.”

**79,5,4b** For if he does not wish angels to be worshipped, how much more her who was born of Anna, who was given to Anna by Joachim, who was granted to father and mother by promise through prayer and all diligence — yet not born in any other way than by the nature of men, but, like all, from the seed of a man and the womb of a woman?

**79,5,5** For even if the story of Mary and traditions hold that it was said to her father Joachim in the desert, “Your wife has conceived”, this does not mean that it came about without marital union, nor without the seed of a man; rather, the angel who was sent foretold what was going to be, so that there might be no hesitation, because of what had in truth been born, and had already been ordained by God, and was born thereafter to the righteous man.

**79,6,1a** And everywhere we see the Scriptures giving such accounts.

**79,6,1b** For Isaiah proclaims beforehand the things that were to be fulfilled in the Son of God, saying, “Behold, the virgin shall conceive, and shall bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel.”

**79,6,2a** And since she who gave birth was a virgin, and he who was being conceived in a woman was God with us, as it is interpreted, so that the truth might not fall into hesitation through suspicion on the prophet’s part, the prophet, constrained by the Holy Spirit, sees in a vision and relates it, and says, “And he went in to the prophetess,” telling of Gabriel’s coming in with the good tidings — he who had been dispatched by God to tell of the entry of the only-begotten Son of God into the world and of his birth from Mary.

**79,6,2b** “And she conceived,” it says, “and bore a son.”

**79,6,3a** “And the Lord said to me, Call his name, Spoil quickly, plunder swiftly; before the child knows how to call father or mother, he will take the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria,” and so on.

**79,6,3b** And none of these things had yet been accomplished.

**79,6,3c** This was to take place in the Son of God, and to be fulfilled after one thousand six hundred years, more or less.

**79,6,4a** And the prophet saw things that were to come after so many generations as though they had already happened.

**79,6,4b** Was it a lie, then?

**79,6,4c** Far from it.

**79,6,4d** Rather, what had been dispensed by God was proclaimed with certainty as already accomplished, so that the truth might not be disbelieved, so that so amazing and astounding a mystery, which was yet to be, might not fall into hesitation in the prophet’s mind.

**79,6,5a** Or do you not see the proclamation itself which follows, in the words of the holy Isaiah himself: “As a sheep he was led to slaughter, and as a lamb is silent before the one who shears him, so he does not open his mouth.”

**79,6,5b** “But who shall declare his generation?”

**79,6,5c** “For his life is taken away from the earth, and I will give the wicked in return for his burial,” and so on.

**79,6,5d** And see how he relates the first things as later, and expounds the later things as having happened, when he says, “As a sheep he was led to slaughter.”

**79,6,6a** And this is spoken of as past.

**79,6,6b** For he did not say “he is led”, and yet the one proclaimed by Isaiah had not yet been led.

**79,6,6c** But the deed was spoken of by the prophet as having already come about.

**79,6,6d** For God’s initiation into the mystery could not be set aside.

**79,6,6e** But going on from it, he no longer spoke of things as having happened, so that he might not, in turn, produce error.

**79,6,6f** Rather, he says, “his life is taken away from the earth.”

**79,6,6g** By the two expressions he shows the truth: that “he was led” was already being accomplished, and “is taken away” was fulfilled afterwards, so that from its having happened you may perceive the truth and the firmness of God’s promise, and from its being yet to come you may infer the time of the mysteries being revealed.

**79,7,1a** So too in the case of Mary the angel foretold what her father was going to receive from God on entering his own house — what had been asked for in prayer through the petition of father and mother: “Behold, your wife has conceived in her womb,” so that he might firmly settle the believer’s mind in the promise.

**79,7,1b** But this has become an occasion of error for some.

**79,7,1c** For it is impossible for anyone on earth to be born otherwise than by the nature of men.

**79,7,1d** For this distinction belonged to him alone; to him alone did nature give way.

**79,7,2** He, as the fashioner and master of the matter, formed himself anew from a virgin as from the earth — God come from heaven, the Word clothed with flesh from a holy virgin; yet not so that the virgin should be worshipped, nor so that he might make her God, not so that we should make offerings in her name, not so that he might again, after so many generations, appoint women as priestesses.

**79,7,3a** God was not pleased for this to happen in Salome, nor in Mary herself.

**79,7,3b** He did not permit her to give baptism, nor to bless disciples; he did not command her to hold rule upon the earth, but only that she should be a sanctuary and be counted worthy of his kingdom.

**79,7,4** Not the one called the mother of Rufus, not the women who followed from Galilee, not Martha the sister of Lazarus, and Mary, not any of the holy women who were counted worthy to be saved by his coming and who ministered to him from their own means, not the Canaanite woman, not the woman with the issue of blood who was saved — not one of the women on earth did he appoint to exercise this dignity.

**79,7,5a** From where, then, does the coiling dragon come upon us again; from where are these crooked counsels renewed?

**79,7,5b** Let Mary be in honour, but let the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit be worshipped; let no one worship Mary.

**79,7,5c** I do not say to a woman — not even to a man; the mystery is assigned to God; not even angels can admit such glorification.

**79,7,6** Let what has been wickedly written in the heart of the deceived be wiped out; let the craving for the tree be dimmed from their eyes; let the creature turn back again to its Master; let Eve, together with Adam, be shamed into honouring God alone; let her not be led by the serpent’s voice, but abide by God’s command, “You shall not eat of the tree.”

**79,7,7a** And the tree was not error, but through the tree came the disobedience of error.

**79,7,7b** Let no one eat of the error that arises on account of holy Mary; for even if the tree was fair, yet it was not for food, and even if Mary is most fair and holy and honoured, yet she is not for worship.

**79,8,1** But these women renew once more the mixed cup for Fortune, and set out the table for the demon, not for God, according to what is written, and they eat food of impiety, as the divine word says, “And the women knead dough, and the sons collect wood to make cakes for the army of heaven.”

**79,8,2a** Let such women be muzzled by Jeremiah, and let them not throw the world into an uproar.

**79,8,2b** Let them not say, “We honour the Queen of heaven.”

**79,8,2c** For Tahpanhes knows how to punish these women; the places of Migdol know how to receive their bodies for rotting.

**79,8,2d** Do not obey a woman, Israel; lift your head up out of the counsel of a bad woman.

**79,8,2e** “For a woman hunts the precious souls of men.”

**79,8,2f** “For her feet lead those who have to do with her down to Hades with death.”

**79,8,3a** Pay no heed to a worthless little woman.

**79,8,3b** For honey drips from the lips of a harlot, which for a season anoints your throat, but afterwards you will find it bitterer than bile and more keenly whetted than a double-edged sword.

**79,8,3c** Do not obey this worthless woman.

**79,8,3d** For every heresy is a worthless woman, and still more this heresy of the women, and that of the one who deceived the first woman.

**79,8,4a** Let Eve our mother be honoured, as one fashioned by God, but let her not be listened to, so that she may not persuade the children to eat from the tree and to break a commandment.

**79,8,4b** And let her too repent of empty babbling; let her turn back, ashamed and clothing herself with fig leaves.

**79,8,4c** And let Adam too take note of her, and no longer obey her.

**79,8,5a** For the persuasion of error and a woman’s counsel to the contrary work death for her own husband, and not only so, but for the children as well.

**79,8,5b** Eve overthrew the creature through the transgression, provoked by the serpent’s voice and promise, led astray from the proclamation and going over to another way of thinking.

**79,9,1a** For this reason the Master and Saviour of all, wishing to heal the pain and build up what had been overthrown and set right what had been diminished, since death came down into the world from a woman, was himself born of a virgin woman, so as to shut death in, and fill up what was lacking, and perfect what had been diminished.

**79,9,1b** But vice turns about upon us again, to bring the diminishment forward into the world once more.

**79,9,1c** But neither the young nor the old are persuaded by the woman, because of the sobriety from above.

**79,9,2a** The Egyptian woman does not make sport of chaste Joseph, nor turn him aside, though she worked the terrible thing of her counsel against the young man with much contrivance.

**79,9,2b** But a man who has received his understanding from the Holy Spirit is not made sport of; he does not destroy his chastity, so as not to cheapen his nobility.

**79,9,2c** He leaves his garments behind and does not lose his body.

**79,9,2d** He flees the place, so as not to fall into the snare.

**79,9,2e** He is punished for a season, but reigns for ever.

**79,9,2f** He is thrown into prison, but it is better to remain in prison “and in a corner of the open air, than with a quarrelsome and talkative woman.”

**79,9,3a** And how much more is there to say?

**79,9,3b** For either these idle women offer the small loaf to Mary herself, as worshipping her, or they undertake to offer this rotten offering already mentioned on her behalf.

**79,9,3c** The whole thing is foolish and alien, an insolence and a deceit from the prompting of demons.

**79,9,4a** But so as not to draw out my discourse, what we have said will suffice.

**79,9,4b** Let Mary be in honour, let the Lord be worshipped; for the righteous work error for no one.

**79,9,4c** “For God cannot be tempted with evils,” and he himself tempts no one — nor do his servants — to deceit.

**79,9,4d** “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire.”

**79,9,4e** “Then desire gives birth to sin, and sin, when it is accomplished, brings forth death.”

**79,9,5** Considering that enough has been said about all these things, beloved, and having crushed with the word of truth this blister beetle too, so to speak — golden in appearance, and winged, so to speak, and flying, yet venomous and holding poison within itself — let us go on to the one that still remains, once more calling on God to stand by us, so that we may track out the parts of the truth and work a complete repulse against what opposes it.

### Sect 80: Massalians

Against the Massalians, with whom are joined the Martyrians, who are of Greek origin, and the Euphemites and the Satanians, the sixtieth, but the eightieth in the series.

**80,1,1** Shamelessness has no surfeit, nor folly any satiety; it has spread out its reasoning over everything and opened its mouth wide to ravage the seed of Adam and of Noah, rubbing off chastity in various ways and sowing the whorish mind in manifold ways in those it wrongs.

**80,1,2a** For after these heresies, once again, another one has risen up against us, a puff of wind, foolish and full of all folly, wholly laughable, having an incoherent mind, and consisting of men and women who have been deceived.

**80,1,2b** These are called Massalians, which interpreted means people who pray.

**80,1,3** Some time ago — from about the times of Constantius until now — there were others again called Euphemites, or else Massalians, from which, I think, this one too perhaps took its imitative zeal.

**80,1,4a** But those set out from the Greeks, neither adhering to Judaism nor being Christians nor deriving from the Samaritans, but being merely Greeks, supposedly; and while they speak of gods, they worship none of them at all, but supposedly pay reverence to one alone and call him the Almighty.

**80,1,4b** And having built for themselves certain houses, or broad places like forums, they called these houses of prayer.

**80,1,5** And in ancient times there were places of prayer both among the Jews, outside the city, and among the Samaritans, as we have also found in the Acts of the Apostles, at the spot where Lydia the purple-seller met Saint Paul and those with him, as the divine writing also tells it: “where,” it says, “there was thought to be a place of prayer”; and they approached, and the apostles taught the women who had come together at that time.

**80,1,6** And there is also a place of prayer in Shechem, in what is now called Neapolis, outside the city, in the plain, about two milestones off, shaped like a theatre, built thus in the air and in an open place by the Samaritans, who imitate everything of the Jews.

**80,2,1** These earlier Massalians, who set out from the Greeks — those before the present ones, who supposedly set out from the name of Christ — they too, in some regions, built certain little enclosures of this kind, called houses of prayer and oratories, and in other places made for themselves buildings in the form and likeness of a church; gathering at evening and at daybreak with abundant kindling of lamps and lights,

**80,2,2** and at great length making certain little chants, by the zealous among them, and certain acclamations, supposedly to God, as though by chants and acclamations they were propitiating God, they deceive themselves.

**80,2,3a** But ignorance, being a kind of blind thing, contrives all these things for those who have gone astray, by a mere seeming of self-conceit.

**80,2,3b** Some time ago one of these structures was struck by lightning; I cannot say in what place, but perhaps we heard that this was in Phoenicia.

**80,2,3c** And certain zealous magistrates also killed many of them for counterfeiting the truth and imitating the manner of the church, though they were not Christians, nor derived from the Jews.

**80,2,3d** I believe that Lupicianus the general was one of those who punished these same Euphemites of the Greeks, and on that occasion a second error sprang up among them in turn.

**80,2,4** For some took the bodies of those who had been killed at that time for this Greek lawlessness and buried them in certain places, and there again they perform the same acclamations, and they named themselves Martyrians, supposedly because of those who bore witness on behalf of the idols.

**80,3,1a** Others of them again, devising something still deeper, as befits their simplicity, and using their own mind as counsellor, said, “Satan is great and stronger, and does much evil to men.”

**80,3,1b** “Why do we not rather take refuge with him and worship him, and honour him and acclaim him, so that through our flattering service he may not work evils against us, but,” they say, “since we have become his servants, may spare us?”

**80,3,1c** And so these too named themselves Satanians.

**80,3,2** We have put the heresy of these together in one place, along with those mentioned before and those who are now to be described by us, since, carried off alike into the open air and having stepped outside the truth, they have given themselves over to praying and singing hymns.

**80,3,3a** But all these things, being ridiculous, were in fact harmless, since they could not turn the mind aside from the truth.

**80,3,3b** For they were not said to be in the name of Christ, but were Greeks entirely; but now, from those ways, there are these who are now called Massalians, who have neither beginning nor end, neither head nor root, but are in everything unstable and without a founder and deceived, having no support at all of a name, or of an ordinance, or of a position, or of legislation.

**80,3,4a** So these people, men and women together, supposedly, give the appearance, saying that they have believed in Christ, of having renounced the world and withdrawn from their own possessions; yet they sleep all mixed together in the same place, men along with women and women along with men, in broad streets, whenever it is the summer season, because, they say, they have no possession on earth.

**80,3,4b** They are unrestrained, and they stretch out their hands to beg, as being without livelihood and without possessions.

**80,3,5a** Their words go beyond those of fools.

**80,3,5b** Whichever of their adherents you question, he says that he is whatever you like.

**80,3,5c** For should you say “prophet”, they will answer, “I am a prophet”; or should you name “Christ”, he declares, “I am Christ”; or “patriarch”, he shamelessly names himself the same; or “angel”, he calls himself that too — and in short, oh, the vain-mindedness of men!

**80,3,6a** Fasting they do not know at all, but, supposedly devoted to prayer, from the second or third hour, or even at night, if hunger overtakes them, they do everything without fear, eating and drinking.

**80,3,6b** Concerning obscenity or lewdness I am not able to know anything for certain.

**80,3,7a** Yet they are not far short of this either, especially as they have made it their practice to lie down in common in the same place, women together with men.

**80,3,7b** These are in Antioch too, having come from Mesopotamia.

**80,4,1a** They got this harmful idea from the immoderate simplicity of certain brethren.

**80,4,1b** For some of our brethren, orthodox ones, not knowing the measure of the life in Christ — which bids us renounce the world, and estrange ourselves from our own possessions and property, and sell what is our own and share it with the poor, and take up the cross and follow in truth, not idle nor workless nor eating out of season, nor like the drone among the bees,

**80,4,2** but working with our own hands, just as the holy apostle Paul too, having renounced the world and being a herald of the truth, he “whose hands supplied not only himself, but also those who were with him” — and those were not idle, but were with him at the same time in the work; as he boasts somewhere when he says it, and he teaches most plainly, “He who does not work, let him not eat either.”

**80,4,3** But some of the brethren mentioned before, having learned perhaps, if I may say so, from Mani, who came up from Persia, things which ought not to be so — the divine word bids us rather to mark such people, who do no work.

**80,4,4a** For the opinion of some has been led astray by the saying recorded from the Saviour, “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures to eternal life.”

**80,4,4b** They think that the food that perishes is the good work, whose labour we have for righteousness; that work which was fulfilled in Abraham through the calf, and in the toil of the widow through Elijah, and in the labour of Job through his children and possessions, and of all the servants of God who toil for righteousness with their own hands, so as to supply those in need as well, just as in every monastery, both in the land of the Egyptians and in all lands, they toil so for righteousness;

**80,4,5** as the bee, holding the wax of its work in its hands and the drop of honey in its mouth, with its own hymn-singing voice hymns the Master of all according to its own perception — as Solomon too testifies, that “honouring wisdom she was advanced” —

**80,4,6a** so too God’s servants, those truly grounded upon the firm rock of the truth and building their house securely, work their fine handiwork with their own hands, each according to his craft.

**80,4,6b** With their mouths they recite almost the whole of divine Scripture, and untiringly and unflaggingly they keep frequent vigils, partly in prayers and partly in psalmody, and constantly the assemblies that have been lawfully appointed by custom;

**80,4,7** and they always pass the day through the unceasing hours at their intervals, sending up their prayers to God blamelessly with much humility and painful groaning, and working with their own hands, as I said, together with the spiritual work, so that they may not come into want and lapse into the hypocrisies of men, and be unable any longer to tell the truth to the ungodly man,

**80,4,8** nor to be free from the defilement of men who are rich from injustice and who defraud the poor, nor to keep clear of their food, being unable to have their daily nourishment from righteous labours, but being forced, through the want that comes from idleness, to share the table of the rich.

**80,5,1a** That is why the divine word gives the charge, saying, “Do not desire the foods of the rich; for these belong to a false life.”

**80,5,1b** And again in another place: that one had to prepare such things, “And if you are rather greedy, do not desire his foods”;

**80,5,2** for in these things the youths in Babylon were glorified, who refused the king’s table and chose to be content with seeds rather than with a table and foods, renouncing riches and renown, even as Moses preferred to be ill-treated together with God’s people rather than to enjoy the treasures that were in Egypt, and by working with his own hands he attained to prophecy.

**80,5,3a** For this man, the well-born, the son of a king’s daughter, became a shepherd of sheep, so as not to eat the bread of idleness, as our father Jacob also teaches in saying to Laban, “Grant me work, that I may labour for my own bread.”

**80,5,3b** And he too, in turn, was set to shepherd the flocks by his own father-in-law, so that the righteous might not eat the bread of idleness.

**80,5,4a** But the apostles were told to be content with preaching the word, so that they might not be kept busy as they made their journey from city to city and from place to place for the preaching.

**80,5,4b** For “the labourer is worthy of his hire”, and “his food is enough for the one who works.”

**80,5,5a** And likewise to the shepherds, because of their constant occupation with the people, and the administration of the church, and their continual ministry, the divine word says, “Who tends a flock and does not eat of its milk?”

**80,5,5b** “Or who plants a vineyard and does not partake of its fruit?”

**80,5,6** And he says, “The labouring farmer must be the first to partake of the fruits,” so that he might ensure that the presbyter or the bishop is not short of his daily food, urging the people to allot to the priests, from their righteous labours, what is needed for food, through first-fruits and offerings and the rest; and though those who have been appointed by God to guide the people have authority over these things, those who profess to please God perfectly do not use even these to excess.

**80,6,1** For even from among God’s priests themselves, these too, together with the preaching of the word, imitate, after God, their holy father in Christ — the holy apostle Paul, I mean — and these too, as far as possible, if not all, yet most of them, work with their own hands at whatever craft they may find to be in due proportion befitting their dignity and the constant demands of the church’s care,

**80,6,2** so that along with the word and the preaching their conscience may rejoice, bearing fruit through its own hands and supplying itself, and sharing willingly with the brethren and the needy the stewardship that is in hand — of first-fruits, I mean, and offerings — and with their neighbours too, from the very things worked by their hands, through an abundance of devotion towards God;

**80,6,3** although they are not compelled, nor condemned, since they have the labours of righteousness and the work of the church and are fed in accordance with righteousness, but they do this through an abundance of free choice.

**80,6,4** For their inspired soul, established in the fear of God and having acquired its knowledge from the Holy Spirit, longs for the heavenly wealth that is according to righteousness, with praise and renown and distinction — the wealth that comes through divine doctrines and the divine study of holy Scripture and the oracles of God, through psalmody and assemblies, holy fasts and purity and way of life, and through the work of the hands done by free choice for the sake of righteousness.

**80,6,5** But these same honoured brethren of ours, those who live in monasteries in Mesopotamia, or rather in what are called folds, have been caught by another fashion, displaying women’s long hair and relying on conspicuous sackcloth.

**80,6,6a** But the children of our holy virgin mother, the church, ought to be modest, keeping at home, serving God in secret, who knows secret things and repays openly, as it is written, and behaving with decorum because of those outside, and not wishing to receive their reward and favour from those who see them.

**80,6,6b** For conspicuous sackcloth and hair that is not cut are foreign to the catholic church, by the preaching of the apostles.

**80,6,6c** “For a man,” it says, “ought not to wear long hair, being the image and glory of God.”

**80,7,1a** And what is worse and contrary?

**80,7,1b** Some cut off the beard, the mark of a man’s form, yet often let the hair of the head grow long.

**80,7,1c** Concerning the beard, in the Apostolic Ordinances the divine word and instruction say not to spoil it, that is, not to cut the hair of the beard, nor to adorn oneself in the manner of harlots, nor to make one’s approach to righteousness a display of pride.

**80,7,2a** For this befitted the Nazoraeans alone, on account of the type.

**80,7,2b** For the ancients were led by a type of what was to come, wearing long hair on the head because of the vow, until the vow of the world came and was fulfilled, and Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, was revealed as the head, and he who always is, yet had not been known to the whole of humanity save to a few who had believed in him, became known to the world; in order that, having come to know the head, we should not bring shame on the head.

**80,7,3a** For he does not speak of one’s own head; rather, from one’s own head the act of mockery strikes at Christ; hence the apostle says, “Does not even nature itself teach you that long hair is a dishonour to a man?”

**80,7,3b** And this dishonour is not praiseworthy like that other, of which it says, “despising the shame.”

**80,7,3c** For the virtue is not for God’s sake, even if it should be supposed to be for God’s sake; rather, the conduct springs from contentiousness, now that what existed only as a type has passed away and the truth has come.

**80,7,4a** And he says, “If anyone is minded to be contentious, we recognize no such custom, nor do the churches of God.”

**80,7,4b** He has therefore excluded those who do and practise such things in contentiousness both from the ordinance of the apostles and from the church of God.

**80,7,5** But we were compelled to say these things on account of the Massalians mentioned above, because they too took the sickness of this way of thinking from that source, turned aside in their understanding and ran aground against the truth; and a sect was formed in the dreadful condition of idleness and the other evils.

**80,8,1a** These are the things we have heard about these people too, who have become a mockery to the world and vomit forth a mind and words of rubbish, being incoherent and without hope and having stepped outside God’s building.

**80,8,1b** Hence, having said a little about them too, we shall next set to work on their refutation.

**80,8,2** And first, that women should be with men in the same place — the righteous word does not prescribe this, not even from the ancient custom of those who were joined in natural unions, but [man, woman] together, one man to one woman, as Adam to Eve, as Sarah had it with Abraham, as Rebecca was joined to Isaac.

**80,8,3a** For even if some of the fathers had two or three wives, the wives did not live in a single house.

**80,8,3b** For such a form belongs to swine, and such coupling to beasts.

**80,8,4a** But these people rather compel us to be astonished, since they profess to have no intercourse with women, while on the contrary they produce mockery instead and display their utter shame.

**80,8,4b** For even if such people had wives, they ought to have kept them separately, not mixed together.

**80,8,5** And if they are indeed in marriage, they ought not to expose what was ordained by God — the union of man with woman, with decorum and dignity and understanding — by bringing it out into the open of their own licence.

**80,8,6** And if some of them, living in purity and continence, have indeed abstained from women, they have outraged what is right through their senselessness, and the way of life of virtue through their reckless conduct in folly — since this was neither the practice of the apostles nor something the prophets before the apostles ordained.

**80,9,1a** Moses, at any rate, in the wilderness, taking up the hymn, sings a song to God when he had come up from the sea, saying, “Let us sing to the Lord, since he has been glorified gloriously; horse and rider he has hurled into the sea.”

**80,9,1b** And the men joined in with him together, and nowhere the women, so that he might show the orderly arrangement, so that he might proclaim the dignity of the good order of God’s law.

**80,9,2a** Then afterwards it says, “And Miriam, taking the timbrel, went at the head of the women, and she said, ‘Let us sing to the Lord, since he has been glorified gloriously.’”

**80,9,2b** And the women joined in together with her who was of like manner and of the same sex and who in some measure led them — on account of the ignorant and rubbishy mind of those who carry on their false teaching all mixed together.

**80,9,3** And concerning the resurrection the prophet says, “And they shall mourn tribe by tribe, tribe over against tribe: Nathan’s tribe on its own, and their wives on their own; Judah’s tribe on its own, and their wives on their own,” and so on.

**80,9,4** So too the apostles ordain for the church; so too the Lord ordained in the gospel, proclaiming the example to us from one woman, when he said to his mother, “Do not touch me; for I have not yet ascended to the Father.”

**80,9,5a** So Gehazi approaches the Shunammite and pushes her away, so as not to destroy the order, so as not to outrage the ordinance of the prophets.

**80,9,5b** But the prophet, borne along by the Holy Spirit, saw that the Shunammite was in deep distress, and for the sake of consolation he went beyond the rule, and allowed it for the moment for the sake of the woman’s consolation, judging the woman’s touching of his feet, contrary to custom, to be equal to the affliction and grief in her mind.

**80,9,5c** And why should I say much about these people who imitate dogs and emulate swine?

**80,9,6a** And as to calling oneself Christ — to whom of those possessed of understanding would the doctrine not appear to be a thing of madness — or to say, “I am a prophet”?

**80,9,6b** For what form of prophecy appears among them, or what wondrous work of Christ is done?

**80,9,6c** And if he himself is Christ, in what Lord has he hoped and believed?

**80,9,6d** What are these empty babblings of error?

**80,9,6e** What are these doctrines of the senseless?

**80,9,6f** But what has been said against this one too will suffice concerning it.

**80,10,1** And let this much stand to seal and complete our whole work concerning these things, God having appeared to us and helped us, so that we may confess with all our soul and mind, and give thanks to the Lord himself, that in the Lord himself we have been counted worthy to complete the undertaking which we promised — having made, I mean, our account and refutation of the heresies, and at the same time having revealed what is done among each of them, as far as our substance of weak humanity allows.

**80,10,2** For having shown up to this point, leaving nothing out, the impulses and causes of eighty heresies — of which we have heard in the world, and of which we have learned the number and the names, and of some the sayings, pretexts and dispositions — we are carried away with wonder and astonished at what is said in the divine Scripture: “Sixty are the queens, and eighty the concubines, and young women past numbering; one is my dove, my perfect one.”

**80,10,3** Since, then, we have spoken from the beginning about these eighty concubines — Barbarism and Hellenism and Scythianism and Judaism and Samaritanism — names of women who are not lawful wives, nor dowered by the king, nor able to have their children inherit under testaments.

**80,10,4** For by nature they are seventy-five, and their mothers are five: such as Hellenism, from which come the Greeks, and Judaism, from which come the Jews and heresies, and the Samaritan, from which Samaritanism, and Christianity,

**80,10,5** from which the heresies that were set apart were broken off like branches, called by the name of Christ but not being his — some of them standing very far off from him, others, for some very slight matter, having made themselves and their children disinherited and strangers to him, being of those who are not lawful wives, but have gone outside, and have only had the name of Christ called upon them — there will remain for us the demonstration concerning the truth, and concerning the dove herself, the only one, who is praised by the bridegroom.

**80,11,1** And when we have had leisure and have earnestly besought God, we shall next make a defence on behalf of the truth too, brief in its discussion but secure in its tradition — the truth not being last, but first, and already called to mind by us far above, among the matters before the heresies,

**80,11,2** at the sojourn of Christ — and now the holy bride, who is first and joined to Christ from his coming in the flesh [and that of his coming],

**80,11,3** she who was formed with Adam, and proclaimed among the patriarchs before Abraham, and believed with Abraham, and revealed through Moses, and prophesied in Isaiah, but made manifest in Christ and existing with Christ, and praised by us last.

**80,11,4** For the contestant must first take his stand in the contest, with its toil and the other bouts of the contest, so that afterwards, having received the crown, he may continue with the crown in exultation — the crown not being last, but set before the wrestling, yet given afterwards for joy and exultation to the one who has toiled.

**80,11,5** Having said these things about them, let us pass on to the discourses mentioned before, to show how there are eighty concubines and sixty queens,

**80,11,6** how the virgin is one, pure and bride together, and dove and ewe-lamb, and the holy city of God and faith, “and the foundation of the truth, and the solid rock over which the gates of Hades shall not prevail.”

**80,11,7a** For calling upon God in all things, and having called upon him, we have succeeded in fulfilling the pledge of our promise — the one against all the heresies, I mean — by which promise we have reached as far as the heresy of the Massalians.

**80,11,7b** And now that we have trodden this one down as well with the sandal of the gospel, like a chameleon of many feet, unsightly, formless, giving off a stench, let us in all things render thanks to God — to the Father in the Son, to the Son in the Father, together with the Holy Spirit — to the ages of ages.

**80,11,7c** Amen.

## De Fide

A concise and true discourse concerning the faith of the church, catholic and apostolic.

**De Fide 1,1** Having dealt with the manifold, multiform and many-branched reckless teachings of the crooked designs of our adversaries, and having divided them by species and genus, we have refuted them, by the power of God, as things vanished and stale; and having swum through the boundless surge, from every heresy, of blasphemies and obscenities and of their most loathsome mysteries, having resolved the questions in every respect, though only with very great difficulty,

**De Fide 1,2** and having passed beyond their wickedness, we have drawn near to the calm regions of the truth — having crossed every stretch of rough sea, and endured every squall and foaming and arching of the waves,

**De Fide 1,3** and having beheld swell, so to speak, and whirlpools, and shoals of no ordinary kind, and places of wild beasts, and having come to experience them through our discourses — now beholding the harbour of peace, into which, in our eagerness to put in, we once more entreat the Lord through prayer;

**De Fide 1,4** already finding respite from all fear and tumult and seasickness, and in the finest condition, breathing in the breezes from the solid land, and strengthened by safety and by the calm harbour, we already rejoice in spirit — having endured,

**De Fide 1,5** if the truth must be told, many hardships in these matters and outrages of no ordinary kind, and having traversed, so to speak, both land and sea, on foot and by voyage — the rough places of the land and the hard country of the desert, and the dangers of the seas mentioned before —

**De Fide 1,6** and at the same time seeing the city, let us hasten to it, holy Jerusalem, the virgin and bride of Christ, the secure foundation and rock, our revered mother, the bride of Christ, saying ourselves too, most fittingly, “Come, let us ascend to the Lord’s mountain, and to the house of Jacob’s God, and he will make known to us his way,” and so on.

**De Fide 2,1** Come then, children of Christ, sons of the holy church of God, who are going gently through this treatise on the eighty heresies, and who have swum with me through such a mass of the wicked teachings mentioned before, and crossed on foot so great a desert, fearful and set in thirst,

**De Fide 2,2** let us invoke the Lord of the universe — having long been in desire of this, and in every place of these heresies, as in the place Marah and in the thirst of the fearful, trackless desert, always encountering their crooked arguments —

**De Fide 2,3a** let us too cry out, “As the hart longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.”

**De Fide 2,3b** And again, “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?”

**De Fide 2,4** Therefore let us too call her the sooner — not as he called the bride, being her bridegroom and Lord and Master and King and God and champion;

**De Fide 2,5** rather let us call her as his servants, saying ourselves too, in harmony with him, “Come from Lebanon, bride, for you are all fair, and there is no blemish in you” —

**De Fide 2,6** the paradise of the great craftsman, the holy King’s city, the bride of the spotless Christ, the chaste virgin, pledged in faith to a single husband only, the radiant one, “peering forth like the morning, lovely as the moon, chosen as the sun, awesome as one set in array,” she whom the queens call blessed and the concubines extol in hymns, who is praised by the daughters, and who comes up from the wilderness made white, leaning upon her beloved, “she who breathes of perfumes, who comes up from the wilderness like pillars of smoke, censed with myrrh and frankincense from the perfumer’s powders, of him who has given his own fragrance” —

**De Fide 2,7a** he whom she foresaw when she said, “Your name is perfume poured out.”

**De Fide 2,7b** “Therefore the maidens have loved you.”

**De Fide 2,7c** “She who stands at the right hand of the King, clothed in fringed garments,” adorned with cloth of gold, she who has nothing dark, though once she was blackened,

**De Fide 2,8** but now is fair and made white — so that, coming to be in you, we may find respite from the hateful affairs of the heresies that we have passed through, and be at rest from the tossing of their great waves, and revive in you, O holy church, our mother, and in the holy teaching within you and the holy and only faith of God in truth.

**De Fide 2,9a** But I shall begin to relate the wonders concerning this holy city of God.

**De Fide 2,9b** For it is glorious things that have been said about her, as the prophet declares, “Glorious things have been said of you, O city of God” — things beyond the reach of all men and alien to unbelievers, but for faithful and true men attainable in part, and in the promise of completion, as things to be bestowed by their own Master in the kingdom of the heavens, where the holy virgin and heir herself, with her own bridegroom, has received her lot and her inheritance in heaven.

**De Fide 3,1** And first, that God who is above all is our God, for us who are born of this holy church; for this is the first proof concerning the truth and the foundation of the faith of this one and only virgin, the holy and guileless dove,

**De Fide 3,2** concerning whom the Lord, by the Spirit, was revealing to Solomon in the Song of Songs, saying, “Sixty are the queens, and eighty the concubines, and young women past numbering; one is my dove, my perfect one” — “my” being added, and “my” again.

**De Fide 3,3a** For the dove is his, and the perfect one is his, the others being so called without being so, whereas she is named twice over.

**De Fide 3,3b** For of the others he did not say, “There are eighty concubines of mine”; but to the queens he assigned, through their glorious title, a share in the honour, while of the concubines he declared their complete estrangement.

**De Fide 3,4** Taking their numbers by name, we are compelled to work them out in this place according to the higher sense of contemplation, so as not to pass over anything, not as men talking idly, but in truth testing the words through the true Scriptures against the true contemplations.

**De Fide 3,5a** For it is a fact that the number written for each subject is inviolable, and that what is set down in number can neither be anything stale nor be measured out in Scripture to no purpose.

**De Fide 3,5b** Now the queens are the souls already named earlier in the genealogy.

**De Fide 3,6** For as great multitudes follow a king, but the king is the head — just as, though a body has many members, the one man will be counted from the head — so from the one king the whole multitude under the king will be reckoned as one.

**De Fide 4,1** Accordingly the generation in Christ has been named queen — not because every generation reigned, but because the one generation which recognised the Lord bears, through the naming of the man, [the cause], the royal dignity and rank; as, for example, Adam and his whole generation will be counted as this queen, both his beginning and the patriarchate having reigned together with those after him because of his knowledge of God, and the first fashioning in which he was deemed worthy to be fashioned, and because he was the first to show repentance, as the sequence has it.

**De Fide 4,2** Then after him Seth and all the humankind with him, and Enosh and Kenan and Mahalalel and Jared and Enoch and Methuselah and Lamech and Noah — these saints being enumerated in a list, by number, generation by generation, whose number is shown in Matthew.

**De Fide 4,3** For sixty-two generations and patriarchates are recorded by him through the names of the more perfect men, who had knowledge of God, or who for some other excellence shared in royal glory and dignity, the list of whose number runs until the coming of Christ.

**De Fide 4,4** For ten generations passed from Adam to Noah, and from Noah to Abraham another ten, and from Abraham to David fourteen generations, and from David to the captivity fourteen generations, and from the captivity to Christ fourteen generations, making sixty-two generations in all from Adam down to Christ, which have been counted as sixty for brevity.

**De Fide 4,5a** For in the wilderness too, though there were seventy-two trunks of palm trees, Scripture named seventy.

**De Fide 4,5b** And of the seventy summoned to the mountain, seventy-two are found, with Eldad and Medad.

**De Fide 4,5c** And seventy-two made the translation under Ptolemy, but for brevity we are accustomed to speak of the translation of the Seventy.

**De Fide 4,6a** So now too, I think, sixty queens are spoken of, the number at the top and the number at the bottom being taken away, because of the central place of the sixty for figures and for the higher sense of perfect contemplation.

**De Fide 4,6b** For since it comes about that the cycle of the six days is completed through six decades, so that from each generation holy souls reigning in God according to faith are joined together.

**De Fide 4,7** Hence too six stone water jars are found in Cana of Galilee, which, having run empty, were filled again, holding two or three measures apiece — concerning the measure of the old and new covenant and of the Trinity of the fullness; and these were changed from water into unmixed wine, being filled for the gladness of a wedding and of the sons of men.

**De Fide 4,8** Hence too in the learning of outsiders there is what is called the hexagonal, measured geometrically through a triad and a heptad into the number twenty-one; and the significance of this hexagonal is the filling of the whole visible vessel, because the square, so to speak, is fourfold, and the base and the covering of the roof above complete the sixth number.

**De Fide 5,1** But, not to extend my account at length, I think again that what has been said about the sixty queens is sufficient — the generations counted up to the coming of Christ — while the generations that have come about since Christ until now are known to the Lord himself alone.

**De Fide 5,2** For the numbers have no longer been recorded by anyone generation by generation, or set in order, because the number of this subject has been sealed and closed off by the number of the queens, counted up to his coming in the flesh.

**De Fide 5,3** For thereafter the later writers, whether compilers or prose authors or chroniclers or historians, no longer count generations, but only the successions of kings and the times according to the number of years of each king, so that the intelligent man knows full well, from every side, that from this inquiry too the whole of time was cut short into the number of the sixty-two generations up to Christ,

**De Fide 5,4** because after Christ the times of the world are no longer counted by genealogies according to this subject, since it is brought to completion in one union, which is signified according to the immovable foundation of God’s good pleasure; as though from her the consummation of the age is cut short and fulfilled in the passing over to the age to come.

**De Fide 5,5** This is why it is said, “One is my dove, my perfect one,” since all things are brought to completion up to her, even if the age should count itself in times and seasons, in years and spans of generations, whether by kings or consuls or Olympiads or governorships.

**De Fide 5,6** And the eighty concubines are those who stand among the queens and before the kingdom in the flesh — that is, the faith — and before this very bride and virgin, the spotless one and dove, the only one to her mother and to her that bore her.

**De Fide 6,1a** For she is the church, born of one faith and brought forth through the Holy Spirit, the only one to the one and only mother who bore her.

**De Fide 6,1b** And all that came after her and before her are named concubines; they have not become altogether strangers to the covenant and the inheritance, but they have not been dowered by the Word, nor have they received the Holy Spirit to dwell in them, but have had only a union with the Word in conscience.

**De Fide 6,2** For the Hebrew expressed the concubine well, calling her phelegestha: pheleg, which is translated ‘half’, and estha, ‘woman’, as if to say ‘half a woman’.

**De Fide 6,3a** For, so far as it concerned the Lord, he has called all to the light of freedom, saying, “As long as you have the light among you, walk in the light,” and so has the holy apostle, saying, “But you are children of day and children of light.”

**De Fide 6,3b** And again in the divine Scripture: “He who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light.”

**De Fide 6,4a** So too concubines are not brought to their husbands openly, nor with the rite of fulfilment, nor with a dowry; even if they have union with the bodies of the men, they cannot have the honour and title and security and marriage portion and bride-gifts and dowry and legitimacy of the free wife.

**De Fide 6,4b** The concubines, then, are the heresies counted in order, eighty, as I said above.

**De Fide 6,5a** And let no one wonder if each of them is also called by other names in each country.

**De Fide 6,5b** But this too must be observed, that often each heresy in turn has split within itself and been divided into many parts and names; for it is no wonder, for that is how it is.

**De Fide 6,6** We find the number eighty and one: the one because of her who is set apart from them all, allotted to the bridegroom alone and acknowledged by him with such a title as this, “My dove is one,” and again, “my perfect one,” since all the concubines are ignoble and are not measured by guilelessness, nor by purity and gentleness.

**De Fide 6,7** So from the beginning there are those connected with what is called Barbarism and Scythianism, up to the Massalians mentioned before, seventy-five in number; and Hellenism, from which come the Hellenic heresies; and Judaism, from which come the Jewish ones; and Samaritanism, from which come the Samaritan ones — the three being added to the seventy-seventh number and filling it up to the number eighty,

**De Fide 6,8** while one remains over, that is, the holy catholic church and Christianity, truly so named from the beginning, believed in alongside Adam, and prior to Adam, and before all ages together with Christ, according to the will of Father and Son and Holy Spirit, and with all who in each generation were well pleasing to God, plainly revealed at his coming into the world, and now, after all these heresies, the concubines indeed, praised again in hymns by us, as in the sequence of the account.

**De Fide 7,1a** For the Word himself counted thus in the Song, speaking of sixty queens and eighty concubines and young women past numbering.

**De Fide 7,1b** “But my dove,” he says, “my perfect one, is one; she is her mother’s only one, the chosen of her who bore her.”

**De Fide 7,2** And afterwards he shows how she will be found among all, as being more honoured than all and ruling over all and alone chosen by him, whose children are heirs of the king and true children, as children born of the promise, not children of the slave woman, nor of a concubine, nor of the others who are described as without number.

**De Fide 7,3** For even if Abraham had children by Keturah the concubine, the children of Keturah are not fellow heirs with Isaac; but they received gifts, by way of a legacy, so that the figure might remain for the higher sense of the account, so that some might not despair of the calling of Christ.

**De Fide 7,4** For the gifts which he gave to Ishmael and to the sons of Keturah were a figure of the good things that were to come for the conversion of souls to the faith and the truth.

**De Fide 7,5** For to Hagar, who was a slave woman and was cast out by Abraham (like the Jerusalem below, which served as a slave together with her children, concerning which it has been said, “I have flung away your mother,” and again, “I gave a bill of divorce into her hands”) — to this slave woman Hagar, I say, he gives, rather symbolically, for the hope of conversion, a skin of water, to show the power of the washing of regeneration, given as a gift of life to the unbelievers and for the conversion of all the nations to the knowledge of the truth.

**De Fide 7,6** But to the sons of Keturah the gifts were a store of goods — gold and silver and clothing — and the things which Abraham, in a mystery, shut up in the bags, frankincense and myrrh and gold, from what came through the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah, that is, through those with Chedorlaomer and Birsha and the rest who had taken the captives from Sodom and Gomorrah and the other cities, and had plundered the horses and carried off the multitude of the people as captives, and seized the possessions and goods of each and a great quantity of other things;

**De Fide 7,7** all this he himself brought back at that time from the slaughter of the kings, and, not daring to give back what had already been set apart for the Lord God, he gave them as gifts, with the other things, to his sons by Keturah, as we have found in the traditions of the Hebrews.

**De Fide 8,1** At the coming of Christ, since these same children of Abraham by Keturah had been sent away by Abraham, and had gone off and settled in the Arabian parts of the country of Magodia, the magi who came from the succession of those seeds offered gifts and presents to Christ in Bethlehem, for a share in the same hope — those same presents — when they came, having seen the star;

**De Fide 8,2a** and of these presents the prophet sets out the clear demonstration, saying, “Before the child knows how to call father or mother, he will take the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria in the presence of the king of the Assyrians.”

**De Fide 8,2b** For these things had been taken from Damascus in the times of Abraham, as I said before, by the kings who came, and from Samaria.

**De Fide 8,3a** When, then, did he take them before he knew how to call father or mother, if not when the magi came and opened their bags — or their treasures, as some of the copies have it — and offered myrrh and frankincense and gold?

**De Fide 8,3b** And do you see how the expressions and sequences of the truth hold together?

**De Fide 8,4** So too these heresies are concubines, and their offspring have obtained gifts, having received the name only, called only by the name of Christ and having accepted the few words from the divine Scripture, so that through them they may understand the truth,

**De Fide 8,5** if they will; but if they will not, but return to Herod (for they are charged not to return to Herod, but to reach their own country by another way) — if they do not do what has been commanded, the gifts are in vain for them, as the journey would have been for those men had they returned to Herod; because these same heresies likewise counterfeit the teachings of the divine words.

**De Fide 9,1a** These, then, are the eighty concubines, whose number is here set down, and those queens are the souls counted by generations, that is, men and patriarchs.

**De Fide 9,1b** And the maidens without number are among the remaining philosophies throughout the whole world and among the ways of life of each soul, one being praiseworthy, another not.

**De Fide 9,2a** For who could count the diversity of this world?

**De Fide 9,2b** For how many others have not sprung up among the Greeks following the four very conspicuous ones already mentioned, and, further, after those heresies and those that followed them, souls and opinions arising each on its own according to each man’s judgement in a show of youthful vigour?

**De Fide 9,3** As some are called Pyrrhonians, and many others, whose names and opinions I shall set out below in order — many indeed are those that have come to our knowledge, but they are a tiny fraction of those that exist in the world.

**De Fide 9,4** And those from the Greeks are these, of which I would place first, from the beginning, the judgement and opinion of Thales of Miletus.

**De Fide 9,5a** For Thales of Miletus himself, being one of the seven wise men, declared water to be the primal origin of all things.

**De Fide 9,5b** For he says that all things are from water and are resolved again into water.

**De Fide 9,6a** Anaximander, the son of Praxiades, himself also of Miletus, said that the boundless is the beginning of all things.

**De Fide 9,6b** For from it all things come into being, and into it all things are resolved.

**De Fide 9,7** Anaximenes, the son of Eurystratus, himself also of Miletus, says that air is the beginning of the universe and that all things are from it.

**De Fide 9,8** Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, the son of Hegesibulus, said that the homoeomeries are the beginnings of all things.

**De Fide 9,9a** Archelaus, the son of Apollodorus, or according to some of Milto, was an Athenian, a natural philosopher; he says that all things have come into being from earth.

**De Fide 9,9b** For this, as he says, is the beginning of the universe.

**De Fide 9,10** Socrates the moralist, the son of Elmaglus, or of Sophroniscus, and of Phaenarete the midwife, said that a man ought to busy himself only with what concerns himself, and with nothing more.

**De Fide 9,11** Pherecydes, for his part, says that earth came to be prior to all things.

**De Fide 9,12a** Pythagoras the Samian, son of Mnesarchus, declared the monad to be God, and that without it nothing has come to be.

**De Fide 9,12b** He said that the wise ought not to sacrifice animals to the gods, nor indeed to eat anything that has a soul, nor beans, nor to drink wine.

**De Fide 9,12c** He said that all things from the moon downward are passible, but that the things above the moon are impassible.

**De Fide 9,12d** He said too that the soul passes into many animals.

**De Fide 9,12e** He also ordered his disciples to keep silence for a period of five years, and at the last he named himself a god.

**De Fide 9,13a** Xenophanes of Colophon, the son of Orthomenes, said that all things come into being from earth and water.

**De Fide 9,13b** And of all things, as he said, nothing is true.

**De Fide 9,13c** Thus the exact truth is unclear to us, and seeming is wrought over all things, especially over things unseen.

**De Fide 9,14** Parmenides, the son of Pyres, an Eleatic by birth, himself also said that the boundless is the beginning of all things.

**De Fide 9,15a** Zeno of Elea, the eristic, holding the same as the other Zeno, says that the earth is motionless and that no place is empty.

**De Fide 9,15b** And he puts it thus: a thing in motion moves either in the place where it is or in the place where it is not.

**De Fide 9,15c** And it moves neither in the place where it is nor in the place where it is not; hence nothing moves.

**De Fide 9,16** Melissus, the son of Ithagenes, a Samian by birth, said that the universe is one, but that nothing is stable by nature, and that all things are perishable in potency.

**De Fide 9,17** Leucippus of Miletus, or according to some of Elea, he too an eristic, also said that the universe is in the boundless, and that all things come about by appearance and seeming and nothing in truth, but that they appear so, like the oar in the water.

**De Fide 9,18a** Democritus the Abderite, son of Damasippus, declared the world to be boundless and to lie over the void.

**De Fide 9,18b** He said also that there is one end of all things, and that cheerfulness is the best, but griefs are the boundaries of vice; and that what seems just is not just, but that what is contrary to nature is unjust.

**De Fide 9,18c** For he called the laws an evil invention, and said that the wise man must not obey laws, but live as a free man.

**De Fide 9,19** Metrodorus of Chios said that no one knows anything, but that the things which we think we know we do not know accurately, and that one ought not to attend to the senses; for all things are in seeming.

**De Fide 9,20** Protagoras the Abderite, son of Menander, declared that gods do not exist, and that there is no god whatever.

**De Fide 9,21** Diogenes of Smyrna, or according to some of Cyrene, held the same opinions as Protagoras.

**De Fide 9,22** Pyrrho of Elis, having collected all the doctrines of the other wise men, wrote counter-arguments to them, overturning their opinions, and was satisfied with no doctrine.

**De Fide 9,23a** Empedocles of Acragas, the son of Meton, introduced fire and earth and water and air as four primal elements, and said that at first there was enmity among the elements.

**De Fide 9,23b** For formerly, he says, they had been separated, but now they have been united, as he says, having become friends with one another.

**De Fide 9,23c** So according to him there are two principles and powers, enmity and friendship, of which the one unites and the other separates.

**De Fide 9,24** Heraclitus of Ephesus, the son of Bleson, said that all things are from fire and are resolved again into fire.

**De Fide 9,25** One Prodicus calls the four elements gods, and then the sun and the moon; for from these, he said, the life-giving power comes to all.

**De Fide 9,26a** Plato of Athens said that God, matter and form exist, and that the world is generated and perishable; and he says that the soul is ungenerated and immortal and divine.

**De Fide 9,26b** And that it has three parts, the rational, the spirited and the appetitive.

**De Fide 9,26c** He used to say that marriages and wives ought to be held in common by everyone, and that no man should keep a single wedded wife privately, but that men who wish should consort with women who are willing.

**De Fide 9,27** Aristippus of Cyrene: being a glutton and a lover of pleasure, he said that pleasure is the end of the soul, and that whoever enjoys pleasure is happy, while he who has no pleasure at all is thrice wretched and ill-starred, as they say.

**De Fide 9,28a** Theodorus, surnamed the Atheist, said that talk about God is nonsense.

**De Fide 9,28b** For he thought that there is no divinity, and for this reason he urged everyone to steal, to swear falsely, to plunder, and not to die for their country.

**De Fide 9,28c** For he said that the world is a single fatherland, and he called only the prosperous man good, and said that the unfortunate man should be shunned, even if he is wise.

**De Fide 9,28d** And that the fool who is rich and unruly is to be preferred.

**De Fide 9,29a** Hegesias of Cyrene: he said that there are neither friendships nor favours.

**De Fide 9,29b** For he said that they do not exist, but that a man gives a favour because he is in need, or does good because he has received something better.

**De Fide 9,29c** He also said that to live is profitable for the worthless man, but to die for the wise, so that some on this account called him the Death-Persuader.

**De Fide 9,30** Antisthenes, born of a Thracian mother but himself an Athenian, at first a Socratic and then a Cynic, said that one must not envy another for his evils, or for the disgraceful things men do among one another; and that the walls of cities are precarious against the betrayer inside, whereas the soul’s walls are unshaken and cannot be breached.

**De Fide 9,31a** Diogenes the Cynic, from Sinope, the city on the Pontus, followed Antisthenes in everything.

**De Fide 9,31b** He said that the good is within the reach of every wise man, and that all other things are nothing but trifles.

**De Fide 9,32** Crates of Boeotian Thebes, himself also a Cynic, said that to own nothing belongs to freedom.

**De Fide 9,33** Arcesilaus maintained that the truth is attainable by God alone, but not by man.

**De Fide 9,34** Carneades held the same opinions as Arcesilaus.

**De Fide 9,35a** Aristotle, the son of Nicomachus, was by birth a Macedonian from Stagira according to some, but according to others a Thracian.

**De Fide 9,35b** He said that there are two principles, God and matter, and that the things above the moon enjoy divine providence, while the things below the moon are without providence and are carried along by some irrational motion, at random.

**De Fide 9,35c** And he says that there exist two worlds, an upper and a lower, the upper being imperishable and the lower perishable.

**De Fide 9,35d** And he calls the soul the entelechy of the body.

**De Fide 9,36** Theophrastus of Eresus held the same opinions as Aristotle.

**De Fide 9,37a** Strato, who was from Lampsacus, said that the hot substance is the cause of all things.

**De Fide 9,37b** And he declared the parts of the world to be boundless, and said that no living creature is receptive.

**De Fide 9,38** Praxiphanes the Rhodian held the same views as Theophrastus.

**De Fide 9,39** Critolaus of Phaselis held the same opinions as Aristotle.

**De Fide 9,40a** Zeno of Citium, the Stoic, said that one ought not to build temples to the gods, but to have the divine in the mind alone, or rather to hold that the mind is God; for it is deathless.

**De Fide 9,40b** And he said that the dead should be thrown to animals, or to fire.

**De Fide 9,40c** And that one may make use of favourite boys without restraint.

**De Fide 9,40d** He said that the divine governs all things.

**De Fide 9,40e** And that the causes of events are in one respect in our power and in another not in our power; that is, some events are in our power and others are not in our power.

**De Fide 9,40f** He also spoke of the soul following its severance from the body, and he named it a long-lived spirit; yet he did not say that it is altogether imperishable, for it is consumed by the length of time into the invisible, as he says.

**De Fide 9,41** Cleanthes says that the good and the noble are pleasures, and he called the soul alone the man, and said that the gods are mystic figures and sacred names, and he maintained that the sun is the torch-bearer and the world the initiates, and he called those possessed by things divine ‘rites’.

**De Fide 9,42** Persaeus taught the same doctrines as Zeno.

**De Fide 9,43a** Chrysippus of Soli wrote unlawful laws.

**De Fide 9,43b** For he said that sons ought to unite with their mothers, and fathers with their daughters.

**De Fide 9,43c** In other matters he agreed with Zeno of Citium.

**De Fide 9,43d** Besides this he said also that men may eat human flesh.

**De Fide 9,44a** And he said that the end of all things is luxurious enjoyment.

**De Fide 9,44b** Diogenes of Babylon said that all things are constituted from pleasure.

**De Fide 9,45a** Panaetius of Rhodes said that the world is immortal and ageless, and paid no heed whatever to divination, and did away with what is said about the gods.

**De Fide 9,45b** For he said that talk about God is idle chatter.

**De Fide 9,46** Posidonius of Apamea said that the greatest good among men is wealth and health.

**De Fide 9,47** Athenodorus the Tarsian shared the opinions of Chrysippus and taught the same as Zeno.

**De Fide 9,48a** Epicurus, son of Neocles, brought up at Athens, followed a pleasure-loving life and did not blush to consort publicly with licentious women, besides what we said about him earlier.

**De Fide 9,48b** Again, he said that there are no gods, but that chance alone governs all things, and that nothing in life is voluntary, neither learning nor want of education nor any other thing, but that everything comes about for everyone against their will.

**De Fide 9,48c** And one ought not, as he says, to blame anyone or to praise anyone; for they do not undergo these things willingly.

**De Fide 9,48d** He said that one ought not to fear death.

**De Fide 9,48e** And he affirmed, as I have already said, that the universe has its constitution from atoms and that the world is in the boundless.

**De Fide 10,1a** These, then, are the ones from the Greeks who have come to our knowledge.

**De Fide 10,1b** But as for the others, as many as there are throughout the barbarian, Greek and Roman lands and the other regions of the inhabited world:

**De Fide 10,2** seventy-two distasteful philosophies are recorded in the brotherhood of the Indians — of the Gymnosophists, of the Brahmans (these alone are praiseworthy), of the Pseudo-Brahmans, of the corpse-eaters, of the doers of shameful things, of the callous; to speak of these one by one, and of the abominable things done among them, we have thought superfluous and not even fitting, because of the great corruption among men, both of vice and of its practice.

**De Fide 10,3** For in Media, again, six different heresies are said to exist; and in Ethiopia how many, and among the Persians, or in Parthia, or in the Elamite country, or the Caspian, or the country of the Germans, or Sarmatia, or how many among the Daunians, or among the Zicchi and the Amazons, the Lazi and the Iberians and the Bosporans, or the Geli, or the Seres, or the other nations — differences of laws, and of philosophies, and of heresies, and a measureless multitude of differences!

**De Fide 10,4a** So among the Seres the men braid their hair, sitting at home, perfuming themselves and making themselves womanish, preparing themselves for the women, while the women, on the contrary, crop the hair of their heads, gird themselves with a man’s girdle, and carry out all the work of the fields.

**De Fide 10,4b** But with the Geli, by contrast, the doers of base deeds win praise from their very laws.

**De Fide 10,5a** And among the Greeks, how many mysteries and rites are there?

**De Fide 10,5b** As the women who keep the Megara and the women who keep the Thesmophoria differ from one another, and so many other things: the mysteries at Eleusis, of Deo and Pherrephatta, and the shameful deeds of the shrines there, the stripping of women — to put it more decently — drums and flat cakes, bull-roarer and basket, wool worked up, and the cymbal, and the kykeon prepared in a cup; and so many others: the mysteries of Archemorus at Pytho,

**De Fide 10,6** and others at the Isthmus, of Athamas and of Melicertes the offspring of Ino; and those who carry the phallus about, and the women who perform the phallic exercises of shamelessness; and the men who serve Rhea, who have cut off the male child and go on living without the form of their parts, no longer able to be men and not become women; and others,

**De Fide 10,7a** the Dionysians, who initiate into the Curetes and the distribution of flesh, wreathed with snakes, crying in their revels “oua, oua”, still calling upon that Eve who was deceived through the serpent, or, with the rough breathing, calling upon the serpent, taking the word from the Hebrew to serve their own error.

**De Fide 10,7b** For the children of the Hebrews call the woman Eua when it is pronounced with the smooth breathing, but the serpent Heuia when it is pronounced with the rough breathing.

**De Fide 11,1a** And what shall I say?

**De Fide 11,1b** For time will fail me as I tell of the things that are unspeakable in number among the differences of men with respect to virtue and wickedness:

**De Fide 11,2a** how many there are in the land of the Egyptians, some initiated to Cronus, shutting themselves up in iron collars, with hair grown very long and with filthy and contemptible clothing, as they pierce their own nostrils with rings each day for Cronus in the place called Astu (this is a small town, a chief village in the so-called Prosopite nome), at the accursed rites of the public gathering of those led astray, and of those who beat out a din and celebrate orgies, putting on a show, so they claim, of frenzied sacred revelations.

**De Fide 11,2b** These men are utterly accursed.

**De Fide 11,3** And among how many others: as those near the Butic nome, or in the little town of Buto itself, who nurse Harpocrates, who are already old men in age, who at the sacred festival are compelled by the demon to perform the fantastic frenzies of Horus.

**De Fide 11,4** Each of the citizens, even one who is already exceedingly old, together with young men of like ways and others of every age from youth upward, priests, so they claim, of this same Horus and of Harpocrates, shaven on the head — or rather, each shamelessly bears the mark, at once servile and accursed and childish, bearing it — given over to playthings besides the clever things that come from the demon, frenzied and senseless, rush about laughing without restraint;

**De Fide 11,5** and first anointing their faces with gruel and fine flour and other vulgar contrivances, putting their faces into a boiling cauldron, and deceitfully goading the crowds into frenzy with a supposed wonder from the face, they wipe it off the face with the hand and share it with each of those who ask, for a partaking of health and as a cure for pains.

**De Fide 12,1** If I were to describe the women of Memphis and Heliopolis who celebrate orgies, who take the enchantment into themselves with drum and pipe, the dancing women and the women of the triennial festivals, and the women at Batheia and at Menouthis who have abandoned modesty and womanly bearing — with how many swellings of tongue, or with how great a breadth of composition, giving myself up to it, shall I be able to devote myself to the unspeakable number mentioned before?

**De Fide 12,2** For even if I were to take upon myself an exceeding labour, I should leave the comprehension of these things incomplete, since it has been said, “maidens without number.”

**De Fide 12,3** The things at Sais, at Pelusium, at Bubastis, at Abydos, the precincts of Antinous and the mysteries there, those at Pharbaethus, those concerning the goat of Mendes, so many at Busiris, how many at Sebennytus, how many at Diospolis — as in some places they perform rites to the ass in the name of Seth, that is, of Typhon, while others perform them to Tithrambo, which is interpreted Hecate, others are initiated to Senephthys, others to Thermouthis, and others to Isis.

**De Fide 12,4a** And how many such things there are to tell, to speak of which one by one would consume much time!

**De Fide 12,4b** Therefore the saying, fulfilled, will embrace them on every side, through the words “maidens without number.”

**De Fide 12,5** And again, of many other mysteries, and of heresiarchs and makers of schisms, the leaders among the Persians are the Magusaeans, and among the Egyptians those called prophets, the leaders of the shrines and temples [and of the magi]; among the Babylonians those called Gazarenes, wise men and enchanters; among the Indians those called Euilaeans and the Brahmans; and among the Greeks the hierophants and the leaders of the temple-wardens, of the multitude of Cynics and of other unspeakable philosophers.

**De Fide 13,1a** So, as I said before, among the Persians there are those called Magusaeans, who abhor idols but worship idols — fire and moon and sun.

**De Fide 13,1b** And others again in Greece, called Mysians, the Abii, who live on mares’ milk and dwell in an altogether wild country.

**De Fide 13,2** And how many of these things, so many and so great, that are named, even among the praiseworthy ones, will the mind of men be able to gather — how many differences there are of the maidens without number: some for praise and others not praised; some gathering for themselves from their own mind the things that pertain to the practice of a way of life and a rule, and going about openly with long hair; other holy brethren sitting at home in sackcloth and ashes; and still others fully assured in their ways of life and exceeding fasts and toil towards God, in youthful vigour, with a perfect conscience towards the bridegroom; and others,

**De Fide 13,3a** as I said before, not rightly, but acting the bold youth tyrannically against the truth according to some preconception of the mind — as Zacchaeus, who died a short while ago in the hill country around Jerusalem, continued praying with no one at all, but also, on the same principle, boldly undertook to touch the holy mysteries and, though a layman, to perform the sacred rite without scruple.

**De Fide 13,3b** And another, whoever that man was, one of those reputed to have lived at the very summit of the way of life, who dwelt in a monastery in the desert parts towards Egypt,

**De Fide 13,4** and another near Sinai, acted the bold youth, receiving the laying on of hands for the episcopate as if from dreams, and they themselves undertook to sit and to perform the functions of bishops.

**De Fide 13,5** And others, and not a few, have dared to make themselves eunuchs contrary to what has been commanded, for the sake, so they claim, of youthful zeal.

**De Fide 13,6** And others, who suppose that they are showing youthful zeal, are so bold — setting out from among the orthodox, in opposition to those who are already there, and drawing a gathering to themselves — as even to rebaptise, without the judgement of an ecumenical council, those who come to them, supposedly, from the Arians,

**De Fide 13,7** though the matter has not yet, as I said, been decided by the judgement of a council, because the peoples are still mixed until now, and many are orthodox but joined in outward pretence to those who hold the priesthood, until an excommunication of this blasphemous heresy takes place, and then what concerns it will be defined.

**De Fide 13,8a** Of those who rebaptise in this way on their own authority, one has come to our hearing, a presbyter in the country of the Lycians.

**De Fide 13,8b** And there are also others, each of whom prays by himself and not with anyone at all, and others who go about in collars, contrary to the rule of the church.

**De Fide 13,9** Therefore at the end of the whole work I spoke of maidens having no number, those which, according to their own notion, act the bold youth for themselves, not, however, towards the good that perfects the forms of wisdom, of prudence and courage and temperance and justice; and from these others, acting the bold youth towards greater tyranny, turn themselves away from the truth too, so that they cannot be numbered.

**De Fide 14,1** But this one dove and holy virgin confesses God, Father and Son and Holy Spirit — a perfect Father, a perfect Son, a perfect Holy Spirit; the Trinity consubstantial, the Trinity not a fusion, but the Son truly begotten of the Father, and the Holy Spirit no stranger to the Father and the Son;
